Palo Alto NGFW — Configuration & Troubleshooting Guide

One guide to configure and troubleshoot Palo Alto Networks firewalls (PAN-OS 11.x), organised by technology. Asked to build a site-to-site tunnel, split a firewall into virtual systems, form an HA pair or add a firewall to Panorama? Search for it, open the ▶ Recipe, and follow it: an animated topology, a complete sample configuration with every command explained, then step-by-step verification and troubleshooting. Every group runs: how it works → configuration → commands → sample output → what breaks → playbook. Legacy virtual-router commands come first, with Advanced Routing equivalents alongside.

Navigating: topics are collapsed to titles. Click one to open it, or use Expand all. Search understands several words at once ("bgp default originate") and common abbreviations (vsys, pbf, gp, dipp, vpn, ha), and ranks the best matches in a results list. Press /, then ↑/↓ and Enter.

CLI convention: bold amber is what you type, green is the line that matters, and grey is annotation. The badge beside each title shows which lab its samples use.

Five habits that raise the success rate

  1. Write the flow down first, including ingress zone, VR and vsys.
  2. Check both directions. Every route and every rule question has a return-path twin.
  3. Work R → A → P in order, and remember: pre-NAT IP, post-NAT zone.
  4. Use the filtered counters, not instinct. The drop counter names the reason.
  5. One change at a time, with before/after output attached to the ticket.

Every CLI block has a Copy button. It copies only the commands (bold amber lines) with prompts stripped.

The Troubleshooting Ladder: Basics, then R·A·P

Most missed faults aren't hard. They're skipped. Someone sees "allow" on a rule and never notices that the route sent the traffic to a different zone, so a different rule applied. This ladder puts every check in a fixed order so nothing gets overlooked.

  1. Basics: physical, ARP, ping. Is the link up, does the firewall know the neighbour's MAC, and can it reach the host from a dataplane address?
  2. R = Routing. On PAN-OS, routing also decides the destination zone. Get the route wrong and the wrong NAT and security rules are evaluated.
  3. A = Address translation. NAT rules match on the pre-NAT addresses and zones. Translation is only applied as the packet leaves.
  4. P = Permissions. Security rules match the pre-NAT IP addresses but the post-NAT destination zone. Then App-ID and security profiles can still block.
  5. Prove it. Session table, global counters and stage-by-stage packet captures confirm what the checks predicted.

R·A·P follows the order a parcel is handled in. Where is it going (Routing)? What will the label say once it's corrected (Address translation)? Is it allowed onto that van (Permissions)? On a Palo Alto the label is only physically rewritten as the parcel leaves, but every decision is made knowing what the new label will be.

On PAN-OS, routing comes first for a second reason: the route lookup decides the egress interface, the interface belongs to a zone, and both NAT and security rules are selected by zone. A wrong route means the wrong zone, which means the wrong rules.

The Six-Step Troubleshooting Method on PAN-OS

  1. Define the flow exactly: source, destination, protocol, port, ingress interface and zone, VR and vsys.
  2. Prove the route in both directions: test routing fib-lookup for the destination (and the post-NAT destination), then for the source on the far side.
  3. Prove the rules: test nat-policy-match, then test security-policy-match with pre-NAT IPs and the post-NAT zone.
  4. Look at the session: show session all filter …, then show session id. No session means the first packet was dropped. A session with no s2c bytes means the reply never came back.
  5. Read the filtered counters: set a packet-diag filter, then show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes twice. The drop counter names the reason.
  6. Capture by stage: receive, firewall, transmit and drop pcaps show exactly where the packet stopped.

Foundations & LabsPACKET FLOW ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

How a Packet Moves Through the Firewall

Everything else in this document hangs off this one picture. If you know which stage a packet died at, you know which command to run — and if you can talk through this diagram out loud, you have answered the question that comes up in almost every Palo Alto interview.

The same ten steps, in plain language

  1. Ingress and parse. The packet arrives on a wire. The firewall reads the outer headers and answers one question: which zone did this come from? That answer comes from the interface, not from the IP address. If the frame is tagged for a VLAN that has no subinterface, the packet dies right here, before any rule has been consulted — which is why flow_rcv_dot1q_tag_err is such a common surprise.
  2. Decapsulation and defragmentation. If it is IPsec or GRE, the wrapper comes off and the real packet inside is what continues. If it arrived in pieces, the pieces are put back together first. Nothing is inspected while it is still fragmented — the firewall wants the whole letter before it reads it.
  3. Session lookup. The pivotal moment. The firewall checks the six-tuple against the session table. Known flow → fast path. Unknown flow → slow path. This single fork explains most of the odd behaviour engineers report: a rule change does not affect traffic that is already flowing, because established sessions never go back through the policy stage.
  4. Forwarding and zone lookup. Now the firewall works out where the packet is going — which virtual router owns it, which route wins, which interface it will leave by, and therefore which zone it is destined for. Routing decides the zone; the zone does not decide the routing. People get this backwards constantly.
  5. NAT policy lookup. The NAT rulebase is consulted and a translation is chosen. The header is not touched yet. This is why the security rule in the next step still sees the original addresses.
  6. Security policy lookup. The rulebase is walked top to bottom, first match wins. It matches on the original addresses but the post-NAT zones. User-ID supplies the username if there is a mapping. If nothing matches, the interzone-default rule denies it and, by default, does not log it — the reason so many "silent drops" are not silent at all, just unlogged.
  7. Session installed. Two flows are written: client-to-server and server-to-client, each carrying the addresses that direction will use. The decisions from steps 4, 5 and 6 are frozen into the session. From here on the answer is cached.
  8. App-ID. The firewall now looks at the payload and names the application — not the port. Because the real application often is not known until several packets in, policy may be re-evaluated once App-ID shifts (say from web-browsing to ms-update). A session that starts allowed and then dies a few packets later is usually this.
  9. Content inspection. The single-pass engine scans once for everything the security profiles ask for: threats, URL category, file types, sensitive data. One pass, many verdicts — that is the architectural claim the platform is built on.
  10. Egress. Only now is the header actually rewritten with the translation chosen back at step 5. QoS is applied, the packet is fragmented if it must be, and it goes out of the interface.

A useful way to say it in an interview: the first packet does all the thinking, and every packet after it just follows the notes. Steps 4 to 7 happen exactly once per session. If your problem affects the very start of a connection, look in the slow path. If a connection starts fine and then misbehaves, look at App-ID and content inspection. If nothing arrives at all, you never got past step 1.

SymptomLikely stageWhere to look
Nothing in the traffic log at all1–3show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes
Session created but never reaches the far end4test routing fib-lookup
Reaches the wrong server, or not translated5test nat-policy-match
Denied when you believe it should be allowed6test security-policy-match
Return traffic dropped, session exists elsewhere3Asymmetric Routing group
Connects, then drops a few seconds in8–9Threat log, App-ID shift, decryption
Works, but capture shows nothing after the first packets3 (fast path)Hardware Offload topic
Foundations & LabsCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Where Routing Sits in the PAN-OS Packet Flow

The first packet of every session takes the slow path. Routing appears twice in it when destination NAT applies: once to find the zone for the NAT rule, and again on the translated destination to find the zone for the security rule. Later packets match the session and take the fast path, so a route change doesn't move existing sessions.

  • Route lookup decides the zone. No route means flow_fwd_l3_noroute and no NAT or security evaluation at all.
  • NAT rules are matched, not applied, before the security rule. Translation happens at egress.
  • Security rules use pre-NAT IP addresses with post-NAT zones.
  • Subsequent packets use the session (fast path). Its stored egress and translations stay until the session ends or is cleared.

Every decision is taken from the original label, but the destination's neighbourhood (zone) is worked out from where the corrected address really is. The sticker is only applied at the door.

Two CLI Modes, and Which Commands Live Where

PAN-OS has an operational mode and a configuration mode, and the single most common reason a copied command is rejected is that it was pasted into the wrong one.

PromptWhere you are
>Operational mode. Look at things, run actions. show, test, ping, debug, request, clear, less, tail. Nothing here is saved config.
#Configuration mode. You got here with configure. set, delete, edit, show (of config), commit. Changes are staged until you commit.
admin@fw-01> configure                       enter configuration mode
Entering configuration mode
[edit]
admin@fw-01# exit                            back to operational mode ("end" also works)
admin@fw-01>

A handful of set commands are operational-mode commands, not config — set system setting target-vsys, set system setting arp-cache-timeout, set cli config-output-format and set cli pager. They change your session or a runtime setting, they are not staged, and they are not committed. If a set is rejected in # mode, try it from >.

Four verbs cover almost everything

VerbWhat it does
showRead-only. Safe on any box at any time, including mid-change.
testAsk the firewall what it would do — policy match, NAT match, route lookup. Changes nothing.
debugTurn on instrumentation. Some of it is free; packet-diag and dump-level daemon debug cost CPU.
clearReset something — a counter, an ARP entry, a session, an SA. Frequently disruptive.

show is looking. test is asking a hypothetical. debug is wiring up a microphone. clear is pulling something out from under live traffic — the only one of the four that can cause an outage on its own.

Finding Commands and Filtering Output

PAN-OS output is frequently enormous. These four pipes and two discovery commands turn a wall of text into an answer, and they work on essentially every show in this guide.

CommandWhat it doesGUI path
?Context-sensitive help at any point in a command. Shows what the box you are standing on actually accepts.Help icon (top-right)
find command keyword <text>Search the entire CLI tree for commands containing <text>. Indispensable on an unfamiliar release.CLI only
| match <text>Keep only lines containing <text>. Accepts a regex, so | match "a|b" works.CLI only
| except <text>Drop lines containing <text>.CLI only
| countCount matching lines instead of printing them.CLI only
| no-moreDisable paging for this one command.CLI only
set cli pager offDisable paging for the whole session. Operational mode.CLI only
admin@fw-01> find command keyword ts-agent       where does this keyword live in the tree?
set template <name> config vsys <vsys> ts-agent <name>
show user ts-agent state all

admin@fw-01> show system info | match "sw-version|serial|model"   regex inside match
model: PA-3420
serial: 013201001234
sw-version: 11.1.4-h7

admin@fw-01> show session all | count              how many sessions, without printing them
Number of lines: 18442

Tab completes a partial command and ? lists what is valid from where you stand. On a release you do not use daily this beats guessing, because CLI syntax genuinely does move between feature releases.

Foundations & LabsSET / XML ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Viewing the Configuration in Set and XML Format

By default, show in configuration mode prints the config as an indented tree. That is fine for reading one branch and useless for copying, diffing or grepping. Switching the output format makes every leaf print as a complete, runnable set line — which is what makes | match genuinely powerful, and what makes a config portable to another box.

The four formats

CommandOutput
set cli config-output-format setFull set commands, one per leaf. Copy-pasteable into another firewall.
set cli config-output-format xmlRaw XML, the on-disk representation. Useful for API work and for exact structure.
set cli config-output-format jsonJSON. Handy when piping into tooling.
set cli config-output-format defaultBack to the indented tree.

The workflow

  1. Set the format. This is an operational-mode command — run it before configure.
  2. Enter configuration mode with configure.
  3. Run show for the whole config, or scope it to a branch such as show network interface.
admin@fw-01> set cli config-output-format set
admin@fw-01> configure
Entering configuration mode
[edit]
admin@fw-01# show
set mgt-config devices localhost.localdomain ip 127.0.0.1
set mgt-config user admin phash fnRL/G5lXVMug
set mgt-config user admin permissions role-based superuser yes
set zone Trust network layer3 ethernet1/2
set zone Untrust network layer3 ethernet1/1
set rulebase security rules Allow-Web from Trust
set rulebase security rules Allow-Web to Untrust
admin@fw-01# show network interface              scope the dump to one branch
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 198.51.100.2/30
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/2 layer3 ip 10.10.10.1/24
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/3 layer3 units ethernet1/3.20 tag 20
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/3 layer3 units ethernet1/3.20 ip 10.10.20.1/24

The output of show is not a runnable script in that order. A line near the top may reference an object defined further down — a security rule that names a zone, a static route that names an interface. Pasting the dump top-to-bottom into a fresh device will throw reference errors. Reorder objects before rules, or paste in branches and commit once at the end.

Think of the default tree view as a folder structure and the set view as the full path to every file. Same information; only one of the two can be copied somewhere else and still mean something.

The format persists for the CLI session only — log out and you are back to default. Note also that the Palo Alto Panorama CLI cheat sheet documents this as set cli config-output-mode set; both forms are accepted, and config-output-format is the form used throughout the knowledge base. Pair it with set cli pager off before dumping a large config.

Management Plane vs Dataplane — Why It Decides Your Command

A PAN-OS firewall is two computers in one chassis. Almost every wrong-tool-for-the-job mistake in troubleshooting comes from asking one plane about the other one's traffic.

PlaneRunsYou inspect it with
Management (MP)Web UI, config, logging, User-ID, IKE negotiation, routing daemon, HA agentshow system resources, less mp-log <file>, tcpdump
Data (DP)Packet forwarding, sessions, App-ID, security policy, NAT, IPsec ESPshow running resource-monitor, show counter global, less dp-log <file>, debug dataplane packet-diag

tcpdump on PAN-OS captures the management interface only. It will never show you traffic transiting the firewall. For transit traffic you want debug dataplane packet-diag. This single misunderstanding accounts for a large share of "the capture showed nothing" tickets.

The management plane is the receptionist — it knows who you are, keeps the records, and negotiates on the phone. The dataplane is the loading dock. Asking the receptionist what came off a truck gets you a blank look.

Log files live in /var/log/pan/. Read them with less mp-log <file>.log or less dp-log <file>.log, and live-tail with tail follow yes mp-log <file>.log. You never cd anywhere — the mp-log / dp-log keywords do the pathing for you.

Foundations & LabsLAB ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

The Lab Used in Every Scenario

Every scenario uses this topology and the baseline configs that follow. A scenario breaks one line of the baseline, so you can always compare against a known-good state.

Design in one paragraph

The hub terminates one route-based IPsec tunnel per spoke (tunnel.1, tunnel.2), both in zone VPN in virtual router vr-wan. iBGP runs over each tunnel, with the hub as route reflector so each spoke learns the other spoke's LAN. The datacentre sits in a second virtual router, vr-dc, joined to vr-wan with next-vr static routes, and learns the server VLANs from CORE-SW1 by OSPF. Both VRs are in the same vsys, so traffic crossing them needs one security rule, from the ingress zone to the final egress zone.

The two virtual routers are two separate road maps inside one building, with a signposted internal corridor (next-vr) between them. There's still only one security desk at the building's exit, so one permission covers the whole trip.

PAN-OS has no ADVPN equivalent. Spoke-to-spoke traffic transits the hub in this lab. Direct spoke-to-spoke options (LSVPN, SD-WAN plugin mesh) are covered in a later group. The intrazone-default allow rule is why hub transit works without an explicit VPN → VPN rule. Many teams override it to deny, which then breaks spoke-to-spoke traffic.

Baseline Config: HUB-PA (set commands)

Shown as configure-mode set commands on a single-vsys firewall, so they paste straight into the CLI. Legacy virtual routers are used. With the Advanced Routing Engine, the same design uses logical routers and routing profiles.

// interfaces and zones
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 203.0.113.10/24
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/3 layer3 ip 10.10.10.1/24
set network interface tunnel units tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.1/30
set network interface tunnel units tunnel.2 ip 10.255.2.1/30
set zone UNTRUST network layer3 ethernet1/1
set zone VPN network layer3 [ tunnel.1 tunnel.2 ]
set zone DC network layer3 ethernet1/3

// virtual routers and inter-VR routes
set network virtual-router vr-wan interface [ ethernet1/1 tunnel.1 tunnel.2 ]
set network virtual-router vr-dc interface ethernet1/3
set network virtual-router vr-wan routing-table ip static-route DEFAULT destination 0.0.0.0/0 interface ethernet1/1 nexthop ip-address 203.0.113.1
set network virtual-router vr-wan routing-table ip static-route TO-DC10 destination 10.10.10.0/24 nexthop next-vr vr-dc
set network virtual-router vr-wan routing-table ip static-route TO-DC20 destination 10.10.20.0/24 nexthop next-vr vr-dc
set network virtual-router vr-wan routing-table ip static-route TO-DC30 destination 10.10.30.0/24 nexthop next-vr vr-dc
set network virtual-router vr-dc routing-table ip static-route DEFAULT destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop next-vr vr-wan

// IPsec: one gateway + tunnel per spoke (SPOKE2 repeats with .2 values)
set network ike crypto-profiles ike-crypto-profiles IKE-AES256 encryption aes-256-cbc hash sha256 dh-group group14
set network ike crypto-profiles ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-AES256 esp encryption aes-256-cbc authentication sha256
set network ike crypto-profiles ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-AES256 dh-group group14
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 protocol version ikev2
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 protocol ikev2 ike-crypto-profile IKE-AES256
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 local-address interface ethernet1/1
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 peer-address ip 198.51.100.11
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 authentication pre-shared-key key [psk]
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 auto-key ike-gateway GW-SPOKE1
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 auto-key ipsec-crypto-profile IPSEC-AES256
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 tunnel-interface tunnel.1

// BGP on vr-wan: iBGP, hub is route reflector, DC prefixes redistributed
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.0.254 local-as 65000
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES type ibgp
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE1 peer-address ip 10.255.1.2 local-address interface tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.1/30
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE1 reflector-client client
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE2 peer-address ip 10.255.2.2 local-address interface tunnel.2 ip 10.255.2.1/30
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE2 reflector-client client
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol redist-profile RP-DC priority 1 filter type static destination [ 10.10.10.0/24 10.10.20.0/24 10.10.30.0/24 ]
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol redist-profile RP-DC action redist
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp redist-rules RP-DC enable yes

// OSPF on vr-dc towards CORE-SW1
set network virtual-router vr-dc protocol ospf enable yes router-id 10.10.10.1
set network virtual-router vr-dc protocol ospf area 0.0.0.0 type normal
set network virtual-router vr-dc protocol ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet1/3 enable yes link-type broadcast

// NAT and security rules
set rulebase nat rules DC-SNAT from DC to UNTRUST source any destination any service any source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/1
set rulebase nat rules WEB-DNAT from UNTRUST to UNTRUST source any destination 203.0.113.80 service service-https destination-translation translated-address 10.10.10.80
set rulebase security rules VPN-TO-DC from VPN to DC source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
set rulebase security rules DC-TO-VPN from DC to VPN source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
set rulebase security rules DC-TO-INTERNET from DC to UNTRUST source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
set rulebase security rules WEB-IN from UNTRUST to DC source any destination 203.0.113.80 application ssl service application-default action allow
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Builds HUB-PA from scratch: interfaces and zones, two virtual routers joined by next-vr routes, one IPsec tunnel per spoke, iBGP with route reflection, OSPF to the core, and the NAT and security rules for DC, spoke and internet traffic.

Interfaces and zones

ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 203.0.113.10/24
WAN interface. It also terminates IKE/IPsec from the spokes.
ethernet1/3 layer3 ip 10.10.10.1/24
Datacentre-facing interface towards CORE-SW1.
tunnel units tunnel.1 / tunnel.2
One logical tunnel interface per spoke, each with a /30 so BGP has a point-to-point peer address.
zone UNTRUST / VPN / DC
Zones are what NAT and security rules match on. Both tunnels share zone VPN, so spoke-to-spoke traffic through the hub is intrazone (VPN → VPN), allowed by default.

Virtual routers

virtual-router vr-wan interface [ ethernet1/1 tunnel.1 tunnel.2 ]
WAN-side routing table: internet and overlays.
virtual-router vr-dc interface ethernet1/3
Separate routing table for the datacentre.
static-route DEFAULT … nexthop ip-address 203.0.113.1
vr-wan default route to the ISP, also the underlay path to the spokes.
static-route TO-DC10/20/30 … nexthop next-vr vr-dc
Hands DC prefixes from vr-wan to vr-dc. A next-vr route has no interface: the lookup continues in the named VR.
vr-dc static-route DEFAULT … nexthop next-vr vr-wan
The return direction. Without it, replies from the DC have no route back (see the inter-VR scenario).

IPsec

ike-crypto-profiles IKE-AES256 · aes-256-cbc · sha256 · group14
Phase 1 algorithms. Must match the spokes.
ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-AES256 · esp aes-256-cbc · sha256 · dh-group group14
Phase 2 (ESP) algorithms. dh-group here is PFS for each rekey.
gateway GW-SPOKE1 protocol version ikev2 · ike-crypto-profile
IKEv2 using the profile above.
local-address interface ethernet1/1 · peer-address ip 198.51.100.11
Which local interface and which remote public IP this IKE gateway talks to.
authentication pre-shared-key key [psk]
Shared secret, identical on the spoke.
tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 auto-key ike-gateway … ipsec-crypto-profile … tunnel-interface tunnel.1
Binds the IKE gateway and phase 2 profile to tunnel.1. Route-based: routing decides what enters tunnel.1, so no proxy-IDs are needed PAN-to-PAN.

BGP on vr-wan

bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.0.254 local-as 65000
Starts BGP with a stable ID. The spokes use the same AS, so the sessions are iBGP.
peer-group SPOKES type ibgp
Groups the spoke peers with shared iBGP behaviour.
peer SPOKE1 peer-address ip 10.255.1.2 local-address interface tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.1/30
The spoke's tunnel IP, and which local interface and address the session is sourced from. A wrong local-address keeps the peer in Active (see scenario).
reflector-client client
Makes the spoke a route-reflector client, so routes learned from SPOKE1 are reflected to SPOKE2 and the other way round.
redist-profile RP-DC … filter type static destination [ 10.10.10.0/24 … ] · action redist
Selects the three DC static routes for redistribution.
bgp redist-rules RP-DC enable yes
Advertises those DC prefixes to the spokes over BGP.

OSPF on vr-dc

ospf enable yes router-id 10.10.10.1
Starts OSPF in the DC virtual router.
area 0.0.0.0 type normal
Backbone area.
area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet1/3 enable yes link-type broadcast
Runs OSPF on ethernet1/3 as a broadcast (Ethernet) segment to learn VLAN 20/30 from CORE-SW1.

NAT and security rules

nat DC-SNAT from DC to UNTRUST … dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/1
DC servers going to the internet are translated to ethernet1/1's address with port translation (DIPP).
nat WEB-DNAT from UNTRUST to UNTRUST destination 203.0.113.80 … translated-address 10.10.10.80
Publishes the web server. Pre-NAT zones on both sides.
security VPN-TO-DC / DC-TO-VPN
Spokes ↔ datacentre. One rule per direction covers the trip across both VRs, because they are in the same vsys.
security DC-TO-INTERNET
DC outbound internet, translated by DC-SNAT.
security WEB-IN from UNTRUST to DC destination 203.0.113.80 application ssl
Inbound to the published server: pre-NAT IP, post-NAT zone.
commit
Nothing takes effect until the candidate configuration is committed.

The hub's BGP peers each set an explicit local-address on their own tunnel interface. If the local address is wrong, the TCP session to the peer never forms and BGP stays in Active or Connect, even though the tunnel is up.

The BGP and OSPF lines show the essential parameters for the lab. Default-route origination to CORE-SW1, timers and authentication are added in the OSPF and BGP groups. Rules use any to keep the lab readable. Narrow them in production.

What each line does

Purpose: Connects a branch firewall to the hub: WAN, LAN and tunnel interfaces with zones, a default route, the IPsec tunnel, iBGP to the hub to exchange LAN prefixes, outbound NAT, and the rules for LAN ↔ VPN and LAN → internet.

Interfaces, zones, routing

ethernet1/1 · ethernet1/2 · tunnel.1
WAN, LAN and the tunnel to the hub (SPOKE2 values in the comments).
zone UNTRUST / TRUST / VPN
Same zone names as the hub, so rule logic reads the same on every site.
virtual-router default interface [ … ]
A single VR is enough at a branch.
static-route DEFAULT … nexthop ip-address 198.51.100.1
Internet, plus the underlay path to the hub's public IP.

IPsec

ike / ipsec crypto profiles
Must match the hub's profiles exactly.
gateway GW-HUB peer-address ip 203.0.113.10
Points the IKE gateway at the hub's public address.
tunnel ipsec VPN-HUB … tunnel-interface tunnel.1
Binds the tunnel to tunnel.1 (zone VPN).

BGP

bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.1.2 local-as 65000
iBGP with the hub. Router ID = tunnel IP.
peer HUB peer-address ip 10.255.1.1 local-address interface tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.2/30
Peers with the hub's end of tunnel.1, sourced from this side's tunnel IP.
redist-profile RP-LAN filter type connect destination 10.10.1.0/24 · action redist
Selects the connected LAN subnet.
bgp redist-rules RP-LAN enable yes
Advertises the LAN to the hub, which reflects it to the other spoke.

NAT and rules

nat LAN-SNAT from TRUST to UNTRUST … dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address
Internet-bound LAN traffic only. TRUST → VPN is untouched, so the hub sees real source addresses.
security LAN-TO-VPN / VPN-TO-LAN
LAN ↔ hub, DC and other spokes, in both directions.
security LAN-TO-INTERNET
Local internet breakout.
commit
Activates the configuration.
SettingSPOKE1-PASPOKE2-PA
ethernet1/1 / gateway198.51.100.11/24 · 198.51.100.1192.0.2.12/24 · 192.0.2.1
ethernet1/2 (TRUST)10.10.1.1/2410.10.2.1/24
tunnel.1 / BGP peer10.255.1.2/30 → 10.255.1.110.255.2.2/30 → 10.255.2.1

The LAN-SNAT rule only matches TRUST → UNTRUST, so traffic into the tunnel (TRUST → VPN) isn't translated. If someone widens the NAT rule's destination zone to any, the spoke LAN gets source-NAT'd into the tunnel, and the hub sees the wrong source address.

What Changed?FIRST MOVE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Ask What Changed Before You Ask What Is Broken

Firewalls do not spontaneously develop faults. If something worked on Tuesday and does not work on Wednesday, something changed — and the odds strongly favour a configuration change, a content update, or a failover over a genuine hardware or software defect. Five minutes here saves an hour of packet captures.

Everyone nods at this and almost nobody does it, because "what changed" feels like admin work rather than troubleshooting. It is troubleshooting. It is the highest-yield five minutes in the whole process, and it is the one step that can end the ticket before it starts.

The configuration log — who touched what

admin@fw-01(active)> show log config direction equal backward
newest first — without "direction equal backward" you start at the oldest entry
Time      Admin    Client   Command  Path
09:41:02  jsmith   Web      commit
09:38:55  jsmith   Web      set      devices/entry/network/virtual-router/entry[@name='VR-OUTSIDE']/routing-table/ip/static-route
09:37:10  jsmith   Web      delete   devices/entry/vsys/entry/rulebase/security/rules/entry[@name='allow-legacy-app']
a route change and a rule deletion, twenty minutes before the tickets started
QueryUse
show log config direction equal backwardEverything, newest first.
show log config direction equal backward receive_time in last-24-hrsScope it to the window the fault appeared in. The time-range keyword varies by release — some builds expose it as receive-time inside last-24-hrs. Tab-complete after backward to see what your box accepts.
show log config direction equal backward admin equal <user>One administrator's changes.
show log config query equal "( cmd eq commit )"Just the commits, to establish a timeline.
show log config query equal "( path contains 'security/rules' )"Only rulebase changes.

Match the timestamps against when the users started complaining, not against when the ticket was raised. Those two are often hours apart, and the gap is where the real change hides.

What Changed?DIFF & COMMITS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Uncommitted Changes, Commit History and Config Diffs

Two questions the config log does not answer directly: is there something sitting in the candidate configuration that has not been committed yet, and was there a commit at the time the fault started.

Is anything pending?

admin@fw-01(active)> configure
enter configuration mode
admin@fw-01(active)# show config diff
candidate versus running — anything listed here is NOT live yet
[edit devices localhost.localdomain vsys vsys1 rulebase security rules]
+  entry allow-new-app {
+    from Trust;
+    to Untrust;
+    action allow;
+  }
admin@fw-01(active)# exit

An uncommitted change is a trap in both directions. Someone may have "fixed" the problem and never committed — so the fix is invisible. Or someone may be halfway through an unrelated change, and your commit will push their work live along with yours. Always run this before you commit anything during an incident.

Was there a commit, and did it succeed?

admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs all
Enqueued          ID  Type          Status  Result    Completed
2026/08/27 09:41  312 Commit        FIN     OK        09:41:38
2026/08/27 06:02  311 AutoCom       FIN     OK        06:02:44
2026/08/26 22:15  310 Commit        FIN     WARN      22:16:09

admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs id 310
read the warnings on any commit that did not come back clean

A commit that finished with WARN is not a commit that finished cleanly. Read the detail — warnings routinely include things like a rule that shadows another, an interface with no zone, or a route that could not be installed. Any of those can be the fault you are chasing.

Comparing against a known-good version

Named configuration snapshots are the cheapest insurance in the product and almost nobody takes them. Before any change window, save one:

admin@fw-01(active)> save config to pre-change-2026-08-27.xml
takes seconds, saves hours
admin@fw-01(active)> show config saved pre-change-2026-08-27.xml
read it back if you need to compare by eye

The GUI equivalent, which is genuinely better for this one task, is Device > Config Audit — pick two versions and it shows you a side-by-side diff. Reach for it when the config log tells you that something changed but not clearly what.

What Changed?INVISIBLE CHANGES ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Changes That Leave No Configuration Log

This is the part that catches experienced engineers. You check the config log, it is clean, and you conclude nothing changed — but plenty of things change a firewall's behaviour without ever appearing there.

ChangeWhy it is invisibleHow to check
Content and application updatesApp-ID and threat content install automatically. A new or modified App-ID signature can reclassify traffic that your rules match by application, silently breaking a rule that has not been edited in years.show system info | match version and compare app/threat versions against when the fault started. show jobs all shows the install job.
Panorama pushThe change was made on Panorama, not here. The local config log may show the push rather than the substance.show config pushed-shared-policy, show config pushed-template
HA failoverThe peer is now active. If the two boxes differ in any way, behaviour changes with no config event at all.show high-availability state, show high-availability flap-statistics, system log
Dynamic address groups and EDLsThe membership changed, not the rule. A rule referencing a dynamic group can start or stop matching without being edited.show object dynamic-address-group all, request system external-list show type ip name <list-name>
Certificate expiryNothing changed — a date passed. Decryption, GlobalProtect and management access all break this way.Device > Certificates; decryption log
Learned routesBGP or OSPF withdrew or added a prefix upstream. Your config is identical; your forwarding table is not.show routing route, protocol neighbour state, show routing protocol bgp summary
DHCP or PPPoE address changeAn interface address moved. NAT rules pinned to an old address stop matching.show interface all, system log
Software upgradeBehaviour and defaults change between versions even when the config is untouched.show system info | match sw-version, debug swm history
Session table pressure or resource exhaustionNothing changed except load.show session info, show running resource-monitor, show running ippool
Somebody ran an operational commandset session offload no, debug levels, clear session all — none of these are configuration and none appear in the config log.debug dataplane packet-diag show setting, show session info, the system log

The lesson is that "no config change" and "nothing changed" are different statements. Content updates and route withdrawals in particular break things that nobody touched, and they are the two most common answers when the config log comes back empty.

What Changed?CHECKLIST ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The Five-Minute Pre-Troubleshooting Check

Run this before the first packet capture, every time. It is short enough that there is no excuse, and it closes a meaningful share of tickets outright.

admin@fw-01(active)> show log config direction equal backward receive_time in last-24-hrs
1. did anyone change anything?

admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs all
2. any commits, auto-commits or content installs? any WARN results?

admin@fw-01(active)> show system info | match "version"
3. what software and content versions is it running now?

admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state
4. is the box you are logged into the one carrying the traffic?

admin@fw-01(active)> show log system direction equal backward
5. link flaps, daemon restarts, HA transitions, failed jobs

admin@fw-01(active)> show session info
6. session count, utilisation, and whether offload is on

admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag show setting
7. did someone leave a filter or a debug running from last time?

admin@fw-01(active)> configure
admin@fw-01(active)# show config diff
8. is there anything uncommitted sitting in the candidate config?
admin@fw-01(active)# exit
If you findDo this before anything else
A commit in the fault windowRead the diff for that change. Do not start capturing.
A content version installed todayCheck whether the affected traffic is matched by application in your rules.
An HA transitionCompare the two peers before assuming the config is at fault.
A commit with WARNRead the warnings. One of them is often the whole answer.
An uncommitted candidate changeFind out whose it is before you commit anything yourself.
A packet-diag filter still armedClear it. Your results will be filtered by somebody else's investigation otherwise.
Nothing at allNow start troubleshooting properly — and you have ruled out the most likely cause in five minutes.

Step 4 deserves more respect than it gets. Logging into the passive HA peer and troubleshooting an absence of traffic is an embarrassingly common way to lose an hour. Check the prompt — it tells you (active) or (passive) — and check it again after any failover during the incident.

Physical & InterfacesRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Layer 3 Interface, VLAN Subinterface and LACP Aggregate

Use it when you bring up a LAN port, add a VLAN on a trunk, or bundle two ports to a switch with LACP.

set network profiles interface-management-profile MGMT-PING ping yes https yes ssh yes
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/2 layer3 ip 10.20.0.1/24
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/2 layer3 interface-management-profile MGMT-PING
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/2 layer3 units ethernet1/2.100 tag 100 ip 10.100.0.1/24
set network interface aggregate-ethernet ae1 layer3 ip 10.50.0.1/24
set network interface aggregate-ethernet ae1 layer3 lacp enable yes mode active
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/5 aggregate-group ae1
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/6 aggregate-group ae1
set network virtual-router default interface [ ethernet1/2 ethernet1/2.100 ae1 ]
set zone TRUST network layer3 [ ethernet1/2 ethernet1/2.100 ae1 ]
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Creates a management profile, a Layer 3 LAN interface with a tagged subinterface, a two-port LACP aggregate, and places them in the virtual router and a zone.

interface-management-profile MGMT-PING ping yes https yes ssh yes
Which services the firewall answers on an interface (to itself). Without a profile, even ping to the interface IP fails.
ethernet1/2 layer3 ip 10.20.0.1/24
A Layer 3 interface with its address.
… interface-management-profile MGMT-PING
Attaches the profile. Use a minimal profile on untrusted interfaces.
units ethernet1/2.100 tag 100 ip 10.100.0.1/24
A subinterface carrying 802.1Q tag 100. The switch port must trunk VLAN 100.
aggregate-ethernet ae1 layer3 ip …
The logical aggregate interface holds the IP.
ae1 layer3 lacp enable yes mode active
Runs LACP, actively negotiating. The switch must run LACP on the same ports.
ethernet1/5 aggregate-group ae1
Adds a physical member. Members carry no configuration of their own.
virtual-router default interface [ … ]
Interfaces must be in a virtual router to route.
zone TRUST network layer3 [ … ]
…and in a zone to match security policy. An interface without a zone drops traffic.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Link and counters

show interface ethernet1/2
show interface all

Good: Link up, the expected speed, the zone and VR shown, errors not rising. If not: Cable/optic, speed or duplex mismatch, or the interface missing from a zone/VR.

2 · VLAN

show interface ethernet1/2.100
ping source 10.100.0.1 host 10.100.0.254

Good: Tag 100 shown. The gateway answers. If not: Switch trunk doesn't allow VLAN 100, or the tag differs.

3 · LACP

show lacp aggregate-ethernet ae1

Good: Both members selected/collecting-distributing. If not: Member not bundled: LACP mode mismatch, or the switch ports aren't in the same port-channel.

⚠ Syntax note. PAN-OS configuration-mode set commands. The structure follows Palo Alto documentation and published configurations. Use Tab/? while typing, run commit validate (or validate full) before commit, and check the GUI equivalent shown in each step.

Physical & InterfacesRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Inserting the Firewall as a Virtual Wire

Use it when you must put a firewall into an existing link without re-addressing: no IPs, no routing, no ARP. The two interfaces are bound together, and traffic between them is inspected and controlled by security policy.

set network interface ethernet ethernet1/7 virtual-wire
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/8 virtual-wire
set network virtual-wire VW-CORE interface1 ethernet1/7 interface2 ethernet1/8
set zone VW-IN network virtual-wire ethernet1/7
set zone VW-OUT network virtual-wire ethernet1/8
set rulebase security rules VW-ALLOW from [ VW-IN VW-OUT ] to [ VW-IN VW-OUT ] source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Turns two ports into a virtual wire pair, gives each side a virtual-wire zone, and allows traffic in both directions.

ethernet1/7 virtual-wire · ethernet1/8 virtual-wire
Sets the interface type. Virtual wire interfaces have no IP addresses.
virtual-wire VW-CORE interface1 … interface2 …
Binds the two interfaces into one virtual wire.
zone VW-IN / VW-OUT network virtual-wire
Virtual wire zones, so rules can tell the two sides apart.
rule VW-ALLOW both directions
Traffic crossing a virtual wire is interzone, so it needs an allow rule (start broad, then tighten with App-ID and profiles).

Verify and troubleshoot

Traffic passes and is logged

show interface ethernet1/7
show session all filter source 10.30.0.1

Good: Both interfaces up as virtual-wire. Sessions between the routers. If not: No traffic: the rule is missing (interzone default deny), or link state differs (consider link state pass-through on the virtual wire).

⚠ Syntax note. Use Tab/? while typing and commit validate before committing. The GUI path is given for every object.

Physical & InterfacesCHECK ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Basics: Physical, ARP and Ping

Check the basics on the interface facing the host (or next hop) that isn't working. They take under a minute.

1 · Physical

admin@HUB-PA> show interface ethernet1/3
// trimmed
Name: ethernet1/3, ID: 18
Link status:
  Runtime link speed/duplex/state: 1000/full/up
  Configured link speed/duplex/state: auto/auto/auto
...
Zone: DC, virtual system: vsys1
Logical interface counters read from CPU:
receive errors                     0
packets dropped                    0

2 · ARP

The firewall can only deliver to a host or next hop on a connected subnet once it has that device's MAC address.

admin@HUB-PA> show arp ethernet1/3
// trimmed · status codes are listed at the top of the output
interface         ip address      hw address         port          status   ttl
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ethernet1/3       10.10.10.2      00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e  ethernet1/3   c        1622
ethernet1/3       10.10.10.99     (incomplete)       ethernet1/3   i        2

admin@HUB-PA> clear arp ethernet1/3      // force fresh ARP on one interface

3 · Ping from a dataplane address

By default, ping on a Palo Alto leaves from the management interface, which has its own routing and proves nothing about the dataplane. Always give a source address that belongs to a dataplane interface. Using the interface the users sit behind also tests the far side's return route.

admin@SPOKE1-PA> ping source 10.10.1.1 host 10.10.20.15 count 3
PING 10.10.20.15 (10.10.20.15) from 10.10.1.1 : 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.10.20.15: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=21.4 ms
...
ResultMeansGo to
Ping from the WAN IP works, from the LAN source failsThe far side has no return route for the LAN subnet, or a rule doesn't allow it.R (return route), then P
Ping fails from any sourceNo forward route, tunnel down, or the host doesn't answer ICMP.R, then test with the real protocol
Ping works, application failsRouting is fine. The difference is port or app based: NAT, service, App-ID or security profile.A, then P

To ping a firewall interface from another device, the interface needs an interface management profile that allows ping. A failed ping to the firewall's own interface often means a missing profile, not a routing fault.

Physical & InterfacesLAYER 1 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Interface State — Where Every L1/L2 Investigation Starts

Before anything else, establish whether the link is up, what it is called logically, and which zone and virtual router it belongs to. show interface all answers all four in one screen and is the correct first command for any physical-layer complaint.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show interface allSummary of every interface — up/down, VLAN tag, virtual router, zone, IP. First command for any L1/L2 issue.Network > Interfaces
show interface <interface>Full counters for one interface: RX/TX bytes and packets, errors, CRC, runts, drops, framing.Network > Interfaces > click the interface
show interface ethernet1/1One dataplane port — hardware state, link, speed, duplex.Network > Interfaces > Ethernet
show interface managementThe out-of-band MGT interface.Device > Setup > Interfaces > Management
show interface logicalLogical interfaces only — VLANs, sub-interfaces, tunnel.x.Network > Interfaces (logical / sub-interfaces)
show interface hardwareHardware view — MAC, link state, transceiver presence.Network > Interfaces (Status column)

Sample — reading the summary

admin@fw-01(active)> show interface all
total configured hardware interfaces: 6
name                    id  speed/duplex/state       mac address
ethernet1/1             16  1000/full/up             b4:0c:25:aa:10:01
ethernet1/2             17  1000/full/up             b4:0c:25:aa:10:02
ethernet1/3             18  1000/full/up             b4:0c:25:aa:10:03
ethernet1/4             19  [n/a]/[n/a]/down         b4:0c:25:aa:10:04

total configured logical interfaces: 5
name             id   vsys  zone          forwarding      tag  addr
ethernet1/1      16   1     Untrust       vr:default      0    198.51.100.2/30
ethernet1/2      17   1     Trust         vr:default      0    10.10.10.1/24
ethernet1/3.20   258  1     Trust         vr:default      20   10.10.20.1/24
ethernet1/3.30   259  1     DMZ           vr:default      30   10.10.30.1/24
tunnel.1         1    1     VPN           vr:default      0    10.255.0.1/30

The two halves answer different questions. The hardware block says "is there a cable and is it electrically alive". The logical block says "does the firewall consider this port part of the network, and which part". A port can be up in the first block and completely missing from the second — that means it is cabled but unconfigured.

The forwarding column carries the virtual router name (vr:default) or logical router on Advanced Routing. If it is blank, the interface has no routing instance and no traffic will be routed through it regardless of how healthy the link looks.

Physical & InterfacesCOUNTERS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Interface and Global Counters

Counters are cumulative since the last dataplane restart, which makes their absolute values close to meaningless. The delta yes option is what converts them into a diagnostic: run the command, generate the traffic, run it again, and the second output shows only what moved in between.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show counter interface <interface>Per-interface counters — drops, errors, queue stats.Network > Interfaces > Hardware
show counter global filter delta yesGlobal counters that changed since the last run. Run it twice. The cornerstone troubleshooting command.CLI only
show counter global filter delta yes severity dropOnly drop counters that changed. This is the one you want when traffic is silently disappearing.CLI only
show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yesOnly counters incremented by packets matching your packet-diag filter. The most targeted view available.CLI only
show counter global | match dropQuick grep for anything with "drop" in the name.CLI only
show counter global | match flow_All flow-engine counters — flow_action_close, flow_policy_deny, flow_no_session_match, and so on.CLI only
clear counter allReset all global counters. Do this before a controlled test if you would rather not use deltas.CLI only

Sample — a drop counter caught in the act

admin@fw-01(active)> show counter global filter delta yes severity drop
Global counters:
Elapsed time since last sampling: 41.288 seconds

name                        value  rate  severity  category  aspect   description
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
flow_policy_deny               64     1  drop      flow      session  Session setup: denied by policy
flow_tcp_non_syn_drop          18     0  drop      flow      session  Packets dropped: non-SYN TCP without session match
flow_no_route                   6     0  drop      flow      forward  Packets dropped: no route
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Total counters shown: 3
CounterWhat it is telling you
flow_policy_denySecurity policy said no. Go to test security-policy-match to find which rule.
flow_tcp_non_syn_dropA mid-stream TCP packet arrived with no matching session. Classic asymmetric routing or a session that was cleared underneath the flow.
flow_no_routeFIB miss. The destination has no route in this virtual router.
flow_fwd_zonechangeThe packet arrived in a zone the existing session does not expect. Routing changed mid-session.
flow_rcv_dot1q_tag_errTagged frame arrived on an interface with no matching sub-interface for that VLAN.

Filter on severity drop, not aspect drop. Severity has four values — info, drop, error, warn. Aspect describes the processing stage a counter belongs to (parse, session, forward, pktproc, resource, mgmt), and drop is not one of its values. filter aspect drop delta yes appears in a lot of circulating cheat sheets and returns nothing useful.

Absolute counters are an odometer; deltas are a speedometer. Nobody diagnoses a car by reading the odometer once.

Physical & InterfacesOPTICS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Transceivers, Optical Levels and PHY State

When a link flaps, errors climb, or a port refuses to come up with a known-good cable, the answer is usually in the PHY. PAN-OS exposes DDM readings from the transceiver through the system state tree rather than through a dedicated command.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show system state | match transceiverInstalled transceivers with vendor, type and DDM information.Network > Interfaces > Hardware Properties
show system state filter sys.s<S>.p<P>.phyPHY detail for slot S port P (e.g. sys.s1.p19.phy) — signal detect, optical RX/TX power, temperature.CLI only
show system state filter-pretty sys.s1.p1.phySame data, human-readable formatting. Use this one by default on 9.x and later.CLI only

Sample — a dying optic

admin@fw-01(active)> show system state filter-pretty sys.s1.p1.phy
sys.s1.p1.phy: {
  media: ethernetCsmacd,
  sfp: {
    connector-type: LC,
    encoding: 64B66B,
    vendor-name: FINISAR CORP,
    vendor-part-number: FTLX8574D3BCL,
    rx-power: -18.42 dBm,          <-- well below the -14 dBm receive sensitivity
    tx-power: -2.31 dBm,
    temperature: 41.7 C,
    voltage: 3.29 V,
  },
  link-partner: { },
  link-speed: 10000, link-duplex: full, link-state: up,
}

Rough optical rules of thumb: for 10G SR expect RX between roughly −1 and −9.5 dBm; for 10G LR, −1 to −14 dBm. A reading below the sensitivity floor, or a TX power near zero, points at the optic, the patch or the far end — not at PAN-OS. A completely absent sfp block usually means an unsupported or unseated module.

Physical & InterfacesCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Link State, Speed and Duplex

These are configuration-mode commands and take effect on commit. The default everywhere is auto, and hard-coding one side while the other autonegotiates is the classic route to a duplex mismatch.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 link-state <up|down|auto>Bring an interface administratively up or down.Network > Interfaces > Ethernet > Advanced
# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 link-speed <10|100|1000|auto>Hard-code speed. Default is auto.Network > Interfaces > Ethernet > Advanced
# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 link-duplex <full|half|auto>Hard-code duplex. Mismatch here is a leading cause of CRC errors.Network > Interfaces > Ethernet > Advanced
admin@fw-01> configure
admin@fw-01# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/4 link-speed 1000
admin@fw-01# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/4 link-duplex full
admin@fw-01# commit
Commit job 1247 ...  Configuration committed successfully

Hard-coding one end and leaving the other on auto produces a link that comes up at the right speed and the wrong duplex — full on the pinned side, half on the negotiating side. It passes ping and collapses under load, with late collisions on one side and CRC errors on the other. Pin both ends or neither.

ARP & Proxy-ARPRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Proxy-ARP for NAT Addresses

PAN-OS has no separate proxy-ARP setting: the firewall answers ARP automatically for NAT addresses that fall inside the subnet of the interface where the request arrives. For addresses outside every interface subnet it does not answer, so you either add the address to the interface or have the upstream router route it to the firewall.

// case 1 · translated address is inside the interface subnet: nothing extra, the firewall proxy-ARPs it
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 203.0.113.10/29
set rulebase nat rules WEB-DNAT from UNTRUST to UNTRUST to-interface ethernet1/1 destination 203.0.113.12 service service-https destination-translation translated-address 10.10.20.40
// case 2 · translated address is NOT in any interface subnet: give the firewall the address (or a route upstream)
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 198.18.50.10/32
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Shows the two cases: an in-subnet NAT address needs nothing extra, while an out-of-subnet address must be added to the interface (or routed upstream).

ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 203.0.113.10/29
The WAN subnet 203.0.113.8/29. NAT addresses from .9 to .14 are inside it.
nat WEB-DNAT … to-interface ethernet1/1 destination 203.0.113.12
A destination NAT rule for an in-subnet address. Naming the to-interface (not only the zone) helps the firewall pick the interface that should proxy-ARP.
ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 198.18.50.10/32
For an address outside every interface subnet, adding it (as a /32 or within a secondary subnet) makes the firewall own and answer for it. The alternative is a static route on the upstream router pointing that address at the firewall.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · ARP requests arrive and are answered

debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match destination 203.0.113.12
show counter global filter delta yes | match arp

Good: ARP counters increase as the router asks. If not: No requests: the router routes the address elsewhere, or has a stale entry (ask the ISP to clear ARP).

2 · The address is in a subnet the firewall owns

show interface ethernet1/1
show running nat-policy

Good: The NAT address falls inside an interface subnet, or is configured on the interface. If not: Out of subnet: add it to the interface, or get an upstream route.

3 · Translation and policy

test nat-policy-match from UNTRUST to UNTRUST source 198.51.100.7 destination 203.0.113.12 protocol 6 destination-port 443

Good: The DNAT rule matches. If not: ARP works but traffic fails: NAT or security rule (see NAT · Destination NAT).

⚠ Syntax note. PAN-OS configuration-mode set commands. The structure follows Palo Alto documentation and published configurations. Use Tab/? while typing, run commit validate (or validate full) before commit, and check the GUI equivalent shown in each step.

ARP & Proxy-ARPLAYER 2 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Viewing the ARP Table

If a directly-connected host is unreachable and the interface is up, ARP is the next thing to check. An incomplete ARP entry means the firewall asked and nothing answered — a VLAN, cabling or far-end problem, not a policy or routing one.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show arp allARP table for every interface. First command for L2 reachability problems.Network > Interfaces > More Runtime Stats > ARP
show arp <interface>Entries learned on one interface only.Network > Interfaces > More Runtime Stats > ARP
show arp managementARP on the MGT interface.Device > Setup > Interfaces
show neighbor interface <interface>The IPv6 neighbour-discovery cache — the ND equivalent of the ARP table.Network > Interfaces > More Runtime Stats > IPv6 Neighbors
admin@fw-01(active)> show arp all
maximum of entries supported :  1500
default timeout:               1800 seconds
total ARP entries in table :   4

interface       ip address      hw address         port            status  ttl
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ethernet1/1     198.51.100.1    00:1c:0f:11:22:33  ethernet1/1     c      1782
ethernet1/2     10.10.10.20     00:50:56:aa:00:11  ethernet1/2     c      1620
ethernet1/3.20  10.10.20.55     00:50:56:aa:00:22  ethernet1/3     c       914
ethernet1/3.30  10.10.30.10     (incomplete)       ethernet1/3     i         0
StatusMeans
cComplete. The firewall has a MAC and can forward.
iIncomplete. ARP was sent, nothing came back. Check VLAN tagging, the switch port, and whether the host is actually on that subnet.
sStatic. Manually configured, never ages out.

An incomplete entry is the firewall shouting a name down a corridor and hearing silence. The problem is not that the firewall is confused about who to call — it is that nobody in that corridor is answering to the name.

ARP & Proxy-ARPTIMERS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

ARP Cache Timeout and Clearing Entries

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show system setting arp-cache-timeoutDisplay the current ARP cache timeout. Default is 1800 seconds.CLI only
set system setting arp-cache-timeout <60-65536>Change the timeout. This is an operational-mode set, not a config-mode one, and it is not committed.CLI only
clear arp <interface> <ip>Clear a single entry to force re-resolution. Safe and targeted.CLI only
clear arp allClear the whole table. Disruptive — every flow pauses while ARP re-resolves.CLI only
admin@fw-01(active)> show system setting arp-cache-timeout
ARP cache timeout: 1800

admin@fw-01(active)> clear arp ethernet1/2 10.10.10.20   surgical: one entry, one interface
arp entry cleared

Lowering the ARP timeout is occasionally suggested as a fix for stale entries after a failover. It increases ARP broadcast load on every attached segment and treats a symptom. If entries go stale after a failover, look at gratuitous ARP behaviour and upstream switch MAC ageing instead.

ARP & Proxy-ARPSTATIC ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Static ARP, IPv6 Neighbours and Proxy-ARP

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 arp <ip> hw-address <mac>Static ARP entry on an L3 Ethernet interface.Network > Interfaces > Ethernet > IPv4 > Add ARP
# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 ipv6 neighbor-discovery neighbor <ipv6> hw-address <mac>Static IPv6 neighbour entry.Network > Interfaces > Ethernet > IPv6
show running nat-policyProxy-ARP is automatic for NAT addresses. Verify the NAT policy is programmed as expected.Policies > NAT
test nat-policy-match from <zone> to <zone> source <ip> destination <ip> destination-port <p> protocol <n>Test which NAT rule — and therefore which proxy-ARP behaviour — applies to a flow.Policies > NAT > right-click > Test Policy Match

PAN-OS proxy-ARPs for a NAT address automatically when that address is inside the subnet of the interface the traffic arrives on. If the NAT address is outside that subnet, no proxy-ARP happens, and the upstream device has no way to reach it — you need a static route pointing at the firewall on that upstream device. This asymmetry catches people out on every second destination-NAT deployment.

ARP & Proxy-ARPCAPTURE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Capturing ARP on the Wire

ARP is not IP, so the ordinary packet-diag filter will not match it. The non-ip include option is what makes ARP, STP and other L2 frames visible to a dataplane capture.

admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match ingress-interface ethernet1/2 non-ip include
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage receive file arp_rx.pcap
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture on
... reproduce, then ...
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture off
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off
admin@fw-01(active)> view-pcap filter-pcap arp_rx.pcap

non-ip include widens the filter considerably — you are now catching every non-IP frame on that interface, and busy segments carry a lot of them. Keep the capture short and always clean up with debug dataplane packet-diag clear all.

DNSRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Firewall DNS and a DNS Proxy for LAN Clients

Use it when the firewall must resolve names itself (always), and optionally answer DNS for a LAN, with internal domains sent to internal servers.

set deviceconfig system dns-setting servers primary 1.1.1.1 secondary 8.8.8.8
set network dns-proxy DNS-LAN enabled yes
set network dns-proxy DNS-LAN interface ethernet1/2
set network dns-proxy DNS-LAN default primary 1.1.1.1 secondary 8.8.8.8
set network dns-proxy DNS-LAN domain-servers CORP domain-name *.corp.example primary 10.10.10.53
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/2 server option dns primary 10.20.0.1
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Sets the firewall's own resolvers, runs a DNS proxy on the LAN interface with a rule for the internal domain, and hands the firewall out as the clients' DNS server.

deviceconfig system dns-setting servers primary/secondary
DNS servers the firewall itself uses (updates, FQDN objects, URL lookups), sourced from the management interface unless service routes change that.
dns-proxy DNS-LAN enabled yes · interface ethernet1/2
A DNS proxy object listening on the LAN interface.
default primary/secondary
Where queries go when no domain rule matches.
domain-servers CORP domain-name *.corp.example primary 10.10.10.53
A per-domain rule: internal names go to the internal DNS server.
dhcp … server option dns primary 10.20.0.1
DHCP clients get the firewall interface as their DNS server.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Firewall resolution

ping host www.paloaltonetworks.com

Good: The name resolves (management plane). If not: Check dns-setting, the management route and service routes.

2 · DNS proxy

show dns-proxy cache all
show dns-proxy statistics all

Good: Cache entries and query counters for DNS-LAN. If not: Empty: clients aren't using the firewall, or the proxy isn't bound to their interface.

3 · Client queries reach it

debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match destination 10.20.0.1 destination-port 53
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes

Good: Packets to 10.20.0.1:53 counted. If not: Interface management profile, or client DNS settings.

⚠ Syntax note. PAN-OS configuration-mode set commands. The structure follows Palo Alto documentation and published configurations. Use Tab/? while typing, run commit validate (or validate full) before commit, and check the GUI equivalent shown in each step.

DNSRESOLUTION ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

System DNS and Testing Name Resolution

The firewall's own DNS — used for update servers, NTP, FQDN address objects and log forwarding — is separate from anything DNS Proxy does for users behind it. When updates fail or an FQDN object resolves to nothing, this is the DNS that matters.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show system info | match dnsThe primary and secondary DNS servers the firewall itself uses.Device > Setup > Services > DNS
# set deviceconfig system dns-setting servers primary <ip> secondary <ip>Configure system DNS servers.Device > Setup > Services > DNS Servers
ping host <fqdn>There is no nslookup on PAN-OS. Ping a hostname and read the resolved address off the first line — that is the resolution test.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
admin@fw-01(active)> ping count 2 host updates.paloaltonetworks.com
PING updates.paloaltonetworks.com (34.120.13.79) 56(84) bytes of data.   <-- resolution worked
64 bytes from 34.120.13.79: icmp_seq=1 ttl=112 time=21.4 ms
64 bytes from 34.120.13.79: icmp_seq=2 ttl=112 time=21.1 ms

ping host <fqdn> resolves using the management interface's DNS. If you have a service route sending DNS out a dataplane interface, this test can succeed while the actual subsystem fails, or the reverse. Check Device > Setup > Services > Service Route Configuration when the two disagree.

DNSDNS PROXY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

DNS Proxy and FQDN Objects

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show dns-proxy allAll configured DNS-proxy rules.Network > DNS Proxy
show dns-proxy fqdn allThe DNS-proxy FQDN cache.Network > DNS Proxy > Cache
show dns-proxy fqdn name <fqdn>Cache entry for one name.Network > DNS Proxy
show dns-proxy statistics allQuery hits, misses and errors.Network > DNS Proxy
clear dns-proxy fqdn allFlush the whole proxy cache.CLI only
clear dns-proxy fqdn name <fqdn>Flush one entry.CLI only
show system fqdnResolved addresses for FQDN address objects used in policy. This is the one that matters when a rule with an FQDN object is not matching.Objects > Addresses (FQDN type)
request system fqdn refreshForce an immediate FQDN object refresh instead of waiting for the timer.Objects > Addresses > More Actions > Refresh
show system setting fqdnThe FQDN refresh timer.Device > Setup > Services > FQDN Refresh Time
admin@fw-01(active)> show system fqdn
FQDN objects:
  vendor-portal.example.com   ->  203.0.113.44, 203.0.113.45      (ttl 300, refreshed 00:02:11 ago)
  saas-api.example.net        ->  198.51.100.90                   (ttl 60,  refreshed 00:00:19 ago)

An FQDN object holds only the addresses returned at the last refresh — default every 30 minutes, floored by the record TTL. A CDN or cloud endpoint that rotates addresses faster than that will produce a rule that works intermittently and looks like a policy fault. It is not; the address set is stale. Shorten the refresh interval or stop using FQDN objects for that destination.

DHCP Server & RelayRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: DHCP Server on One VLAN, DHCP Relay on Another

Use it when the firewall hands out addresses itself (small sites, guest VLANs) or forwards DHCP to central servers (corporate VLANs). The interface must be Layer 3, in a virtual router and a zone.

// e1/2 · firewall as DHCP server
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/2 server mode enabled
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/2 server ip-pool 10.20.0.100-10.20.0.200
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/2 server option gateway 10.20.0.1 subnet-mask 255.255.255.0
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/2 server option lease timeout 1440
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/2 server option dns primary 10.20.0.1
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/2 server reserved 10.20.0.50 mac 00:11:22:33:44:55
// e1/3 · relay to the central DHCP server
set network dhcp interface ethernet1/3 relay ip enabled yes server 10.10.10.50
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Runs a DHCP server on one interface and relays DHCP to a central server on another.

server mode enabled
enabled serves addresses. auto turns the server off if another DHCP server is detected on the segment.
server ip-pool 10.20.0.100-10.20.0.200
The pool handed out. Keep it clear of static addresses.
option gateway · subnet-mask
The default gateway (the firewall interface) and mask sent to clients.
option lease timeout 1440
The lease length in minutes (unlimited also exists).
option dns primary 10.20.0.1
The DNS server clients get (here the firewall's DNS proxy).
server reserved 10.20.0.50 mac …
A fixed address for one device.
relay ip enabled yes server 10.10.10.50
The interface relays DHCP to this server (up to eight per family). A security rule must allow DHCP from the relay interface to the server.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Leases (server mode)

show dhcp server lease interface ethernet1/2
show dhcp server settings ethernet1/2

Good: Clients listed with their MACs and lease times. If not: No leases: the interface isn't in a zone/VR, mode is auto with another server present, or the pool is exhausted.

2 · Relay path

debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match destination 10.10.10.50 destination-port 67
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes

Good: Relayed packets to the server, replies coming back. If not: A missing security rule, or no route back from the server to the relay interface subnet.

⚠ Syntax note. Use Tab/? while typing and commit validate before committing. The GUI path is given for every object.

Ping, Traceroute & MTUREACHABILITY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Ping — and the Source Option That Changes Everything

A bare ping host <ip> sources from the management interface. That is almost never the test you meant to run. Adding source <dataplane-ip> puts the packet on the dataplane, through the real routing table and the real policy, which is the path production traffic takes.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
ping host <ip>Ping from the MGT interface.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping count 5 host <ip>Bound the number of probes. Without it, ping runs until Ctrl-C.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping source <dataplane-ip> host <ip>The important one. Ping from a dataplane interface IP — the only way to test reachability of networks behind data interfaces.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping (Source field)
ping source <ip> count <n> host <ip>Source and count together.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping source <ip> interval <sec> host <ip>Time between probes.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping source <ip> ttl <n> host <ip>Set the IP TTL of the request.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping source <ip> tos <0-255> host <ip>Set the ToS / DSCP byte — useful for QoS path testing.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping source <ip> bypass-routing yes host <ip>Force the probe out the directly-connected interface, ignoring the routing table. Isolates "is it L2" from "is it routing".Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping inet6 yes source <ipv6> host <ipv6>IPv6 ping from a dataplane interface.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
admin@fw-01(active)> ping count 4 source 10.10.20.1 host 10.10.30.10   DMZ host, sourced from the VLAN 20 SVI
PING 10.10.30.10 (10.10.30.10) from 10.10.20.1 : 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.10.30.10: icmp_seq=1 ttl=63 time=0.712 ms
64 bytes from 10.10.30.10: icmp_seq=2 ttl=63 time=0.688 ms
64 bytes from 10.10.30.10: icmp_seq=3 ttl=63 time=0.701 ms
64 bytes from 10.10.30.10: icmp_seq=4 ttl=63 time=0.694 ms

--- 10.10.30.10 ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss, time 3003ms

Pinging from the management interface to test a user's path is like testing the loading bay by walking out the front door. Both are exits from the building; only one of them is the one the trucks use.

A dataplane-sourced ping is subject to security policy in the same way transit traffic is. A failed ping can mean "unreachable" or it can mean "your own intrazone/interzone rule denies ICMP from the firewall". Check with test security-policy-match before concluding the network is broken.

Ping, Traceroute & MTUMTU ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Path MTU Discovery with Ping

Intermittent failures that only affect large transfers — SMB, backups, TLS handshakes with big certificate chains — while ping and SSH work fine are almost always MTU. Setting the DF bit and walking the size down finds the real path MTU.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
ping source <ip> size <bytes> host <ip>Set the ICMP payload size.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping (Size)
ping source <ip> do-not-fragment yes size 1472 host <ip>DF-bit probe at the standard 1500-byte-MTU ceiling. Decrease size until it succeeds.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping (Don't Fragment)
ping count 5 size 9000 do-not-fragment yes source <ip> host <ip>End-to-end jumbo frame test.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
ping count 100 source <ip> host <ip>Sustained run for spotting intermittent loss.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping

Sample — finding the real MTU

admin@fw-01(active)> ping count 2 do-not-fragment yes size 1472 source 10.10.20.1 host 10.10.30.10
PING 10.10.30.10 (10.10.30.10) from 10.10.20.1 : 1472(1500) bytes of data.
ping: local error: Message too long, mtu=1400            <-- path MTU is 1400, not 1500

admin@fw-01(active)> ping count 2 do-not-fragment yes size 1372 source 10.10.20.1 host 10.10.30.10
1380 bytes from 10.10.30.10: icmp_seq=1 ttl=63 time=0.9 ms    <-- 1372 + 28 = 1400. Confirmed.
Payload sizeTotal on the wireProves an MTU of
14721500Standard Ethernet
14221450Typical IPsec overhead
13721400Common tunnel MTU
1372 − 241376GRE inside the above

Add 28 to the ping size to get the on-the-wire figure: 20 bytes of IP header plus 8 bytes of ICMP header. So 1472 tests a 1500 MTU, and 1372 tests a 1400 MTU.

Traceroute

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
traceroute host <ip>Trace from the MGT interface.Device > Troubleshooting > Traceroute
traceroute source <dataplane-ip> host <ip>Trace from a dataplane interface. As with ping, this is the one that reflects production.Device > Troubleshooting > Traceroute (Source)
