admin@fw-01(active)> traceroute source 10.10.20.1 host 8.8.8.8
traceroute to 8.8.8.8 (8.8.8.8), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  198.51.100.1   0.874 ms   0.812 ms   0.795 ms
 2  * * *                                            <-- hop hides itself; not necessarily a fault
 3  203.0.113.17   8.221 ms   8.109 ms   8.334 ms
 4  8.8.8.8        9.104 ms   9.012 ms   8.998 ms       <-- destination replied; path is fine

A row of asterisks in the middle of a trace means one router declined to send ICMP time-exceeded. It is a policy choice on that device, not evidence of loss. Only treat a trace as showing a break when every hop from a given point onward is starred and the destination never replies. Middle-of-path stars followed by a good final hop are noise.

Ping, Traceroute & MTUPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

Slow, or Large Transfers Fail

time-box 20 minMTU / MSSdataplane load
  1. MTU symptoms: ping works, small pages load, but big downloads, SMB or TLS handshakes hang. Check filtered counters for flow_fwd_mtu_exceeded.
  2. Through IPsec, PAN-OS adjusts the TCP MSS of tunnelled TCP automatically, using the lower of the tunnel interface MTU − 40 and a value calculated from the encryption overhead. Setting a lower MTU on tunnel.x lowers it further.
  3. On other encapsulations (MPLS, PPPoE, VLAN-tagged transits), enable MSS adjustment on the Layer 3 interface: 
    set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 adjust-tcp-mss enable yes ipv4-mss-adjustment 40
    What each line does

    Purpose: Lowers the TCP MSS for TCP sessions leaving ethernet1/1, so endpoints send segments that fit a path with extra encapsulation.

    set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3
    Applies to this Layer 3 interface.
    adjust-tcp-mss enable yes
    Turns on MSS rewriting in the TCP SYN/SYN-ACK passing through this interface.
    ipv4-mss-adjustment 40
    The firewall sets MSS = interface MTU − this value. The default of 40 covers the IP and TCP headers. Increase it when extra encapsulation (PPPoE, MPLS, GRE) sits on the path. Traffic through IPsec tunnels is already adjusted automatically.
  4. Interface errors: show interface ethernetX/Y. Rising errors point to physical faults.
  5. Dataplane load: show running resource-monitor (dataplane CPU and buffers) and show session info (session table usage).

debug dataplane set ip4-df-ignore yes makes the firewall fragment IPv4 packets even when DF is set. It's global. Use it only as a deliberate, documented workaround, and revert with debug dataplane set ip4-df-ignore no.

Routing CoreRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Floating Default Route, Path Monitoring and Policy Based Forwarding

Use it when a site has two ISPs without SD-WAN: use ISP-A, fail over to ISP-B when ISP-A stops reaching the internet, and send one subnet out of ISP-B deliberately.

// primary and floating default routes (same admin distance, metric decides)
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route DEF-ISPA destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop ip-address 198.51.100.1 interface ethernet1/1 metric 10
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route DEF-ISPB destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop ip-address 203.0.113.1 interface ethernet1/4 metric 20
// withdraw DEF-ISPA when the internet stops answering via ISP-A
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route DEF-ISPA path-monitor enable yes failure-condition any
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route DEF-ISPA path-monitor monitor-destinations GOOGLE enable yes source 198.51.100.2 destination 8.8.8.8 interval 3 count 5
// send one subnet out of ISP-B on purpose (PBF), with symmetric return
set rulebase pbf rules BACKUP-NET from zone TRUST source 10.20.5.0/24 destination any service any
set rulebase pbf rules BACKUP-NET action forward egress-interface ethernet1/4 nexthop ip-address 203.0.113.1
set rulebase pbf rules BACKUP-NET enforce-symmetric-return enabled yes nexthop-address-list 203.0.113.1
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Two default routes with different metrics, path monitoring that withdraws the primary on failure, and a PBF rule that sends one subnet out of ISP-B with symmetric return.

static-route DEF-ISPA … nexthop 198.51.100.1 interface ethernet1/1 metric 10
Primary default route. Both statics have admin distance 10, so the lower metric wins.
static-route DEF-ISPB … metric 20
Floating default: inactive (no A flag) until DEF-ISPA is removed.
path-monitor enable yes failure-condition any
Enables monitoring for DEF-ISPA. any = remove the route when any monitored destination fails (all = only when all fail).
monitor-destinations GOOGLE … source 198.51.100.2 destination 8.8.8.8 interval 3 count 5
Pings 8.8.8.8 from the ISP-A interface every 3 s. 5 misses mark it down. When the route is withdrawn, a path-monitor-failure system log is written.
pbf rules BACKUP-NET from zone TRUST source 10.20.5.0/24
Matches the first packet of new sessions from that subnet, before the routing table.
action forward egress-interface ethernet1/4 nexthop ip-address 203.0.113.1
Forces those sessions out of ISP-B.
enforce-symmetric-return enabled yes nexthop-address-list 203.0.113.1
Returns replies via the same ISP, avoiding asymmetric return.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Active route

show routing route virtual-router default destination 0.0.0.0/0
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 8.8.8.8

Good: DEF-ISPA with the A flag. fib-lookup returns ethernet1/1. If not: Both active: equal metrics (ECMP if enabled). Neither: interface down.

2 · Path monitor

show routing path-monitor
show log system direction equal backward | match path-monitor

Good: GOOGLE up. If not: Down while ISP-A works: the source or destination is unreachable, or blocked upstream.

3 · PBF

test pbf-policy-match from TRUST source 10.20.5.10 destination 8.8.8.8 protocol 6 destination-port 443
show running pbf-policy

Good: BACKUP-NET matches. If not: No match: source/zone. Remember PBF applies to new sessions only.

⚠ Syntax note. PAN-OS configuration-mode set commands. The structure follows Palo Alto documentation and published configurations. Use Tab/? while typing, run commit validate (or validate full) before commit, and check the GUI equivalent shown in each step.

Routing CoreORIENTATION ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Virtual Routers vs Logical Routers — Two Command Trees

PAN-OS 10.2 introduced Advanced Routing, which replaces the legacy virtual router with a logical router built on FRR. Both exist in the field, they are enabled per-device, and the command trees are completely separate. Running a legacy command on an Advanced Routing box does not give a syntax error — it gives an empty table, which is far more misleading.

Legacy (virtual router)Advanced Routing (logical router)
show routing routeshow advanced-routing route
show routing fibshow advanced-routing fib
show routing protocol bgp summaryshow advanced-routing bgp summary logical-router <lr>
show routing protocol ospf neighborshow advanced-routing ospf neighbor
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip <ip>test routing fib-lookup logical-router <lr> ip <ip>
nexthop next-vr <vr>nexthop next-lr <lr>

Which one am I on?

admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing route
Advanced routing is not enabled                    <-- legacy VR box; use "show routing ..."

admin@fw-01(active)> show routing route
flags: A:active, ?:loose, C:connect, H:host, S:static, ...   <-- you are on legacy

Same firewall, same routes, two vocabularies. Guessing which one applies wastes the first five minutes of every routing ticket — run one command from each tree first and let the box tell you.

Advanced Routing is a per-device setting under Device > Setup > Management and it requires a reboot to change. In a Panorama-managed estate you will commonly have both kinds of firewall under one template stack, so never assume the tree from the last box you were on.

⚠ Verification note. Palo Alto's Networking cheat sheet lists the Advanced Routing lookup commands as show advanced-routing route destination <ip/netmask>, show advanced-routing route logical-router <name> and show advanced-routing fib. The test routing fib-lookup logical-router … form isn't in that cheat sheet. Confirm it with test routing fib-lookup ? on your release, and fall back to the documented commands if it isn't offered. The legacy form test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip <ip> is documented in the KB.

Routing CoreCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs

How PAN-OS Picks a Route: Prefix, Distance, Metric, ECMP

  1. Longest prefix match. A /24 beats a /16, which beats the default route, whatever the distance.
  2. Lowest administrative distance between different sources (static vs OSPF vs BGP).
  3. Lowest metric between routes from the same source. Metrics are never compared across protocols.
  4. Still tied → ECMP, but only if ECMP is enabled on the virtual router. Otherwise one path is used.
SourceDefault AD · legacy virtual routerDefault AD · Advanced Routing (logical router)Notes
Static1010Raise it above a dynamic route to make a floating backup.
eBGP2020 (BGP AS External) · BGP Local Route 20Learned from a different AS.
OSPF intra-area30 (OSPF Int)10The two engines differ. Legacy uses one internal value. Advanced Routing splits intra-area (10) and inter-area (30).
OSPF inter-area30
OSPF external110110Redistributed into OSPF.
RIP120n/aRIP is a legacy-engine protocol.
iBGP200200 (BGP AS Internal)What the spokes use in this lab. A static route to the same prefix silently wins.

OSPF internal routes beat a "floating" static at AD 100. On a legacy VR, OSPF internal is AD 30. On Advanced Routing, intra-area is 10 (it ties with static, and then a static wins only on other criteria) and inter-area is 30. If someone floats a static at AD 100 expecting OSPF to win like on a Cisco router, OSPF already wins, and the static never activates. Check the router's admin distance settings before assuming another vendor's numbers. ✎ Advanced Routing values added from the logical router reference

ECMP facts (Palo Alto docs): off until you enable it on the virtual or logical router. Up to four equal-cost paths, with Max Path defaulting to 2 on virtual routers. Load balancing is per session, not per packet. Enabling or changing ECMP restarts the virtual router and can drop sessions. ECMP isn't supported when any of the equal-cost routes has a virtual router or logical router as its next hop, which matters for next-vr designs.

RIB, FIB and the Runtime Lookup

QuestionLegacy virtual routerAdvanced Routing Engine (logical router)
All routes, with active flagshow routing routeshow advanced-routing route
Routes for one destinationshow routing route destination <prefix>show advanced-routing route destination <ip/mask>
Forwarding tableshow routing fib virtual-router <vr>show advanced-routing fib
Which interface would this IP use?test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip <ip>Filter the FIB or route output by destination

The runtime lookup is the most honest answer: it asks the dataplane, so it includes everything that affects forwarding for that destination. Use it before reading the whole table.

Routing CoreLEGACY VR ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

RIB and FIB — Legacy Virtual Routers

The RIB is every route the firewall knows. The FIB is the subset it has actually programmed for forwarding, after recursive next-hop resolution and best-path selection. When they disagree, the FIB is the truth.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show routing routeThe routing table across all virtual routers. First command for any routing issue.Network > Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats > Route Table
show routing route virtual-router <vr-name>One VR only. Essential on multi-VR boxes.Network > Virtual Routers > select VR
show routing route type <static|connect|bgp|ospf|rip>Filter by protocol.Route Table (Type filter)
show routing route destination <ip/mask>Just the route to one prefix.Route Table
show routing fibThe forwarding table — what actually forwards packets.Network > Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats > Forwarding Table
show routing fib virtual-router <vr-name>FIB for one VR.Forwarding Table
show routing fib virtual-router <vr> | match <ip/mask>The FIB entry for a specific destination.Forwarding Table

Sample — reading the route table

admin@fw-01(active)> show routing route virtual-router default
flags: A:active, ?:loose, C:connect, H:host, S:static, ~:internal, R:rip, O:ospf, B:bgp,
       Oi:ospf intra-area, Oo:ospf inter-area, O1:ospf ext-type-1, O2:ospf ext-type-2, E:ecmp, M:multicast

VIRTUAL ROUTER: default (id 1)
  destination        nexthop         metric  flags  age    interface       next-AS
  0.0.0.0/0          198.51.100.1        10  A S            ethernet1/1
  10.10.10.0/24      10.10.10.1           0  A C            ethernet1/2
  10.10.10.1/32      0.0.0.0              0  A H
  10.10.20.0/24      10.10.20.1           0  A C            ethernet1/3.20
  10.10.30.0/24      10.10.30.1           0  A C            ethernet1/3.30
  10.20.0.0/16       10.255.0.2         110  A Oi   41221   tunnel.1
  172.16.0.0/12      198.51.100.1        20    S            ethernet1/1   <-- no A: known but NOT active

total routes shown: 7
FlagMeans
AActive. This route is in the FIB and will be used. Its absence is the single most important thing to notice in this output.
CConnected — derived from an interface address.
HHost route for the interface's own address.
SStatic.
O / Oi / Oo / O1 / O2OSPF, and which LSA class it came from.
BBGP.
EECMP — multiple equal-cost next hops installed.
?Loose — the next hop is not directly connected and needed recursive resolution.

A route without A is present in the table and doing nothing. It lost best-path selection to something else — usually a more specific prefix, a lower administrative distance, or a better metric. Reading the table without checking the flags column is how people conclude "the route is there, so routing is fine" while traffic goes somewhere else entirely.

Sample — the FIB

admin@fw-01(active)> show routing fib virtual-router default | match 10.20
id  destination      nexthop        flags  interface       mtu
17  10.20.0.0/16     10.255.0.2     ug     tunnel.1        1400

FIB flags: u up, g gateway (next hop is another router), h host, e ECMP member. The MTU column here is the value actually used for forwarding — worth checking when large packets fail across a tunnel.

Reading show routing route

Each virtual router has its own table. Always name the VR you mean. Reading the default VR while the traffic lives in vr-wan is the most common multi-VR mistake.

// illustrative, trimmed

VIRTUAL ROUTER: vr-wan (id 1)

destination        nexthop        metric flags      age   interface
0.0.0.0/0          203.0.113.1    10     A S              ethernet1/1
10.10.1.0/24       10.255.1.2     0      A Bi       2461  tunnel.1

admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing route logical-router LR-CORE type static
Codes: K - kernel, C - connected, S - static, O - OSPF, B - BGP
       > - selected route, * - FIB route

S>* 0.0.0.0/0        [10/0] via 198.51.100.1, ethernet1/1, 09w2d
S>* 10.20.0.0/16     [10/0] via 10.255.0.2, tunnel.1, 04d11h
S   172.16.0.0/12    [200/0] via 198.51.100.1, ethernet1/1 inactive

Advanced Routing output uses FRR conventions rather than PAN-OS flags: > marks the selected route and * marks the one installed in the FIB. The bracketed pair is [distance/metric]. A route with neither > nor *, or marked inactive, is the Advanced Routing equivalent of a missing A flag.

Routing CoreFIB LOOKUP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

test routing fib-lookup — The Best Command in the Routing Section

Reading a route table and working out which entry wins is error-prone. test routing fib-lookup asks the firewall to do the longest-prefix match itself and report the answer, including the source address it would use. It is the correct starting point for asymmetric routing, for tunnel steering questions, and for "which interface does this leave by".

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr-name> ip <destination-ip>Which route wins for this destination on a legacy VR.Network > Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats
test routing fib-lookup logical-router <lr-name> ip <ip>Same under Advanced Routing.Network > Routing > Logical Routers

Sample — egress lookup

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 203.0.113.90
runtime route lookup
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
virtual-router:  default
destination:     203.0.113.90
result:
   interface  ethernet1/1
   nexthop    198.51.100.1
   source     198.51.100.2
   metric     10
   flags      ug

Sample — ingress lookup (which interface is the source behind?)

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 10.10.20.55
   interface  ethernet1/3.20
   nexthop    0.0.0.0              <-- directly connected
   source     10.10.20.1
   flags      uh

Run it twice — once on the source address and once on the destination — and you have both ends of the path through this firewall before you have looked at a single policy. That pair of lookups is step one and step two of the end-to-end flow trace.

A fib-lookup that returns the default route for an address you expected to be internal means the specific route is missing or inactive — not that the destination is unreachable. Check the RIB for the prefix and look at its flags before you go hunting on other devices.

The legacy form test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip <ip> is documented in the KB.

Routing CoreSTATIC ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Static Routes and Path Monitoring

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
# set network virtual-router <vr> routing-table ip static-route <name> destination <ip/mask> nexthop ip-address <gw> metric <n> interface <intf>Static route on a legacy VR.Network > Virtual Routers > Static Routes > Add
# set network logical-router <lr> vrf <vrf> routing-table ip static-route <name> destination <ip/mask> nexthop ip-address <gw>Static route under Advanced Routing. Note the extra vrf level.Network > Routing > Logical Routers > Static Routes
show advanced-routing static-route-path-monitorPath-monitor status for monitored static routes.Static Routes > Path Monitoring column
admin@fw-01# set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route To-DC2 destination 10.20.0.0/16 nexthop ip-address 10.255.0.2 interface tunnel.1 metric 10
admin@fw-01# commit
admin@fw-01# exit
admin@fw-01> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 10.20.5.10   always verify after commit
   interface  tunnel.1
   nexthop    10.255.0.2

A static route pointing at a tunnel interface stays active even when the tunnel is down, unless the tunnel interface itself goes down or path monitoring is configured. That is how traffic gets black-holed into a dead VPN with a perfectly healthy-looking route table. Either enable tunnel monitoring on the tunnel interface or attach path monitoring to the static route.

Routing CoreCLI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Inactive Routes, Floating Statics and Path Monitoring

A configured static route that doesn't forward is usually present but without the A flag: it lost on admin distance, its interface is down, or path monitoring removed it.

When path monitoring for a static route fails, the firewall logs a critical path-monitor-failure event, and a path-monitor-recovery event when it comes back. After recovery, the route only returns once the preemptive hold time has passed.

show routing path-monitor                          // legacy VR
show advanced-routing static-route-path-monitor    // ARE
show log system direction equal backward | match path-monitor

On an active/passive HA pair, the passive firewall blocks the egress pings for path monitoring because it isn't processing traffic. Don't read "monitor down" on the passive peer as a fault.

Routing CoreCLI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Policy Based Forwarding: Before the Routing Table

PBF rules are matched for the first packet of a new session, before the routing table. A matching forward rule sends the session out of the PBF egress interface, so the zone, NAT and security evaluation follow that interface, not the routing table.

admin@SPOKE1-PA> test pbf-policy-match from TRUST source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.20.15 protocol 6 destination-port 443
// a match means the routing table will NOT be used for this session
admin@SPOKE1-PA> show running pbf-policy
Common PBF problemFix
Internal destinations caught by an "all to ISP-B" ruleAdd a no-pbf rule above it for internal ranges and tunnels.
Return traffic leaves via a different ISPEnable symmetric return on the PBF rule with the right next hop.
PBF monitor failed, traffic droppedCheck the monitor profile action (fail-over vs wait-recover) and the target.
Routing CorePBF / MCAST ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Policy-Based Forwarding and Multicast

PBF is evaluated before the route lookup, so a PBF rule silently overriding the FIB is a standard reason for "the route says X but traffic goes to Y".

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show pbf rule allAll PBF rules with hit counts. Hit counts are the fast way to see whether PBF is involved at all.Policies > Policy Based Forwarding
show pbf rule name <name>One rule in detail.Policies > Policy Based Forwarding
show pbf return-mac allThe return-MAC table PBF uses for symmetric return traffic.Policies > Policy Based Forwarding
test pbf-policy-match from <zone> source <ip> destination <ip> protocol <n>Would PBF catch this flow?Policies > Policy Based Forwarding
show routing multicast fib virtual-router <vr>Multicast forwarding table.Network > Virtual Routers > Multicast
show routing multicast pim group <group> virtual-router <vr>PIM (S,G) state for a group.Network > Virtual Routers > Multicast
admin@fw-01(active)> show pbf rule all
Rule           ID  State   Action    Egress IF  NextHop        NextHop Status
Guest-Breakout  1  Active  Forward   ethernet1/5  198.51.100.65  UP
Legacy-App      2  Active  Forward   ethernet1/1  198.51.100.1   UP

PBF is a shortcut that runs before the map is consulted. If somebody tells you the route table is correct and traffic still leaves the wrong way, PBF is where to look next — the route table is correct, it just is not being asked.

The routed Daemon — Logs and Debug

CommandDescription / usage
less mp-log routed.logThe routing daemon log — BGP, OSPF and RIP events all land here.

admin@fw-01(active)> tail follow yes mp-log routed.log
Apr 27 14:02:11 routed: BGP: 172.16.9.1 [FSM] Timer (connect timer expire)
Apr 27 14:02:11 routed: BGP: 172.16.9.1 went from Connect to Active
Apr 27 14:02:41 routed: BGP: 172.16.9.1 [Error] Connect failed: Connection timed out

Set debug routing global on debug only for as long as you need it, and always put it back to info. On a box carrying a full internet table, debug-level routed logging generates enough volume to fill a partition and slow the management plane noticeably.

⚠ Verification note. debug routing global on debug with less/tail of mp-log routed.log is the form Palo Alto's community material uses for legacy routing debug (✎ replaced debug routed log-level …, which isn't a documented command). The name of the default level to return to can differ by release: check with debug routing global on ?. On Advanced Routing, use the debug advanced-routing … tree instead.

BGPHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

BGP in This Design: Sessions, States and Route Reflection

Every BGP problem is one of two kinds: the session isn't Established, or it is Established but the routes aren't what you expect. Check the session first. A session walks through six states, and the state it gets stuck in tells you where to look.

Route reflection in the hub-and-spoke lab

Stuck inCheck
IdlePeer disabled, or no route to the peer address: test routing fib-lookup to the peer.
Connect / ActiveTCP 179 not completing: tunnel down, wrong local-address, security rule (intrazone deny), management profile.
OpenSent / OpenConfirmAS number, authentication (MD5) or router-ID mismatch. Read show routing protocol bgp peer peer-name <n>.
Established, 0 prefixesNothing advertised: redistribution profile or export rules. Read rib-out on the sender.

A BGP session is two offices agreeing to share address books. First the phone line has to connect (TCP), then they check each other's ID (OPEN), then they swap books (UPDATE). A reflector is the receptionist who, unlike other staff, is allowed to forward one office's book to another.

BGPCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

BGP Lab Configuration, Explained

The BGP part of the hub-and-spoke baseline, pulled out here so the whole BGP story sits in one place. The full baseline is in Foundations & Labs.

// HUB-PA · vr-wan
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.0.254 local-as 65000
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES type ibgp
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE1 peer-address ip 10.255.1.2 local-address interface tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.1/30
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE1 reflector-client client
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE2 peer-address ip 10.255.2.2 local-address interface tunnel.2 ip 10.255.2.1/30
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE2 reflector-client client
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol redist-profile RP-DC priority 1 filter type static destination [ 10.10.10.0/24 10.10.20.0/24 10.10.30.0/24 ]
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol redist-profile RP-DC action redist
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp redist-rules RP-DC enable yes
// SPOKE1-PA · default VR
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.1.2 local-as 65000
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group HUB type ibgp
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group HUB peer HUB peer-address ip 10.255.1.1 local-address interface tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.2/30
set network virtual-router default protocol redist-profile RP-LAN priority 1 filter type connect destination 10.10.1.0/24
set network virtual-router default protocol redist-profile RP-LAN action redist
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp redist-rules RP-LAN enable yes
What each line does

Purpose: Runs iBGP between the hub and both spokes over the IPsec tunnels, with the hub reflecting each spoke's LAN to the other and advertising the datacentre prefixes.

Hub

bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.0.254 local-as 65000
Starts BGP in vr-wan with a stable ID. Every site uses AS 65000, so all sessions are iBGP.
peer-group SPOKES type ibgp
A group for the spoke peers, sharing iBGP behaviour.
peer SPOKE1 peer-address ip 10.255.1.2 local-address interface tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.1/30
Who to peer with (the spoke's tunnel IP) and where to source the session (the hub's tunnel.1 IP). They must mirror the spoke's config.
reflector-client client
Lets the hub pass routes learned from one spoke to the other. Plain iBGP never re-advertises iBGP-learned routes.
redist-profile RP-DC … filter type static destination […] · action redist
Selects the DC static routes (next-vr) for advertisement.
bgp redist-rules RP-DC enable yes
Applies the profile to BGP, so the spokes learn the DC prefixes.

Spoke

bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.1.2 local-as 65000
Same AS as the hub. Router ID = tunnel IP.
peer HUB peer-address ip 10.255.1.1 local-address interface tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.2/30
Peers with the hub's tunnel address, sourced from the spoke's own.
redist-profile RP-LAN filter type connect destination 10.10.1.0/24
Selects the connected LAN.
bgp redist-rules RP-LAN enable yes
Advertises the LAN to the hub, which reflects it to SPOKE2.

BGP Scenarios: the Lab and What Each Config Solves

The scenarios run on FW-EDGE (AS 65010, public prefix 192.0.2.0/24) with two internet providers and an internal iBGP peer. They build on the iBGP hub-and-spoke config above.

#ScenarioProblem it solves
B1eBGP to an ISP: accept only a default, advertise only your prefixInternet routing without becoming a transit AS or importing a full table.
B2Default-originate to a downstream peerA branch or customer router receives a default from the firewall.
B3Dual ISP: primary/backup with local preference and AS-path prependDeterministic outbound and inbound paths with automatic failover.
B4Originating an aggregate with a discard routeAdvertise one stable summary even when individual subnets flap.
B5eBGP multihop between loopbacks, with MD5 and BFDPeering across an intermediate device, fast failure detection, protected sessions.
B6Import filtering, max-prefixes and BGP ↔ OSPF redistributionProtecting the firewall from route leaks, and sharing BGP routes with the internal IGP safely.
BGPCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Routing scenarios

B1 · eBGP to an ISP: Accept a Default, Advertise Only Your Prefix

// B1 · eBGP to ISP-A
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.255.1 local-as 65010
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp reject-default-route no
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group ISP-A type ebgp import-nexthop original export-nexthop resolve
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group ISP-A peer ISPA-R1 peer-as 64500 peer-address ip 198.51.100.1 local-address interface ethernet1/1 ip 198.51.100.2/30
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route PI-NULL destination 192.0.2.0/24 nexthop discard
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp redist-rules 192.0.2.0/24 enable yes set-origin igp
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules ISPA-DEFAULT-ONLY used-by ISP-A match address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 exact yes
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules ISPA-DEFAULT-ONLY action allow
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules ISPA-DENY-REST used-by ISP-A action deny
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules ISPA-OWN-PREFIX used-by ISP-A match address-prefix 192.0.2.0/24 exact yes
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules ISPA-OWN-PREFIX action allow
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules ISPA-DENY-REST used-by ISP-A action deny
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Peers with ISP-A, accepts only a default route from it, and advertises only the organisation's own prefix. This is the safest standard edge design.

bgp enable yes router-id … local-as 65010
Starts BGP with your public (or private) AS number.
reject-default-route no
PAN-OS rejects default routes learned through BGP unless this is cleared. Needed here because the ISP sends 0.0.0.0/0.
peer-group ISP-A type ebgp
External peering. import-nexthop original keeps the ISP's next hop, export-nexthop resolve sends our own address as the next hop.
peer ISPA-R1 peer-as 64500 peer-address … local-address …
The ISP router's AS and IP, sourced from our WAN address on ethernet1/1.
static-route PI-NULL 192.0.2.0/24 nexthop discard
A route for our own prefix that always exists, so the advertisement never flaps. Traffic to unused parts of the range is dropped.
redist-rules 192.0.2.0/24 enable yes set-origin igp
Redistributes our prefix into BGP. A redist rule can name an IP subnet directly, as here, or a redistribution profile.
import rules ISPA-DEFAULT-ONLY … exact yes · allow
Accepts the default route and nothing longer than /0.
import rules ISPA-DENY-REST · deny
Rules are evaluated in order: everything else from ISP-A is rejected. This protects the firewall if the ISP sends a full table by mistake.
export rules ISPA-OWN-PREFIX … allow
Advertises only 192.0.2.0/24.
export rules ISPA-DENY-REST · deny
Nothing else leaves. Above all, routes learned from ISP-B are never advertised to ISP-A, so you never become a transit path between providers.

⚠ Syntax note. These are legacy virtual router commands. The option names follow Palo Alto's documented GUI fields and published configurations. Keyword spellings can vary slightly between releases, so press Tab or ? while typing, and run commit validate first. On the Advanced Routing Engine the same scenarios are built in Network > Routing > Logical Routers, with filters and redistribution profiles under Network > Routing > Routing Profiles.

BGPCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Routing scenarios

B2 · Default-Originate to a Downstream Peer

// B2 · send a default route to a downstream branch router (iBGP or eBGP)
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp allow-redist-default-route yes
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp redist-rules 0.0.0.0/0 enable yes set-origin incomplete
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules DEFAULT-TO-BRANCH used-by BRANCH match address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 exact yes
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules DEFAULT-TO-BRANCH match route-table unicast
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules DEFAULT-TO-BRANCH action allow
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules BRANCH-DENY-REST used-by BRANCH action deny
commit
What each line does

Purpose: The PAN-OS equivalent of "default-originate": the firewall redistributes its own default route into BGP and sends only that to the BRANCH peer group.

allow-redist-default-route yes
The safety catch. BGP won't redistribute a default route unless explicitly allowed (GUI: Redist Rules > Allow Redistribute Default Route).
redist-rules 0.0.0.0/0 enable yes
Redistributes the firewall's active default route (static, or learned from the ISP) into BGP.
set-origin incomplete
Marks the route as redistributed rather than an IGP origin.
export rules DEFAULT-TO-BRANCH … 0.0.0.0/0 exact yes · route-table unicast · allow
Sends exactly the default route to peers in group BRANCH.
export rules BRANCH-DENY-REST · deny
Nothing else goes to the branch: it only needs a default.

The default is only advertised while the firewall itself has an active default route. If the ISP default is withdrawn (or a monitored static is removed), the advertisement disappears and the branch fails over to its own backup. Usually that's exactly the behaviour you want.

⚠ Syntax note. These are legacy virtual router commands. The option names follow Palo Alto's documented GUI fields and published configurations. Keyword spellings can vary slightly between releases, so press Tab or ? while typing, and run commit validate first. On the Advanced Routing Engine the same scenarios are built in Network > Routing > Logical Routers, with filters and redistribution profiles under Network > Routing > Routing Profiles.

BGPCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Routing scenarios

B3 · Dual ISP: Primary/Backup with Local Preference and AS-Path Prepend

// B3 · add ISP-B as backup (ISP-A from B1 stays primary)
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group ISP-B type ebgp import-nexthop original export-nexthop resolve
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group ISP-B peer ISPB-R1 peer-as 64510 peer-address ip 203.0.113.1 local-address interface ethernet1/2 ip 203.0.113.2/30
// outbound: prefer ISP-A
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules ISPA-DEFAULT-ONLY action allow update local-preference 200
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules ISPB-DEFAULT-ONLY used-by ISP-B match address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 exact yes
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules ISPB-DEFAULT-ONLY action allow update local-preference 100
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules ISPB-DENY-REST used-by ISP-B action deny
// inbound: make the path via ISP-B look longer
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules ISPB-OWN-PREFIX used-by ISP-B match address-prefix 192.0.2.0/24 exact yes
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules ISPB-OWN-PREFIX action allow update as-path prepend 3
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules ISPB-DENY-REST used-by ISP-B action deny
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Adds a second provider as a backup. Outbound traffic prefers ISP-A through local preference, inbound traffic prefers ISP-A because the route via ISP-B carries a longer AS path, and both fail over automatically when the ISP-A session drops.

peer-group ISP-B … peer ISPB-R1 peer-as 64510 …
The second eBGP session, on ethernet1/2.
ISPA-DEFAULT-ONLY … update local-preference 200
The default from ISP-A gets local preference 200. Higher wins, so all outbound traffic uses ISP-A.
ISPB-DEFAULT-ONLY … update local-preference 100
ISP-B's default keeps the normal value 100 and becomes the backup.
ISPB-OWN-PREFIX … update as-path prepend 3
Our AS is added three extra times when advertising to ISP-B, so the internet sees a longer path through ISP-B and prefers ISP-A for inbound traffic.
ISPB-DENY-REST · deny
As with ISP-A: no transit between providers.

Prepending influences, but doesn't guarantee, inbound traffic: other networks may prefer ISP-B because of their own policies. For stronger control, ask the providers about BGP community values they support.

Keyword spellings can vary slightly between releases, so press Tab or ? while typing, and run commit validate first. BGPCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Routing scenarios

B4 · Originating an Aggregate with a Discard Route

// B4 · advertise one summary for several internal /24s
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route AGG-10-40 destination 10.40.0.0/16 nexthop discard
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp redist-rules 10.40.0.0/16 enable yes set-origin igp
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules IBGP-AGG used-by HUB match address-prefix 10.40.0.0/16 exact yes
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy export rules IBGP-AGG action allow
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Originates a stable /16 summary for a block of internal /24s, so peers carry one route and individual subnet flaps never reach them.

static-route AGG-10-40 10.40.0.0/16 nexthop discard
A discard (null) route anchors the summary. Longer, more specific routes still forward normally, and only unused parts of the /16 hit the discard and are dropped, which also prevents routing loops.
redist-rules 10.40.0.0/16 … set-origin igp
Brings the summary into BGP.
export rules IBGP-AGG … exact yes · allow
Sends the summary only, exactly as a /16. Add deny rules for the specifics if they would otherwise be advertised.

B5 · eBGP Multihop Between Loopbacks, with MD5 and BFD

// B5 · eBGP multihop between loopbacks, MD5, BFD
set network interface loopback units loopback.1 ip 10.255.255.1/32
set network virtual-router default interface loopback.1
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route TO-PEER-LO destination 10.255.255.9/32 nexthop ip-address 10.60.0.2 interface ethernet1/7
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp auth-profile BGP-MD5 secret [secret]
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PARTNER type ebgp
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PARTNER peer PARTNER-R1 peer-as 64600 peer-address ip 10.255.255.9 local-address interface loopback.1 ip 10.255.255.1/32
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PARTNER peer PARTNER-R1 connection-options multihop 2
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PARTNER peer PARTNER-R1 connection-options authentication BGP-MD5
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PARTNER peer PARTNER-R1 bfd profile Inherit-vr-global-setting
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp routing-options graceful-restart enable yes
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Peers between loopback addresses through an intermediate device, signs the session with MD5, and uses BFD to detect a dead path in under a second instead of waiting for the BGP hold timer.

loopback.1 10.255.255.1/32 · interface loopback.1
A loopback that never goes down, used as the BGP source address. It must be in the virtual router (and a zone).
static-route TO-PEER-LO 10.255.255.9/32
eBGP between loopbacks needs a route to the peer's loopback, here via the directly connected next hop 10.60.0.2.
auth-profile BGP-MD5 secret …
A TCP MD5 signature profile. Both ends need the same secret, or the session never leaves Connect/Active.
peer-address 10.255.255.9 · local-address interface loopback.1
Peer with the partner's loopback, sourced from ours.
connection-options multihop 2
eBGP normally expects the peer one hop away (TTL 1). Multihop raises the TTL so loopback peering through one router works.
connection-options authentication BGP-MD5
Applies the MD5 profile to this peer.
bfd profile Inherit-vr-global-setting
Uses the virtual router's BFD profile. When BFD declares the path down, BGP tears the session down immediately.
graceful-restart enable yes
Neighbours keep forwarding on stale routes while the firewall's routing process restarts (for example during an HA failover), instead of withdrawing everything.

⚠ Syntax note. These are legacy virtual router commands. The option names follow Palo Alto's documented GUI fields and published configurations. Keyword spellings can vary slightly between releases, so press Tab or ? while typing, and run commit validate first. BGPCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Routing scenarios

B6 · Import Filtering, Max-Prefixes and BGP ↔ OSPF Redistribution

// B6a · protect against route leaks from a partner
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PARTNER peer PARTNER-R1 max-prefixes 100
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules PARTNER-ALLOW used-by PARTNER match address-prefix 172.16.0.0/12 exact no
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules PARTNER-ALLOW action allow
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp policy import rules PARTNER-DENY-REST used-by PARTNER action deny
// B6b · share partner routes with the internal OSPF domain, tagged
set network virtual-router default protocol redist-profile RP-BGP-TO-OSPF priority 20 filter type bgp destination 172.16.0.0/12
set network virtual-router default protocol redist-profile RP-BGP-TO-OSPF action redist
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf export-rules RP-BGP-TO-OSPF new-path-type ext-2 metric 30 new-tag 200
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Limits what a partner can send (prefix list and maximum count), then hands only the partner's networks to OSPF, tagged so they can be recognised and kept from looping back.

max-prefixes 100
If the partner sends more than 100 prefixes (a leak or misconfiguration), the session is protected from flooding the firewall's routing table.
import rules PARTNER-ALLOW 172.16.0.0/12 exact no
Accepts any prefix inside 172.16.0.0/12, including longer ones.
import rules PARTNER-DENY-REST · deny
Everything else from the partner is dropped, including a default route or your own prefixes.
redist-profile RP-BGP-TO-OSPF filter type bgp destination 172.16.0.0/12
Selects only BGP-learned partner routes.
export-rules RP-BGP-TO-OSPF … ext-2 metric 30 new-tag 200
Injects them into OSPF as external type 2 with tag 200. If OSPF is also redistributed into BGP elsewhere, exclude tag 200 there to prevent loops.

What you received (after import rules)show routing protocol bgp loc-rib
What you send (after export rules)show routing protocol bgp rib-out

BFD for the peershow routing bfd details

BGPBGP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

BGP — Legacy Virtual Routers

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show routing protocol bgp summaryPer-neighbour summary across all VRs — state, AS, uptime, prefixes received. The primary BGP command.Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats > BGP > Summary
show routing protocol bgp peerList all peers.BGP > Peer
show routing protocol bgp peer peer-name <name>One peer in detail — capabilities, timers, counters.BGP > Peer
show routing protocol bgp loc-ribThe local BGP RIB — best paths after selection.BGP > Local RIB
show routing protocol bgp rib-out peer <peer>What we are advertising to a peer.BGP > RIB Out
show routing protocol bgp rib-in peer <peer>What we received from a peer, pre-policy. Requires soft-reconfiguration to be enabled.BGP > RIB In
clear routing protocol bgp peer <peer>Hard-reset a peer. Disruptive — the session drops and all its prefixes are withdrawn.BGP > clear

Sample — BGP summary

admin@fw-01(active)> show routing protocol bgp summary
virtual router:  default
  router id:     10.10.10.1     local AS: 65001
  BGP state:     Enabled

  peer            peer-AS  state         uptime      prefix-rcvd  prefix-sent
  198.51.100.1     65100   Established   09w2d04h            412           14
  10.255.0.2       65002   Established   04d11h27m            36           22
  172.16.9.1       65003   Active        never                 0            0   <-- never came up
StateWhat to check next
IdlePeer administratively down, or the peer address is unreachable. Start with test routing fib-lookup to the peer address.
Connect / ActiveTCP 179 is not completing. Security policy on the intrazone path, a firewall in between, or the peer is not listening. Cycling between the two means each attempt is being refused or timing out.
OpenSent / OpenConfirmTCP is up, BGP parameters disagree — AS number mismatch, router-ID collision, or an unsupported capability.
EstablishedThe session is fine. If prefixes are still missing, the problem is import/export policy, not adjacency.

Established with prefix-rcvd 0 is a policy problem, not a peering problem. Check the inbound route-map or prefix-list, and confirm the peer is actually advertising. Restarting the session will not change anything and will cost you a convergence event.

show advanced-routing bgp filters access-list logical-router <lr> [ipv4|ipv6] name <access-list>Inspect an access-list.
clear advanced-routing bgp peer <peer> logical-router <lr> [soft in|out]Reset a peer. Always try soft in first — it re-applies policy without dropping the session.
admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing bgp peer filtered-routes peer-name ISP-A afi ipv4 logical-router LR-CORE
   Network            Next Hop        Metric  LocPrf  Weight  Path
   172.16.0.0/12      198.51.100.1         0     100       0  65100 i   (filtered: RM-IN-DENY-RFC1918)
   192.168.0.0/16     198.51.100.1         0     100       0  65100 i   (filtered: RM-IN-DENY-RFC1918)

filtered-routes has no legacy-VR equivalent and is one of the clearest reasons to be pleased about Advanced Routing. On a legacy VR the same question requires soft-reconfiguration to be enabled in advance so that rib-in holds the pre-policy view.

BGPSCENARIO ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

BGP Stuck in Active: Wrong Local Address or Intrazone Deny

Change made (A): SPOKE2's peer on the hub is copied from SPOKE1 and keeps local-address interface tunnel.1. Change made (B): a hardening project overrides intrazone-default to deny.

Symptom: both tunnels are up, but SPOKE2's BGP peer never reaches Established (A), or all peers drop after the commit (B). Spoke routes disappear, and traffic to them follows the default route.

  1. R: show routing protocol bgp summary shows the peer in Active/Connect. test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-wan ip 10.10.2.20 returns ethernet1/1, the default route.
  2. Transport: ping source 10.255.2.1 host 10.255.2.2 works, so the tunnel is fine.
  3. Config: show config running | match "local-address" reveals tunnel.1 / 10.255.1.1 on the SPOKE2 peer (A).
  4. Counters: filtered on 10.255.2.2 and TCP 179, counters show flow_policy_deny (B): BGP to the firewall's own tunnel address is VPN → VPN, now denied.
// fix A
set network virtual-router vr-wan protocol bgp peer-group SPOKES peer SPOKE2 local-address interface tunnel.2 ip 10.255.2.1/30
// fix B: explicit rule above the overridden default
set rulebase security rules ALLOW-BGP-OVERLAY from VPN to VPN source any destination any application bgp service application-default action allow
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Two independent fixes for the "BGP stuck in Active" scenario.

peer SPOKE2 local-address interface tunnel.2 ip 10.255.2.1/30
Fix A: sources the SPOKE2 session from the hub's tunnel.2 address, which is the address SPOKE2 is configured to peer with.
rules ALLOW-BGP-OVERLAY from VPN to VPN … application bgp
Fix B: explicitly allows BGP to and from the firewall's tunnel addresses when intrazone-default has been overridden to deny.
commit
Applies both changes.

A phone call made from the wrong extension gets no answer, even though both phones work. And if the building suddenly bans calls between offices on the same floor (intrazone deny), every internal call fails at once.

BGPPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

BGP Neighbour Down, Routes Missing

time-box 20 mincontrol plane

BGP

  1. State: show routing protocol bgp summary (ARE: show advanced-routing bgp summary logical-router <lr>). Established with a prefix count, or stuck in Idle/Active/Connect?
  2. Transport: is the tunnel up? Does ping source <local-tunnel-ip> host <peer> work? Is the peer's local-address the right interface and IP?
  3. Permission to reach the firewall itself: BGP to the firewall's tunnel IP arriving on tunnel.x is intrazone (VPN → VPN). If intrazone-default was overridden to deny, BGP silently breaks. Add an explicit rule for BGP.
  4. Up but routes missing: show routing protocol bgp rib-out on the sender, show routing protocol bgp loc-rib on the receiver. A redistribution profile that matches nothing advertises nothing.
OSPF, RIP & BFDHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

OSPF Adjacency: the Six States

An OSPF neighbour must reach Full before routes are exchanged. Like BGP, where it stops tells you what's wrong.

Stuck inUsual cause
Down / no neighbourOSPF not enabled on the interface, area mismatch, hello/dead timer mismatch, authentication mismatch, or hellos filtered.
InitOne-way hellos: the neighbour doesn't see ours (filtering, multicast issue).
2-Way (between DROthers)Normal on broadcast segments for non-DR routers.
ExStart / ExchangeMTU mismatch, the classic.
Full but routes missingArea type (stub/NSSA), export rules, or a route with a better admin distance wins.

OSPF Scenarios: the Lab and What Each Config Solves

The configurations that follow build up one OSPF design on FW-EDGE, one scenario at a time. Each scenario adds a few lines to the previous one, and each has a "What each line does" panel.

#ScenarioProblem it solves
O1Basic area 0 with the core, plus a passive LANLearn internal VLANs dynamically. Advertise the users' LAN without forming adjacencies on it.
O2Default-originate into OSPFThe core and branches send internet traffic to the firewall without static defaults on every switch.
O3Learning a default route from OSPFAn internal firewall that should follow an upstream router's default.
O4Stub and totally stubby area with a default routeA branch area that only needs a default route, not the full LSDB.
O5NSSA with a default routeA partner area that must inject its own external routes but should otherwise be stubby.
O6Redistributing static/connected routes, and area summarisationAdvertising non-OSPF networks, and shrinking the backbone LSDB.
O7OSPF over an IPsec tunnel with MD5 authenticationDynamic routing to a remote site through a route-based VPN, protected against rogue neighbours.
OSPF, RIP & BFDCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Routing scenarios

O1 · Basic Area 0 with a Passive LAN Interface

// O1 · basic OSPF
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf enable yes
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf router-id 10.255.255.1
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.0 type normal
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet1/3 enable yes passive no link-type broadcast metric 10 priority 1
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ethernet1/6 enable yes passive yes
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Forms a full OSPF adjacency with the core switch on ethernet1/3, and advertises the users' LAN on ethernet1/6 without sending hellos there.

protocol ospf enable yes
Turns OSPF on in this virtual router.
router-id 10.255.255.1
A unique 32-bit identity. Use a stable value (often a loopback): changing it later resets every adjacency.
area 0.0.0.0 type normal
The backbone. Every other area must attach to it.
interface ethernet1/3 enable yes passive no
Runs OSPF on the core-facing interface and forms neighbours there.
link-type broadcast
Ethernet with automatic neighbour discovery by multicast hellos, and DR/BDR election.
metric 10 · priority 1
Interface cost (default 10), and DR election priority. 0 means never DR/BDR.
interface ethernet1/6 enable yes passive yes
The LAN subnet is included in the LSDB and advertised, but no OSPF packets are sent or received. Users can't form a rogue adjacency.

⚠ Syntax note. These are legacy virtual router commands. The option names follow Palo Alto's documented GUI fields and published configurations. Keyword spellings can vary slightly between releases, so press Tab or ? while typing, and run commit validate first. On the Advanced Routing Engine the same scenarios are built in Network > Routing > Logical Routers, with filters and redistribution profiles under Network > Routing > Routing Profiles.

O2 · Default-Originate: Advertise the Firewall's Default Route into OSPF

On PAN-OS there's no single default-information originate command for a normal area. The firewall advertises its default route by redistributing it: the route must exist in the routing table, OSPF must be allowed to redistribute a default, and an export rule must match 0.0.0.0/0.

// O2 · advertise 0.0.0.0/0 into OSPF
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route DEFAULT destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop ip-address 203.0.113.1 interface ethernet1/1
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf allow-redist-default-route yes
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf export-rules 0.0.0.0/0 new-path-type ext-2 metric 10
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Makes FW-EDGE an ASBR that advertises its internet default route to the whole OSPF domain.

static-route DEFAULT … nexthop 203.0.113.1
The route being advertised must be active in the firewall's RIB. If the ISP route disappears (path monitoring), the advertisement is withdrawn too.
allow-redist-default-route yes
OSPF refuses to export a default route unless explicitly allowed. This is PAN-OS's safety catch against accidentally injecting a default.
export-rules 0.0.0.0/0
The export rule names what to redistribute: an IP subnet, as here, or a redistribution profile.
new-path-type ext-2
External type 2: the metric stays fixed through the domain (E1 adds internal cost). E2 is the usual choice for a single exit.
metric 10
The external metric. With two edge firewalls, give the backup a higher metric so the primary wins.

Receiving side: other PAN-OS firewalls in the domain ignore this default unless their own Reject Default Route is cleared (scenario O3). Reject is the documented, recommended default setting.

O3 · Learning a Default Route from OSPF

// O3 · on an INTERNAL firewall that should follow the edge default
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf reject-default-route no
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Lets an internal PAN-OS firewall install a default route learned from OSPF, for example the one FW-EDGE advertises in O2.

reject-default-route no
By default PAN-OS rejects any 0.0.0.0/0 learned through OSPF. Clear it only on firewalls that should follow an upstream default, and make sure no static default with a lower admin distance overrides it.
CheckCommand

O4 · Stub and Totally Stubby Area with a Default Route

// O4 · area 10 towards BRANCH-SW (FW-EDGE is the ABR)
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.10 type stub accept-summary yes default-route advertise metric 10
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.10 interface ethernet1/4 enable yes link-type broadcast
// totally stubby: stop Type-3 summaries as well
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.10 type stub accept-summary no default-route advertise metric 10
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Keeps the branch area small: no external routes enter it, and the ABR gives it a default route instead. The totally stubby variant also removes inter-area summaries.

type stub
No Type-5 external LSAs enter this area. The branch switch only needs a default to reach outside.
accept-summary yes
Inter-area (Type-3) summaries are still accepted, so the branch knows specific routes to other areas.
default-route advertise metric 10
The ABR injects a default route into the stub area with this metric (range 1-255).
interface ethernet1/4 …
Puts the branch-facing interface in area 10.
accept-summary no
Totally stubby area: the ABR stops propagating summary LSAs, so the branch sees only intra-area routes plus the default.

Every router in the area must agree that it is a stub. A mismatch in the stub flag prevents adjacency, and the neighbour never appears.

O5 · NSSA with a Default Route and External Ranges

// O5 · area 20 towards PARTNER-RTR, which redistributes 172.20.0.0/16
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.20 type nssa accept-summary yes default-route advertise metric 20 type ext-2
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.20 type nssa nssa-ext-range 172.20.0.0/16 advertise
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.20 interface ethernet1/5 enable yes link-type broadcast
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Lets the partner router inject its own external networks (Type-7 LSAs), while the area stays protected from the rest of the domain's externals and gets a default route from FW-EDGE.

type nssa
Not-So-Stubby Area: like a stub, but an ASBR inside it may originate Type-7 LSAs. The ABR translates them to Type-5 for the backbone.
accept-summary yes
Keep inter-area summaries. Set it to no for a totally-NSSA area.
default-route advertise metric 20 type ext-2
The ABR advertises a default into the NSSA as an external type 2 route with metric 20.
nssa-ext-range 172.20.0.0/16 advertise
When translating Type-7 to Type-5, advertise the partner's externals as one summary. Use suppress to keep them out of the backbone entirely.
interface ethernet1/5 …
Partner-facing interface in area 20.

O6 · Redistributing Static and Connected Routes, and Summarising an Area

// O6a · advertise a static and a connected network that are not in OSPF
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route LAB-NET destination 10.50.0.0/16 nexthop ip-address 10.10.10.254 interface ethernet1/3
set network virtual-router default protocol redist-profile RP-TO-OSPF priority 10 filter type [ static connect ] destination [ 10.50.0.0/16 192.168.99.0/24 ]
set network virtual-router default protocol redist-profile RP-TO-OSPF action redist
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf export-rules RP-TO-OSPF new-path-type ext-1 metric 20 new-tag 100
// O6b · ABR summarises area 10 into one route for the backbone
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.10 range 10.20.0.0/16 advertise
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Advertises networks OSPF doesn't own (a static route and a connected DMZ), tagged so they can be recognised later, and replaces area 10's individual subnets with one summary in the backbone.

static-route LAB-NET 10.50.0.0/16
A non-OSPF network reachable via a router on the core segment.
redist-profile RP-TO-OSPF priority 10
A redistribution profile: a reusable filter selecting which routes to export. Lower priority numbers are evaluated first.
filter type [ static connect ] destination [ … ]
Only static and connected routes whose destination matches these prefixes. Always filter by destination: redistributing "all statics" leaks more than you intend.
action redist
Routes that match are redistributed (no-redist excludes them).
export-rules RP-TO-OSPF new-path-type ext-1 metric 20
Exports the profile's matches as external type 1, so internal cost is added, which helps when several ASBRs advertise the same network.
new-tag 100
Marks the routes. In mutual redistribution (OSPF ↔ BGP), filter on the tag to stop the same routes being redistributed back in a loop.
area 0.0.0.10 range 10.20.0.0/16 advertise
On the ABR, area 10's subnets are advertised to the backbone as one Type-3 summary. A flapping branch subnet no longer causes SPF runs across the domain.

⚠ Syntax note. These are legacy virtual router commands. The option names follow Palo Alto's documented GUI fields and published configurations. Keyword spellings can vary slightly between releases, so press Tab or ? while typing, and run commit validate first. OSPF, RIP & BFDCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Routing scenarios

O7 · OSPF over an IPsec Tunnel with MD5 Authentication

// O7 · tunnel.30 to a remote site (route-based IPsec already up)
set network interface tunnel units tunnel.30 ip 10.255.30.1/30
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf auth-profile OSPF-MD5 md5 1 key [secret] preferred yes
set network virtual-router default protocol ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface tunnel.30 enable yes link-type p2p metric 50 authentication OSPF-MD5
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Runs OSPF across a route-based VPN to a remote site, with MD5 so only a router that knows the key can become a neighbour.

tunnel.30 ip 10.255.30.1/30
OSPF needs an IP on the tunnel interface to source hellos.
auth-profile OSPF-MD5 md5 1 key … preferred yes
An MD5 profile with key ID 1. The preferred key signs outgoing packets. Several keys allow a hitless key rollover. MD5 is recommended over a simple password.
link-type p2p
Point-to-point: the neighbour is discovered automatically, with no DR/BDR election. Right for tunnels.
metric 50
A higher cost than LAN links, so the tunnel is preferred only when it is the better path.
authentication OSPF-MD5
Applies the profile to the interface. Both ends need the same key ID and key, or the neighbour never forms.

OSPF hellos on tunnel.30 travel inside the tunnel, from the firewall's own tunnel IP. If the tunnel zone's intrazone traffic is denied by an overridden default rule, add an explicit rule for OSPF, just as the BGP scenario does.

OSPFv2 and OSPFv3

Legacy VRAdvanced RoutingShows

show routing protocol ospf interfaceshow advanced-routing ospf interfacePer-interface area, hello/dead, cost, network type.

Sample — neighbours

admin@fw-01(active)> show routing protocol ospf neighbor
virtual router:  default
  neighbor address  interface        state     inactivity-time  neighbor-id
  10.10.10.2        ethernet1/2      full             00:00:36  10.10.10.2
  10.255.0.2        tunnel.1         full             00:00:31  10.20.0.1
  10.10.30.9        ethernet1/3.30   exstart          00:00:38  10.10.30.9   <-- stuck: MTU mismatch
Stuck atAlmost always
Down / InitHellos are one-way. Check subnet mask, area ID, hello/dead timers, authentication, and whether security policy permits OSPF on that intrazone path.
2-Way (and you expected Full)Normal on a broadcast segment between two DROTHERs. Only a fault if one of the pair should be DR or BDR.
ExStart / ExchangeMTU mismatch in the vast majority of cases. The DBD exchange fails because the two ends disagree on interface MTU. Second most common: duplicate router-ID.
LoadingAn LSA request is going unanswered. Rare; usually transient.

OSPF adjacency across a firewall zone boundary needs security policy permitting it. Intrazone traffic is allowed by default, interzone is not — and an OSPF neighbour on a different zone will silently fail to form with no log entry that obviously says so.

OSPF, RIP & BFDSCENARIO ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

OSPF Neighbour Stuck in ExStart

Change made: CORE-SW1's VLAN 10 interface is set to MTU 9000. ethernet1/3 stays at 1500.

Symptom: show routing protocol ospf neighbor shows CORE-SW1 stuck in ExStart/Exchange. vr-dc loses 10.10.20.0/24 and 10.10.30.0/24, and the spokes still receive the hub's static-based BGP routes but traffic dies in vr-dc with flow_fwd_l3_noroute.

  1. show routing protocol ospf neighbor: state ExStart/Exchange, never Full.
  2. show routing protocol ospf interface and the switch's interface: the MTUs differ.
  3. Fix: match the MTU on both sides (or ignore-MTU on both, only if you understand the risk).

This scenario also shows a design weakness. The hub advertises 10.10.20/30.0/24 into BGP from static routes, so the spokes keep sending traffic even when OSPF has lost those networks. Path monitoring on those statics, or redistributing the OSPF routes instead, would withdraw them cleanly.

OSPF, RIP & BFDPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

OSPF Neighbour Down, Routes Missing

time-box 20 mincontrol plane

OSPF

  1. State: show routing protocol ospf neighbor. Missing: area, hello/dead or authentication mismatch. Stuck in ExStart/Exchange: MTU mismatch.
  2. Interface: show routing protocol ospf interface. Link type matters over tunnels: use point-to-point there.
  3. Default route to the core: needs an export rule plus allowing redistribution of the default route.
