RIP and BFD

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show routing protocol rip interfaceRIP per-interface state (legacy VR).Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats > RIP
show routing protocol rip databaseThe RIP database.Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats > RIP
show routing bfd active-profile [<name>]Active BFD profiles and their timers.Network > Network Profiles > BFD Profile
show routing bfd details [interface <name>] [local-ip <ip>] [multihop] [peer-ip <ip>] [session-id] [virtual-router <name>]Session state, negotiated timers and counters. Filter by whichever key you have.Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats > BFD
show routing bfd drop-counters session-id <id>Drop counters for a BFD session — the command for diagnosing a flapping session.Virtual Routers > BFD
show counter global | match bfdTransmitted, received and dropped BFD packets at the dataplane.CLI only
clear routing bfd session-state session-id <all|1-1024>Clear a session for testing.CLI only
clear routing bfd counters session-id <all|1-1024>Reset BFD counters.CLI only
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing bfd details interface tunnel.1
session-id       : 3
interface        : tunnel.1
local-ip / peer  : 10.255.0.1 / 10.255.0.2
protocol         : BGP
state            : up          (last state change 04d11h)
tx-interval(cfg/neg) : 300 ms / 300 ms
rx-interval(cfg/neg) : 300 ms / 1000 ms          <-- peer imposed a slower rx
detect-multiplier    : 3         detection-time: 3000 ms

Aggressive BFD timers over a tunnel or a WAN with variable latency cause false failovers — the protocol does exactly what you configured, which is to declare a peer dead after three missed packets. If BFD flaps, check drop-counters and the negotiated intervals before blaming the tunnel. Negotiated values, not configured ones, are what the detection time is built from.

Virtual Systems & Inter-VRRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Multi-VSYS with Inter-VSYS Traffic (WAN, CORP, GUEST)

Use it when one firewall must act as several independent firewalls that share one internet connection, with controlled traffic between them. Each vsys has its own zones, policies and administrators. Traffic between vsys uses external zones, and every vsys on the path applies its own security policy.

Steps 0–2 · Multi-vsys, virtual routers, virtual systems

// 0 · operational mode: enable multi-vsys (needs the vsys licence on most models)
set system setting multi-vsys on
configure
// 1 · virtual routers (one per vsys) and inter-VR routes
set network virtual-router vr-wan interface ethernet1/1
set network virtual-router vr-corp interface ethernet1/2
set network virtual-router vr-guest interface ethernet1/3
set network virtual-router vr-wan routing-table ip static-route DEFAULT destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop ip-address 198.51.100.1 interface ethernet1/1
set network virtual-router vr-wan routing-table ip static-route TO-CORP destination 10.20.0.0/24 nexthop next-vr vr-corp
set network virtual-router vr-wan routing-table ip static-route TO-GUEST destination 10.30.0.0/24 nexthop next-vr vr-guest
set network virtual-router vr-corp routing-table ip static-route DEFAULT destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop next-vr vr-wan
set network virtual-router vr-corp routing-table ip static-route TO-GUEST destination 10.30.0.0/24 nexthop next-vr vr-guest
set network virtual-router vr-guest routing-table ip static-route DEFAULT destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop next-vr vr-wan
set network virtual-router vr-guest routing-table ip static-route TO-CORP destination 10.20.0.0/24 nexthop next-vr vr-corp
// 2 · virtual systems: import interfaces and VRs, make them visible to each other
set vsys vsys1 display-name WAN
set vsys vsys1 import network interface ethernet1/1
set vsys vsys1 import network virtual-router vr-wan
set vsys vsys1 import visible-vsys [ vsys2 vsys3 ]
set vsys vsys2 display-name CORP
set vsys vsys2 import network interface ethernet1/2
set vsys vsys2 import network virtual-router vr-corp
set vsys vsys2 import visible-vsys [ vsys1 vsys3 ]
set vsys vsys3 display-name GUEST
set vsys vsys3 import network interface ethernet1/3
set vsys vsys3 import network virtual-router vr-guest
set vsys vsys3 import visible-vsys [ vsys1 vsys2 ]
What each line does

Purpose: Enables multi-vsys, builds one virtual router per tenant with next-vr routes between them, and creates three vsys that own their interfaces and VRs and can see each other.

set system setting multi-vsys on
Operational command that enables multiple virtual systems (licence-dependent). Configuration is then per vsys.
virtual-router vr-wan / vr-corp / vr-guest
A separate routing table per tenant.
vr-wan … TO-CORP / TO-GUEST … nexthop next-vr
Return routes from the WAN VR to each tenant VR.
vr-corp / vr-guest DEFAULT … next-vr vr-wan
Each tenant's default route hands traffic to the WAN VR.
vr-corp TO-GUEST / vr-guest TO-CORP
Direct inter-tenant routes for the printer access, in both directions.
vsys … import network interface / virtual-router
Assigns the interface and VR to the vsys (GUI: Device > Virtual Systems).
import visible-vsys [ … ]
Visible Virtual System: required for virtual systems that need to communicate with each other.

Steps 3–4 · External zones, security and NAT

// 3 · zones: one internal zone per vsys, plus external zones pointing at the other vsys
set vsys vsys1 zone UNTRUST network layer3 ethernet1/1
set vsys vsys1 zone TO-TENANTS network external [ vsys2 vsys3 ]
set vsys vsys2 zone TRUST network layer3 ethernet1/2
set vsys vsys2 zone TO-WAN network external vsys1
set vsys vsys2 zone TO-GUEST network external vsys3
set vsys vsys3 zone TRUST network layer3 ethernet1/3
set vsys vsys3 zone TO-WAN network external vsys1
set vsys vsys3 zone TO-CORP network external vsys2
// 4 · security rules in every vsys the traffic crosses, NAT only in vsys1
set vsys vsys2 rulebase security rules CORP-OUT from TRUST to TO-WAN source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
set vsys vsys2 rulebase security rules CORP-PRINT from TRUST to TO-GUEST source any destination 10.30.0.200/29 application [ ping ssl ] service application-default action allow
set vsys vsys3 rulebase security rules GUEST-OUT from TRUST to TO-WAN source any destination any application [ web-browsing ssl dns ] service application-default action allow
set vsys vsys3 rulebase security rules CORP-PRINT-IN from TO-CORP to TRUST source 10.20.0.0/24 destination 10.30.0.200/29 application [ ping ssl ] service application-default action allow
set vsys vsys1 rulebase security rules TENANTS-OUT from TO-TENANTS to UNTRUST source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
set vsys vsys1 rulebase nat rules TENANTS-SNAT from TO-TENANTS to UNTRUST source any destination any service any source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/1
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Creates internal and external zones in each vsys, and the security and NAT rules for each leg of the traffic.

zone TO-TENANTS network external [ vsys2 vsys3 ]
An external zone in vsys1 that represents traffic to or from vsys2/vsys3 (GUI: Network > Zones, Type External).
zone TO-WAN / TO-GUEST / TO-CORP … external …
Each tenant's view of the other vsys.
vsys2 CORP-OUT TRUST → TO-WAN
CORP's own rule for internet traffic.
vsys1 TENANTS-OUT TO-TENANTS → UNTRUST
WAN's rule for the same traffic as it continues out. Both rules must allow it.
vsys1 nat TENANTS-SNAT … interface ethernet1/1
Source NAT once, at the edge vsys.
vsys2 CORP-PRINT / vsys3 CORP-PRINT-IN
The printer access needs an allow rule in CORP (outbound to TO-GUEST) and in GUEST (inbound from TO-CORP). There is no GUEST → CORP rule, so guests can't start sessions into CORP.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Vsys and assignments

show system info | match multi-vsys
show interface all

Good: multi-vsys: on. Each interface shows its vsys and zone. If not: An interface still in vsys1, or a VR not imported.

2 · Routing across VRs

test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-corp ip 8.8.8.8
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-wan ip 10.20.0.50

Good: vr-corp → next-vr vr-wan. vr-wan → next-vr vr-corp. If not: A missing return route in the other VR.

3 · Policy in each vsys

set system setting target-vsys vsys2
test security-policy-match from TRUST to TO-WAN source 10.20.0.50 destination 8.8.8.8 protocol 6 destination-port 443
set system setting target-vsys vsys1
test security-policy-match from TO-TENANTS to UNTRUST source 10.20.0.50 destination 8.8.8.8 protocol 6 destination-port 443
set system setting target-vsys none

Good: An allow rule in both vsys. If not: The vsys with no match is where the traffic is denied.

4 · Counters on the flow

debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.20.0.50 destination 10.30.0.201
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes

Good: No drop counters. If not: flow_policy_deny: a rule missing in one vsys. flow_fwd_l3_noroute: an inter-VR route.

⚠ Syntax note. PAN-OS configuration-mode set commands. The structure follows Palo Alto documentation and published configurations. Use Tab/? while typing, run commit validate (or validate full) before commit, and check the GUI equivalent shown in each step.

Virtual Systems & Inter-VRNEXT-VR ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Routing Between Virtual Routers

Virtual routers do not talk to each other by default. PAN-OS joins them with a static route whose next hop is another VR rather than an IP address — and the route has to exist in both directions or you get a one-way path that looks fine from whichever side you happened to check.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
# set network virtual-router <vr-A> routing-table ip static-route <name> destination <ip/mask> nexthop next-vr <vr-B>Static route in VR-A whose next hop is VR-B. This is how legacy inter-VR routing is built.Virtual Routers > VR-A > Static Routes > Add > Next Hop = Next VR
# set network logical-router <lr-A> vrf <vrf> routing-table ip static-route <name> destination <ip/mask> nexthop next-lr <lr-B>The Advanced Routing equivalent.Logical Routers > LR-A > VRF > Static > Next Hop = Next LR
show routing route virtual-router <vr-A> | match <network>Confirm the route is installed in VR-A.VR-A > More Runtime Stats > Route Table
show routing fib virtual-router <vr-A>Confirm the FIB resolved recursively into VR-B.VR-A > Forwarding Table
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr-A> ip <destination>Confirm VR-A actually selects the VR-B path.VR-A > More Runtime Stats
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing route virtual-router VR-TRUST | match 10.30
  10.30.0.0/16   vr VR-DMZ   10  A S              <-- next hop is a VR, not an IP

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router VR-TRUST ip 10.30.5.20
   virtual-router  VR-DMZ                        <-- recursion into the second VR resolved
   interface       ethernet1/3.30
   nexthop         0.0.0.0

Inter-VR traffic still crosses a zone boundary and still needs a security policy in each direction. A working next-vr route with no matching rule produces a clean route table, a clean FIB lookup, and no traffic. Verify with test security-policy-match using the zones on both interfaces, not just the route.

Two virtual routers on one chassis are two separate buildings that happen to share a car park. A next-vr route is the corridor between them; the security policy is whether the door in that corridor is unlocked. You need both.

Virtual Systems & Inter-VRWORKED LAB ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Two Virtual Routers, End to End — Topology, Config and Flow

A single firewall, two virtual routers, and traffic that has to cross from one to the other. This is a common design — internal routing kept separate from the internet edge — and it confuses people because the packet crosses a routing boundary without crossing a security boundary in the way they expect. Here is the whole thing on one page.

A virtual router is a routing table, nothing more. It is not a firewall inside a firewall, it has no policy of its own, and crossing from one to another does not create a second inspection point. Zones are where security lives; VRs are where routing lives. The two are separate axes, and confusing them is the root of most inter-VR tickets.

Sample configuration — interfaces and zones

# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/2 layer3 ip 10.10.20.1/24
# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 ip 198.51.100.2/30
# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/3 layer3 units ethernet1/3.30 tag 30 ip 10.10.30.1/24
# set zone Trust network layer3 ethernet1/2
# set zone DMZ network layer3 ethernet1/3.30
# set zone Untrust network layer3 ethernet1/1

Sample configuration — the two virtual routers

# set network virtual-router VR-INSIDE interface [ ethernet1/2 ethernet1/3.30 ]
# set network virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE interface [ ethernet1/1 ]

VR-INSIDE: send everything unknown to the other VR
# set network virtual-router VR-INSIDE routing-table ip static-route to-outside destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop next-vr VR-OUTSIDE

VR-OUTSIDE: default to the ISP, and the return routes back inside
# set network virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE routing-table ip static-route default destination 0.0.0.0/0 nexthop ip-address 198.51.100.1
# set network virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE routing-table ip static-route back-trust destination 10.10.20.0/24 nexthop next-vr VR-INSIDE
# set network virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE routing-table ip static-route back-dmz destination 10.10.30.0/24 nexthop next-vr VR-INSIDE

The return routes on VR-OUTSIDE are the step people skip. Without them the outbound packet leaves happily, the reply arrives on ethernet1/1, VR-OUTSIDE has no route for 10.10.20.0/24, and the packet is dropped with flow_no_route. The symptom — outbound works, nothing comes back — looks like a NAT or policy problem and is neither.

Sample configuration — security policy

Note what is not here: there is no rule mentioning virtual routers, because policy cannot see them. One rule, one session, zone to zone.

# set rulebase security rules trust-to-internet from Trust to Untrust source 10.10.20.0/24 destination any application any service application-default action allow
# set rulebase security rules trust-to-dmz from Trust to DMZ source 10.10.20.0/24 destination 10.10.30.20 application any service application-default action allow

trust-to-dmz stays entirely inside VR-INSIDE — same VR, two zones, so policy applies and routing is local. trust-to-internet crosses the VR boundary, and policy treats it identically. That is the point: the VR hop is invisible to the rulebase.

Sample configuration — NAT

NAT rules are also written in zones, not virtual routers. The source zone is where the packet came from (Trust, in VR-INSIDE) and the destination zone is where it is headed (Untrust, in VR-OUTSIDE) — the rule spans both VRs without ever naming them.

# set rulebase nat rules outbound-hide from Trust to Untrust source 10.10.20.0/24 destination any
# set rulebase nat rules outbound-hide to-interface ethernet1/1
# set rulebase nat rules outbound-hide source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/1

Setting to-interface matters more than usual in a multi-VR design. Without it, a NAT rule written zone-to-zone can match traffic that ends up leaving by a different interface than you intended once routes change. Pinning the egress interface makes the rule mean what you think it means.

How the flow actually runs

  1. Packet arrives on ethernet1/2. Ingress zone is Trust; the interface belongs to VR-INSIDE.
  2. VR-INSIDE is consulted for 203.0.113.90. The best match is the default route, whose next hop is next-vr VR-OUTSIDE. The lookup is handed over, not finished.
  3. VR-OUTSIDE is consulted for the same destination. Its default route points at 198.51.100.1 via ethernet1/1. Egress interface and therefore egress zone Untrust are now known.
  4. NAT policy is evaluated: Trust → Untrust matches outbound-hide, translation chosen but not applied.
  5. Security policy is evaluated: Trust → Untrust, source 10.10.20.55 (pre-NAT), matches trust-to-internet, allowed.
  6. One session is created. Not two — the two-VR hop does not create a second session, and show session id will show a single entry with Trust on the c2s side and Untrust on the s2c side.
  7. The reply returns on ethernet1/1 into VR-OUTSIDE, matches the existing session, and is forwarded back through VR-INSIDE using the back-trust route.

Verifying it — the lookup has to be done twice

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router VR-INSIDE ip 203.0.113.90
runtime route lookup
virtual-router:  VR-INSIDE
destination:     203.0.113.90
result:
  next-vr:       VR-OUTSIDE
note there is no interface here — the lookup is not finished

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE ip 203.0.113.90
virtual-router:  VR-OUTSIDE
destination:     203.0.113.90
result:
  interface:     ethernet1/1
  nexthop:       198.51.100.1
  metric:        10
now you have the real egress interface

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE ip 10.10.20.55
result:
  next-vr:       VR-INSIDE
the return path — run this too, it is the half that is usually missing

Any time a fib-lookup answers with next-vr and no interface, you are only halfway. Run it again against the named VR. A surprising number of "the route is there, I checked" conversations end when someone finally runs the second lookup and finds the far VR has nothing.

admin@fw-01(active)> show routing route virtual-router VR-INSIDE
flags: A:active, ?:loose, C:connect, H:host, S:static, ~:internal, R:rip, O:ospf, B:bgp, E:ecmp

VIRTUAL ROUTER: VR-INSIDE (id 2)
  destination        nexthop         metric  flags  age  interface
  0.0.0.0/0          VR-OUTSIDE      10      A S
  10.10.20.0/24      10.10.20.1      0       A C          ethernet1/2
  10.10.30.0/24      10.10.30.1      0       A C          ethernet1/3.30

admin@fw-01(active)> show session all filter source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90
ID     Application  State   Type Flag  Src[Sport]/Zone/Proto (translated IP[Port])
                                       Dst[Dport]/Zone (translated IP[Port])
88210  ssl          ACTIVE  FLOW NS    10.10.20.55[51204]/Trust/6  (198.51.100.2[40119])
                                       203.0.113.90[443]/Untrust  (203.0.113.90[443])
one session, Trust on one side and Untrust on the other — the VR hop leaves no trace here

When it breaks

SymptomCauseCommand that proves it
Outbound fine, nothing returnsMissing next-vr return route on VR-OUTSIDEtest routing fib-lookup virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE ip 10.10.20.55
flow_no_route climbingEither VR has no path for that destinationshow counter global filter severity drop delta yes
Session created, never leavesInterface not assigned to the expected VRshow routing route virtual-router VR-OUTSIDE
Traffic denied unexpectedlyEgress zone is not what you assumed after the VR hoptest security-policy-match ... to Untrust
NAT does not applyNAT rule zones do not match the post-hop egress zonetest nat-policy-match from Trust to Untrust ...
Routing loop between the VRsBoth VRs point their default at each otherCompare both route tables side by side

If the firewall is running the Advanced Routing engine, this design is expressed differently — logical routers with explicit route leaking rather than a next-vr static route, and the show commands move to the show advanced-routing tree. The packet flow and the zone logic are unchanged; only the configuration syntax differs. Check which engine is enabled before copying the config above.

Virtual Systems & Inter-VRSCENARIO ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Inter-VR: Forward Works, Return Has No Route

Change made: during a clean-up, the default route in vr-dc (next-vr vr-wan) is deleted.

Symptom: spokes can't reach DC servers. Sessions appear on the hub with c2s bytes but no s2c bytes.

  1. Forward: test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-wan ip 10.10.20.15 → next-vr vr-dc, then in vr-dc → ethernet1/3. Fine.
  2. Return: test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-dc ip 10.10.1.50 → no route.
  3. Counters: filtered on the flow, flow_fwd_l3_noroute for the reply packets.
  4. Fix: restore the vr-dc default (or specific routes) with nexthop next-vr vr-wan.

Next-vr routes are needed in both VRs. Avoid next-vr routes that point at each other for the same prefix: a packet bouncing between VRs until TTL expiry shows up as flow_fwd_l3_ttl_zero.

Virtual Systems & Inter-VREXTERNAL ZONE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Routing Between Virtual Systems

Traffic between two vsys uses an External Zone — a zone in vsys1 that points at vsys2, and a mirror of it in the other direction. Both halves plus a security rule in each vsys are required.

An external zone is a doorway between two apartments in the same building, not a corridor with its own address. You need one on each side, and you need a rule on each side that mentions it, because each vsys enforces policy independently. Configure only one half and the traffic goes out of vsys1 and is never let into vsys2 — and the deny will be logged in the other vsys, which is where people stop looking.

What crossesvsys1 seesvsys2 sees
Zone pairTrust → ext-to-v2ext-to-v1 → Server
SessionSession 1Session 2 — a separate ID
Rulebasevsys1 rules onlyvsys2 rules only
Security profilesWhatever vsys1 attachesWhatever vsys2 attaches — inspected twice
LogsLogged in vsys1Logged in vsys2

Before you troubleshoot anything inter-vsys, set your CLI context: set system setting target-vsys vsys2. Session and log commands are vsys-scoped, and running them from the wrong context is why half the conversation appears to be missing. Set it back to none when you finish.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show vsysList virtual systems. Inter-vsys communication needs external zones between them.Device > Virtual Systems
# set vsys vsys1 zone external-zone-A network external <vsys2>Define an external zone in vsys1 pointing at vsys2. Repeat in the other direction.Network > Zones > Add > Type = External
# set rulebase security rules <name> from external-zone-A to <internal-zone> source any destination any application any service any action allowPermit the traffic. Needed in each vsys, not once.Policies > Security > Add (in each vsys)
test security-policy-match from <ext-zone-A> to <int-zone> source <ip> destination <ip> destination-port <p> protocol <n>Verify the rule matches the flow.Policies > Security > Test Policy Match
ping source <vr-A-interface-ip> host <ip-in-vr-B>Active reachability test across the boundary.Device > Troubleshooting > Ping
show session all filter source <ip> destination <ip>Confirm sessions are being created across the boundary.Monitor > Session Browser
show session id <session-id>Inspect zones, ingress/egress interfaces and the rule hit for one inter-vsys session.Monitor > Session Browser

A single inter-vsys flow is inspected twice — once on the way out of vsys1 and once on the way into vsys2 — and creates a session in each. When you go looking in the session browser, expect two entries per conversation, and remember that the security profiles applied are those of whichever vsys you are looking at.

Virtual Systems & Inter-VRVSYS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Multi-VSYS State and Scoping the CLI

On a multi-vsys firewall, dataplane show commands return a global view by default, which on a busy box is useless. target-vsys scopes the rest of your session to one vsys, and forgetting to unset it afterwards is a classic way to convince yourself something has disappeared.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show system info | match vsysWhether multi-vsys is on, and the current count.Device > Setup > Management > Multi Virtual System Capability
show vsysList all configured virtual systems.Device > Virtual Systems
show system setting target-vsysWhich vsys your session is currently scoped to.CLI only
set system setting target-vsys vsys2Scope subsequent dataplane queries — sessions, IP-user mappings — to vsys2. Operational mode.VSYS selector, top-right of the web UI
set system setting target-vsys noneRevert to global. Always run this when you finish.VSYS selector
set system setting target-vsys ?List available vsys names for targeting.VSYS selector
# set system setting multi-vsys onEnable multi-vsys mode. Requires a capacity licence on some platforms and a commit.Device > Setup > Management
show high-availability state | match vsysPer-vsys HA state.Device > High Availability
admin@fw-01(active)> show vsys
vsys1  (Corporate)      interfaces: ethernet1/2, ethernet1/3.20
vsys2  (Partner-Extranet) interfaces: ethernet1/4, ethernet1/5

admin@fw-01(active)> set system setting target-vsys vsys2
admin@fw-01(active)> show session all filter destination 10.40.0.10   now scoped to vsys2 only
ID    Application  State   Src[Sport]/Zone/Proto  Dst[Dport]/Zone
9922  ldap         ACTIVE  10.40.1.5[43112]/PartnerTrust/6  10.40.0.10[389]/PartnerDMZ
admin@fw-01(active)> set system setting target-vsys none            put it back

target-vsys persists for the life of your CLI session. Leave it set, walk away, come back, and the next twenty minutes of "the sessions are gone" is entirely self-inflicted. Make set system setting target-vsys none a reflex, the same way you would clean up a packet-diag filter.

Virtual Systems & Inter-VRRESOURCES ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Per-VSYS Resource Verification

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show session meterPer-vsys session-table usage against the configured limit. The command to reach for when one tenant is starving the others.Dashboard > Session Information
show session infoOverall session-table info. Combine with target-vsys for a scoped view.Dashboard > Session Information
show user ip-user-mapping allIP-to-user mappings. Scope with target-vsys first on multi-vsys.Monitor > Logs > User-ID

show zone-protection zone <zone-name>Zone-protection profile applied to a zone.Network > Network Profiles > Zone Protection
admin@fw-01(active)> show session meter
vsys      maximum    current    throttled
vsys1      262144      41022            0
vsys2       65536      65530          118   <-- at the ceiling and dropping new sessions

A non-zero throttled count means new sessions in that vsys are being refused because it has hit its configured maximum. The symptom users report is "some connections work and some do not, at random" — which is exactly what a full session table produces. Raise the limit under Device > Setup > Session or find what is consuming them.

Security PolicyTEST ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Policy Match Tests — Asking Instead of Guessing

These three commands ask the firewall which rule would match a described flow, without generating any traffic. On a rulebase of several hundred rules this replaces an afternoon of reading with about ten seconds.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
test security-policy-match from <src-zone> to <dst-zone> source <ip> destination <ip> destination-port <p> protocol <n>Which security rule would this flow hit, and what is the action?Policies > Security > right-click > Test Policy Match
test nat-policy-match from <zone> to <zone> source <ip> destination <ip> destination-port <p> protocol <n>Which NAT rule applies, and what is the translation?Policies > NAT > right-click > Test Policy Match
test pbf-policy-match from <zone> source <ip> destination <ip> protocol <n>Which policy-based-forwarding rule applies.Policies > Policy Based Forwarding

Sample — security policy match

admin@fw-01(active)> test security-policy-match from Trust to Untrust source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90 destination-port 443 protocol 6
"Allow-Web-Outbound" {
        from Trust;
        source any;
        source-region none;
        to Untrust;
        destination any;
        destination-region none;
        user any;
        category any;
        application/service [ ssl/tcp/any/443 web-browsing/tcp/any/80 ];
        action allow;
        icmp-unreachable: no
        terminal yes;
}

Sample — NAT policy match

admin@fw-01(active)> test nat-policy-match from Trust to Untrust source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90 destination-port 443 protocol 6
Source-NAT: rule "Outbound-PAT"
        source translation: dynamic-ip-and-port
        translated source: 198.51.100.2  (interface address ethernet1/1)
        translated destination: unchanged
You seeIt means
A named rule with action allowPolicy is not your problem. Move on to NAT, routing or the far end.
A named rule with action denyThat is your rule. Note the name and read it in the GUI.
No rule returnedNothing matched, so the default interzone-deny applies. Frequently the zones you supplied were wrong — confirm them from show interface all first.
No nat-policyNo translation applies. If the source is RFC 1918 heading for a public address, NAT is happening somewhere else — go look upstream.

The App-ID in the result is what the rule permits, not what the session will be identified as. A rule allowing ssl matches the test but will still drop the session if App-ID later decides the traffic is something else on port 443. A clean policy-match result does not guarantee the session survives identification.

Security PolicyCHECK ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Permissions: Rule Match, Order, Hit Counts and the Default Rules

Only check permissions once routing and NAT are confirmed, because they decide the zones and addresses the rule is matched on. Then answer three questions: which rule matches, is it the one you expect, and is it actually being hit?

Which rule would match?

// pre-NAT addresses, post-NAT destination zone
admin@SPOKE1-PA> test security-policy-match from TRUST to VPN source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.20.15 protocol 6 destination-port 443
"LAN-TO-VPN; index: 1" {
        from TRUST;
        to VPN;
        ...
        action allow;
}

admin@SPOKE1-PA> test security-policy-match from TRUST to VPN source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.20.15 protocol 6 destination-port 3389 application ms-rdp
// no output, or a deny rule = not permitted

Is an earlier rule shadowing it?

Security rules are evaluated top-down and the first match wins. PAN-OS warns about shadowed rules at commit time. Read the commit warnings rather than clicking past them.

Is it actually being hit?

admin@HUB-PA> show rule-hit-count vsys vsys-name vsys1 rule-base security rules all
// trimmed · zero hits on the rule you expect and rising hits on another confirms shadowing
Rule Name          Hit Count     Last Hit Timestamp          Last Reset Timestamp
old-block          304           Tue Oct 27 10:41:53 2026
WEB-IN             0             -

The default rules, and why drops look silent

Default ruleActionTroubleshooting impact
intrazone-defaultAllowTraffic within one zone passes without an explicit rule. In this lab, spoke-to-spoke at the hub is VPN → VPN, so it's allowed by default.
interzone-defaultDenyNot logged by default, so denied traffic leaves no traffic log. Override the rule to enable logging at session end, or rely on flow_policy_deny in the global counters.

Other permission layers that look like routing faults

LayerSymptomCheck
App-IDRule allows ssl, traffic identified as something else and denied part-way through.Traffic log application column, show session id application.
Security profilesSession allowed, content blocked.Threat and URL logs for that rule.
Management profilePings or BGP to the firewall fail.Interface management profile, flow_host_service_deny counter.
Zone protection / DoSDrops under load or for specific patterns.Zone protection profile on the ingress zone, flow_dos counters.

Never test by adding an any-any allow at the top of the rulebase in production. test security-policy-match and the counters tell you exactly which rule catches the traffic without changing anything.

Security PolicyRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Zone Protection on the Internet-Facing Zone

Use it when hardening the edge. A zone protection profile defends the whole ingress zone against floods, reconnaissance and malformed packets, before security policy is evaluated.

Network > Network Profiles > Zone Protection   ZP-UNTRUST
  Flood Protection                             SYN (SYN cookies) · UDP · ICMP · Other IP: alarm/activate/max rates sized from your baseline
  Reconnaissance Protection                    TCP/UDP port scan, host sweep: alert or block
  Packet Based Attack Protection               drop spoofed IPs, strict IP address check, discard malformed/fragment abuse as appropriate
Network > Zones > UNTRUST                      Zone Protection Profile: ZP-UNTRUST
CLI equivalent (attach)                        set zone UNTRUST network zone-protection-profile ZP-UNTRUST
What each line does

Purpose: Creates a zone protection profile and attaches it to the internet-facing zone.

Flood Protection · SYN cookies
Protects the firewall and servers from SYN floods. Alarm/activate/maximum rates must come from your real traffic baseline, or legitimate bursts get dropped.
Reconnaissance Protection
Detects port scans and host sweeps from the internet.
Packet Based Attack Protection
Drops spoofed or malformed packets early.
zone UNTRUST zone-protection-profile ZP-UNTRUST
Applies the profile to all traffic entering that zone.

Verify

Is it acting?

show counter global filter delta yes | match flow_dos
show zone-protection zone UNTRUST

Good: Counters steady in normal operation. If not: Counters rising during normal business: the thresholds are too low. Logs appear as threat log subtypes flood/scan/packet.

⚠ Syntax note. Use Tab/? while typing and commit validate before committing. The GUI path is given for every object.

Security PolicyRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Moving From Port-Based Rules to App-ID with Policy Optimizer

Use it when a rulebase has legacy "any application on port X" rules. Policy Optimizer (Policies > Policy Optimizer) shows what applications actually used each rule, so you can convert it to App-ID safely.

Policies > Policy Optimizer > No App Specified   list rules with application "any"
  select a rule > Compare                        applications seen on the rule (needs enough traffic history)
  Create Cloned Rule                             new rule with the observed applications, placed above the original
Monitor hit counts                               new rule takes the traffic. The old rule's hits drop to zero.
Disable, later delete                            the original port-based rule
Unused Apps / Rule Usage                         remove apps never seen, and rules unused for months
What each line does

Purpose: A safe, reversible way to tighten rules using observed traffic.

No App Specified
Port-based rules: the candidates for conversion.
Compare (applications seen)
What really used the rule. Let it run long enough to cover monthly or quarterly business cycles.
Create Cloned Rule above the original
The App-ID rule catches known applications first, and the old rule remains as a safety net.
Monitor, then disable
Once the old rule shows no new hits, disable it (keeping it lets you roll back), then delete it.

Rule usage relies on hit counts. Check that rule hit counting is enabled and that hit counts weren't reset recently before you trust "unused".

DecryptionHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Concept

SSL Forward Proxy: How Decryption Works

With SSL Forward Proxy, the firewall sits in the middle of an outbound TLS session. It connects to the real server and validates its certificate, then presents the client with a copy of that certificate signed by the firewall's Forward Trust CA. The client accepts it only if that CA is in its trusted store. Inside the tunnel the firewall now sees cleartext, so App-ID, threat prevention, URL filtering and file controls work fully. The traffic is re-encrypted on both sides.

TermMeaning
Forward Trust certificateCA certificate the firewall uses to sign certificates for sites whose real certificate it trusts. Clients must trust it. An enterprise-CA-signed certificate is Palo Alto's recommended best practice.
Forward Untrust certificateCA the firewall uses when the real server certificate is invalid or untrusted. It must not be trusted by clients, so users still get a warning for bad sites.
Decryption policyRules (zones, addresses, users, URL categories, service) that decide decrypt or no-decrypt. Separate from security policy.
Decryption profileChecks on decrypted (and undecrypted) sessions: block expired or untrusted certificates, unsupported versions/ciphers, client authentication.
SSL Inbound InspectionDecrypting traffic to your own server, using the server's own certificate and key loaded on the firewall.
DecryptionRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Enabling SSL Forward Proxy for Users

Use it when you must inspect users' outbound HTTPS. Build it in this order. Start with a narrow pilot group, and keep sensitive categories excluded.

// GUI objects, in build order                     
Device > Certificate Management > Certificates     FWD-TRUST-CA: enterprise sub-CA (or generated root CA) · Forward Trust Certificate ✓
                                                   FWD-UNTRUST-CA: self-signed CA · Forward Untrust Certificate ✓ (never deployed to clients)
Clients (GPO / MDM)                                deploy FWD-TRUST-CA to the trusted root store (skip if it chains to your enterprise CA)
Objects > Decryption Profile                       DEC-STD · SSL Forward Proxy: block expired certs, block untrusted issuers,
                                                     block unsupported versions/ciphers · SSL Protocol Settings: min TLS1.2
Policies > Decryption (order matters)              1 NO-DECRYPT-SENSITIVE: TRUST → UNTRUST · category financial-services, health-and-medicine ·
                                                     action No Decrypt · profile DEC-STD (still validates server certificates)
                                                   2 NO-DECRYPT-PINNED: destination = EDL/objects for apps that pin certificates · No Decrypt
                                                   3 DECRYPT-PILOT: TRUST → UNTRUST · source user grp-decrypt-pilot · action Decrypt ·
                                                     type SSL Forward Proxy · profile DEC-STD
Objects > Log Forwarding / Device > Log Settings   decryption logs: success and failures (PAN-OS 10.0+ has a dedicated decryption log)
What each line does

Purpose: Creates the two forwarding CAs, a decryption profile with sane certificate checks, and decryption rules that exclude sensitive and pinned traffic before decrypting a pilot group.

FWD-TRUST-CA · Forward Trust Certificate
Signs the impersonated certificates for valid sites. Must be a CA certificate. Enterprise-CA-signed avoids having to distribute a new root.
FWD-UNTRUST-CA · Forward Untrust Certificate
Used when the real server certificate fails validation. Clients must not trust it, so users still see a warning for bad sites.
deploy FWD-TRUST-CA to clients
Without it every decrypted site shows a certificate error. This is the most common pilot failure.
DEC-STD · block expired / untrusted issuer / unsupported
Keeps the protection users would have had without decryption: bad server certificates are blocked rather than silently accepted.
rule 1 NO-DECRYPT-SENSITIVE
Privacy and legal: banking and health sites are not decrypted. The profile still checks their certificates.
rule 2 NO-DECRYPT-PINNED
Apps that pin certificates or use mutual TLS break under decryption. Exclude them by destination.
rule 3 DECRYPT-PILOT · source user group
Decrypt a pilot group first. Widen it once the exclusions are proven. Decryption rules are evaluated top-down like security rules.
decryption log
Shows each session's decryption result, versions, cipher and error reasons. The first stop when a site breaks.

Decryption doesn't replace security policy: the security rule still needs to allow the (now visible) application, with the security profiles attached. Decrypt-and-inspect is what makes those profiles effective on HTTPS.

DecryptionPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs Concept

Decryption: Step-by-Step Troubleshooting

When users report "site broken" or "certificate error" after decryption, work through it in this order.

1 · Was the session decrypted, and by which rule?

show session all filter source 10.20.0.50 destination-port 443
show session id <id>

Good: The session shows it was decrypted (proxy/decrypt flags), and the traffic log shows the decryption rule. If not: Not decrypted: check the decryption rule order and match (zone, user, category). The GUI test is Device > Troubleshooting > Decryption/SSL Policy Match.

2 · Read the decryption log for that session

show log decryption direction equal backward

Good: Success, with TLS version, cipher and the certificate used. If not: An error reason such as unsupported version/cipher, client certificate requested, or certificate expired points straight at the fix.

3 · Certificates the firewall uses

show system setting ssl-decrypt certificate

Good: Forward Trust and Forward Untrust certificates present, with the expected names and validity. If not: The wrong certificate is flagged as Forward Trust, or it has expired.

4 · Sites excluded automatically

show system setting ssl-decrypt exclude-cache

Good: Shows servers the firewall stopped decrypting (for example after errors or client authentication). If not: A site keeps failing: add it to a no-decrypt rule or the exclusion list deliberately.

5 · Dataplane counters

show counter global filter delta yes | match proxy

Good: Proxy counters steady. If not: Rising proxy failure or "no resource" counters mean capacity or unsupported traffic.

What the user seesMost likely causeFix
Certificate warning on every decrypted siteForward Trust CA not trusted by the clientDeploy the CA (GPO/MDM). Check the browser uses the OS store.
One app fails, browsers workCertificate pinning or mutual TLSNo-decrypt rule for that app's destinations
Some sites blocked with a firewall pageDecryption profile blocking expired/untrusted/unsupportedCorrect behaviour for bad sites. For a business exception, a no-decrypt rule with care.
Warning only for one site, others fineThe real server certificate is invalid (signed with Forward Untrust)Expected protection. Confirm with the site owner.
Slow browsing after enablingDecryption load or resource limitsNarrow the scope, check proxy counters and dataplane load

⚠ Verification note. show system setting ssl-decrypt certificate and exclude-cache are widely used and appear in PCNSE material, but the decryption-specific CLI isn't on Palo Alto's CLI cheat sheets. The decryption log and Device > Troubleshooting > Decryption/SSL Policy Match are the documented first stops.

How a Session Is Inspected: App-ID, Content-ID and the Logs They Leave

A security rule that allows traffic can still block parts of it: the security profiles attached to the rule inspect the content. Understanding the order explains every "the rule allows it, but it's blocked" ticket.

ProfileActs onLook in
Antivirus / WildFireMalicious filesThreat log (virus, wildfire-virus), WildFire submissions
Anti-SpywareCommand-and-control, spyware, DNS securityThreat log (spyware)
Vulnerability ProtectionExploits against clients and serversThreat log (vulnerability)
URL FilteringWeb categories, credential phishingURL filtering log (action block-url / alert)
File BlockingFile types by directionData filtering log
Security Profiles & ThreatsRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: A Security Profile Group on the Internet Rule

Use it when you build or harden an outbound rule. A profile group keeps the profiles together, so every internet rule gets the same protection.

set profiles url-filtering CORP-URL block [ malware phishing command-and-control grayware ]
set profiles url-filtering CORP-URL alert [ unknown newly-registered-domain ]
set profile-group STD-INTERNET virus default spyware strict vulnerability strict url-filtering CORP-URL file-blocking basic-file-blocking wildfire-analysis default
set rulebase security rules LAN-TO-INTERNET profile-setting group STD-INTERNET
set rulebase security rules LAN-TO-INTERNET log-end yes
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Creates a URL filtering profile, bundles it with Palo Alto's predefined threat profiles into a group, attaches the group to the internet rule, and logs session ends.

url-filtering CORP-URL block [ malware phishing command-and-control grayware ]
Categories that are always blocked.
… alert [ unknown newly-registered-domain ]
Allowed but logged, for visibility into risky categories without breaking work.
profile-group STD-INTERNET virus default spyware strict vulnerability strict …
Bundles antivirus (default), anti-spyware and vulnerability protection (strict, predefined), URL, file blocking and WildFire profiles.
rules LAN-TO-INTERNET profile-setting group STD-INTERNET
Attaches the group. Profiles only act on traffic the rule allows.
log-end yes
Logs at session end (the default), giving the end reason and byte counts in the traffic log.

⚠ Syntax note. The predefined profile names (default, strict, basic-file-blocking) exist on every firewall. Check the exact keywords with Tab/?, and remember HTTPS content is only inspected when it is decrypted.

Security Profiles & ThreatsPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs Concept

"It's Blocked": Finding Which Rule or Profile Did It

1 · Traffic log: which rule, which action, which end reason?

show log traffic direction equal backward query "( addr.src in 10.20.0.50 ) and ( addr.dst in 203.0.113.80 )"

Good: The rule name, action allow/deny, and session end reason. If not: action deny → a security rule (or default). end reason threat → a security profile. policy-deny → rule order.

2 · Threat or URL log for the same session

show log threat direction equal backward query "( addr.src in 10.20.0.50 )"
show log url direction equal backward query "( addr.src in 10.20.0.50 )"

Good: The threat name and ID, or URL category and action, plus the profile. If not: Nothing logged: the block happened elsewhere (decryption, rule, App-ID).

3 · URL category (miscategorised site?)

test url www.example.com
test url-info-cloud www.example.com

Good: The category the firewall uses (local database and cloud). If not: Wrong category: submit a change request to Palo Alto. Meanwhile use a custom URL category with allow.

4 · App-ID

show session id <id>

Good: The application identified, and whether it matches the rule's application list. If not: incomplete/insufficient-data: the handshake failed. A different app than expected: adjust the rule or use an application override only if justified.

5 · Confirm the rule logic

test security-policy-match from TRUST to UNTRUST source 10.20.0.50 destination 203.0.113.80 protocol 6 destination-port 443 application ssl

Good: The expected allow rule. If not: Shadowed by an earlier rule.

False positives: threat exceptions

If a signature blocks legitimate traffic: find the threat ID in the threat log, add a threat exception for it in the vulnerability or anti-spyware profile (optionally limited to specific IP addresses), commit, then open a TAC case.

Palo Alto's guidance: create an exception only when you're sure the signature is a false positive, open a support case so the signature can be fixed, and remove the exception once it is resolved. With IP address exemptions (up to 100 per signature), the exception applies only to the listed addresses.

App-ID & Log LabelsHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Concept

App-ID and TCP: Why an Application Needs Several Packets

Applications that use TCP usually need several packets before App-ID can identify them. The handshake carries no application data, so the firewall first matches the session on zones, addresses and port, then watches the payload. Once App-ID has seen enough, it labels the session with the application (for example gmail-base) and re-checks the security policy against that application. If it can't identify it, the session gets one of the special labels below.

Because identification needs data, a rule that allows only specific applications must also let the first packets through until the application is known. That's why application-based rules use service application-default or explicit ports rather than "any" on both. If the final application isn't allowed, the session is denied at that point.

App-ID & Log LabelsREFERENCE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Concept

Classifying TCP Traffic: not-applicable, incomplete, insufficient-data, unknown-tcp, unknown-p2p

When App-ID receives enough packets it assigns an application label such as gmail-base. When it can't identify the application, it assigns one of these labels. Each one is a diagnosis in itself.

LabelWhat App-ID is telling you (Palo Alto definition)Typical causesNext check
not-applicableThe firewall discarded the traffic because security policy did not allow it. For example, a rule allows HTTP only on TCP 80, but the traffic arrives on another port: it is blocked and labelled not-applicable.Port not allowed by any rule (application-default mismatch), interzone default deny, wrong zoneRule column (interzone-default?), test security-policy-match with the real port, the rule's service setting
incompleteThe three-way handshake did not complete, or it completed but no data followed. Not really an application.No SYN-ACK: routing/return path, server down, filtered upstream, asymmetric routing. Handshake but no data: client gave up, health checks, port scansBytes received (0?), end reason aged-out or tcp-rst-*, show session id, packet-diag counters, return route
insufficient-dataThe handshake completed, but not enough payload data followed to identify the application.Very short sessions, keepalives, probes, an application that sends little before closingBytes and packets, end reason (tcp-fin / rst), whether it matters (often benign monitoring traffic)
unknown-tcpThe handshake completed and data is flowing, but App-ID can't identify the application.Internally developed app, commercial app without a signature, encrypted proprietary protocol, or malwareDestination and volume. If legitimate: a custom application (or application override, as a last resort). If not: investigate as suspicious
unknown-udpThe UDP counterpart: data flows but no application matched.As for unknown-tcpAs for unknown-tcp
unknown-p2pNo specific application matched, but the traffic shows generic peer-to-peer behaviour.Unidentified P2P or tunnelling software, or malwareTreat as suspicious until proven otherwise: source host, destinations, user

unknown-tcp, unknown-udp and unknown-p2p can be internally developed or commercial applications, or malware the firewall has no signature for. Never write a broad allow rule for them. Identify the traffic first, then create a custom application with a signature where possible.

Check it from the CLI

show session all filter application incomplete
show session all filter application unknown-tcp
show session id <id>
show log traffic direction equal backward query "( app eq insufficient-data )"
show log traffic direction equal backward query "( app eq not-applicable )"
What each line does

Purpose: Finding sessions and logs with each special label.

show session all filter application <label>
Live sessions currently carrying that label.
show session id <id>
Application, rule, bytes per direction and end state for one session.
show log traffic … query "( app eq … )"
Historical traffic logs filtered by application label.

Every Action and Subtype You Will See in Traffic and Threat Logs

Traffic log

FieldValueMeaning
Type (subtype)start · end · drop · denystart = session started, end = session ended, drop = dropped before the application was identified and no rule allows it, deny = dropped after the application was identified and a rule blocks it (or none allows it)
ActionallowThe session was allowed by policy
ActiondenyThe session was denied by policy
ActiondropThe session was dropped silently
Actionreset-client · reset-server · reset-bothThe session was terminated with a TCP reset to the client, the server or both
Session end reasonsee Session End Reason, DecodedOnly the highest-priority reason is shown when there were several. Priority order: threat → policy-deny → decrypt-cert-validation → decrypt-unsupport-param → decrypt-error → tcp-rst-from-client → tcp-rst-from-server → resources-unavailable → tcp-fin → tcp-reuse → decoder → aged-out → unknown

Threat log

ActionMeaning
alertA threat or URL was detected but not blocked
allowFlood detection alert
denyThe flood detection mechanism activated and denied traffic based on configuration
dropA threat was detected and the session remains, but all its packets are dropped
drop-all-packetsSame family: the session's packets are all discarded
reset-client · reset-server · reset-bothA threat was detected and a TCP RST was sent to the client, the server, or both

block-override / override / override-lockoutURL only: an override page was shown / the correct passcode was given / too many failed passcodes, so the source is locked out

Threat log subtypes

SubtypeProduced by
virus · wildfire-virusAntivirus / WildFire
spywareAnti-spyware, including DNS security

urlURL filtering
fileFile blocking

flood · scan · packetZone protection / DoS protection

A profile signature's default action is usually alert or reset-both. A profile can override it per signature or severity. The allow action in a security profile generates no threat log at all, so "nothing in the threat log" can also mean "allowed without logging".

Reading a Log Line: What Each Combination Means

The fastest diagnosis comes from reading application + action + session end reason + bytes together. Common combinations and what they point to:

ApplicationAction / end reasonBytesMost likely meaningNext step
incompleteallow · aged-outreceived 0SYN sent, nothing came back: no route back, server down, filtered, or asymmetric returnReturn route on the far side, server reachability, packet-diag counters
incompleteallow · tcp-rst-from-serversmallThe server refused the connection (port closed)The server / service, not the firewall
incompleteallow · tcp-rst-from-clientsmallThe client gave up (timeout, or reset by another device)Client side, an intermediate proxy or IPS
insufficient-dataallow · tcp-finsmall, both waysA short legitimate session: health check, keepalive, monitoringUsually benign. Confirm the source
not-applicabledeny / drop · policy-deny0 / tinyPort or zone not allowed by any rule (often interzone-default)Rule column, test security-policy-match with the real port

unknown-tcpallow · tcp-finlargeUnidentified application in active useIdentify it: custom application, or investigate
anyreset-both · threatvariesA security profile terminated the sessionThreat log for the same session ID: name, ID, profile

anyallow · decrypt-unsupport-paramsmallThe TLS version or cipher isn't supported for decryptionDecryption profile, or a no-decrypt rule
anyallow · resources-unavailablevariesA resource limit was hit (e.g. too many out-of-order packets per flow)Dataplane load, counters, path quality

1 · Find the session in the traffic log

show log traffic direction equal backward query "( addr.src in 10.20.0.50 ) and ( addr.dst in 203.0.113.80 )"

Good: Application, action, end reason and bytes for the flow. If not: No log: the rule doesn't log, or the session is still open (show session).

2 · Match it to a row above

show session id <id>

Good: The combination and live counters confirm the diagnosis. If not: Unclear: packet-diag counters for the flow (Debug & Capture group).

3 · Follow the pointer

show log threat direction equal backward query "( addr.src in 10.20.0.50 )"
show log decryption direction equal backward

Good: The threat or decryption log explains a threat or decrypt-* end reason. If not: Nothing there: back to routing and policy (R·A·P).

User-ID: How an IP Address Becomes a User

Security rules can match users and groups instead of addresses. To do that, the firewall needs two things: an IP-to-user mapping (who is on 10.20.0.50 right now) and a user-to-group mapping (which groups that user belongs to).

Mapping sourceTypical use
Server monitoring (PAN-OS integrated agent, or Windows User-ID agent)Domain users on corporate PCs, from DC security logs
GlobalProtectRemote users: the mapping comes from the GP login
Authentication policy / portalUsers with no other mapping are prompted to log in
Syslog / XML APINAC, Wi-Fi controllers and proxies that already know the user
User-ID & AuthenticationRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Agentless User-ID with Group-Based Rules

// GUI objects, in build order                                      
AD                                                                  service account svc-userid with read access to the DC security logs (Event Log Readers)
Device > Server Profiles > LDAP                                     LDAP-CORP · servers dc1/dc2 10.10.10.11/.12 · base DN DC=corp,DC=example · bind svc-userid
Device > User Identification > Group Mapping                        GM-CORP · server profile LDAP-CORP · include groups grp-vpn-users, grp-finance
Device > User Identification > User Mapping                         PAN-OS agent account svc-userid · Server Monitoring: dc1, dc2 (Microsoft Active Directory)
Network > Zones > TRUST                                             Enable User Identification ✓ (only on internal zones, never on UNTRUST)
Policies > Security                                                 FINANCE-APPS: TRUST → DC · source user grp-finance · apps finance-erp · allow
Device > Authentication Profile (for login portals / GP / admins)   AUTH-LDAP · type LDAP · server LDAP-CORP · allow list grp-vpn-users
What each line does

Purpose: Lets the firewall learn who is behind each internal IP from the domain controllers, learn group membership from LDAP, and use groups in rules.

service account svc-userid
The firewall reads DC security logs with this account. Least privilege (Event Log Readers), not a domain admin.
LDAP-CORP · base DN · bind
How the firewall queries AD for groups. Use two servers for redundancy, and LDAPS where possible.
GM-CORP · include groups
Only the groups you use in policy. Including everything slows group mapping on large directories.
Server Monitoring: dc1, dc2
Agentless mapping from logon events (the PAN-OS integrated agent).
zone TRUST · Enable User Identification
User-ID only maps addresses in zones where it is enabled. Never enable it on untrusted zones.
rule source user grp-finance
The rule matches only mapped users in that group. Unknown users don't match it.
AUTH-LDAP · allow list
Authenticates logins (GP, portal, admins). Only allow-listed groups may log in.

The CLI paths for these objects are set shared server-profile ldap …, set group-mapping … and set user-id-agent … (vsys-scoped variants exist). The GUI is the documented way to build them.

User-ID & AuthenticationPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs Concept

User-ID and Authentication: Step-by-Step Troubleshooting

1 · Is there a mapping for the user's IP?

show user ip-user-mapping ip 10.20.0.50
show user ip-user-mapping all | match corp\\jdoe

Good: The IP maps to the right user, with a remaining timeout. If not: No mapping: continue with step 2. A wrong user (shared PC, terminal server) means the mapping is outdated. Use clear user-cache ip 10.20.0.50/32, then log on again.

2 · Are the mapping sources healthy?

show user server-monitor state all
show user user-id-agent state all
show log userid direction equal backward

Good: Server monitors connected, agents connected, recent mapping log entries. If not: Not connected: service account rights, DC reachability, or WMI/WinRM blocked.

3 · Group membership

show user group-mapping state all
show user group name "cn=grp-finance,ou=groups,dc=corp,dc=example"

Good: The group is listed, and the user is a member. If not: Missing group: not in the include list, LDAP bind/base DN issue, or the next refresh hasn't run yet.

4 · Does the rule match the user?

test security-policy-match from TRUST to DC source 10.20.0.50 destination 10.10.20.30 protocol 6 destination-port 443 source-user corp\jdoe

Good: FINANCE-APPS matches. If not: Wrong rule: order, or the user isn't in the group the firewall knows.

5 · Authentication (GP, portal, admin logins)

test authentication authentication-profile AUTH-LDAP username jdoe password
less mp-log authd.log

Good: Authentication succeeded for user jdoe. If not: Failed: server reachability, bind account, user not on the allow list, or the wrong username format.

6 · Deep dive (only if needed)

debug user-id log-ip-user-mapping yes
tail follow yes mp-log useridd.log
debug user-id log-ip-user-mapping no

Good: Mapping events as users log on. If not: Always turn debug off afterwards.

NAT · How It WorksEVALUATION ORDER ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The Order Addresses Are Evaluated

Almost every NAT ticket that turns into an argument comes from one sentence, so it is worth committing to memory: security policy is matched on the original, pre-NAT addresses — but on the post-NAT zones. The firewall works out where the packet will end up before it decides whether it is allowed, and it does that without having rewritten the header yet.

Think of it as a customs desk. The officer reads the passport you arrived with (pre-NAT addresses) but stamps you for the terminal you are actually leaving from (post-NAT zone). The new identity is only issued as you walk out of the door.

NAT rules and security rules are two separate rulebases, both top-down, first match wins, evaluated independently. A packet can match a NAT rule and still be denied by security policy — and that is the normal outcome when someone writes the security rule against the translated address.

NAT · How It WorksCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

How PAN-OS Interprets NAT in the Flow

PAN-OS decides everything on the original packet and only rewrites the addresses on the way out. Palo Alto's NAT overview gives the order: route lookup to find the egress interface and zone, then the NAT rule match on the original zones and addresses, then the security rule on the pre-NAT addresses with the post-NAT zone, and finally translation as the packet leaves.

Rule typeSource / destination IPDestination zone
NAT rulePre-NAT (original packet)From the route lookup of the pre-NAT destination
Security rulePre-NAT (original packet)From the route lookup of the post-NAT destination, i.e. where the host really is

Destination NAT · publishing a DC web server on the hub

Lab addition: WEB-DNAT maps 203.0.113.80:443 (UNTRUST) to the server 10.10.10.80 in zone DC.

Source NAT · DC servers browsing the internet

Rule DC-SNAT (DC → UNTRUST, dynamic IP and port, interface address of ethernet1/1). Here routing, NAT and security all see the same zones, DC → UNTRUST, and the security rule uses the server's real address.

A Palo Alto works like a sorting office that decides everything from the original label: which van, which corrected address, which permission. Only at the loading bay door does someone stick the new label on. So when you check the permissions, look for the original address. When you check which van, look for where the corrected address actually lives.

For DNAT, the NAT rule's destination zone is the pre-NAT zone. Here the public IP routes to UNTRUST, so the rule is UNTRUST → UNTRUST. The security rule's destination zone is the post-NAT zone, UNTRUST → DC. Mixing these up is the most common PAN-OS NAT mistake.

NAT · How It WorksEXAMPLE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Verifying NAT: Rule, Test, Session

Check NAT at three levels: what's configured, what the firewall says it would do, and what the session actually recorded.

1 · The rules

admin@HUB-PA# show rulebase nat rules WEB-DNAT
WEB-DNAT {
  from UNTRUST;
  to UNTRUST;                         // pre-NAT zone: 203.0.113.80 routes out of eth1/1
  source any;
  destination 203.0.113.80;
  service service-https;
  destination-translation {
    translated-address 10.10.10.80;
  }
}

admin@HUB-PA# show rulebase security rules WEB-IN
WEB-IN {
  from UNTRUST;
  to DC;                              // post-NAT zone: where 10.10.10.80 lives
  source any;
  destination 203.0.113.80;           // pre-NAT IP
  application ssl;
  service application-default;
  action allow;
}
What each line does

Purpose: Shows the two rules that publish the DC web server, and why their zones differ even though they describe the same traffic.

NAT rule · WEB-DNAT

from UNTRUST
Zone the traffic arrives in: internet clients on ethernet1/1.
to UNTRUST
The pre-NAT destination zone: 203.0.113.80 is on the WAN subnet, so the route lookup for it points to ethernet1/1 (UNTRUST). NAT rules always use the zones of the original packet.
destination 203.0.113.80 · service service-https
Only the public IP on TCP/443 is translated.
destination-translation · translated-address 10.10.10.80
Rewrites the destination to the real server. The rewrite is applied as the packet leaves, but the decision is made here.

Security rule · WEB-IN

from UNTRUST · to DC
The post-NAT zone pair: 10.10.10.80 routes out of ethernet1/3 in zone DC.
destination 203.0.113.80
The pre-NAT IP. Security rules match the original addresses, so using 10.10.10.80 here would never match.
application ssl · service application-default
Allows TLS on its standard port. App-ID identifies the traffic as ssl.
action allow
Permits the session. Translation and logging follow.

2 · Ask the firewall

admin@HUB-PA> test nat-policy-match from UNTRUST to UNTRUST source 198.51.100.77 destination 203.0.113.80 destination-port 443 protocol 6
// illustrative output
Destination-NAT: Rule matched: WEB-DNAT
198.51.100.77:12345 => 10.10.10.80:443

admin@HUB-PA> test security-policy-match from UNTRUST to DC source 198.51.100.77 destination 203.0.113.80 protocol 6 destination-port 443
"WEB-IN; index: 4" {
        from UNTRUST;
        to DC;
        ...
        action allow;
}

3 · The session

                                          Vsys    Dst[Dport]/Zone (translated IP[Port])
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

                                          vsys1   203.0.113.80[443]/DC  (10.10.10.80[443])

FieldRead it as
Flag ND / NS / NBDestination NAT / source NAT / both, in the session list.
c2s / s2c flowClient-to-server and server-to-client. The s2c source shows the real (post-NAT) server.
rule / nat-ruleExactly which security and NAT rules created the session.
egress interfaceWhere routing sent it. This must be the interface in the security rule's destination zone.

Common NAT mistakes

SymptomLikely cause
DNAT never matchesNAT rule destination zone set to DC (post-NAT) instead of UNTRUST (pre-NAT).
DNAT matches, traffic deniedSecurity rule uses the private IP, or the pre-NAT zone, as destination.
Session with no s2c trafficServer's default gateway isn't the firewall, or no route back from the server side.
Internal users can't use the public IPU-turn NAT needed: a rule from the internal zone that also source-NATs. Covered in a later group.
Public IP doesn't answerThe upstream doesn't route it to the firewall, or the address isn't on the egress subnet and no route exists.
NAT · How It WorksDESTINATION NAT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Destination NAT — Inbound to a Published Server

The classic inbound publish: the internet reaches a public address, the firewall rewrites the destination to a private server. This is the scenario where the pre-NAT / post-NAT split bites hardest, because the destination address and the destination zone come from different sides of the translation.

RulebaseSource zoneDest zoneDest address
NAT ruleUntrustUntrust — the zone the original packet was headed to198.51.100.10
Security ruleUntrustDMZ — post-NAT zone198.51.100.10 — pre-NAT address

Those two destination zone values are different, and that is not a typo. On the NAT rule it is Untrust; on the security rule it is DMZ. Writing DMZ on the NAT rule is the number-one reason an inbound publish silently fails to translate.

Verify it without waiting for traffic

admin@fw-01(active)> test nat-policy-match from Untrust to Untrust source 203.0.113.50 destination 198.51.100.10 destination-port 443 protocol 6
note: to-zone is the PRE-NAT zone here
Destination-NAT-Rule: publish-web
Rule: publish-web; Index: 3
  From Untrust, Source: any, To Untrust, Destination: 198.51.100.10
  Service: tcp/any/443, Translated Destination: 10.10.30.20, Translated Port: 443

admin@fw-01(active)> test security-policy-match from Untrust to DMZ source 203.0.113.50 destination 198.51.100.10 destination-port 443 protocol 6
to-zone is POST-NAT, destination is PRE-NAT
"allow-inbound-web" {
	from Untrust;
	source any;
	to DMZ;
	destination 198.51.100.10;
	action allow;
}

If the NAT test matches but the security test returns no rule, you have almost certainly written the security rule against 10.10.30.20. Change the address object back to the public one and leave the zone as DMZ.

What the session looks like afterwards

admin@fw-01(active)> show session id 91442
Session          91442
        c2s flow:
                source:      203.0.113.50 [Untrust]
                dst:         198.51.100.10
                proto:       6
                sport:       51204          dport:      443
                state:       ACTIVE         type:       FLOW
        s2c flow:
                source:      10.10.30.20 [DMZ]
                dst:         203.0.113.50
                sport:       443            dport:      51204
        rule                       : allow-inbound-web
        NAT rule                   : publish-web
        destination translation    : 198.51.100.10/443 => 10.10.30.20/443

Read the two flows as a mirror. The c2s flow carries the addresses as they arrived; the s2c flow carries the addresses the server will reply with. If the NAT rule line says None on a session you expected to translate, the NAT rulebase never matched — go back to test nat-policy-match, not to the security rules.

NAT · How It WorksSOURCE NAT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Source NAT — Outbound Hide Behind the Egress Interface

The everyday outbound case. Internal clients leave through a public address, usually the egress interface IP with dynamic port translation. The evaluation order is the same seven steps; the difference is that here the zones agree, so the only trap is the source address.

RulebaseSource zoneDest zoneSource address
NAT ruleTrustUntrust10.10.20.0/24
Security ruleTrustUntrust10.10.20.0/24 — pre-NAT, never the public IP
admin@fw-01(active)> test nat-policy-match from Trust to Untrust source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90 destination-port 443 protocol 6
Source-NAT-Rule: outbound-hide
  From Trust, Source: 10.10.20.0/24, To Untrust, Destination: any
  Translated Source: 198.51.100.2, Type: dynamic-ip-and-port, Port: dynamic

admin@fw-01(active)> show session id 88210 | match translation
        source translation         : 10.10.20.55/51204 => 198.51.100.2/40119

When outbound NAT runs out of room

DIPP oversubscription is finite. When the pool is exhausted, new sessions are dropped and the symptom looks like intermittent internet loss for a subset of users — not an obvious NAT failure.

admin@fw-01(active)> show running ippool
Rule            Type              Used     Available
--------------------------------------------------------
outbound-hide   Dynamic IP/Port   63488    1536
admin@fw-01(active)> show counter global filter severity drop delta yes | match nat
flow_dnat_pool_exhaust     0    0  drop  flow  session  Packets dropped: NAT pool exhausted
flow_snat_pool_exhaust   214   11  drop  flow  session  Packets dropped: source NAT pool exhausted

show running ippool is the one to keep in your back pocket. A high Used figure against a shrinking Available is a capacity problem, and the fix is another public IP in the pool or a higher oversubscription setting, not a policy change.

Useful NAT commands, both directions

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
test nat-policy-match from <z> to <z> source <ip> destination <ip> destination-port <n> protocol <n>Which NAT rule matches, and what the translation will be. to is the pre-NAT zone.—
show running nat-policyThe NAT rulebase as the dataplane actually holds it, in evaluation order.Policies > NAT
show running ippoolDIPP pool utilisation per rule.—
show session all filter nat-rule <name>Every live session translated by one rule.Monitor > Session Browser
show session all filter source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90Find the session, then show session id <n> for the translation lines.Monitor > Session Browser
show counter global filter severity drop delta yes | match natNAT-specific drops, including pool exhaustion.—

Two questions settle nearly every NAT case. Did the NAT rule match — test nat-policy-match. Did the security rule match the pre-NAT address with the post-NAT zone — test security-policy-match. If both say yes and traffic still fails, the problem is no longer NAT; go back to routing and counters.

GuidePAN-OS session flagPAN-OS rule zonesFortiGate equivalent
Source NATNStrust → untrustdir=org act=snat

Source NAT changes who a letter is from. Destination NAT changes where it goes. U-turn changes both, for a letter that never leaves the school.

NAT · Destination NATOVERVIEW ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Destination NAT at a Glance

Destination NAT changes where the packet is going on the way in, so the outside world can reach a private server. Five scenarios, each with CLI and web interface config, verification, and the commands for when it doesn't work. Same lab as the PAN-OS SNAT guide: PA-EDGE, untrust on ethernet1/1 (203.0.113.10/29), dmz on ethernet1/3 with web server 10.10.20.40, public address 203.0.113.11.

NAT · Destination NATTHE PAN-OS RULE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

The zone puzzle: untrust → untrust in NAT, untrust → dmz in Security

This is where most PAN-OS DNAT mistakes live. The firewall does two route lookups: one on the original destination (to find the NAT rule's zones) and one on the translated destination (to find where the packet really goes, which the security rule uses). Both rules still use the original public address.

FieldNAT ruleSecurity rule
From zoneuntrustuntrust
To zoneuntrust (zone of the public IP)dmz (zone of the real server)
Destination address203.0.113.11203.0.113.11 (pre-NAT)
Port / serviceOriginal portOriginal (external) port

A visitor asks for "the school" at the front gate. The gate list (NAT) is about the front gate. The hallway pass (Security) is about the classroom they'll really walk into, but the pass still says "visitor for the school", not the room number.

Coming from FortiGate, this is backwards in two places: the security rule uses the public address (not the internal one), and the external port (not the mapped one).

NAT · Destination NATTRANSLATION TYPES ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Destination translation options

Sometimes one gate leads to one classroom (Static IP). Sometimes the gate number chooses the room: gate 2222 goes to room 22 (translated port). Sometimes the visitor goes to whichever helper is next on today's list (session distribution).

OptionBehaviourScenario
Static IP1:1 destination translation — a single IP, range or netmask, to the same number of addressesA
Static IP + Translated PortPort forwarding / port translation (external 2222 → internal 22)B
Dynamic IP (with session distribution)Translated address is an FQDN or dynamic group that may resolve to several servers; sessions are spread across themC
Bi-directional Static IP (source NAT rule)One outbound static rule that also creates an implied inbound translationD
Source + destination in one pathBoth addresses rewritten; needed for true subnet overlapE

Static NAT rules should sit above dynamic rules in the NAT rulebase; a broad DIPP rule above a static one can take its traffic first.

NAT · Destination NATPRE-CHECK ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Before you publish anything

# where does the public address route? (gives the NAT rule's to-zone)
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 203.0.113.11
# where does the server route? (gives the security rule's to-zone)
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 10.10.20.40

# is the server reachable and listening? (from the firewall's management plane)
ping source 10.10.20.1 host 10.10.20.40

# what is already published — avoid reusing a public IP/port
show running nat-policy

# interface and zone of each side
show interface ethernet1/1
show interface ethernet1/3

# pending changes from someone else?
configure ; check pending-changes ; exit

Before opening the gate, make sure the classroom's door leads back to the same gate. If the teacher answers through the back door, the visitor never hears the answer.

NAT · Destination NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario A — one public IP for one web server, HTTPS only

The web server 10.10.20.40 must be reachable from the internet at 203.0.113.11, on HTTPS only. On PAN-OS the NAT rule's service and the security rule's application/service together decide what gets through.

NAT · Destination NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — static destination NAT plus its security rule

CLI

configure
set address PUB_WEB   ip-netmask 203.0.113.11/32
set address SRV_WEB01 ip-netmask 10.10.20.40/32

# NAT: untrust → untrust, public destination, HTTPS only
set rulebase nat rules Web-DNAT from untrust to untrust source any destination PUB_WEB service service-https
set rulebase nat rules Web-DNAT destination-translation translated-address SRV_WEB01
move rulebase nat rules Web-DNAT top

# Security: untrust → dmz (post-NAT zone), destination = PUBLIC address (pre-NAT)
set rulebase security rules Allow-Web from untrust to dmz source any destination PUB_WEB application [ ssl web-browsing ] service application-default action allow
set rulebase security rules Allow-Web log-end yes

commit description "DNAT: publish web01 on 203.0.113.11:443"
exit

Web interface

  1. Objects › Addresses: PUB_WEB (203.0.113.11), SRV_WEB01 (10.10.20.40).
  2. Policies › NAT › Add → Original Packet: Source Zone untrust, Destination Zone untrust, Service service-https, Destination Address PUB_WEB.
  3. Translated Packet: Source Address Translation None; Destination Address Translation Static IP, Translated Address SRV_WEB01, Translated Port empty.
  4. Policies › Security › Add: Source Zone untrust, Destination Zone dmz, Destination Address PUB_WEB, Application ssl, web-browsing, Service application-default, Allow.
  5. Commit.

We don't change the visitor's name tag, so the teacher knows exactly who came to visit.
