NAT · Destination NATTROUBLESHOOT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Troubleshoot — published but unreachable

# does the packet even arrive?
debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 198.51.100.7 destination 203.0.113.11
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage receive  file rx.pcap
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage transmit file tx.pcap
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage drop     file dp.pcap
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture on
   ... connect from outside ...
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture off
show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes
view-pcap filter-pcap tx.pcap     # destination should be 10.10.20.40 here
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off

# does upstream ARP resolve the public address to us?
show arp ethernet1/1
SymptomLikely causeFix
rx.pcap emptyTraffic never reaches the firewall (DNS, ISP, upstream ACL)Test by IP from a known-good external host
NAT test failsNAT to-zone set to dmz instead of untrustNAT zones come from the public IP's route
NAT matches, security deniesSecurity rule uses the private IP, or to-zone untrustDestination = public IP, to-zone = dmz
Session exists, no server replyServer down, host firewall, or wrong gatewayCapture on the dmz side; check server routing
flow_policy_deny risingSecurity policy denialTraffic log with deny; test security-policy-match
Works for one port onlyNAT rule service is specific (correct)Add another rule for another service, deliberately

Follow the visitor step by step: did they reach the gate? Was their name on the gate list? Did they get a hallway pass? Did they reach the room? Did the teacher answer? The first step that goes wrong is the problem.

NAT · Destination NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario B — one public IP, several internal services

One public address, three services: HTTPS to web01, SSH to a jump host published on external port 2222, and an app listening on 8443 for a partner range only.

NAT · Destination NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — translated-port, and a security rule on the EXTERNAL port

CLI

configure
# service object for the external port — destination port only, source port left blank
set service tcp-2222 protocol tcp port 2222
set service tcp-8443 protocol tcp port 8443
set address SRV_JUMP01   ip-netmask 10.10.20.45/32
set address SRV_APP01    ip-netmask 10.10.20.50/32
set address NET_PARTNER  ip-netmask 198.51.100.0/24
set address NET_ADMINS   ip-netmask 192.0.2.0/28

# external 2222 → jump01:22
set rulebase nat rules SSH-DNAT from untrust to untrust source NET_ADMINS destination PUB_WEB service tcp-2222
set rulebase nat rules SSH-DNAT destination-translation translated-address SRV_JUMP01 translated-port 22

# external 8443 → app01:8443, partner only
set rulebase nat rules App-DNAT from untrust to untrust source NET_PARTNER destination PUB_WEB service tcp-8443
set rulebase nat rules App-DNAT destination-translation translated-address SRV_APP01

# security: post-NAT zone, public IP, EXTERNAL port
set rulebase security rules Allow-SSH-Jump from untrust to dmz source NET_ADMINS destination PUB_WEB application ssh service tcp-2222 action allow
set rulebase security rules Allow-App-Partner from untrust to dmz source NET_PARTNER destination PUB_WEB application any service tcp-8443 action allow

commit description "DNAT: SSH 2222 to jump01, 8443 to app01"
exit

Two traps here. First, the security rule's service is the external port (tcp-2222): the policy is evaluated against the original packet. Second, application ssh with service application-default would fail, because SSH's default port is 22 and the session arrives on 2222. Use an explicit service object.

Web interface

  1. Objects › Services › Add: tcp-2222, TCP, Destination Port 2222, Source Port blank.
  2. Policies › NAT › Add: untrust → untrust, Service tcp-2222, Destination PUB_WEB; Destination Address Translation Static IP → SRV_JUMP01, Translated Port 22.
  3. Policies › Security › Add: untrust → dmz, Destination PUB_WEB, Application ssh, Service tcp-2222.
  4. Restrict sources on both rules (admins, partner) → Commit.

Only letting known visitors onto the gate list is a second lock. Even if a hallway pass is too generous, strangers never get past the gate.

NAT · Destination NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario C — one public IP in front of a pool whose members change

The application runs on several servers that are added and removed by the platform team, all published in DNS as app-pool.corp.example. Destination NAT with Dynamic IP (with session distribution) translates to that FQDN and spreads new sessions across whatever it resolves to.

Visitors are sent to whichever helper is next on today's list. But nobody checks whether that helper is awake. If a sleepy helper is still on the list, visitors still get sent to them.

This is distribution, not load balancing with health checks. There's no probe of the real servers; the membership is whatever DNS returns. If you need health-checked balancing, SSL offload or persistence, put an ADC (such as an F5) behind the firewall and publish its VIP with Scenario A.

NAT · Destination NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — FQDN address and dynamic destination translation

CLI

configure
set address FQDN_APP_POOL fqdn app-pool.corp.example

set rulebase nat rules AppPool-DNAT from untrust to untrust source any destination PUB_WEB service service-https
set rulebase nat rules AppPool-DNAT dynamic-destination-translation translated-address FQDN_APP_POOL translated-port 443 distribution round-robin

set rulebase security rules Allow-AppPool from untrust to dmz source any destination PUB_WEB application ssl service application-default action allow

commit description "DNAT: app pool via FQDN session distribution"
exit

Web interface

  1. Objects › Addresses › Add: FQDN_APP_POOL, Type FQDN, app-pool.corp.example.
  2. Policies › NAT › Add: untrust → untrust, Destination PUB_WEB, Service HTTPS.
  3. Destination Address Translation: Translation Type Dynamic IP (with session distribution), Translated Address FQDN_APP_POOL, Port 443, Session Distribution Method Round Robin.
  4. Security rule as in Scenario A → Commit.
Distribution methodUse when
Round Robin (default)Stateless servers, even spread
Source IP HashKeep a client on the same server (simple affinity)
IP Modulo / IP HashDeterministic mapping from source (and destination) addresses
Least SessionsServers with uneven session lengths

The firewall uses at most the first 32 IPv4 addresses returned for the FQDN.

Scenario D — one identity both ways with one NAT rule

A partner allowlists 203.0.113.14 for a server that both receives connections from them and calls out to them. A bi-directional static source NAT rule translates the server's outbound traffic to 203.0.113.14 and creates an implied inbound rule back to it.

One sign on the door works both ways: visitors come in by it, and the teacher goes out by it. Handy, but it opens every door into that room, so the hallway pass has to be strict.

NAT · Destination NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — one static rule, two security rules

CLI

configure
set address SRV_02    ip-netmask 10.10.20.60/32
set address PUB_SRV02 ip-netmask 203.0.113.14/32

# outbound static source NAT + implied inbound destination NAT
set rulebase nat rules Srv02-Static from dmz to untrust source SRV_02 destination any service any
set rulebase nat rules Srv02-Static source-translation static-ip translated-address PUB_SRV02 bi-directional yes
move rulebase nat rules Srv02-Static top

# outbound permission
set rulebase security rules Srv02-Out from dmz to untrust source SRV_02 destination HOST_PARTNER application ssl service application-default action allow
# inbound permission: public address (pre-NAT), post-NAT zone dmz, only what's needed
set rulebase security rules Srv02-In from untrust to dmz source HOST_PARTNER destination PUB_SRV02 application ssl service application-default action allow

commit description "Static bi-directional NAT for srv02"
exit

Web interface

  1. Policies › NAT › Add: dmz → untrust, Source SRV_02.
  2. Source Address Translation: Static IP, Translated Address PUB_SRV02, Bi-directional ticked.
  3. Two security rules: dmz → untrust (outbound) and untrust → dmz with destination PUB_SRV02 (inbound), both narrow.
  4. Commit.

The implied inbound translation has no port or source restrictions of its own, so the inbound security rule is the only thing limiting exposure. Keep it tight, or use a separate unidirectional DNAT rule (Scenario A) when you want the NAT itself to be scoped.

NAT · Destination NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario E — both sides of the VPN use 10.10.10.0/24

After an acquisition, both sites use 10.10.10.0/24. You can't route to a remote subnet that's also directly connected, and translating a remote destination back into 10.10.10.x on your own firewall lands on your connected route. The clean design splits the work: each side hides behind a unique range and addresses the other by its unique range.

Two schools both have a "Room 10". So each school gives the other a nickname for its rooms. You only ever send letters to their nickname, and their office turns it back into their real Room 10. Nobody gets confused.

NAT · Destination NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — our half of the agreement

Agree the two ranges in writing: 172.31.99.0/24 represents our LAN, 172.31.98.0/24 represents theirs. Both are /24 so Static IP keeps the host part.

CLI (our firewall)

configure
set address NET_US_ALIAS   ip-netmask 172.31.99.0/24
set address NET_THEM_ALIAS ip-netmask 172.31.98.0/24

# we reach them by THEIR alias, so route the alias into the tunnel
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route PARTNER-ALIAS destination 172.31.98.0/24 interface tunnel.1

# hide our source behind our alias, host part preserved
set rulebase nat rules LAN-to-Overlap from trust to vpn-partner source NET_LAN_USERS destination NET_THEM_ALIAS service any
set rulebase nat rules LAN-to-Overlap source-translation static-ip translated-address NET_US_ALIAS bi-directional no

set rulebase security rules Allow-Overlap-Out from trust to vpn-partner source NET_LAN_USERS destination NET_THEM_ALIAS application any service application-default action allow

# phase 2 carries only the aliases
set network tunnel ipsec IPSEC_PARTNER auto-key proxy-id PID-OVL local 172.31.99.0/24 remote 172.31.98.0/24 protocol any

commit description "Overlap: SNAT to 172.31.99.0/24, reach partner via 172.31.98.0/24"
exit

The partner's half (their firewall)

# if the partner also runs PAN-OS — adjust zone names to theirs
# their NAT to-zone comes from THEIR route for the alias 172.31.98.0/24,
# so they route the alias towards their LAN interface first
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route US-SEES-US destination 172.31.98.0/24 interface ethernet1/2
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route TO-US destination 172.31.99.0/24 interface tunnel.1

# destination static /24 → /24 for traffic arriving from the tunnel
set rulebase nat rules Overlap-In from vpn-us to trust source 172.31.99.0/24 destination 172.31.98.0/24 service any
set rulebase nat rules Overlap-In destination-translation translated-address 10.10.10.0/24
# + security vpn-us → trust, destination 172.31.98.0/24 (pre-NAT)
# + proxy-ID mirrored: local 172.31.98.0/24, remote 172.31.99.0/24

Web interface

  1. Network › Virtual Routers › default › Static Routes: 172.31.98.0/24 → tunnel.1.
  2. Policies › NAT › Add: trust → vpn-partner, Destination NET_THEM_ALIAS; Source Translation Static IP → NET_US_ALIAS.
  3. Policies › Security: trust → vpn-partner, source real LAN, destination NET_THEM_ALIAS.
  4. Network › IPSec Tunnels › Proxy IDs: Local 172.31.99.0/24, Remote 172.31.98.0/24.
  5. Users connect to partner servers by their alias address (172.31.98.80) — update internal DNS accordingly.

Don't try to do both translations for the remote side on your own firewall. After translating the destination back to 10.10.10.x, your post-NAT route lookup resolves to your own connected LAN, not the tunnel. Separating routing domains (virtual routers) can make it work, but splitting the NAT across the two firewalls is simpler and easier to troubleshoot.

NAT · Destination NATPITFALLS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Ten things that catch people out

  1. NAT rule to-zone set to dmz. It's the zone of the public IP: untrust → untrust.
  2. Security rule destination set to the private IP. It's the public (pre-NAT) address.
  3. Security rule to-zone set to untrust. It's the post-NAT zone: dmz.
  4. Security service set to the internal port when using port translation. It's the external port.
  5. application-default with a non-standard external port. Use an explicit service object.
  6. Custom service with a source port. Leave it blank.
  7. NAT service any — every port translated, security rule becomes the only lock.
  8. Static rules below DIPP rules. Static NAT belongs at the top.
  9. Bi-directional NAT with a broad inbound security rule. All ports are translated inbound.
  10. Testing from inside. Reaching the public IP from the LAN is U-turn (hairpin) NAT — the next guide.
NAT · Destination NATPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

Inbound NAT / Published Server Broken

time-box 15 minA: NAT zones = pre-NATP: rule zone = post-NAT

From the internet

  1. Does it arrive? Filtered counters or a receive-stage capture on the public IP. Nothing means upstream routing or ARP for the public IP.
  2. NAT rule: zones must be the pre-NAT pair (UNTRUST → UNTRUST for a public IP on the WAN subnet). test nat-policy-match must return it.
  3. Route to the private IP: test routing fib-lookup … ip <private-ip> gives the real egress zone.
  4. Security rule: destination = public IP, destination zone = that real zone.
  5. Reply path: the server's default gateway must lead back through this firewall.

From inside, using the public IP (U-turn)

Internal users hitting the public address need their own NAT rule from the internal zone, with the destination public IP translated to the server. If the client and server share a zone or subnet, the rule must also source-NAT to the firewall, or the server replies directly to the client and the session breaks. Full scenario: U-turn NAT in the Routing Scenarios group.

NAT · Source NATOVERVIEW ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Source NAT at a Glance

Source NAT changes who the packet claims to be on the way out. Four real scenarios on PAN-OS, each with CLI and web interface config, verification, and the commands for when it doesn't work. Lab: PA-EDGE, zone trust on ethernet1/2 (10.10.10.1/24), zone untrust on ethernet1/1 (203.0.113.10/29, gateway 203.0.113.9), PAN-OS 11.1. Same addressing as the FortiGate series, so the two can be read side by side.

NAT · Source NATCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Why SNAT exists, in one page

Private (RFC 1918) addresses aren't routable on the internet, so a reply to 10.10.10.25 has nowhere to go. Source NAT lends the packet a routable source address and records, in the session, who the packet really was.

Reason to SNATWhat breaks without itScenario in this guide
Private users need internetReplies never come backA — DIPP, interface address
A partner allowlists one IPThey drop you, or you can't separate appsB — DIPP, dedicated address
One host must always be one public IPShared NAT means unpredictable identityC — Static IP
Partner requires a unique range over VPNYour subnet collides with someone else's in their networkD — Static IP into the tunnel

Your classroom writes letters to a pen-pal. Your desk number means nothing outside the school, so the school office writes the school's address on your letter and remembers it was yours. When the reply comes back, the office walks it to your desk.

NAT · Source NATTHE PAN-OS RULE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Two rulebases: NAT decides the translation, Security decides the permission

This is the biggest difference from FortiGate. On PAN-OS a NAT rule never allows traffic, and a security rule never translates it. Every NAT'd flow needs one of each, and they're matched with different views of the same packet.

FieldNAT rule seesSecurity rule sees
Source addressOriginal (10.10.10.25)Original (10.10.10.25)
Destination addressOriginalOriginal
Destination zoneFrom the route lookup (untrust)Post-NAT zone (untrust — same for SNAT)
ApplicationNot a match fieldApp-ID

Two grown-ups stand at the school door. One decides which address goes on the letter (NAT). The other decides whether the letter may leave at all (Security). Both read the letter exactly as you handed it in. If either one says no, the letter stays inside.

NAT · Source NATPACKET FLOW ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Where NAT sits in the PAN-OS session setup

Before the office can write an address, it has to know which road leads to your pen-pal. No road means no address, and the letter never leaves.

Existing sessions keep the NAT decision they were created with. After changing a NAT rule and committing, clear the affected sessions (clear session all filter source …) before re-testing.

NAT · Source NATTRANSLATION TYPES ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

The three source translation types

TypeBehaviourUse it when
Dynamic IP and Port (DIPP)Many hosts share one or more addresses; source ports are translated. Each address/port pair can be reused concurrently (oversubscription, 2/4/8×)Internet access, dedicated app egress — the default choice
Dynamic IP (DIP)1:1 dynamic mapping, address only, no port change. When the pool is used up, new sessions are dropped unless DIPP fallback is configuredProtocols that break with port translation, with a pool big enough for concurrent hosts
Static IPFixed 1:1 mapping of an address or range to an equal-sized range; source port kept. Optional bi-directional flag also allows inboundOne host = one public identity; subnet-to-subnet mapping

DIPP is the whole class sharing the school's one address, with a different sticker number on each letter so replies find the right kid. Dynamic IP is a few spare mailboxes handed out to whoever asks first; when they're all taken, the next kid waits. Static IP is one kid with their very own mailbox, always the same one.

A NAT rule can reference at most 256 translated addresses (model limits also apply across all rules). PAN-OS answers ARP (proxy ARP) for translated addresses in the same subnet as the egress interface; addresses outside it need a route on the upstream router.

# version, HA state, vsys

# (advanced routing engine)

Value in this guideWhat it is
trust · ethernet1/2 · 10.10.10.1/24User zone, subnet 10.10.10.0/24
untrust · ethernet1/1 · 203.0.113.10/29Internet zone, gateway 203.0.113.9

PAN-OS only applies what you commit. Nothing in this guide takes effect until commit, and a commit pushes every pending change in the candidate config — including a colleague's. Check pending changes first.

⚠ Verification note. The legacy form test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip … is documented in the KB. The Advanced Routing line (test advanced-routing fib-lookup logical-router …) isn't in Palo Alto's Networking cheat sheet. Confirm with ?, or use the documented show advanced-routing route destination <ip/netmask> and show advanced-routing fib.

NAT · Source NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario A — the whole office needs internet

200 users in trust need the internet and there's one public address on ethernet1/1. DIPP with the interface address lets everyone share it, separated by source port.

NAT · Source NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — one NAT rule, one security rule, one commit

CLI

configure

# address object for the user subnet
set address NET_LAN_USERS ip-netmask 10.10.10.0/24

# 1. NAT rule: translate, nothing more
set rulebase nat rules LAN-to-Internet from trust to untrust source NET_LAN_USERS destination any service any
set rulebase nat rules LAN-to-Internet source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/1

# 2. Security rule: permit — pre-NAT source, post-NAT zone
set rulebase security rules Allow-LAN-Internet from trust to untrust source NET_LAN_USERS destination any application any service application-default action allow
set rulebase security rules Allow-LAN-Internet log-end yes

commit description "SNAT: LAN to internet via ethernet1/1"
exit

Web interface

  1. Objects › Addresses › Add: NET_LAN_USERS, IP Netmask 10.10.10.0/24.
  2. Policies › NAT › Add → General: name LAN-to-Internet, NAT Type ipv4.
  3. Original Packet: Source Zone trust, Destination Zone untrust, Destination Interface any, Service any, Source Address NET_LAN_USERS.
  4. Translated Packet: Translation Type Dynamic IP And Port, Address Type Interface Address, Interface ethernet1/1, IP address 203.0.113.10/29 → OK.
  5. Policies › Security › Add: trust → untrust, source NET_LAN_USERS, destination any, Allow, log at session end.
  6. Commit (top right) with a description.

"Interface address" means "use whatever address is painted on the school gate". If the school gets a new address, the letters still work, because the painted sign changes by itself.

If ethernet1/1 has more than one IP, pick the right one explicitly (interface-address interface ethernet1/1 ip 203.0.113.10/29). Otherwise the translated address may not be the one you expect.

        nat-type ipv4; from trust; source 10.10.10.0/24; to untrust; to-interface ;

}

# 2. which security rule WOULD allow it?

# 3. the live session: flag NS = source NAT
show session all filter source 10.10.10.25 destination 8.8.8.8

   ... reproduce from PC-01 ...

NAT · Source NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario B — a partner allowlists one IP, not your whole office

The payments app on 10.10.20.40 (zone dmz) must reach a partner at 198.51.100.50, whose firewall only accepts 203.0.113.12. A dedicated NAT rule, placed above the general one, gives that app its own identity.

NAT · Source NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — DIPP to a specific translated address

CLI

configure
set address SRV_PAYAPP   ip-netmask 10.10.20.40/32
set address HOST_PARTNER ip-netmask 198.51.100.50/32
set address PUB_PAYAPP   ip-netmask 203.0.113.12/32

set rulebase nat rules PayApp-to-Partner from dmz to untrust source SRV_PAYAPP destination HOST_PARTNER service any
set rulebase nat rules PayApp-to-Partner source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port translated-address PUB_PAYAPP

# first match wins: put it above the general rule
move rulebase nat rules PayApp-to-Partner top

set rulebase security rules Allow-PayApp-Partner from dmz to untrust source SRV_PAYAPP destination HOST_PARTNER application ssl service application-default action allow

commit description "SNAT: payments app to partner as 203.0.113.12"
exit

Web interface

  1. Create address objects SRV_PAYAPP, HOST_PARTNER, PUB_PAYAPP.
  2. Policies › NAT › Add: dmz → untrust, source SRV_PAYAPP, destination HOST_PARTNER.
  3. Translated Packet: Dynamic IP And Port, Address Type Translated Address → PUB_PAYAPP.
  4. Select the rule and use Move › Move Top (or drag it) above LAN-to-Internet.
  5. Add the matching security rule, then Commit.

Pick a spare address on the same street as the school. The postman already walks that street, so he'll find it. An address on a different street only works if someone tells the postman the way.

Scenario C — one host must always be one public IP

The SFTP host 10.10.20.50 uploads to a bank that pins its source address and dislikes port translation. Static IP source NAT gives that host a fixed public address and keeps its source port.

Some pen-pals only open letters from one exact mailbox. So that kid always uses the same mailbox, every single time, and keeps their own sticker number too.

NAT · Source NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — Static IP source translation

CLI

configure
set address SRV_SFTP  ip-netmask 10.10.20.50/32
set address HOST_BANK ip-netmask 198.51.100.60/32
set address PUB_SFTP  ip-netmask 203.0.113.13/32

set rulebase nat rules SFTP-to-Bank from dmz to untrust source SRV_SFTP destination HOST_BANK service any
set rulebase nat rules SFTP-to-Bank source-translation static-ip translated-address PUB_SFTP bi-directional no
move rulebase nat rules SFTP-to-Bank top

set rulebase security rules Allow-SFTP-Bank from dmz to untrust source SRV_SFTP destination HOST_BANK application ssh service application-default action allow

commit description "SNAT: SFTP host static to 203.0.113.13"
exit

Web interface

  1. Policies › NAT › Add: dmz → untrust, source SRV_SFTP, destination HOST_BANK.
  2. Translated Packet: Translation Type Static IP, Translated Address PUB_SFTP, Bi-directional unticked.
  3. Move it above broader rules, add the security rule, Commit.

Leave Bi-directional off unless you really want inbound connections to that host too. Ticking it quietly publishes the server to anything a security rule allows towards 203.0.113.13. Inbound publishing belongs in a deliberate destination NAT rule (DNAT guide).

For a small group of hosts that need no port translation but don't need fixed identities, Dynamic IP with Advanced (Dynamic IP/Port Fallback) hands out addresses 1:1 and falls back to DIPP instead of dropping when the pool is exhausted.

NAT · Source NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario D — the partner says "present yourselves as 172.31.99.0/24"

A partner already has another customer using 10.10.10.0/24, so they assign you a unique range to appear as across the tunnel. Their servers live on 192.168.50.0/24. Static IP maps your /24 host-for-host into their assigned /24 before traffic enters tunnel.1.

If both ends use the same subnet (true overlap), source NAT alone isn't enough: you can't route to a remote subnet that's also directly connected. That needs source and destination translation (double NAT), covered in the DNAT guide.

NAT · Source NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — Static IP subnet mapping into the tunnel

CLI

configure
set address NET_ASSIGNED     ip-netmask 172.31.99.0/24
set address NET_PARTNER_SRV  ip-netmask 192.168.50.0/24

# NAT: /24 to /24, host part preserved
set rulebase nat rules LAN-to-Partner-VPN from trust to vpn-partner source NET_LAN_USERS destination NET_PARTNER_SRV service any
set rulebase nat rules LAN-to-Partner-VPN source-translation static-ip translated-address NET_ASSIGNED bi-directional no

# security: pre-NAT source, post-NAT zone
set rulebase security rules Allow-LAN-Partner from trust to vpn-partner source NET_LAN_USERS destination NET_PARTNER_SRV application any service application-default action allow

# route to the partner servers via the tunnel
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route PARTNER-SRV destination 192.168.50.0/24 interface tunnel.1

# proxy-ID must name the TRANSLATED local range
set network tunnel ipsec IPSEC_PARTNER auto-key proxy-id PID-1 local 172.31.99.0/24 remote 192.168.50.0/24 protocol any

commit description "SNAT: LAN presented as 172.31.99.0/24 to partner"
exit

Web interface

  1. Policies › NAT › Add: trust → vpn-partner, source NET_LAN_USERS, destination NET_PARTNER_SRV; Translated Packet Static IP → NET_ASSIGNED.
  2. Policies › Security: trust → vpn-partner, source NET_LAN_USERS (the real subnet).
  3. Network › Virtual Routers › default › Static Routes: 192.168.50.0/24 → interface tunnel.1.
  4. Network › IPSec Tunnels › IPSEC_PARTNER › Proxy IDs: Local 172.31.99.0/24, Remote 192.168.50.0/24, Protocol any.
  5. Agree the proxy-IDs with the partner, then Commit.

Your pen-pal's school already has a kid with your name. So you agree to sign your letters with a nickname. Everything they see uses the nickname; inside your own school you keep your real name.

Proxy-IDs must match exactly on both ends, and if the partner's device is policy-based, a mismatch stops phase 2 from coming up at all. Change both sides in the same window.

How DIPP stretches one public address

DIPP can reuse the same translated address and port in several concurrent sessions — 2, 4 or 8 times, depending on the platform — on the assumption that the sessions go to different destinations and so remain unique.

# pool size, memory and oversubscription ratio per rule
show running ippool
show running nat-rule-ippool rule LAN-to-Internet
Oversubscription Ratio: 2
Number of Allocates: 9327

show counter global filter delta yes | match nat
OptionWhat it buys you
Add translated addresses to the ruleMore address/port pairs; up to 256 translated addresses per NAT rule
Split heavy sources onto their own rule and addressOne noisy application stops starving the rest
Oversubscription rate (Device › Setup › Session › Session Settings › NAT Oversubscription Rate)Platform Default, 1x, 2x, 4x or 8x; higher = more reuse per pair

One mailbox can be shared a little more if the letters go to different towns, because the postman never mixes them up. It only gets crowded when everyone writes to the same town at the same time.

When a letter gets lost, check in order: did you post it (commit)? Is there a road (route)? Which address was written (NAT)? Was it allowed out (security)? Did it actually leave (session, capture)? The first "no" is where it got lost.

NAT · Source NATPITFALLS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Ten things that catch people out

  1. Forgetting to commit. The candidate config looks right; the firewall is running the old one.
  2. A NAT rule without a security rule. NAT never allows traffic on PAN-OS.
  3. Security rule written with translated addresses. For SNAT it uses the real internal source.
  4. Rule order. NAT is first-match; a broad rule above yours takes the traffic.
  5. Old sessions. Clear them after changing NAT.
  6. Translated address outside the interface subnet. No proxy ARP, so the upstream router needs a route.
  7. Multiple IPs on the egress interface. Specify which one DIPP should use.
  8. Bi-directional static NAT ticked by habit. It publishes the host inbound.
  9. Proxy-IDs still naming the real subnet after introducing VPN NAT.
  10. Committing someone else's half-finished change. Check pending changes before every commit.

A Zone Can't Reach the Internet

time-box 10 minR: default routeA: DIPPP: rule + App-ID
  1. Can the firewall get out from the dataplane? ping source 203.0.113.10 host 8.8.8.8.
  2. R: test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip 8.8.8.8 returns the WAN interface? Also check PBF.
  3. A: test nat-policy-match from <zone> to UNTRUST source <client> destination 8.8.8.8 protocol 6 destination-port 443 returns the source-NAT rule. In the session, flag NS and the translated source.
  4. P: test security-policy-match from <zone> to UNTRUST … returns the allow rule.
  5. Pool health: show running ippool. An exhausted DIPP pool only affects some users.
NAT · U-Turn NATOVERVIEW ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

U-Turn NAT at a Glance

A user in the office opens https://app.example.com. DNS answers 203.0.113.11, the public address of a server in the DMZ. PAN-OS calls the fix U-Turn NAT (Fortinet calls it hairpin): the request goes to the firewall and turns straight back inside. Three scenarios, one alternative that often beats them all, and the commands for when it fails. Same lab as the PAN-OS SNAT and DNAT guides: trust ethernet1/2 10.10.10.0/24, dmz ethernet1/3 with web01 10.10.20.40, public 203.0.113.11.

NAT · U-Turn NATCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Why the published server doesn't work from inside

The DNAT rule from the DNAT guide is untrust → untrust. An office user's packet arrives in zone trust, so that rule never matches it. Without a rule written for trust users, the packet follows the default route towards the internet, usually through the general outbound source NAT rule, and dies.

Missing pieceWhat happens without it
A NAT rule from trust to untrust with the public destinationNo destination translation for internal users
That rule placed above the general trust → untrust source NAT ruleThe general rule matches first and sends it to the internet
Source translation on the same rule (when needed)Server replies straight to the client, which drops the reply
A security rule trust → dmz, destination the public IPNAT decided, then denied by policy

You're inside the school and you post a letter to the school's own street address. The mailroom has to be told: "letters from inside, addressed to us, go straight to Room 40". Otherwise the letter travels all the way to the post office and gets lost.

NAT · U-Turn NATTHE KEY IDEA ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Why U-turn usually needs source NAT as well

Where the server sitsDoes the reply come back via the firewall?Source NAT on the U-turn rule?
Different zone (dmz), server's gateway is the firewallYesOptional — recommended (Scenario A)
Same zone and subnet as the clientsNo — the server talks to the client directlyMandatory (Scenario B)
Behind another router with a direct path to clientsOften noMandatory

If Room 40 answers by walking straight across the hall to you, you won't recognise the answer, because you were waiting for a reply from the office. So the office pretends it asked the question. Room 40 answers the office, and the office hands the answer to you.

NAT · U-Turn NATPAN-OS TRAP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Rule order: the outbound DIPP rule steals U-turn traffic

The U-turn rule and the everyday internet rule have the same zones (trust → untrust) because the public address routes out of untrust. NAT is first-match, so whichever is higher wins.

The mailroom reads its list from the top. If "send everything to the post office" is written first, it never reaches "walk letters for Room 40". Put the special instruction at the top.

The reverse trap exists too. If your inbound DNAT rule was written with source zone any instead of untrust, it will also match trust users — performing DNAT without source NAT. That breaks the same-zone case. Keep inbound DNAT rules at source zone untrust and give internal users their own U-turn rule.

NAT · U-Turn NATWHY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Scenario A — office users reach the DMZ web server by its public name

Staff and bookmarks use app.example.com, which resolves to 203.0.113.11. The server sits in dmz, a different zone from the users. One U-turn rule translates both addresses so the conversation is symmetric.

Your tablet works at home and at school with the same web address. You never have to remember two names.

NAT · U-Turn NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — one NAT rule translating both ways, one security rule

CLI

configure
# NAT: source zone = clients (trust), destination zone = zone of the PUBLIC IP (untrust)
set rulebase nat rules U-Turn-Web from trust to untrust source NET_LAN_USERS destination PUB_WEB service service-https
set rulebase nat rules U-Turn-Web destination-translation translated-address SRV_WEB01
# source NAT to the firewall's dmz interface, so web01 replies to the firewall
set rulebase nat rules U-Turn-Web source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/3
move rulebase nat rules U-Turn-Web top

# Security: trust → dmz (post-NAT zone), destination = PUBLIC address (pre-NAT)
set rulebase security rules Allow-UTurn-Web from trust to dmz source NET_LAN_USERS destination PUB_WEB application [ ssl web-browsing ] service application-default action allow

commit description "U-turn NAT: trust users to web01 via 203.0.113.11"
exit

Web interface

  1. Policies › NAT › Add → Original Packet: Source Zone trust, Destination Zone untrust, Destination Address PUB_WEB, Service HTTPS.
  2. Translated Packet: Source Address Translation Dynamic IP And Port → Interface Address → ethernet1/3; Destination Address Translation Static IP → SRV_WEB01.
  3. Move › Move Top so it sits above LAN-to-Internet.
  4. Policies › Security › Add: trust → dmz, Destination PUB_WEB, Application ssl / web-browsing → Commit.

Source NAT is technically optional here, because web01's gateway is the firewall and the reply returns through it anyway. Palo Alto's own U-turn example translates only the destination for this layout. Keep source NAT if you want one design that also survives future routing changes; drop it if the server team needs real client IPs in their logs.

Choose the source NAT interface on the server's side (ethernet1/3). Using the trust interface address would make web01 reply to 10.10.10.1, which it reaches via the firewall anyway, but the address it logs is less meaningful and harder to recognise.

Scenario B — client and server in the same zone and subnet

A small site has no DMZ. The NAS 10.10.10.60 in trust is published as 203.0.113.14:5001, and office users reach it on that address from the mobile app. The traffic enters and leaves on ethernet1/2. This is exactly the layout of Palo Alto's own U-turn example.

NAT · U-Turn NATCLI + GUI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Config — source NAT to the trust interface is mandatory

CLI

configure
set address PUB_NAS ip-netmask 203.0.113.14/32
set address SRV_NAS ip-netmask 10.10.10.60/32
set service tcp-5001 protocol tcp port 5001

set rulebase nat rules U-Turn-NAS from trust to untrust source NET_LAN_USERS destination PUB_NAS service tcp-5001
set rulebase nat rules U-Turn-NAS destination-translation translated-address SRV_NAS
set rulebase nat rules U-Turn-NAS source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/2
move rulebase nat rules U-Turn-NAS top

# security: trust → trust (the NAS lives in trust), destination = public IP
set rulebase security rules Allow-UTurn-NAS from trust to trust source NET_LAN_USERS destination PUB_NAS application any service tcp-5001 action allow

commit description "U-turn NAT: trust users to NAS via 203.0.113.14"
exit

Web interface

  1. NAT rule: trust → untrust, destination PUB_NAS, service tcp-5001.
  2. Translated Packet: Source Dynamic IP And Port, Interface Address ethernet1/2; Destination Static IP SRV_NAS. Move to top.
  3. Security rule: trust → trust, destination PUB_NAS. Commit.

Intrazone traffic (trust → trust) is allowed by PAN-OS's default intrazone-default rule, so it may appear to work without an explicit rule. Write one anyway: it gives you logging, security profiles, and a rule you can find later.

Room 40 will now think every question comes from the office. That's fine, but it can't tell which kid asked any more.

Scenario C — the public address is routed to you, not configured on an interface

Config — same pattern, confirm the zone with a route lookup

# which zone does the routed public address fall into? (default route → untrust)

configure
set address PUB_PORTAL ip-netmask 198.18.50.10/32

Web interface

  1. Same NAT rule as Scenario A with PUB_PORTAL / SRV_PORTAL; destination zone = the zone the route lookup returned.
  2. Security rule trust → dmz, destination PUB_PORTAL. Move to top, commit.

If the public block is routed to a zone other than untrust (for example a dedicated "public-servers" zone with a static route to null or a loopback), the NAT to-zone is that zone. Always write it from test routing fib-lookup, never from memory.

Scenario D — skip U-turn: give internal users the private address

If internal DNS answers app.example.com with 10.10.20.40, users go straight to the server through a normal trust → dmz rule. No double NAT, and the server logs keep real client IPs. Palo Alto's community experts routinely recommend this over U-turn where it's possible.

U-turn NATSplit DNS

Config — a static entry on the firewall's DNS proxy

If Active Directory DNS hosts example.com internally, add an A record there and you're done. If clients use the firewall as their DNS server, add a static entry to its DNS proxy.

CLI

configure
set network dns-proxy DNSP-LAN enabled yes
set network dns-proxy DNSP-LAN interface ethernet1/2
set network dns-proxy DNSP-LAN default primary 10.10.1.53
set network dns-proxy DNSP-LAN static-entries APP-INTERNAL domain app.example.com address 10.10.20.40
# DNS proxy is documented through the web interface; confirm these keywords with tab completion on your release
set rulebase security rules Allow-Web-Internal from trust to dmz source NET_LAN_USERS destination SRV_WEB01 application [ ssl web-browsing ] service application-default action allow
commit description "Split DNS: app.example.com → 10.10.20.40 for trust"
exit

Web interface

  1. Network › DNS Proxy › Add: Name DNSP-LAN, Interfaces ethernet1/2, Primary server 10.10.1.53.
  2. Static Entries tab: Name APP-INTERNAL, FQDN app.example.com, Address 10.10.20.40.
  3. A normal trust → dmz security rule to the private address (no NAT involved).
  4. Make sure DHCP hands out 10.10.10.1 as DNS to trust clients → Commit.
PC-01> ipconfig /flushdns
PC-01> nslookup app.example.com
Address: 10.10.20.40

The easiest trick of all: tell the kids the inside room number in the first place. Then nobody has to walk to the office and back.

QuestionCommand

Look at the little sticker on the letter. NS means only the sender's name changed. ND means only the address changed. NB means both changed, and that's the one you want for a U-turn.

NAT · U-Turn NATPITFALLS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · PA-EDGE

Eight things that catch people out

  1. U-turn rule below the outbound DIPP rule. Same zones; first match wins.
  2. Inbound DNAT rule with source zone any. It catches internal users and skips source NAT.
  3. NAT to-zone set to dmz. It's the zone of the public IP (untrust).
  4. Security rule destination set to the private IP. It's the public, pre-NAT address.
  5. No source NAT in the same-zone case. Guaranteed asymmetric failure.
  6. Relying on intrazone-default for trust → trust. Write an explicit rule for logging and profiles.
  7. Old sessions and DNS caches after the change — clear both before re-testing.
  8. Server ACLs by client IP. With source NAT every internal user looks like the firewall.
NAT · U-Turn NATSCENARIO ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

U-Turn NAT: Internal Users on the Public IP

A DC client (10.10.10.60) resolves the web server's public name to 203.0.113.80. The inbound rule WEB-DNAT only matches from UNTRUST, so without a U-turn rule the request is source-NAT'd out to the internet and never reaches the server.

Because client and server share the DC subnet, the U-turn rule must translate both addresses. If it only translated the destination, the server would reply directly to the client and the client would discard a reply from an address it never contacted.

// NAT zones = pre-NAT: the public IP routes to UNTRUST
set rulebase nat rules UTURN-WEB from DC to UNTRUST source any destination 203.0.113.80 service service-https
set rulebase nat rules UTURN-WEB source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/3
set rulebase nat rules UTURN-WEB destination-translation translated-address 10.10.10.80
move rulebase nat rules UTURN-WEB before DC-SNAT
commit
// security: pre-NAT destination IP, post-NAT zone DC → DC (intrazone, allowed by default)
test security-policy-match from DC to DC source 10.10.10.60 destination 203.0.113.80 protocol 6 destination-port 443
What each line does

Purpose: Lets DC clients reach the web server through its public IP, by translating both destination and source so the reply returns through the firewall.

nat rules UTURN-WEB from DC to UNTRUST
Pre-NAT zones: the client is in DC, and the public IP routes to UNTRUST.
destination 203.0.113.80 service service-https
Matches internal users hitting the public address on 443.
source-translation dynamic-ip-and-port interface-address interface ethernet1/3
Source NAT to the firewall's DC address (10.10.10.1). The server then replies to the firewall, not directly to the client in the same subnet.
destination-translation translated-address 10.10.10.80
Rewrites the public IP to the real server.
move rulebase nat rules UTURN-WEB before DC-SNAT
NAT rules are first match. The specific U-turn rule must sit above the general outbound rule.
test security-policy-match from DC to DC … destination 203.0.113.80
Confirms permission: pre-NAT IP, post-NAT zone DC → DC (intrazone, allowed by default).
MistakeSymptom
U-turn rule below the outbound DIPP ruleOutbound rule matches first, and flow_policy_nat_land or a hairpin to the internet follows.
Destination translation only, same subnetSYN reaches the server, SYN-ACK goes straight to the client, connection fails.
NAT zones set DC → DCNever matches: the pre-NAT destination routes to UNTRUST.

When the client is in a different zone from the server (e.g. TRUST clients, DC server), destination translation alone is enough, because replies already route back through the firewall. The rule then goes from TRUST to UNTRUST with only destination translation, placed above the outbound rule.

Sessions & Flow TracingSESSIONS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The Session Table

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show session infoTotals — active, allocated, packet rate, throughput, and the configured maximum.Dashboard > Session Information
show session allEvery session. On a production box this is unusable without a filter.Monitor > Session Browser
show session all filter source <ip> destination <ip> destination-port <p>Filter by 5-tuple. This is the one you will use.Session Browser (filter row)

Sample — a single session in detail

admin@fw-01(active)> show session id 84213
Session          84213
        c2s flow:
                source:      10.10.20.55 [Trust]
                dst:         203.0.113.90
                proto:       6
                sport:       51022           dport:      443
                state:       ACTIVE          type:       FLOW
                src user:    corp\jsmith
        s2c flow:
                source:      203.0.113.90 [Untrust]
                dst:         198.51.100.2
                sport:       443             dport:      51022

        start time      : Mon Apr 27 14:11:02 2026
        timeout         : 1800 sec
        time to live    : 1774 sec
        c2s octets      : 8842
        s2c octets      : 214905
        application     : ssl
        rule            : Allow-Web-Outbound
        session to be logged at end : True
        nat-rule        : Outbound-PAT (vsys1)
        layer7 processing : completed
What you seeWhat it means
c2s octets > 0, s2c octets = 0One-way traffic. The problem is beyond this firewall — missing upstream NAT, a remote ACL, or return traffic taking a different path.
state INIT in both directionsThe TCP handshake never completed. SYN went out, no SYN-ACK came back.
application: incompleteApp-ID saw packets but could not classify — too few bytes, a very short session, or a non-standard port.
application: undecidedClassification is still in progress. Normal for a young session.
end-reason: aged-outTimed out rather than closing cleanly. Paired with s2c = 0, this confirms a reachability problem downstream.
end-reason: policy-denyExplicitly denied. Go find the rule with test security-policy-match.
end-reason: tcp-rst-from-serverThe server refused. Application or host problem, not a firewall one.

clear session all has no confirmation prompt and no undo. Every established connection through the firewall is torn down. Use a filter — clear session all filter source 10.10.20.55 — or clear by ID.

Sessions & Flow TracingREADING SESSIONS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Session Interpretation Guide

Almost every conclusion in the workflow above comes out of one show session id. This is what the fields mean and where each one sends you next.

What you seeWhat it meansWhere to look next
c2s > 0, s2c = 0One-way traffic. The client sent, the server sent nothing back.Beyond this firewall — upstream NAT, remote ACL or cloud security group, or return-path asymmetry.
State INIT, both directionsThe TCP handshake never completed. SYN out, no SYN-ACK.Next-hop and destination reachability.
Application: incompleteApp-ID saw packets but could not classify — too few bytes, very short session, or non-standard port.Not necessarily an error. Becomes one if App-ID enforcement blocks it after the identification timeout.
Application: undecidedClassification still in progress on a live session.Normal. Investigate only if it stays that way.
End-reason: aged-outTimed out rather than closing cleanly. INIT-state sessions age out in about 5 seconds.Paired with s2c = 0, confirms a downstream reachability problem.
End-reason: policy-denyExplicitly denied by a rule.test security-policy-match to name the rule.
End-reason: tcp-rst-from-serverThe server actively refused.Application or host, not the firewall.
End-reason: tcp-rst-from-clientThe client gave up and reset.Usually a timeout on the client side. Check what it was waiting for.
Translated address = original addressNo NAT applied on this box.Expected for internal-to-internal; a finding for private-to-public.

incomplete in the traffic log with Bytes Received: 0 is the same signal seen from the log side, and it is the fastest fleet-wide version of this check — filter Monitor > Logs > Traffic for it in Panorama and the Device Name column tells you which firewall handled the flow.

Sessions & Flow TracingWORKFLOW ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Tracing a Flow End to End — The Order That Works

"Traffic is not getting through" is not a diagnosis, it is a starting position. This sequence takes it apart in the order the firewall itself processes a packet, and each step feeds the next. Worked throughout on one real flow: 10.10.20.55 attempting to reach 203.0.113.90:20100.

StepQuestionCommand
1Where does the source enter?test routing fib-lookup ... ip <source>
2Where does it leave for the destination?test routing fib-lookup ... ip <destination>
3What zones are those interfaces in?show interface all | match <interface>
4Does policy allow it?test security-policy-match ...
5Is it being translated?test nat-policy-match ...
6Is traffic flowing right now?show session all filter ...
7What does the session say?show session id <id>
8Are packets physically arriving and leaving?debug dataplane packet-diag ...
9Which counter is incrementing?show counter global filter ... delta yes

Steps 1 to 5 cost nothing, generate no traffic and touch no CPU. Most faults are found before step 6. People reach for packet capture first because it feels thorough; it is actually the slowest way to answer questions the firewall will simply tell you.

Sessions & Flow TracingSTEPS 1-3 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Steps 1–3 — Interfaces and Zones

Step 1 — where does the source enter?

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 10.10.20.55 ✎ /32 removed: the command takes an IP address
   interface  ethernet1/3.20
   nexthop    0.0.0.0
   source     10.10.20.1
   flags      uh

The source sits behind ethernet1/3.20. That is the ingress interface, and you now have it without asking anyone.

Step 2 — where does it leave?

admin@fw-01(active)> test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 203.0.113.90
   interface  ethernet1/1
   nexthop    198.51.100.1
   source     198.51.100.2
   metric     10

Egress is ethernet1/1 via 198.51.100.1. Note that the source is RFC 1918 and the destination is public — NAT has to happen somewhere, and step 5 will tell you whether it happens here.

Step 3 — what zones are those?

admin@fw-01(active)> show interface all | match ethernet1/3.20
ethernet1/3.20   258   1   Trust    vr:default   20   10.10.20.1/24

admin@fw-01(active)> show interface all | match ethernet1/1
ethernet1/1      16    1   Untrust  vr:default   0    198.51.100.2/30

You now have Trust → Untrust, which is what steps 4 and 5 need. Supplying the wrong zones to test security-policy-match produces a confident, wrong answer — usually "no rule matched" — which is why the zones are derived here rather than assumed.

Sessions & Flow TracingSTEPS 4-5 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Steps 4–5 — Security Policy and NAT

Step 4 — will the firewall allow it?

admin@fw-01(active)> test security-policy-match source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90 destination-port 20100 protocol 6 from Trust to Untrust
"Factory-Telemetry-Egress" {
        from Trust;
        source any;
        to Untrust;
        destination any;
        application/service [ ssl/tcp/any/20100 ];
        action allow;
        terminal yes;
}

Allowed, by a named rule, covering the right port. Policy is not the problem — move on.

Step 5 — is anything being translated?

admin@fw-01(active)> test nat-policy-match source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90 destination-port 20100 protocol 6 from Trust to Untrust
No nat-policy

This is the finding. An RFC 1918 source heading for a public destination with no NAT rule on this firewall means the packet leaves with 10.10.20.55 intact. Either something upstream translates it, or the return traffic has nowhere to come back to. Go and confirm on the next-hop device — the firewall has just told you it is not the one doing the translation.

ResultNext move
A rule with action allow and a NAT rule that translatesBoth fine. Go to step 6.
A rule with action denyFound it. Read that rule.
No security rule returnedDefault interzone deny. Re-check the zones from step 3 before concluding a rule is missing.
No nat-policy with a private source and public destinationNAT is upstream, or absent. Verify on the next hop.
Sessions & Flow TracingSTEPS 6-7 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Steps 6–7 — Sessions and What They Reveal

admin@fw-01(active)> show session all filter source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90 destination-port 20100
ID     Application  State  Type  Src[Sport]/Zone/Proto (translated IP[Port])
                                 Dst[Dport]/Zone (translated IP[Port])
91204  incomplete   INIT   FLOW  10.10.20.55[44118]/Trust/6  (10.10.20.55[44118])
                                 203.0.113.90[20100]/Untrust (203.0.113.90[20100])
91188  incomplete   INIT   FLOW  10.10.20.55[44102]/Trust/6  (10.10.20.55[44102])
                                 203.0.113.90[20100]/Untrust (203.0.113.90[20100])

Two things stand out immediately. The translated source equals the original source — confirming step 5's No nat-policy finding on the wire. And the state is INIT with incomplete App-ID, meaning the client keeps trying and the handshake never finishes. Repeated session IDs with rising source ports are retries.

admin@fw-01(active)> show session id 91204
Session          91204
        c2s flow: 10.10.20.55[44118] -> 203.0.113.90[20100]  [Trust]
        s2c flow: 203.0.113.90[20100] -> 10.10.20.55[44118]  [Untrust]
        start time    : Mon Apr 27 15:02:11 2026
        timeout       : 5 sec
        c2s octets    : 132
        s2c octets    : 0                          <-- nothing came back. At all.
        application   : incomplete
        rule          : Factory-Telemetry-Egress
        end-reason    : aged-out

c2s octets > 0 with s2c octets = 0 is close to conclusive: the firewall sent the packet and nothing returned. Combined with aged-out, the fault is beyond this firewall — and given step 5, the missing upstream NAT is the leading candidate. Everything from here is confirmation rather than investigation.

Sessions & Flow TracingSTEPS 8-9 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Steps 8–9 — Proving It on the Wire

Steps 1 to 7 have already produced an answer. Steps 8 and 9 exist to prove it to somebody who owns the upstream router and would prefer not to believe you.

admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set log feature flow basic
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set log on
... reproduce for ~10 seconds ...
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set log off       log off FIRST
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag aggregate-logs
admin@fw-01(active)> less dp-log pan_packet_diag.log
...
Policy lookup, matched rule "Factory-Telemetry-Egress", action allow
NAT policy lookup: no rule matched
Packet transmitted at forwarding stage, egress ethernet1/1       <-- it left, untranslated
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all

Step 9 — the counters, for completeness

admin@fw-01(active)> show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes
name                     value  rate  severity  category  aspect   description
pkt_recv                    18     1  info      packet    pktproc  Packets received
pkt_sent                    18     1  info      packet    pktproc  Packets transmitted
session_installed            6     0  info      session   resource Sessions installed
                                        no drop counters at all — the firewall is not the problem

Received equals transmitted, and there is not a single drop counter in the output. The firewall did exactly what it was asked to do, forwarded the packet unchanged, and never saw a reply. That is a finished piece of work — hand it to whoever owns 198.51.100.1.

Sessions & Flow TracingPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

Route Changed, but Traffic Still Uses the Old Path

time-box 10 minsessions

The egress interface is decided for the first packet and stored with the session. Long-lived sessions keep their old egress after a route change, failover or new PBF rule.

test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-wan ip 10.10.2.20      // the new path
show session all filter destination 10.10.2.20                     // the old sessions
show session id <id>                                                 // check "egress interface" and start time
clear session id <id>                                                // clear one
clear session all filter destination 10.10.2.20                   // clear only matching sessions

clear session all without a filter drops every session on the firewall. Always run show session all filter … with the same filter first.

Debug & CaptureMAP ✓ checked vs PAN docs

Which Tool Answers Which Question

QuestionTool
Where would it go?test routing fib-lookup · test pbf-policy-match
Which NAT / security rule?test nat-policy-match · test security-policy-match
Did a session form, and in which state?show session all filter … · show session id
Why was it dropped?Packet-diag filter + show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes
Where exactly did it stop?Stage captures: receive, firewall, transmit, drop
What did the dataplane decide, step by step?Packet-diag flow basic log
Why is the tunnel or neighbour down?mp-log ikemgr.log · system log · show routing protocol …

The tests are the planning office ("where would this go?"), the session table is the visitor log, counters are the reasons stamped on rejected parcels, and stage captures are CCTV at each door of the building.

The logs worth knowing by name

LogCovers

less mp-log ha_agent.logHA transitions, link and path monitoring.

Live-tail the relevant log in one window and trigger the thing in another. Reading a log after the fact tells you what happened; watching it as you trigger the event tells you what happened because of what you just did, which is a much shorter path to an answer.

Debug & CaptureCOUNTERS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Counter-Driven Debugging

With a packet-diag filter armed, the global counters become flow-specific. This pairing — a narrow filter plus packet-filter yes delta yes — is the quickest route from "traffic is disappearing" to a named reason, and it costs far less CPU than Flow Basic.

CommandDescription / usage
show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yesOnly counters incremented by packets matching the filter. The most targeted view available.
show counter global filter delta yes severity dropEvery increasing drop counter on the box, filter or no filter.
show counter global filter category <cat> delta yesFilter by process category — flow, ssl, dfa, pktproc, nat, appid.
show counter global filter aspect <aspect> delta yesFilter by processing stage — parse, session, forward, pktproc, resource, offload, mgmt.
show counter global | match tcp_dropTCP-specific drop events.
show counter global | match flow_no_routeFIB misses.
admin@fw-01(active)> show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes
Global counters:
Elapsed time since last sampling: 12.402 seconds

name                     value  rate  severity  category  aspect   description
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
pkt_recv                    24     2  info      packet    pktproc  Packets received
flow_policy_deny            24     2  drop      flow      session  Session setup: denied by policy
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Total counters shown: 2

Two lines, and the case is closed: 24 packets arrived and all 24 were denied by policy. No Flow Basic, no pcap, no CPU cost worth mentioning. Reach for this before reaching for Flow Basic — a large share of "silent drop" tickets end here.

Remember that severity takes drop and aspect does not. filter aspect drop delta yes is a common copy-paste error that returns nothing and looks like the box is healthy.

Debug & CaptureWORKED SAMPLE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Worked Sample — Source, Destination, Filter, Delta

This is the whole counter technique on one page, run against a single pair of addresses. The complaint: 10.10.20.55 cannot reach 203.0.113.90 on TCP/443. Nothing in the traffic log. Four commands answer it.

Step 1 — Arm the filter on the two addresses

Index 1 is the client-to-server direction. Add index 2 reversed so return traffic is caught too — without it you are only seeing half the conversation, and a return-path fault looks identical to a forward-path fault.

admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90 destination-port 443
c2s direction — filter index 1
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 203.0.113.90 destination 10.10.20.55 source-port 443
s2c direction — filter index 2
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
nothing is filtered until this line runs
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag show setting
Packet filter
  Enabled:                   yes
  Match pre-parsed packet:   no
Index 1: 10.10.20.55[0]->203.0.113.90[443], proto 0
         ingress-interface any, egress-interface any, exclude non-IP
Index 2: 203.0.113.90[443]->10.10.20.55[0], proto 0
         ingress-interface any, egress-interface any, exclude non-IP

set filter on is a separate command from set filter match. Defining the match without turning the filter on is the single most common reason this workflow "shows nothing" — always confirm with show setting before you trust an empty result.

Step 2 — Clear the counters so the delta means something

admin@fw-01(active)> show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes
run once and discard — this establishes the baseline

delta yes reports the change since the last time you ran the command, not since boot — so you do not need to clear anything. The first run simply establishes the baseline and is thrown away. Re-run it, then have the user reproduce the failure, then run it a third time — that third output is your evidence.

Step 3 — Reproduce, then read the drop deltas

admin@fw-01(active)> show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes severity drop
Global counters:
Elapsed time since last sampling: 18.114 seconds

name                        value  rate  severity  category  aspect   description
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
flow_rcv_dot1q_tag_err          9     0  drop      flow      parse    Packets dropped: 802.1q tag not configured
flow_no_interface               9     0  drop      flow      parse    Packets dropped: invalid interface
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Total counters shown: 2

Nine packets in, nine packets dropped at parse — before policy, before session setup, before NAT. The firewall is receiving tagged frames on an interface that has no matching subinterface for that VLAN. This is a configuration or trunk problem on the switch side, not a rulebase problem, and no amount of policy troubleshooting would have found it.

Delta you seeWhat it usually meansWhere to go next
flow_rcv_dot1q_tag_err, flow_no_interfaceVLAN tag arriving with no subinterface for itSwitch trunk config; show interface ethernet1/3
flow_policy_denySecurity policy denied session setuptest security-policy-match
flow_no_routeNo FIB entry for the destinationtest routing fib-lookup
flow_tcp_non_syn_dropMid-stream packet with no session — classic asymmetryAsymmetric Routing group
flow_fwd_l3_mcast_drop, flow_fwd_zonechangeEgress zone differs from the zone the session was built withRoute change or interface move
flow_ipfrag_recv rising with no matching dropFragmentation, usually MTU/tunnel relatedPath-MTU topic
Only pkt_recv, nothing elsePackets arrive and are forwarded cleanly — the fault is not on this firewallCheck the far end or the return path
Nothing at allTraffic is not reaching this box, or the filter is wrongRe-check the filter, then the upstream device

Step 4 — Clean up

admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag show setting
look at the output — do not assume

Filter narrow, clear, reproduce, read the delta. Because the filter is scoped to two addresses, anything that appears in the output was caused by the traffic you care about — there is no busy-firewall noise to argue about. That is what makes this faster than reading logs, and far cheaper than Flow Basic.

Debug & CaptureCLI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Filtered Global Counters: the Drop Reason in Two Commands

Global counters count every event in the dataplane. Filtered by a packet-diag filter and shown as a delta, they show only what happened to your flow since the last run.

debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.2.20
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes      // run once to reset the delta
// reproduce the problem
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes severity drop   // drops only
Drop counterMeansNext check
flow_policy_denyDenied by a security rule or interzone-default.test security-policy-match, pre-NAT IP / post-NAT zone
flow_fwd_l3_norouteNo route.test routing fib-lookup in the right VR
flow_fwd_l3_noarpRoute exists, no ARP reply from next hop or host.show arp on the egress interface
flow_tcp_non_syn_dropNon-SYN TCP without a session.Asymmetric routing: the One Way playbook
flow_fwd_zonechangeForwarded to a different zone than the session.Route or PBF changed mid-session, asymmetry
flow_host_service_denyTraffic to the firewall itself denied.Interface management profile, rules for BGP/IKE
flow_no_interfaceInvalid ingress interface (no zone / VR).Interface config
flow_fwd_mtu_exceededPacket larger than egress MTU.MTU/MSS playbook
flow_policy_nat_landSource NAT caused a LAND situation.U-turn NAT order and translation

Check pkt_recv in the filtered output. If it doesn't increase while you reproduce, the packets aren't reaching this firewall, or the filter doesn't match them. Before enabling a capture, a very high pkt_recv rate means the filter is too broad.

Debug & CaptureCLI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Stage Captures: Receive, Firewall, Transmit, Drop

Packet captures are taken on the dataplane at four stages. Comparing them shows exactly where a packet stopped.

debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.20.15 destination-port 443 protocol 6
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage receive file rx.pcap
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage firewall file fw.pcap
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage transmit file tx.pcap
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage drop file drop.pcap
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture on
// reproduce, then:
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture off
view-pcap filter-pcap rx.pcap
view-pcap filter-pcap tx.pcap
view-pcap filter-pcap drop.pcap

How the stages use the filter (per Palo Alto's docs): the receive stage copies individual packets that match the filter, while the firewall, drop and transmit stages mark new sessions that match it and then capture both directions of those sessions. So a session that already existed when you started is not captured at those stages, and offloaded packets never reach the dataplane CPU. Clear the matching session (clear session id <id>) before capturing, so the next packets build a fresh, marked session. ✎ clarified The same settings are available in the GUI under Monitor → Packet Capture, where the pcaps can be downloaded.

Debug & CapturePCAP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Dataplane Packet Capture and the Four Stages

Packet capture uses the same filter as Flow Basic but writes pcap files instead of a text log. The four stages are what make it diagnostic rather than merely informative: comparing which stages a packet appears in localises the drop precisely.

StageCapturesMissing here means
receiveJust after ingress, before parsing.The packet never arrived. Look upstream.
firewallAfter policy lookup.Dropped between ingress and policy — parse error, no session, no route.
transmitLeaving the dataplane.Dropped between policy and egress — policy deny, NAT failure, no ARP for next hop.
dropPackets explicitly discarded.If it appears here, the firewall deliberately dropped it — and the counters will say why.
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage receive file rx.pcap
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage firewall file fw.pcap
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage transmit file tx.pcap
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage drop file drop.pcap
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture on
... reproduce the traffic ...
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture off
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag show setting       confirm everything is off
admin@fw-01(active)> view-pcap filter-pcap drop.pcap
admin@fw-01(active)> scp export filter-pcap from drop.pcap to jay@10.10.0.50:/tmp/
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
CommandDescription / usage
debug dataplane packet-diag show settingCurrent filters, stages, log status and captured byte counts. Run this to confirm cleanup actually happened.
view-pcap filter-pcap <file>View a capture on the device.
scp export filter-pcap from <file> to <user>@<ip>:<path>Export for analysis off-box.
scp export packet-capture from <file> to <user>@<ip>:<path>Alternative export form used for GUI-initiated captures.

Pre-Parse Match captures every packet regardless of filter and is extremely heavy. Only enable it when TAC specifically asks — it exists for cases where the problem is in route lookup or a pre-policy stage, before the filter can even be applied.

Debug & CaptureFLOW BASIC ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Flow Basic — The Packet-Path Trace

Flow Basic logs every stage a matched packet passes through inside the dataplane. It is the PAN-OS equivalent of FortiGate's diagnose debug flow, and it is the most powerful thing in this document — and the most capable of hurting a production firewall if you leave it running.

  1. Clear everything first. debug dataplane packet-diag clear all — a leftover filter from someone else's session will silently ruin your results.
  2. Clear the old log. debug dataplane packet-diag clear log log
  3. Set a narrow filter. debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source <ip> destination <ip> — up to four filter indices are supported.
  4. Turn the filter on. debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
  5. Enable the log feature. debug dataplane packet-diag set log feature flow basic
  6. Turn logging on. debug dataplane packet-diag set log on — CPU cost starts here.
  7. Reproduce the traffic. Keep it to seconds, not minutes.
  8. Log off FIRST. debug dataplane packet-diag set log off
  9. Then filter off. debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off
  10. Aggregate. debug dataplane packet-diag aggregate-logs merges the per-core logs.
  11. Read it. less dp-log pan_packet_diag.log
  12. Clean up. debug dataplane packet-diag clear all

Step 8 before step 9, always. If you turn the filter off while logging is still on, the firewall briefly logs every packet on the box — because with no filter, everything matches. On a busy firewall that is a CPU spike and a flood of useless log. Log off, then filter off. Every time.

Sample — reading the output

admin@fw-01(active)> less dp-log pan_packet_diag.log
== 2026-04-27 14:41:02.118 ==
Packet received at ingress stage, tag 0, type ORDERED
Packet info: len 74 port 17 interface 258 vsys 1
  wqe index 21044 packet 0x0x80000004d1a2b100
Packet decoded dump:
L2:    00:50:56:aa:00:22->b4:0c:25:aa:10:03, type 0x0800
IP:    10.10.20.55->203.0.113.90, protocol 6
TCP:   sport 51022, dport 443, flags 0x02 (SYN)
Session setup: vsys 1
PBF lookup (vsys 1) with application none
Session setup: ingress interface ethernet1/3.20 egress interface ethernet1/1
Policy lookup, matched rule index 14, rule "Allow-Web-Outbound"
Session setup: rule "Allow-Web-Outbound" action allow
NAT policy lookup, matched rule "Outbound-PAT"
Session allocated 84213
Packet transmitted at forwarding stage              <-- it left. Problem is downstream.
Line to look forTells you
Packet received at ingress stageThe packet reached the firewall at all. If this is missing, nothing is arriving — look upstream.
Session setup: ingress ... egress ...Both interfaces the firewall chose. Wrong egress means routing, not policy.
Policy lookup, matched rule ...The exact rule. Named right here, no guessing.
Session setup: ... action denyDenied by policy. You have the rule name on the line above.
NAT policy lookup, matched rule ...Which NAT rule applied, if any.
Packet dropped / discardedRead the reason on the same line, then confirm with show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes.
Packet transmitted at forwarding stageIt left the firewall. Whatever is wrong is beyond this box.

Flow Basic is a body camera on one packet. Everything else in this guide tells you the state of the firewall; this tells you what happened to your traffic, in order, with the rule names written down.

Debug & CaptureHARDWARE OFFLOAD ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Hardware Offload — and Why Your Capture Goes Quiet

If you have come from FortiGate you already know this problem by a different name. On a FortiGate, once a session is offloaded to the NP ASIC, diagnose sniffer packet stops showing you packets — the traffic is flying past the CPU entirely, and you have to set auto-asic-offload disable on the policy before the sniffer becomes truthful again.

Palo Alto has exactly the same behaviour, and exactly the same trap. The mechanism is different — an FPGA rather than a purpose-built NP ASIC — but the operational consequence is identical: offloaded traffic does not appear in a PAN-OS packet capture, because captures are taken strictly in the dataplane CPU and offloaded packets never visit it.

What offload actually is

Once the slow path is finished with a session — the application is identified, the policy verdict is in, and there is nothing left that requires the CPU to look at every byte — the session can be handed to the offload processor. From that moment the FPGA forwards the remaining packets: it applies the NAT rewrite, updates the counters, checks the sequence numbers, and pushes the packet out. The dataplane CPU is not involved and does not see them.

Picture a supervisor who checks the first few items on a production line, decides the batch is fine, and then waves the rest straight through a side door. The goods still get out — but the CCTV camera is pointed at the supervisor's desk, so the footage shows almost nothing. Your packet capture is that camera.

Which platforms this applies to

Offload is an FPGA feature and only exists on the larger chassis. Palo Alto documents it as supported on the PA-3200, PA-5200, PA-5450, PA-7000 and PA-7500 Series. The PA-220, PA-400 Series and VM-Series have no offload hardware — on those, everything is software and your capture always sees the whole flow. That is worth knowing before you spend an afternoon chasing a capture problem on a PA-440 that cannot have one.

What gets offloaded

Traffic typeWhy it is a candidate
Encrypted traffic that is not being decrypted (SSL, SSH)The firewall cannot inspect the payload anyway, so there is nothing for the CPU to do.
Network control protocols — LACP, OSPF, BGP, RIPWell-known, high-rate, no content inspection value.
Application override sessionsYou have explicitly told the firewall to stop doing App-ID on them.
Terminating applications, once identifiedApp-ID has finished and no further decoding is required.

The pattern behind all four rows: offload happens when inspection is finished or was never going to happen. A session under active threat scanning or SSL decryption stays on the CPU, which is also why a heavily-inspected firewall shows a much lower offload rate than a lightly-inspected one.

Advantages

  • Throughput. The datasheet numbers for large-packet, low-inspection traffic assume offload is working. Turning it off drops real capacity substantially.
  • Latency. Hardware forwarding is far more predictable than software forwarding on a busy CPU.
  • CPU headroom. Elephant flows — backups, replication, file transfers — stop consuming dataplane cores, leaving them for sessions that actually need inspection.
  • Session capacity. More concurrent sessions per box, because their steady state costs almost no CPU.

Disadvantages, which are all troubleshooting disadvantages

  • Packet capture goes blind. The first packets appear, then nothing, even though the connection is clearly working. This looks like the firewall dropped the flow when it did the opposite.
  • Flow Basic logging thins out. Same cause — if the CPU does not see the packet, it cannot log a decision about it.
  • The fix is global by default. Disabling offload affects every session on the box, not just the one you care about. On a busy production firewall that is a real performance event, not a free debug toggle.
  • Counters can look inconsistent. A session's byte counts advance while your capture file stays empty — confusing if you have not met this before.
