  • It hides the interesting half. The packets that are offloaded are, by definition, the ones nothing was inspecting. If your fault lies in the steady state of a long session, offload removes exactly the evidence you need.

Troubleshooting steps

  1. Confirm the box even has offload. Check the model first, then look at what the session table reports. 
    admin@fw-01(active)> show session info
Number of sessions supported:              2097152
Number of active sessions:                 41203
Number of active TCP sessions:             30112
Session table utilization:                 1%
Hardware session offloading:               True
Hardware UDP session offloading:           True
Packet rate:                               84210/s

    If Hardware session offloading reads False, offload is not the reason your capture is empty and you should go back to your filter.

  2. Prefer the surgical option first (PAN-OS 11.1.0 and later). ✎ corrected: was 10.1 Rather than switching offload off for the whole firewall, disable it only for the sessions matching your packet-diag filter. Set the filter as usual, then: 
    admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter offload no
only the filtered sessions stay on the CPU — the rest of the box is untouched

    This is the equivalent of disabling ASIC offload on a single FortiGate policy instead of the whole unit, and it is the right first move on anything carrying production load.

  3. Re-establish the session. Offload is decided when the session is set up, so a session that is already offloaded stays offloaded. Clear it and let the client reconnect, otherwise you will change the setting and still see nothing: 
    admin@fw-01(active)> clear session all filter source 10.10.20.55 destination 203.0.113.90
the new session will honour the new offload setting
  4. If you must go global, use the temporary form. Operational mode, effective immediately, and deliberately not persistent: 
    admin@fw-01(active)> set session offload no
every session now stays on the dataplane CPU

    This does not survive a commit or a reboot — and that is a feature. Any commit, including an automatic one, silently puts offload back. If your capture worked and then went quiet again mid-session, ask who committed.

  5. Only make it persistent if you truly need it across a reboot. 
    admin@fw-01(active)> configure
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig setting session offload no
admin@fw-01(active)# commit

    Reverse it with set deviceconfig setting session offload yes or delete deviceconfig setting session offload, followed by a commit. Put a calendar reminder on this. A firewall left with offload disabled after a debug session is a performance ticket waiting to be raised by someone who has no idea why the box got slower.

  6. Take the capture, then verify you actually put it back. 
    admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter offload yes
admin@fw-01(active)> set session offload yes
admin@fw-01(active)> show session info | match offload
Hardware session offloading:               True
Hardware UDP session offloading:           True
look at the output — do not assume the command worked

⚠ Verification note. Palo Alto's Disable Hardware Offload page documents the operational commands set session offload no / yes, and, from PAN-OS 11.1.0, debug dataplane packet-diag set filter offload no for capture traffic only. The configuration-mode form (set deviceconfig setting session offload) and the "reverts on commit" behaviour described here could not be confirmed in official documentation. Check them with ? on your release before relying on them.

Two commands that look interchangeable are not. set session offload no is operational mode and temporary; set deviceconfig setting session offload no is configuration mode and permanent. Note also that some builds accept set session udp-offload no for UDP only, and some do not — if the CLI rejects it, that is the known platform limitation, not a typo on your part.

One more capture blind spot worth pairing with this: packets discarded during ingress parsing never reach the capture either, for the same reason. So an empty capture has two innocent explanations before you reach "the traffic is not arriving" — it was offloaded, or it was dropped at parse. The global counters cover both, which is why they, not the capture, should be your first stop.

Debug & CaptureMGT CAPTURE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

tcpdump — Management Interface Only

CommandDescription / usage
tcpdump filter "host <ip>"Capture on the MGT interface. Never transit traffic.
tcpdump snaplen 0 filter "not port 22"Full-length capture excluding your own SSH session — otherwise you capture yourself capturing.
view-pcap mgmt-pcap mgmt.pcapView the resulting capture on-box.
admin@fw-01(active)> tcpdump snaplen 0 filter "host 10.10.0.30 and not port 22"
... reproduce, Ctrl-C to stop ...
admin@fw-01(active)> view-pcap mgmt-pcap mgmt.pcap

This is worth stating twice because it costs people entire afternoons: tcpdump on PAN-OS sees management-plane traffic only. Use it for User-ID agent conversations, LDAP, syslog, NTP, update-server traffic and the firewall's own DNS. For anything passing through the firewall, use debug dataplane packet-diag.

Debug & CaptureCLEANUP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Cleanup — Not Optional

Forgetting to clean up after a debug session is the leading cause of a firewall that has been mysteriously slow "since last Tuesday". Everything below should be part of closing the ticket, not something you remember later.

CommandWhy
debug dataplane packet-diag set log offStops Flow Basic logging. Do this before turning the filter off.
debug dataplane packet-diag set capture offStops writing pcap files.
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter offDisarms the filter.
debug dataplane packet-diag clear allRemoves filters, capture stages and log settings entirely.
debug dataplane packet-diag show settingVerify. Do not trust that the previous command worked — look.
debug <process> offEvery daemon whose level you raised.
debug routing global on infoSpecifically the routing daemon, which is easy to forget.
set system setting target-vsys noneIf you scoped your session to a vsys.
set cli config-output-format defaultIf you changed the output format.
admin@fw-01(active)> debug dataplane packet-diag show setting
Packet diagnosis setting:
Packet filter
  Enabled:           no
  Match pre-parsed packet: no
Logging
  Enabled:           no
  Log-throttle:      no
Counters
  Enabled:           no
Packet capture
  Enabled:           no
  Snaplen:           0
  Stage receive     : file rx.pcap  (0 bytes)

Treat packet-diag like a circuit breaker you have racked out. The job is not finished when the fault is found; it is finished when everything is back the way you found it and you have looked to confirm it.

Debug & CaptureRUNBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

One-Flow Capture Pack (Before You Open a Case)

Log the SSH session to a file and run this for the failing flow on every firewall in the path, closest to the source first. It covers the six steps and what support usually asks for first.

show system info
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-wan ip 10.10.2.20
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router vr-wan ip 10.10.1.50
test nat-policy-match from VPN to VPN source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.2.20 protocol 1
test security-policy-match from VPN to VPN source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.2.20 protocol 1
show session all filter source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.2.20
debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.1.50 destination 10.10.2.20
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes
// reproduce
show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off
debug dataplane packet-diag clear all

For support cases, also generate a tech support file (Device → Support) shortly after reproducing, so its logs cover the event.

Asymmetric RoutingSCENARIO ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Two Independent Firewalls, One ECMP Upstream

This is the non-HA case: two firewalls sharing load because an upstream router is doing ECMP across them, with no session synchronisation between them. Outbound SYN goes via FW-A and creates a session there. Return SYN-ACK comes back via FW-B, which has never seen the flow, and drops it. The handshake never completes.

Run every command in this group on both firewalls, ideally at the same time while traffic is flowing. The whole diagnosis rests on comparing the two, and a single-box view of this fault looks completely normal on one of them.

Asymmetric RoutingSTEPS 1-2 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Confirm No HA, Then Compare Routing

Step 1 — is HA genuinely absent?

admin@fw-01> show high-availability all
HA not enabled

admin@fw-02> show high-availability all
HA not enabled

Two independent devices, no session sync, sharing load. That is the precondition for everything below. If HA is enabled, this is a different problem entirely — go and look at HA2 and session synchronisation instead.

Step 2 — do both boxes route the destination the same way?

CommandDescription / usage
show routing route virtual-router <vr-name> destination <ip/mask>The route to the destination in a specific VR. Confirm next hop and egress interface on each box.
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr-name> ip <ip>Which route each firewall would actually select.
admin@fw-01> show routing route virtual-router VR-TRUST destination 10.10.40.10/32
  10.10.40.10/32   10.10.0.33    10  A S   ethernet1/2

admin@fw-01> show routing route virtual-router VR-PEERING destination 10.10.40.10/32
  10.10.40.10/32   vr VR-TRUST   10  A S          leaked between VRs — consistent

In a multi-VR design, check the destination in every VR that could carry the flow. Inconsistent inter-VR leaking between the two firewalls produces the same symptom as upstream ECMP and is worth ruling out before you go and argue with the routing team.

Asymmetric RoutingSTEP 3 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The Session Table Comparison — This Is the Proof

This is the step that confirms the diagnosis. Run the identical filter on both firewalls while the client is actively retrying. Asymmetric routing is proven when the session exists on one box and not the other.

admin@fw-02> show session all filter source 10.10.20.55 destination 10.10.40.10 destination-port 636
ID       Application  State   Type  Src[Sport]/Zone/Proto
2159791  undecided    ACTIVE  FLOW  10.10.20.55[40331]/Trust-Inside
                                    10.10.40.10[636]/Trusted-Peering
2144672  undecided    ACTIVE  FLOW  10.10.20.55[32251]/Trust-Inside
                                    10.10.40.10[636]/Trusted-Peering

admin@fw-01> show session all filter source 10.10.20.55 destination 10.10.40.10 destination-port 636
No Active Sessions                                <-- and yet return traffic is arriving here

FW-02 is handling the conversation. FW-01 has never heard of it. Any packet for that flow reaching FW-01 has nothing to match and is dropped as a non-SYN TCP packet without a session. That is the entire fault, in two commands.

Sessions showing undecided rather than an identified application is expected here — App-ID cannot classify a conversation whose handshake never completed. It is a symptom, not a second problem.

Asymmetric RoutingSTEPS 4-5 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Capture on the Firewall With No Session

Capture on the box that has no session — that is where the return packets are landing and dying. Capturing on the healthy firewall shows you a healthy flow and proves nothing.

admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match source 10.10.20.55 destination 10.10.40.10 destination-port 636
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage receive file asym_rx.pcap
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage firewall file asym_fw.pcap
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage transmit file asym_tx.pcap
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture stage drop file asym_drop.pcap
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter on
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture on
... reproduce ...
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set capture off
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag set filter off
admin@fw-01> scp export filter-pcap from asym_drop.pcap to jay@10.10.0.50:/tmp/
admin@fw-01> debug dataplane packet-diag clear all

What the captures show

ComparisonConclusion
SYN in rx and txForwarded correctly. The problem is downstream of this firewall.
SYN in rx, absent from txThis firewall dropped it. Check policy and NAT.
SYN-ACK in rx with no matching SYNAsymmetric routing confirmed. The session was created on the other firewall.
Return packets in drop.pcapReceived and discarded for want of a session. Same conclusion, stated by the firewall itself.
asym_drop.pcap, opened in Wireshark:
1   10.10.40.10:636 -> 10.10.20.55   [RST]        stale session reset
2   10.10.40.10:636 -> 10.10.20.55   [SYN, ACK]   the LB did respond
3   10.10.40.10:636 -> 10.10.20.55   [SYN, ACK]   retransmit — no ACK came back
4   10.10.40.10:636 -> 10.10.20.55   [SYN, ACK]   retransmit again

The server is responding. FW-01 receives the SYN-ACK, has no session for it, and drops it — so the client never sends the final ACK and the handshake stalls forever. Confirm on the dataplane with show counter global filter delta yes severity drop, where flow_tcp_non_syn_drop will be incrementing on the firewall that has no session.

Asymmetric RoutingSTEP 6 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Confirming From Panorama Logs

The traffic log gives the same answer without touching either CLI, and it scales — you can see the pattern across every affected flow at once.

Monitor > Logs > Traffic, filter:
( addr.src in 10.10.20.55 ) and ( addr.dst in 10.10.40.10 ) and ( port.dst eq 636 )

Result:
Device Name      Application  Bytes Sent  Bytes Received  Type   Session End Reason
site-fw-02       incomplete           66               0   end   aged-out
site-fw-02       incomplete           66               0   end   aged-out
site-fw-02       incomplete           66               0   end   aged-out
ColumnWhat it is telling you
Device NameWhich physical firewall handled the flow. Every entry naming one box means all outbound traffic went that way.
Application: incompleteApp-ID never classified it — the handshake did not finish.
Bytes Received: 0Nothing came back on this firewall. The reply exists; it went to the other one.
Session End Reason: aged-outTimed out waiting rather than closing cleanly.

Three log columns say the same thing the session tables and the pcaps said. That is what makes this diagnosis defensible in a bridge call — four independent views agreeing, none of which require the other team to take your word for anything.

Asymmetric RoutingFIXES ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Root Cause and the Fix Options

Root cause: an upstream router load-balancing across two independent firewalls that share no session state. The outbound SYN creates a session on one; the return SYN-ACK arrives at the other, which has nothing to match it against and drops it.

OptionWhat it doesWhere
1. Flow-based ECMP hashing (best)Configure the upstream router to hash on the 5-tuple — source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol — so a given flow always takes the same firewall. No firewall change required.Upstream router
2. Policy-based routingForce return traffic for specific flows down the same path as the outbound.Upstream router, or Policies > Policy Based Forwarding
3. Static route on the destinationMake the destination host or load balancer return traffic via the specific firewall that handles the inbound direction.Destination host / LB
4. Put the pair into HAWith session synchronisation over HA2, both firewalls share the session table and asymmetry stops mattering.Device > High Availability

Option 4 is a design change, not a fix — it alters the failure domain and the licensing model, and it may not be what the architecture intended. Confirm the intended design with whoever owns it before proposing it. Option 1 solves the immediate problem without touching the firewalls at all, which is why it is first.

Two things make this fault hard to spot from a single box: everything on the healthy firewall looks perfect, and the traffic log on the other one shows sessions that were permitted by policy. Nothing anywhere says "asymmetric routing". The comparison between the two session tables is the only place the fault is visible.

Asymmetric RoutingPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

Works One Way Only, or Non-SYN Drops

time-box 20 minR: asymmetric return

The signature: flow_tcp_non_syn_drop rising in the filtered counters, sessions that never progress past the first packet, or the reply seen on a different firewall or interface. The forward and return paths differ.

  1. Confirm with counters filtered on the flow: flow_tcp_non_syn_drop means a non-SYN packet arrived with no session, i.e. this firewall didn't see the start of the conversation.
  2. Find where the other half goes: run test routing fib-lookup for the source address on each device that could carry the reply.
  3. Check the return route on the far side for the original source (or the SNAT address).
  4. Check PBF and ECMP: a PBF rule without symmetric return, or ECMP across two firewalls, splits directions.

set session tcp-reject-non-syn no makes the symptom go away, but it weakens TCP state checking. Use it only as a short, documented workaround while you fix the routing.

Reading the LogsRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Forwarding Logs to a SIEM / Syslog Server

Use it when the SOC needs firewall logs in the SIEM. Three pieces must line up: a syslog server profile (where to send), a log forwarding profile attached to rules (which traffic/threat logs), and Device > Log Settings (system, config, User-ID, HIP logs).

set shared log-settings syslog SIEM-SYSLOG server SIEM1 server 10.10.40.20 transport UDP port 514 format BSD facility LOG_USER
set shared log-settings profiles LF-SIEM match-list TRAFFIC log-type traffic filter "All Logs" send-syslog SIEM-SYSLOG
set shared log-settings profiles LF-SIEM match-list THREAT log-type threat filter "All Logs" send-syslog SIEM-SYSLOG
set rulebase security rules LAN-TO-INTERNET log-setting LF-SIEM
set rulebase security rules LAN-TO-INTERNET log-end yes
set shared log-settings system match-list SYS-ALL filter "All Logs" send-syslog SIEM-SYSLOG
set shared log-settings config match-list CFG-ALL filter "All Logs" send-syslog SIEM-SYSLOG
set deviceconfig system route service syslog source interface ethernet1/2 address 10.20.0.1/24
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Defines the SIEM as a syslog server, forwards traffic and threat logs from the internet rule, forwards system and config logs, and sends syslog from a dataplane interface that can reach the SIEM.

log-settings syslog SIEM-SYSLOG server … transport UDP port 514 format BSD
The syslog server profile (Device > Server Profiles > Syslog). Up to four servers per profile. TCP or SSL (with certificates) for reliable delivery.
log-settings profiles LF-SIEM match-list TRAFFIC / THREAT … send-syslog
A log forwarding profile (Objects > Log Forwarding): which log types and filters go to which server.
rules LAN-TO-INTERNET log-setting LF-SIEM · log-end yes
The profile only forwards logs from rules it is attached to, and only logs that are generated (log at session end).
log-settings system / config match-list … send-syslog
System and config logs are forwarded from Device > Log Settings, not from rules.
route service syslog source interface ethernet1/2
By default syslog leaves the management interface. A service route sends it from a dataplane interface when the SIEM is only reachable that way.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Logs are generated

show log traffic direction equal backward

Good: Entries for the rule, with the LF-SIEM profile attached. If not: No logs: log-end disabled, or the traffic matches another rule.

2 · Syslog leaves the firewall

show logging-status
tcpdump filter "port 514"
view-pcap mgmt-pcap mgmt.pcap

Good: Syslog packets to 10.10.40.20 (tcpdump captures on the management interface). If not: Nothing on mgmt: check the service route (traffic may leave a dataplane port). Then use packet-diag on that interface.

3 · The SIEM receives and parses

test a syslog with a config change, e.g. commit

Good: The config log arrives at the SIEM. If not: Firewall in between, wrong port/transport, or parsing: check the format (BSD/IETF) and the SIEM's Palo Alto parser.

⚠ Syntax note. Use Tab/? while typing and commit validate before committing. The GUI path is given for every object.

Reading the LogsTRAFFIC LOG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The Traffic Log — Which Columns Actually Tell You Something

Most engineers look at three columns in the traffic log: source, destination, action. Those three tell you almost nothing you did not already know. The columns that solve tickets are the ones people scroll past — bytes in each direction, session end reason, and the NAT fields.

FieldWhat it really meansWhat to notice
Typestart, end, drop, denyA start log with no matching end means the session is still open, or the box lost it. Most rules log at session end only, so a missing log often means the session never ended, not that it never happened.
ActionWhat the firewall did — allow, deny, drop, reset-client, reset-server, reset-bothdeny means a rule matched and denied. drop means discarded silently. reset-* means the firewall actively tore it down — usually a threat or decryption verdict, so go look at those logs next.
RuleThe security rule that matchedIf this says interzone-default you have no rule for that traffic at all. That is a policy gap, not a deny you wrote.
ApplicationWhat App-ID concludedincomplete and not-applicable are diagnoses in themselves — see the byte-pattern topic.
Bytes Sent / Bytes ReceivedClient-to-server and server-to-client, at the firewallThe single most useful pair of numbers in the log. An asymmetry here localises the fault to one direction immediately.
Packets Sent / ReceivedSame, counted in packetsSent climbing while received stays at zero is retransmission — the client is trying repeatedly and nothing is coming back.
Session End ReasonHow the session finishedIts own topic below. This is the field that turns "it didn't work" into a cause.
NAT Source IP / Port, NAT Dest IP / PortThe translated values actually usedBlank or unchanged means no NAT rule matched. This is faster than test nat-policy-match for confirming what happened after the fact.
Elapsed TimeSession duration in secondsNear zero with bytes in both directions is a connect-then-immediately-close pattern. Long elapsed with tiny byte counts is an idle session that eventually aged out.
Repeat CountIdentical sessions collapsed into one log entryA high count on a deny log means something is hammering the firewall, not that it happened once.
Session IDThe key that links every log type togetherTake it from the traffic log and search the threat, URL and decryption logs with it. That correlation is the whole technique.

Read a traffic log line the way a doctor reads a chart, not the way you read a receipt. Action tells you the outcome; the byte counts and the end reason tell you the story that produced it.

Reading the LogsEND REASONS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Session End Reason — Decoded

This one field carries more diagnostic weight than anything else in the traffic log, and almost nobody adds it to their column layout. Add it. Then use this table.

ValueIn human termsWhat to do next
tcp-finBoth ends said goodbye properly. A normal, healthy close.Nothing. If the user still complains, the problem is above the firewall.
tcp-rst-from-clientThe client gave up and sent a reset.Usually an application timeout on the client side, or the client was told to stop by something else.
tcp-rst-from-serverThe server actively refused or aborted.Port closed, service down, or the server did not like what it received. The firewall did its job — go to the server.
aged-outNobody spoke for the length of the idle timeout, so the session was removed.Combine with byte counts. Zero received bytes plus aged-out is the classic "nothing came back" signature.
policy-denyA rule with a deny, drop or reset action matched.Look at the Rule column. If it is interzone-default, you never had a rule.
threatA security profile decided to end the session.Go straight to the threat log with the same session ID. The threat log tells you which signature and which direction.
decrypt-cert-validationDecryption was on and the server certificate failed validation — expired, untrusted issuer, name mismatch, revoked.Decryption log, then check the certificate chain and your trusted CA list.
decrypt-unsupport-paramThe TLS version, cipher suite or extension in use is not one the firewall can decrypt.Decryption log for the exact parameter. Usually the answer is a decryption exclusion for that destination.
decrypt-errorDecryption was attempted and failed for another reason, including resource limits.Check decryption resource usage before assuming it is the site's fault.
tcp-reuseA new SYN arrived matching a session that was already in the table, so the old one was torn down and reused.Seen with fast source-port cycling and with NAT pool pressure. Check show running ippool.
decoderThe protocol decoder saw something malformed or out of spec and ended the session.Often a non-standard application on a standard port, or genuine protocol abuse.
resources-unavailableThe firewall ran out of something — buffers, session slots, proxy resources.This is a capacity event. show running resource-monitor and show session info.
unknownThe firewall never saw a clean end. The session was cleared manually, the box failed over, or the close happened somewhere it could not observe.Suspect asymmetric routing, an HA event, or somebody running clear session.
n/aNot an end log — a start, drop or deny entry.Nothing. It is not an error.

Two of these get misread constantly. aged-out is not a firewall fault — it means the conversation stopped, and the interesting question is why. unknown is not "no information" — it is a strong hint that the firewall lost visibility of the flow, which is exactly what asymmetric routing and failovers produce.

Reading the LogsBYTE PATTERNS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Byte and Packet Patterns — Reading the Shape of a Failure

Pair the byte counts with the end reason and the application, and the traffic log stops being a record of what happened and starts being a diagnosis. These are the shapes you will meet.

Bytes sentBytes receivedUsually also showsWhat it means
Small, fixed (a few hundred)0aged-out, app incompleteThe classic. The client's SYNs left the firewall and nothing ever came back. The firewall is not the problem — the destination, the return route, or something downstream is. Start with test routing fib-lookup on the reply direction.
0 or near 00policy-denyDenied at session setup. Nothing was ever forwarded. Check the Rule column.
SmallSmalltcp-rst-from-server, app incompleteThe handshake completed or nearly completed and the server reset it. Port closed or service not listening. Firewall exonerated.
SubstantialSubstantialtcp-finHealthy session. If the user still reports a problem, it is application-level, not network.
SubstantialStops mid-flowthreat, reset-bothThe firewall killed a working session part-way through. Threat log, same session ID.
SmallSmalldecrypt-*TLS setup failed. The decryption log names the parameter or certificate at fault.
Climbing, packets rising0, packets 0long elapsedRetransmissions. The client keeps trying. Same conclusion as row one but with more patience from the client.
AnyAnyapp not-applicableThe firewall never got far enough to identify an application — usually because the traffic was denied, or the port did not match the service in the rule. This is not the same as incomplete.
AnyAnyapp incompleteThe TCP handshake never finished, so App-ID had nothing to inspect. Almost always a reachability problem, not a policy one.
AnyAnyhigh repeat count, denySomething is retrying hard. Look at the source before you look at the rule.

incomplete versus not-applicable is worth committing to memory because they point in opposite directions. Incomplete means the conversation never really started — look at routing and reachability. Not-applicable means the firewall refused to have the conversation — look at your rule's service and action.

admin@fw-01(active)> show log traffic direction equal backward src in 10.10.20.55 dst in 203.0.113.90
Time      Src          Dst            App          Rule                Action  Bytes-S  Bytes-R  End-Reason
10:14:02  10.10.20.55  203.0.113.90   incomplete   trust-to-internet   allow   264      0        aged-out
10:14:33  10.10.20.55  203.0.113.90   incomplete   trust-to-internet   allow   198      0        aged-out
allowed by policy, zero bytes back, app never identified — this is a reachability fault, not a firewall fault

Notice that Action says allow. People stop reading at that word and conclude the firewall is fine, which is true — but the log still tells you exactly where to look next. Allowed and working are different things.

Reading the LogsTHREAT LOG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The Threat Log — When the Firewall Was the One That Hung Up

You arrive here from a traffic log line whose end reason was threat, or whose action was reset-both. The question to answer is not "was there a threat" but "which direction was it in, and was the verdict right".

FieldWhat to read into it
Threat / Content Name and IDThe specific signature. Take the ID — it is what you need to build an exception, and what you give to support.
SeverityCritical through informational. Informational entries are noise in most environments; do not let them derail a real investigation.
Actionalert means it was logged and allowed through. drop, reset-client, reset-server, reset-both mean it was stopped. If the user is complaining and the action is alert, this log is not your cause.
DirectionClient-to-server or server-to-client. The most under-used field in the log. A server-to-server-side detection on a download means the far end sent something objectionable; a client-to-server detection means your own host did. Those are entirely different tickets.
Category / Sub-typevulnerability, virus, spyware, wildfire, file, data, url. Tells you which profile made the decision, so you know which one to adjust.
Session IDPair it back to the traffic log line to see how much data moved before the verdict.
admin@fw-01(active)> show log threat direction equal backward query equal "( sessionid eq 88210 )"
Time      Src          Dst           Threat/Content                  Sev       Action      Direction
10:22:41  10.10.20.55  203.0.113.90  suspicious-file-download(39284)  medium   reset-both  server-to-client
the far end sent it, and the firewall tore the session down in both directions

A false positive and a genuine block look identical in the traffic log — both just say threat. The threat log is where you find out which, and the Direction field is what stops you accusing the wrong host.

Before you create an exception for a signature, check whether it fires for other sessions too. A signature that only ever matches one destination is a candidate for an exception; one that fires across many hosts is telling you something and should not be silenced to close a ticket.

Reading the LogsURL FILTERING ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The URL Filtering Log — Category Timing and Block Actions

URL filtering complaints almost always come down to one of two things: the site is in a category the user did not expect, or the block happened before the category could be resolved.

ActionWhat the user experienced
alertAllowed, but logged. Not your cause if the user reports a block.
block-urlBlocked and the response page was served. The user saw a block page.
continue / block-continueThe user was shown a warning page they can click through. If they say "it worked the second time", this is why.
overrideAllowed after a password prompt.
block-overrideThe prompt was shown and not satisfied.
What you seeWhat it means
Category not-resolvedThe cloud lookup did not return in time and no local entry existed. Intermittent, and worth checking cloud connectivity rather than the policy.
Category unknownThe site genuinely has no category. Your policy decides what to do with those — check what it does.
Category differs between the URL log and the traffic logNormal. The traffic log records the category known at the time the session was logged; the URL log records the per-request result.
An HTTPS site blocked with only the domain visible, no pathDecryption is not enabled for that traffic, so the firewall can only see SNI. Categorisation is domain-level only.
Site allowed by category but still failingLook for a threat log or a decryption log on the same session ID before touching the URL policy.
admin@fw-01(active)> show log url direction equal backward src in 10.10.20.55
Time      Src          URL                       Category            Action
10:31:08  10.10.20.55  files.example.net/get     online-storage      block-url
10:31:44  10.10.20.55  files.example.net/get     online-storage      continue
blocked, then the user clicked through the warning page — both are expected behaviour, not a fault
Reading the LogsDECRYPTION LOG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

The Decryption Log — Why That One Site Will Not Load

The symptom is always the same and always misleading: one site fails while everything else is fine, and the traffic log shows the session allowed. The decryption log is where the actual reason lives.

What the log showsCauseFix direction
Certificate validation failure — untrusted issuerThe server's CA is not in the firewall's trusted listAdd the CA, or exclude the destination from decryption
Certificate expired or name mismatchThe far end's certificate is genuinely badThis is the site's problem. Confirm from an undecrypted path before excusing it.
Unsupported cipher suite or TLS versionThe negotiated parameters are outside what the firewall can proxyDecryption exclusion for that destination
Client certificate required by the serverMutual TLS. The proxy cannot present the client's certificate.Exclude. This one cannot be worked around.
Application appears to ignore the firewall's certificate entirelyCertificate pinning in the client applicationExclude by application or destination
Resource-related decryption errors under loadDecryption capacity, not configurationCheck utilisation before changing policy

The pattern to recognise: a single destination failing, TLS handshake never completing, and a clean traffic log. Nine times out of ten that is decryption, and nine times out of ten the fix is an exclusion rather than a certificate change. Pinned applications and mutual TLS simply cannot be decrypted, and no amount of policy work changes that.

The decryption log is its own log type on current PAN-OS versions. If you cannot find it, decryption logging may not be enabled on the decryption rule — the session end reason in the traffic log will still start with decrypt-, which is enough to point you the right way.

Reading the LogsCORRELATION ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Working the Logs From the CLI — One Session, Every Log Type

The GUI is better for browsing. The CLI is better when you know what you are looking for and want it in one screen — especially over a slow link or during an incident bridge.

CommandUseGUI path
show log traffic direction equal backwardNewest entries first. Always include this — the default order starts at the oldest.Monitor > Traffic
show log traffic direction equal backward src in <ip> dst in <ip>The everyday query.Monitor > Traffic
show log traffic query equal "( addr.src in 10.10.20.55 ) and ( action eq deny )"Full filter syntax, same expressions as the GUI filter bar.Monitor > Traffic
show log threat direction equal backward query equal "( sessionid eq <n> )"Threat verdicts for one session.Monitor > Threat
show log url direction equal backward src in <ip>Per-request URL decisions.Monitor > URL Filtering
show log decryption direction equal backward src in <ip>TLS failures.Monitor > Decryption
show log system direction equal backwardLink flaps, HA events, commits, daemon restarts.Monitor > System
show log config direction equal backwardWho changed what. See the What Changed group.Monitor > Configuration
show log traffic csv-output equal yes ...Machine-readable output for pasting into a ticket or a sheet.Export button

The correlation pattern

  1. Find the session in the traffic log and note three things: the session ID, the byte counts, and the end reason.
  2. If the end reason is threat, query the threat log by that session ID and read the Direction field.
  3. If the end reason starts with decrypt-, query the decryption log by source and time.
  4. If the application is incomplete with zero received bytes, stop reading logs. This is a routing or reachability problem and no log will tell you more — go to test routing fib-lookup and the global counters.
  5. If the log is missing entirely, check whether the rule logs at session start or end, and whether the session is still open. Then check the counters — traffic dropped before session setup never reaches the traffic log at all.

A dropped packet is not always a logged packet. Anything discarded during ingress parsing, denied by the default interzone rule with logging off, or dropped by zone protection may leave no traffic log line whatsoever. An empty log is evidence of nothing — go to show counter global filter severity drop delta yes before you conclude the traffic never arrived.

IPsec VPNRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Site-to-Site IPsec Between Two Palo Alto Firewalls

Use it when you are asked to "connect site A to site B". A complete route-based tunnel. PA-B is the mirror image.

// ===== PA-A (e1/1 203.0.113.10, LAN 10.0.1.0/24) =====
set network interface tunnel units tunnel.10 ip 10.255.10.1/30
set zone VPN network layer3 tunnel.10
set network virtual-router default interface tunnel.10
set network ike crypto-profiles ike-crypto-profiles IKE-S2S encryption aes-256-cbc hash sha256 dh-group group14
set network ike crypto-profiles ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-S2S esp encryption aes-256-cbc authentication sha256
set network ike crypto-profiles ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-S2S dh-group group14
set network ike gateway GW-SITEB protocol version ikev2
set network ike gateway GW-SITEB protocol ikev2 ike-crypto-profile IKE-S2S
set network ike gateway GW-SITEB local-address interface ethernet1/1
set network ike gateway GW-SITEB peer-address ip 198.51.100.20
set network ike gateway GW-SITEB authentication pre-shared-key key [psk]
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SITEB auto-key ike-gateway GW-SITEB
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SITEB auto-key ipsec-crypto-profile IPSEC-S2S
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SITEB tunnel-interface tunnel.10
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route TO-SITEB destination 10.0.2.0/24 interface tunnel.10
set rulebase security rules A-TO-B from TRUST to VPN source 10.0.1.0/24 destination 10.0.2.0/24 application any service any action allow
set rulebase security rules B-TO-A from VPN to TRUST source 10.0.2.0/24 destination 10.0.1.0/24 application any service any action allow
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Builds PA-A's side: tunnel interface and zone, crypto profiles, IKE gateway, IPsec tunnel, a route to site B and two rules.

tunnel units tunnel.10 ip 10.255.10.1/30
The tunnel interface. An IP is optional for pure static routing, but useful for monitoring and dynamic routing.
zone VPN · virtual-router default interface tunnel.10
A tunnel interface needs a zone and a VR, or it drops traffic.
ike-crypto-profiles IKE-S2S … group14
Phase 1 proposal. Must match PA-B.
ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-S2S … dh-group group14
Phase 2 proposal. The DH group here is PFS: a mismatch fails phase 2 only.
gateway GW-SITEB … local-address ethernet1/1 · peer-address 198.51.100.20
Which local interface and which peer IP. A wrong peer IP gives "couldn't find configuration for IKE phase-1 request".
authentication pre-shared-key key
The shared key, identical on both sides.
tunnel ipsec VPN-SITEB … tunnel-interface tunnel.10
Binds the gateway and phase 2 profile to tunnel.10. Route-based PAN-to-PAN needs no proxy-IDs. For a policy-based peer, add mirrored proxy-IDs.
static-route TO-SITEB 10.0.2.0/24 interface tunnel.10
Routes site B traffic into the tunnel.
rules A-TO-B / B-TO-A
Security rules per direction between TRUST and VPN.

PA-B: the same structure with peer-address ip 203.0.113.10, a route to 10.0.1.0/24 via its tunnel interface, and the rules reversed.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Underlay

ping source 203.0.113.10 host 198.51.100.20

Good: Replies (or UDP 500/4500 reaches the peer). If not: ISP or upstream filtering.

2 · Phase 1

test vpn ike-sa gateway GW-SITEB
show vpn ike-sa gateway GW-SITEB
tail follow yes mp-log ikemgr.log

Good: IKE SA established. If not: Crypto, PSK or peer IP. Match the log message with the IPsec playbook table.

3 · Phase 2

test vpn ipsec-sa tunnel VPN-SITEB
show vpn ipsec-sa tunnel VPN-SITEB

Good: IPsec SA present. If not: IPsec crypto/PFS, or proxy-IDs against a policy-based peer.

4 · Route, rule, encap/decap

test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 10.0.2.20
test security-policy-match from TRUST to VPN source 10.0.1.10 destination 10.0.2.20 protocol 1
show vpn flow name VPN-SITEB

Good: tunnel.10. A-TO-B allows. encap and decap rising. If not: encap only: the far side isn't returning traffic (its route or rule).

⚠ Syntax note. PAN-OS configuration-mode set commands. The structure follows Palo Alto documentation and published configurations. Use Tab/? while typing, run commit validate (or validate full) before commit, and check the GUI equivalent shown in each step.

IPsec VPNHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

IPsec on PAN-OS: Phase 1, Phase 2, Encap and Decap

A route-based IPsec tunnel on PAN-OS has three layers you can test separately: phase 1 (IKE SA between the public addresses), phase 2 (the IPsec SAs that carry data), and the data path (routes into tunnel.x, zone, rules, encap/decap counters).

LayerProofIf it fails
Phase 1show vpn ike-sa gateway <gw>Underlay, peer IP, IKE crypto, PSK/ID. See the IKE debug topic.
Phase 2show vpn ipsec-sa tunnel <t>IPsec crypto, PFS, proxy-IDs.
Data pathshow vpn flow name <t>: encap and decap risingRoute to tunnel.x, zone, rules, NAT into tunnel, far side.
IPsec VPNCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

IPsec Lab Configuration, Explained

The IPsec part of the hub baseline, so the whole tunnel story sits in this group.

// HUB-PA · one gateway + tunnel per spoke (SPOKE2 repeats with tunnel.2 and its own peer IP)
set network interface tunnel units tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.1/30
set zone VPN network layer3 [ tunnel.1 tunnel.2 ]
set network virtual-router vr-wan interface [ ethernet1/1 tunnel.1 tunnel.2 ]
set network ike crypto-profiles ike-crypto-profiles IKE-AES256 encryption aes-256-cbc hash sha256 dh-group group14
set network ike crypto-profiles ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-AES256 esp encryption aes-256-cbc authentication sha256
set network ike crypto-profiles ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-AES256 dh-group group14
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 protocol version ikev2
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 protocol ikev2 ike-crypto-profile IKE-AES256
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 local-address interface ethernet1/1
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 peer-address ip 198.51.100.11
set network ike gateway GW-SPOKE1 authentication pre-shared-key key [psk]
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 auto-key ike-gateway GW-SPOKE1
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 auto-key ipsec-crypto-profile IPSEC-AES256
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 tunnel-interface tunnel.1
What each line does

Purpose: Builds the route-based IPsec tunnel from the hub to SPOKE1: the tunnel interface and its zone, the crypto profiles, the IKE gateway, and the tunnel that binds them together.

tunnel units tunnel.1 ip 10.255.1.1/30
Logical tunnel interface. Its IP is used for BGP and monitoring. Traffic is routed into it.
zone VPN network layer3 [ tunnel.1 tunnel.2 ]
Without a zone a tunnel interface drops everything. Both spokes share VPN, so hub transit is intrazone.
virtual-router vr-wan interface [ … tunnel.1 … ]
Places the tunnel in vr-wan so routes can point at it.
ike-crypto-profiles IKE-AES256 · aes-256-cbc · sha256 · group14
Phase 1 proposal. Must match the peer exactly.
ipsec-crypto-profiles IPSEC-AES256 · esp aes-256-cbc · sha256 · dh-group group14
Phase 2 proposal. The DH group here is PFS: a mismatch fails phase 2 only.
gateway GW-SPOKE1 protocol version ikev2 · ike-crypto-profile
IKEv2 with the phase 1 profile.
local-address interface ethernet1/1 · peer-address ip 198.51.100.11
The local WAN interface and the spoke's public IP. A wrong peer IP gives "couldn't find configuration for IKE phase-1 request".
authentication pre-shared-key key [psk]
Shared secret. A mismatch fails at IKE AUTH.
tunnel ipsec VPN-SPOKE1 auto-key ike-gateway … ipsec-crypto-profile … tunnel-interface tunnel.1
Binds gateway, phase 2 profile and tunnel interface. No proxy-IDs: route-based to another PAN-OS peer.
IPsec VPNSTATUS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Tunnel and Gateway Status

Two phases, two commands. show vpn ike-sa covers Phase 1 (the IKE negotiation between gateway addresses) and show vpn ipsec-sa covers Phase 2 (the actual encrypted data SAs). Knowing which of the two is missing narrows the problem enormously before you open a log.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show vpn gatewayAll configured IKE gateways with peer IP, local IP and IKE version.Network > Network Profiles > IKE Gateways
show vpn gateway name <gw-name>Full configuration of one gateway.IKE Gateways > select
show vpn ike-saPhase 1. Active IKE SAs — state, peer, encryption.Network > IPSec Tunnels > Status (IKE Info)
show vpn ike-sa gateway <gw-name>Phase 1 for one gateway.IPSec Tunnels > Status
show vpn ipsec-saPhase 2. Active IPsec SAs — SPI, encryption, anti-replay.IPSec Tunnels > Status (Tunnel Info)
show vpn ipsec-sa tunnel <tunnel-name>Phase 2 for one tunnel.IPSec Tunnels > Status
show vpn tunnelAll configured auto-key tunnel definitions.Network > IPSec Tunnels
show vpn tunnel name <tunnel-name>One tunnel's configuration.IPSec Tunnels > select
show vpn flowPer-tunnel counters: bytes encrypted and decrypted, errors. Compare the two directions — the fastest way to spot one-way traffic.IPSec Tunnels > Status
show vpn flow tunnel-id <id>Counters for one tunnel by ID, including tunnel-monitor hits and misses.Network > IPSec Tunnels

Sample — both phases up

admin@fw-01(active)> show vpn ike-sa
IKE Gateway              Peer Address     Local Address   Ver  State      Established  Expires
GW-DC2                   203.0.113.200    198.51.100.2    IKEv2  Established  04d11h    03h41m
GW-Partner               192.0.2.50       198.51.100.2    IKEv2  Established  09d02h    06h12m

admin@fw-01(active)> show vpn ipsec-sa
Tunnel            Gateway     TunnelId  Proto  Local SPI   Remote SPI  Expires
Tun-DC2           GW-DC2             3   ESP   0x8f2a1b44  0x1c99e207  00h41m
Tun-Partner       GW-Partner         5   ESP   0x2b7cc019  0x99a01f3e  01h22m

Sample — the asymmetry that matters

admin@fw-01(active)> show vpn flow tunnel-id 3
tunnel  Tun-DC2
        id:                     3
        state:                  active
        encap packets:          1284402      encap bytes:  1188442019
        decap packets:                0      decap bytes:           0   <-- nothing coming back
        anti-replay errors:           0
        decrypt errors:               0
PatternWhere the fault is
encap climbing, decap at zeroYour ESP is leaving and nothing is returning. The peer is not sending, or ESP is being dropped on the return path — check for a device in between that does not pass IP protocol 50.
Both climbing, users still complainThe tunnel is fine. The problem is routing inside it, policy on the tunnel zone, or MTU.
decrypt errors climbingKey mismatch or corruption. Usually one side rekeyed and the other did not follow.
anti-replay errors climbingPackets arriving out of order beyond the replay window. Common on paths with per-packet load balancing upstream.

Phase 1 up and Phase 2 missing is the two ends having agreed on who they are and then failing to agree on what they will carry — nearly always proxy-IDs or the Phase 2 proposal. Phase 1 itself missing means they never got as far as introductions.

IPsec VPNACTIONS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Bringing Tunnels Up and Tearing Them Down

CommandImpactDescription / usage
test vpn ike-sa gateway <gw-name>SafeManually trigger Phase 1 against a gateway. Watch ikemgr.log at the same time and you see the negotiation live.
test vpn ipsec-sa tunnel <tunnel-name>SafeManually trigger Phase 2 on a tunnel.
clear vpn ike-sa gateway <gw-name>One tunnelClear Phase 1 for one gateway, forcing renegotiation.
clear vpn ipsec-sa tunnel <tunnel-name>One tunnelClear Phase 2 for one tunnel.
clear vpn ike-saAll tunnelsClears every Phase 1 SA on the box.
clear vpn ipsec-saAll tunnelsClears every Phase 2 SA on the box.
debug software restart process ikemgrAll tunnelsRestart the IKE manager. Last resort — every IPsec tunnel drops.
admin@fw-01(active)> test vpn ike-sa gateway GW-DC2
Initiate 1 IKE SA.
admin@fw-01(active)> show vpn ike-sa gateway GW-DC2
GW-DC2   203.0.113.200   198.51.100.2   IKEv2  Established  00h00m02s  07h59m

clear vpn ike-sa and clear vpn ipsec-sa with no gateway or tunnel argument hit everything. On a hub firewall with two hundred branch tunnels, that is a site-wide outage typed as a diagnostic. Always name the gateway or tunnel.

IPsec VPNDEBUG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

IKE Logs and Debug

IKE negotiation happens on the management plane, which is good news: debug ike affects one process rather than the dataplane, so it is far safer than packet-diag.

CommandDescription / usage
less mp-log ikemgr.logThe IKE manager log. Every negotiation failure is explained here in plain text.
tail follow yes mp-log ikemgr.logLive-tail while you run test vpn ike-sa. This pairing is the core IPsec workflow.
debug ike global on debugVerbose IKE debug. Affects only the ikemgr process. Revert with debug ike global on info.
debug ike pcap on / offCapture IKE packets to a pcap on the box.
view-pcap no-dns-lookup yes debug-pcap ikemgr.pcapView the IKE debug capture on-box.
debug ike statistics showIKE process statistics.

Common messages and what they actually mean

In ikemgr.logCauseWhere to fix
no SA proposal chosenEncryption, hash, DH group or lifetime mismatch.Network > Network Profiles > IKE Crypto / IPSec Crypto
AUTHENTICATION_FAILED / Invalid Hash InformationPre-shared key mismatch, or certificate validation failure.Network > Network Profiles > IKE Gateways
INVALID_ID_INFORMATIONLocal-ID or Peer-ID mismatch — FQDN, IP, KeyID or DN.IKE Gateways > Local / Peer Identification
Received Notify type INVALID_KE_PAYLOADDH group mismatch.IKE Crypto profile
TS_UNACCEPTABLE / Phase 2 selector mismatchProxy-IDs do not match the remote traffic selectors.IPSec Tunnels > Proxy IDs
admin@fw-01(active)> tail follow yes mp-log ikemgr.log
(in another window: test vpn ike-sa gateway GW-Partner)
ike-nego-p1-fail-common: IKE phase-1 negotiation is failed as initiator, main mode.
Failed SA: 198.51.100.2[500]-192.0.2.50[500] cookie:1f2c... 
Due to timeout. Please check the network connectivity and the peer configuration.

PAN-OS is route-based. A peer running a policy-based VPN expects traffic selectors, and the only way to give it those is to configure proxy-IDs on the PAN-OS tunnel that exactly mirror the remote selectors. Phase 1 will come up perfectly without them and Phase 2 will never establish — which is the single most common cause of "the tunnel is half up" with a non-Palo peer.

⚠ Verification note. debug ike global on debug, debug ike pcap on and view-pcap … debug-pcap ikemgr.pcap are documented in Palo Alto KB material. debug ike statistics couldn't be confirmed in official sources. Check with debug ike ?.

IPsec VPNON THE WIRE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Capturing IPsec and Verifying Routing

When the logs say the negotiation timed out, the next question is whether the packets are leaving at all — and whether anything is coming back.

CommandCaptures
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match destination <peer-ip> proto 50ESP — the encrypted payload itself.
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match destination <peer-ip> destination-port 500IKE.
debug dataplane packet-diag set filter match destination <peer-ip> destination-port 4500IKE with NAT-T. If there is any NAT on the path, this is the port in use.
CommandDescription / usage
show routing route | match <tunnel-name>Confirm routes point at tunnel.<n> as their next hop.
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip <ip-behind-tunnel>Confirm the firewall would actually forward into the tunnel for that destination.

Use the drop capture stage as well as receive and transmit. If ESP is arriving and being discarded, drop.pcap is where it shows up, and pairing that with show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes names the exact reason.

IPsec VPNPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

IPsec Tunnel Won't Come Up

time-box 20 minR: underlay to peerP: UNTRUST → UNTRUST ike/ipsec
  1. Bring it up on demand and watch the log: 
    test vpn ike-sa gateway GW-HUB
show vpn ike-sa gateway GW-HUB
test vpn ipsec-sa tunnel VPN-HUB
show vpn ipsec-sa tunnel VPN-HUB
tail follow yes mp-log ikemgr.log     // in a second session while testing
  2. Underlay: ping source <wan-ip> host <peer-ip>. Check that UDP 500/4500 reaches the peer. A firewall in between, or the peer's own rules, may block it.
  3. Match the error to the cause:
System / ikemgr log saysUsual cause
Couldn't find configuration for IKE phase-1 request for peer IP …Peer IP in the IKE gateway is wrong, or the request arrives on a different local address.
Unable to process peer's SA payload / no proposal chosenIKE crypto profile mismatch: encryption, authentication or DH group.
pfs group mismatched / no suitable proposal found in peer's SA payload (phase 2)IPsec crypto profile mismatch, often the PFS DH group.
Phase-2 negotiation failed when processing Proxy IDThe peer is policy-based. Configure proxy-IDs that mirror the peer's.
No ikemgr entries for the peer at allNothing arrives. Check underlay, NAT-T, upstream filtering, or the peer isn't initiating.

Proxy-IDs on the two peers must be mirrors of each other: your local ID is their remote ID, and the other way round. PAN-to-PAN route-based tunnels like this lab normally need none.

For more detail, enable debug ike global on debug while reproducing, then set it back with debug ike global on normal. Leaving IKE debug on fills the log and hides the next problem.

IPsec VPNPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

VPN Up, but No Traffic Passes

time-box 15 minR: route to tunnel.xA: NAT into the tunnelP: zone of tunnel.x
  1. Read encap/decap first. It tells you which side is at fault. 
    show vpn flow name VPN-HUB
// compare two runs a few seconds apart
encap packets: 48        // rising: we are sending into the tunnel
decap packets: 0         // flat: nothing comes back, so look at the far side
    Encap rising and decap flat: the far side isn't sending back (its route, rules or proxy-IDs). Both flat: traffic isn't entering the tunnel here.
  2. Route into the tunnel: test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip <remote-host> must return tunnel.x. If it returns the WAN, the BGP or static route is missing.
  3. Zone of the tunnel: tunnel.x must be in a zone (VPN here), and a security rule must allow LAN → VPN and VPN → LAN. A tunnel interface with no zone drops everything.
  4. NAT into the tunnel: a broad source-NAT rule (destination zone any) can translate traffic entering the tunnel. Check test nat-policy-match from TRUST to VPN returns no match.
  5. Proxy-IDs (to policy-based peers): traffic outside the negotiated proxy-IDs isn't sent. show vpn ipsec-sa tunnel <name> shows the negotiated pairs.
  6. Counters: filter on the flow and read show counter global filter delta yes packet-filter yes.

An "up" tunnel is a phone line with a dial tone. Encap and decap counters tell you whether anyone is actually talking, and who has gone quiet.

IPsec VPNVPN ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Proxy-IDs with Policy-Based Peers

PAN-OS tunnels are route-based. Peers that are policy-based (many ASA, Check Point and cloud gateways) negotiate specific subnet pairs, so the Palo Alto must offer exactly those pairs as proxy-IDs, mirrored: your local = their remote.

set network tunnel ipsec VPN-PARTNER auto-key proxy-id P1 local 10.10.20.0/24 remote 172.16.5.0/24 protocol any
show vpn ipsec-sa tunnel VPN-PARTNER     // one SA per proxy-ID pair
What each line does

Purpose: Defines one phase 2 subnet pair for a tunnel to a policy-based peer.

tunnel ipsec VPN-PARTNER auto-key proxy-id P1
Adds a proxy-ID entry named P1 to this tunnel.
local 10.10.20.0/24
Your side's subnet. It must equal the peer's remote subnet.
remote 172.16.5.0/24
The peer's subnet. It must equal the peer's local subnet.
protocol any
Any IP protocol. A protocol or port here must match the peer as well.
show vpn ipsec-sa tunnel VPN-PARTNER
Each proxy-ID pair builds its own phase 2 SA. Check that every expected pair is listed.
SymptomCause
Phase 2 fails "processing Proxy ID"No proxy-ID, or not a mirror of the peer's.
Some subnets work, others don'tMissing proxy-ID pair for those subnets (one SA per pair).
Tunnel up, traffic droppedTraffic outside every proxy-ID pair, or no route to tunnel.x for that subnet.

Each proxy-ID pair is a separate phase 2 SA. Supernetting on both sides (one /16 instead of many /24s) reduces the number of SAs and the chances of a mismatch, but both ends must agree.

IPsec VPNVPN ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Tunnel Monitoring and Routing Failover

Without monitoring, a static route to tunnel.x stays active even when the far end stopped passing traffic, because the interface is still up. Tunnel monitoring pings a destination through the tunnel. With a monitor profile set to fail over, a failed monitor brings the tunnel down, and routes using it can be withdrawn so a backup takes over.

set network tunnel ipsec VPN-HUB tunnel-monitor enable yes destination-ip 10.255.1.1
show vpn flow name VPN-HUB          // monitor status shown with the tunnel
What each line does

Purpose: Turns on tunnel monitoring so a tunnel that stops passing traffic is detected, even though its interface stays up.

tunnel-monitor enable yes
Sends periodic pings through the tunnel.
destination-ip 10.255.1.1
Target on the far side of the tunnel (the hub's tunnel.1 IP). It must answer pings through the tunnel.
(monitor profile, optional)
A monitor profile sets the action on failure: wait-recover or fail-over. Use fail-over when a backup route or tunnel should take over.
show vpn flow name VPN-HUB
Shows tunnel state including the monitor status.

The monitor destination must answer pings through the tunnel, and the tunnel interface needs an IP for the source. A monitor pointed at an address that never answers takes a working tunnel down. Test with ping source first.

With dynamic routing over the tunnel (BGP as in this lab), failover comes from the routing protocol itself. Tunnel monitoring is still useful to detect a dead tunnel faster, or BFD can do the same for BGP.

Recipe: GlobalProtect Remote Access in Build Order

Use it when you build GlobalProtect from nothing. This is the order and the checkpoints. Each object is explained in detail in "GlobalProtect on the Firewall: Configuration, Explained".

1 Device > Certificate Management      server cert gp.example.com (CN/SAN), from a CA clients trust · SSL/TLS profile SSL-GP
2 Device > Authentication Profile      AUTH-GP (SAML/LDAP/RADIUS) · allow list grp-vpn-users · test with test authentication
3 Network > Interfaces > Tunnel        tunnel.10 · zone GP-USERS · virtual router default
4 Network > GlobalProtect > Portals    interface ethernet1/1 · SSL-GP · AUTH-GP · agent config Staff → external gateway gp.example.com
5 Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways   ethernet1/1 · SSL-GP · AUTH-GP · tunnel.10 · IPsec on · pool 10.70.0.0/24 · DNS · split include
6 Policies + routing                   GP-USERS → CORP rule · internal routers route 10.70.0.0/24 back to the firewall
Checkpoint                             browser: https://gp.example.com/global-protect/prelogin.esp returns XML · then connect a test user

Verify

Users connect and get addresses

show global-protect-gateway current-user
show global-protect-gateway statistics

Good: The test user listed with a pool IP and ESP in use. If not: Follow the GlobalProtect playbooks: can't connect, no access, slow.

GlobalProtect (Firewall)HOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · GP edge

How a GlobalProtect Client Connects

GlobalProtect has two roles, which can live on the same firewall or on different ones. The portal authenticates the user and hands the app its configuration, including the list of gateways. The gateway authenticates again, assigns an IP address from its pool, and builds the tunnel. Almost every "can't connect" problem fails at one of the six steps below, and the app's status, the GlobalProtect log and the client logs tell you which.

StepFails asFirst place to look
Portal"Portal unreachable", certificate warningDNS for the portal name, TLS certificate chain and name, reachability of TCP 443
Auth"Authentication failed"Authentication profile, allow list, server reachability, the GlobalProtect log
ConfigConnects to portal, no gatewayAgent config selection criteria (users, OS), gateway list in the agent config
GatewayPortal OK, gateway failsGateway certificate, authentication, IP pool exhausted, max users
TunnelConnected but slow, or SSL instead of IPsecUDP 4501 blocked on the path, MTU
HIPConnected, blocked by a HIP-based ruleHIP Match log, the HIP profile, HIP report from the client

The portal is reception: it checks your badge and gives you a floor plan with the list of doors you may use. The gateway is the door: it checks your badge again, gives you a visitor sticker (pool IP) and lets you into the building through a private corridor (the tunnel).

GlobalProtect (Firewall)CONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · GP edge

GlobalProtect on the Firewall: Configuration, Explained

A typical single-firewall deployment: portal and gateway on the same internet interface, user tunnels on tunnel.10, split tunnelling for corporate subnets. Shown as the GUI objects in the order you build them.

// GP-EDGE · GlobalProtect remote access (GUI objects, shown as a settings sheet, not CLI)
Device > Certificate Management        Server cert gp.example.com (CN/SAN match the portal and gateway FQDN), issued by a CA the laptops trust
Device > SSL/TLS Service Profile        SSL-GP · certificate gp.example.com · min TLS 1.2
Device > Authentication Profile         AUTH-GP · SAML (or LDAP/RADIUS) · allow list: grp-vpn-users
Network > Interfaces > Tunnel          tunnel.10 · zone GP-USERS · virtual router default · no IP needed
Network > GlobalProtect > Portals      GP-PORTAL · interface ethernet1/1 (203.0.113.10) · SSL-GP · AUTH-GP
                                        agent config "Staff": users grp-vpn-users · external gateway gp.example.com
                                        connect method user-logon (always on) · save credentials as policy allows
Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways     GP-GATEWAY · interface ethernet1/1 · SSL-GP · AUTH-GP · tunnel mode on tunnel.10
                                        enable IPsec (UDP 4501), SSL as fallback
                                        client settings: IP pool 10.70.0.0/24 · DNS 10.20.0.53 · DNS suffix corp.example
                                        split tunnel: include 10.20.0.0/16 · exclude the rest (internet stays local)
Policies > Security                     GP-TO-CORP   from GP-USERS to CORP · src 10.70.0.0/24 · user grp-vpn-users · allow
                                        (portal/gateway traffic to ethernet1/1 itself is UNTRUST → UNTRUST: allowed by intrazone-default unless that rule was overridden)
Network > Virtual Routers               route for 10.70.0.0/24 is connected via tunnel.10 · inside routers need 10.70.0.0/24 → firewall
What each line does

Purpose: Publishes a GlobalProtect portal and gateway on the firewall's internet interface, so staff laptops authenticate, receive a pool address, and reach corporate subnets through tunnel.10 while their internet traffic stays local (split tunnel).

Certificates and authentication

Server cert gp.example.com
The name users type and the gateway names in the agent config must appear in the certificate's CN or SAN, and the issuing CA must be trusted by the laptops. Most "can't connect" tickets on day one are certificate tickets.
SSL/TLS Service Profile SSL-GP
Binds the certificate and TLS versions to the portal and gateway.
Authentication Profile AUTH-GP · allow list
How users prove who they are, and which groups may log in. A user outside the allow list fails authentication even with the right password.

Tunnel interface

tunnel.10 · zone GP-USERS
All connected users' traffic arrives on this interface, so this zone is the source zone in every GlobalProtect security rule. It doesn't need an IP address.

Portal

GP-PORTAL · ethernet1/1 · SSL-GP · AUTH-GP
Where the app connects first. It authenticates and returns the agent configuration.
agent config "Staff" · users grp-vpn-users
Selection criteria decide which config a user gets. A user who matches no agent config gets no gateway list.
external gateway gp.example.com
The gateway the app connects to next. It must match the gateway certificate name.
connect method user-logon
Always-on: the app connects as the user logs in to Windows/macOS. On-demand leaves it to the user.

Gateway

GP-GATEWAY · tunnel mode on tunnel.10
Terminates user tunnels on tunnel.10.
enable IPsec (UDP 4501), SSL fallback
IPsec is preferred for performance. If UDP 4501 is blocked on the user's network, the app falls back to SSL over TCP 443, which works but is slower.
IP pool 10.70.0.0/24
Addresses handed to connected users. Size it for peak users: an exhausted pool means new users can't connect. Internal routers must route this range back to the firewall.
DNS 10.20.0.53 · suffix corp.example
DNS settings pushed to the client, so internal names resolve while connected.
split tunnel include 10.20.0.0/16
Only corporate destinations use the tunnel. Everything else uses the user's local internet. Without an include list, all traffic is tunnelled and the firewall needs an outbound rule and NAT for GP-USERS.

Policy and routing

GP-TO-CORP from GP-USERS to CORP · user grp-vpn-users
The rule that actually grants access. Without it, users connect fine but reach nothing (interzone default deny).
route back for 10.70.0.0/24
The firewall knows the pool through tunnel.10, but core switches and servers must route 10.70.0.0/24 back to the firewall, or replies go nowhere.
GlobalProtect (Firewall)CLI ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · GP edge

Checking Connected Users, Tunnels and Their Traffic

Start with who is connected, then what their tunnel looks like, then what their traffic is doing. The pool IP from the first step is the key that links a user to their sessions and logs.

show global-protect-gateway current-user                         // everyone connected now
show global-protect-gateway current-user gateway GP-GATEWAY user jdoe   // one user (part of the name works)
show global-protect-gateway current-user | match "User Name"       // names only
show global-protect-gateway previous-user                        // who was connected, and when they left
show global-protect-gateway statistics                           // user counts per gateway
show global-protect-gateway flow                                 // dataplane view of the gateway tunnels
show global-protect-gateway gateway                              // gateway configuration as the firewall sees it
show global-protect-gateway summary all
admin@GP-EDGE> show global-protect-gateway current-user user jdoe
// illustrative, trimmed
GlobalProtect Gateway: GP-GATEWAY (1 users)
Tunnel Name          : GP-GATEWAY-N
Domain-User Name     : corp\jdoe
Computer             : LAPTOP-0142
Client               : Microsoft Windows 11 Enterprise, 64-bit
Private IP           : 10.70.0.25                 // the address the user's traffic will carry
Public IP            : 198.51.100.77              // where the user is connecting from
ESP                  : exist                      // IPsec tunnel in use
SSL                  : exist
Login Time           : Oct.27 08:12:34
Inactivity TTL       : 10760
FieldRead it as
Private IPPool address. Use it in session filters, packet-diag filters and log queries.
Public IPThe user's home or hotel address. Behind CGNAT this can be shared by many users.
ESP / SSL"ESP removed, SSL exist" means the tunnel fell back to SSL: UDP 4501 isn't getting through on the user's path. Expect slower performance.
Inactivity TTLTime left before an idle user is logged out.

Then follow the user's traffic

show session all filter source 10.70.0.25                       // everything this user has open
show session all filter source 10.70.0.25 destination 10.20.0.10 destination-port 443
test security-policy-match from GP-USERS to CORP source 10.70.0.25 destination 10.20.0.10 protocol 6 destination-port 443
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip 10.70.0.25      // should point at tunnel.10

Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways > Remote Users (current and previous users) · Monitor > Logs > GlobalProtect (connection events) · Monitor > Logs > HIP Match.

GlobalProtect (Firewall)LOGS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · GP edge

GlobalProtect Logs: Firewall Side and Client Side

Every GlobalProtect connection leaves evidence in three places. Look in the order below: the GlobalProtect log usually names the failing stage outright.

WhereWhatUse it for
Monitor > Logs > GlobalProtectPortal and gateway events per user: prelogin, auth, config, gateway connect, logout, with the stage and errorThe first stop for every connect problem.
Monitor > Logs > Traffic / HIP MatchThe user's sessions (source = pool IP) and HIP resultsConnected-but-no-access and HIP-based blocks.
Firewall mp-logsgpsvc.log (PAN-OS 10.2 and later), appweb3-sslvpn.log (earlier releases)Detail behind portal/gateway errors.
Client logsPanGPS.log (service), PanGPA.log (app), PanGPHip.log (HIP), collected with the app's "Collect Logs"What the laptop saw: DNS, certificate, tunnel and HIP errors.
less mp-log gpsvc.log
tail follow yes mp-log gpsvc.log                      // watch while the user reconnects
show log system direction equal backward | match globalprotect

Quick browser tests

From the user's machine, these URLs prove that TLS to the portal and gateway works and the certificate is trusted, without the app being involved:

https://gp.example.com/global-protect/prelogin.esp     // portal
https://gp.example.com/ssl-vpn/prelogin.esp            // gateway

An XML reply means the portal or gateway is reachable and TLS is fine, so look at authentication next. A certificate warning in the browser is the same warning the app hits.

Users Can't Connect

time-box 15 minGlobalProtect log first
SymptomCheck, in this order
Portal unreachableDNS for the portal name, reachability of TCP 443 to the firewall interface, an upstream device or ISP blocking it, the portal bound to the right interface/IP. Browser test: prelogin.esp.
Certificate warning or errorPortal/gateway names must be in the certificate CN/SAN. The issuing CA (and intermediates) must be trusted by the client. Check expiry and the SSL/TLS service profile.
Authentication failedGlobalProtect log stage and reason. Authentication profile and server reachability (test authentication authentication-profile AUTH-GP username jdoe password). Allow list and group mapping (show user group name …). SAML: IdP clock, certificates, redirect URL.
Portal OK, gateway failsGateway name in the agent config matches the gateway certificate. Gateway authentication (it can differ from the portal's). IP pool not exhausted (show global-protect-gateway statistics). Licence or max-user limits.
Wrong agent config or no gateway listAgent config selection criteria (user/group, OS). The order of agent configs: the first match wins.
GlobalProtect (Firewall)PLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

Connected, but Can't Reach Resources

time-box 15 minGlobalProtect log first
SymptomCheck, in this order
Nothing internal worksSecurity rule from GP-USERS to the internal zone (traffic log for the pool IP). Internal routers route the pool back to the firewall (test routing fib-lookup on both sides). Pool overlapping an internal or home subnet.
Some subnets work, others don'tSplit-tunnel include list missing that subnet, so the traffic goes out of the user's local internet. Check the routes the client received (the app's Route Details or PanGPS.log).
Names don't resolveDNS servers and suffix pushed by the gateway. The rule allows DNS from GP-USERS to the DNS servers. Split DNS settings if used.
Internet broken while connected (full tunnel)No split tunnel means all traffic enters the tunnel: the firewall needs a GP-USERS → UNTRUST rule and source NAT for the pool.
Blocked by a HIP ruleHIP Match log for the user. HIP profile conditions. The HIP report has arrived (it is sent after connecting and on change).
GlobalProtect (Firewall)PLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

Slow, Unstable or Disconnecting

time-box 15 minGlobalProtect log first
SymptomCheck, in this order
Tunnel uses SSL instead of IPsecUDP 4501 blocked on the user's network (hotel, guest Wi-Fi, CGNAT devices). current-user shows "ESP removed". Expected to be slower. Confirm IPsec is enabled on the gateway.
Large transfers stall, small ones workMTU on the tunnel path. Lower the GlobalProtect client MTU setting on the gateway, or check fragmentation on the user's link.
Disconnects after a fixed timeLogin lifetime and inactivity logout in the gateway client settings (Inactivity TTL in current-user).
Reconnects when the laptop changes networkExpected behaviour while the tunnel rebuilds. Frequent drops on one network point at that network (NAT timeouts, UDP filtering).
Firewall under load at peakshow global-protect-gateway statistics against the platform limit, show running resource-monitor for dataplane load.
Prisma AccessHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Prisma

How Prisma Access Fits Together

Prisma Access is a cloud-delivered security service run by Palo Alto Networks. Instead of traffic hairpinning through your own firewalls, mobile users, branches and your HQ/data centre all connect to Prisma Access locations. Prisma Access joins them with an internal backbone built from the infrastructure subnet you supply, and forwards all logs to Strata Logging Service.

TermWhat it is
MU-SPNMobile-user security processing node: the cloud gateway in a Prisma Access location that GlobalProtect users connect to.
RN-SPNRemote-network security processing node: terminates IPsec from branches and secures their traffic.
SC-CANService connection corporate access node: IPsec (static or BGP) from Prisma Access into your HQ or data centre.
Infrastructure subnetA subnet you provide that Prisma Access uses for its internal backbone. It must not overlap anything else you use.
Mobile user IP poolsAddresses handed to GlobalProtect users, allocated per region.
Strata Logging ServiceWhere all Prisma Access logs are stored and queried.
Management planeEither Strata Cloud Manager (cloud-managed) or Panorama with the Cloud Services plugin. Steps, menu paths and some features differ between the two.

Service connections are needed for more than HQ access. Remote networks are fully meshed with each other, but the mobile user infrastructure isn't, so mobile users reach branch networks through a service connection. Palo Alto recommends creating one even if you have no HQ or data centre to connect.

Prisma Access is a global chain of security checkpoints run for you. Travellers (mobile users) and regional offices (branches) each walk into their nearest checkpoint. The checkpoints are joined by a private corridor (the infrastructure subnet), and service connections are the doors from that corridor into your headquarters.

Prisma AccessPLAN ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Prisma

Before You Configure: the Addressing and Inputs Prisma Needs

Most Prisma Access problems that appear months later were baked in at planning time: overlapping subnets, an undersized infrastructure subnet, a missing service connection. Fill this in first.

InputGuidance from Palo AltoLab value
Infrastructure subnetMust not overlap any other subnet. Around a /24 for fewer than 50 sites and 2,500 mobile users. A /23 is sufficient in most cases (fewer than 100 sites and 5,000 users). Larger needs: contact Palo Alto.172.16.55.0/23
Infrastructure BGP ASRequired if service connections or remote networks use BGP. A private AS (RFC 6996).65534
Mobile user IP poolsOne address per connected device. Must not overlap the infrastructure subnet, branch subnets or corporate subnets.10.80.0.0/16
Portal hostnameDefault domain <name>.gpcloudservice.com, or a custom domain with your own certificate.acme.gpcloudservice.com
Explicit Proxy URLDefault <name>.proxy.prismaaccess.com on port 8080. A CNAME lets you use your own domain.acme.proxy.prismaaccess.com:8080
HQ/DC IPsec deviceIPsec-capable firewall, router or SD-WAN device. The whole infrastructure subnet must be reachable from HQ/DC: Prisma uses it for control-plane traffic.DC-PA 203.0.113.20
Routing per connectionStatic subnets, BGP, or both.BGP to DC, static for a small branch
AuthenticationSAML (and Kerberos for Explicit Proxy). The Cloud Identity Engine provides user and group mapping.SAML (Entra ID / Okta)

Overlap is the classic mistake: the mobile user pools, branch subnets, corporate (service connection) subnets and infrastructure subnet must all be mutually exclusive.
