Mobile Users with GlobalProtect: Configuration, Explained

The GlobalProtect app connects to a Prisma Access portal and gateway instead of your own firewall. The client experience is the same as on-prem GlobalProtect (see the GlobalProtect (Firewall) group for how the app connects). What changes is where the portal and gateways live, and that Palo Alto runs them.

// Prisma Access · Mobile Users—GlobalProtect (settings sheet; SCM path first, Panorama in brackets)
Service infrastructure                   infrastructure subnet 172.16.55.0/23 · infra BGP AS 65534
  (Panorama: Cloud Services > Configuration > Service Setup)
Mobile Users—GlobalProtect > Onboarding  portal hostname acme.gpcloudservice.com (default domain)
  (Panorama: Cloud Services > Configuration > Mobile Users—GlobalProtect)
Authentication                          SAML profile to the IdP · Cloud Identity Engine for user/group mapping
Locations                               select the Prisma Access locations near your users
IP pools                                10.80.0.0/16 (allocated per region, must not overlap anything)
Network services                        DNS for internal domains (corp.example → 10.20.0.53) · public DNS for the rest
Agent / app settings                    connect method user-logon · split tunnel per policy
Security policy                         rules in the Mobile Users scope / Mobile_User_Device_Group
Service connection                      at least one, so users reach HQ/DC and branch networks (next topics)
What each line does

Purpose: Turns on GlobalProtect for mobile users in Prisma Access: the backbone, the portal users connect to, how they authenticate, which cloud locations serve them, what addresses they get, and how internal names resolve.

infrastructure subnet 172.16.55.0/23 · infra BGP AS
Builds the internal backbone. Set once, and plan it carefully: it can't overlap any of your networks.
portal hostname acme.gpcloudservice.com
What users enter in the GlobalProtect app. The default domain avoids certificate work. A custom domain needs your certificate.
SAML · Cloud Identity Engine
Users authenticate at your IdP. The Cloud Identity Engine supplies groups for policy.
Locations
The cloud gateways users can connect to. The app selects among them automatically, normally the best-performing nearby one.
IP pools 10.80.0.0/16
Each connected device needs an address. Prisma advertises pool blocks to your sites over BGP (by default in /24 blocks), so your HQ/DC must accept and route them.
DNS for internal domains
Internal names resolve to internal servers through the tunnel. The usual cause of "connected but internal sites don't load".
Security policy in the Mobile Users scope
The rules that grant access. Being connected grants nothing by itself.
Service connection
Without one, mobile users can't reach HQ/DC resources or branch networks.
Prisma AccessCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Prisma

Mobile Users with Explicit Proxy

Explicit Proxy secures web and SaaS traffic without a VPN client. The browser uses a PAC file to send proxy-aware HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the Prisma Access proxy. Users authenticate through SAML (or Kerberos) via the Authentication Cache Service (ACS), and policy is applied in the cloud.

// Explicit Proxy (settings sheet)
Infrastructure settings      explicit proxy URL acme.proxy.prismaaccess.com · port 8080
Authentication               SAML IdP + authentication profile (Kerberos also supported for PAC deployments)
                             Panorama: IdP ACS URL https://global.acs.prismaaccess.com/saml/acs
                                       Entity ID     https://global.acs.prismaaccess.com/saml/metadata
                             Cloud Identity Engine: use mail or userPrincipalName for group mapping
Locations                    a subset of Prisma Access locations supports Explicit Proxy
PAC file                     return "PROXY acme.proxy.prismaaccess.com:8080"; plus DIRECT bypasses for the ACS
                             (*.acs.prismaaccess.com), the PAC file URL itself, and internal/private apps
Security policy              allow web access to known (authenticated) users
CheckWhy
Cloud Services > Status > Network Details > Mobile Users—Explicit Proxy (Panorama)Shows the Explicit Proxy URL, ACS FQDN and SAML metadata actually in use.
Traffic and Authentication logsPalo Alto's first stops for authentication issues. IdP-side failures are only visible in the IdP's own logs.
PAC file contentIt must contain at least one valid Explicit Proxy URL in a PROXY statement. If you change the proxy URL, upload a new PAC file, or the change isn't applied.

URL filtering continue and override actions aren't supported with Explicit Proxy. Only proxy-aware HTTP/HTTPS traffic is covered: use GlobalProtect for everything else.

Remote Networks: Connecting a Branch

// Prisma side · Remote Networks (settings sheet)
Remote network "BR-LONDON"   location UK · IPSec termination node (chosen per location)
Primary tunnel               IPsec to the branch public IP 198.51.100.40 · predefined IPsec template matching the CPE
Routing                      static: branch subnet 10.30.40.0/24   — or —   BGP: peer IP / local IP, branch AS 65040
ECMP (optional)              up to 4 tunnels; BGP required; QoS and static routes not supported with ECMP
Service IP address           read from Network Details / serviceability "Service IP Address" → used as the CPE peer
// Branch side · PAN-OS firewall BR-LONDON (CLI)
set network interface tunnel units tunnel.50 ip 10.255.50.2/30
set zone PRISMA network layer3 tunnel.50
set network virtual-router default interface tunnel.50
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA protocol version ikev2
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA protocol ikev2 ike-crypto-profile IKE-PRISMA
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA local-address interface ethernet1/1
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA peer-address ip 192.0.2.50
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA authentication pre-shared-key key [psk]
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-PRISMA auto-key ike-gateway GW-PRISMA
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-PRISMA auto-key ipsec-crypto-profile IPSEC-PRISMA
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-PRISMA tunnel-interface tunnel.50
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route TO-PRISMA-MU destination 10.80.0.0/16 interface tunnel.50
set network virtual-router default routing-table ip static-route TO-PRISMA-INFRA destination 172.16.55.0/23 interface tunnel.50
set rulebase security rules BRANCH-TO-PRISMA from TRUST to PRISMA source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
set rulebase security rules PRISMA-TO-BRANCH from PRISMA to TRUST source any destination any application any service application-default action allow
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Connects a branch firewall to its Prisma Access remote network over IPsec. Branch traffic gets secured in the cloud, and branch users can reach other branches, the DC and mobile users through Prisma.

Prisma side

location UK · IPSec termination node
The Prisma Access location that serves this branch, and the node its tunnel terminates on.
predefined IPsec template
Prisma offers predefined IKE/IPsec templates for common devices. The branch crypto profiles must match the template exactly.
static branch subnet / BGP
Static: you list the branch subnets and must update them on change. BGP: Prisma learns them and advertises its routes (including mobile user pools) to the branch.
ECMP up to 4 tunnels
Load balancing across tunnels. It requires BGP, and doesn't support QoS or static routes.
Service IP address
The Prisma endpoint the branch must use as its IKE peer. Retrieve it from the network details or the serviceability commands. Don't guess it.

Branch side

tunnel.50 · zone PRISMA
A dedicated tunnel interface and zone, so rules for Prisma traffic are explicit.
ike gateway GW-PRISMA … peer-address ip 192.0.2.50
Points IKE at the Prisma Service IP (lab value). IKEv2 and the crypto profiles match the Prisma template.
tunnel ipsec VPN-PRISMA … tunnel-interface tunnel.50
Binds the IKE gateway and phase 2 profile to tunnel.50.
static routes 10.80.0.0/16 and 172.16.55.0/23 → tunnel.50
With static routing, the branch must route mobile user pools and the infrastructure subnet (plus any other remote sites and DC subnets) into the tunnel. With BGP, these are learned.
rules BRANCH-TO-PRISMA / PRISMA-TO-BRANCH
Allow traffic both ways between the LAN and the Prisma zone.

Service Connections: Connecting HQ and the Data Centre

A service connection is an IPsec tunnel (with static routes or BGP) from Prisma Access to an IPsec-capable device in your HQ or data centre. It does two jobs: access to corporate resources, and the hub that lets mobile users reach remote networks.

// Prisma side · Service Connections (settings sheet)
Service connection "SC-DC1"    location near the DC (and near the branches mobile users visit most)
Tunnel                         IPsec to DC-PA public IP 203.0.113.20 · secondary tunnel optional
Routing                        BGP: peer IP = DC router ID · Prisma advertises MU pools, branch and infra routes
                               (or static routes to each DC subnet)
Source NAT (optional)          NAT mobile user pool / infrastructure addresses at this service connection
// DC side · PAN-OS firewall DC-PA (CLI, BGP)
set network interface tunnel units tunnel.60 ip 10.255.60.2/30
set zone PRISMA network layer3 tunnel.60
set network virtual-router default interface tunnel.60
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA-SC peer-address ip 192.0.2.60
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA-SC local-address interface ethernet1/1
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA-SC protocol version ikev2
set network ike gateway GW-PRISMA-SC authentication pre-shared-key key [psk]
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-PRISMA-SC auto-key ike-gateway GW-PRISMA-SC
set network tunnel ipsec VPN-PRISMA-SC tunnel-interface tunnel.60
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp enable yes router-id 10.255.60.2 local-as 65020
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PRISMA type ebgp
set network virtual-router default protocol bgp peer-group PRISMA peer SC-DC1 peer-as 65534 peer-address ip 10.255.60.1 local-address interface tunnel.60 ip 10.255.60.2/30
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Connects Prisma Access to the data centre over IPsec with eBGP, so mobile users and branches can reach DC applications, and DC routers learn where the mobile user pools and branches live.

Prisma side

location near the DC
Latency matters: also place service connections near the branches mobile users access most.
BGP · peer IP = DC router ID
Prisma advertises mobile user pools (by default in /24 blocks), branch routes and the infrastructure subnet. The DC advertises its own subnets.
static routes (alternative)
You list every DC subnet manually, and the DC needs static routes back for every Prisma range.
source NAT (optional)
Hides mobile user/infrastructure addresses behind a subnet at this service connection, when the DC can't route those ranges.

DC side

tunnel.60 · zone PRISMA
Dedicated interface and zone for traffic from Prisma.
ike gateway … peer-address ip 192.0.2.60
The service connection's Prisma endpoint (lab value). Crypto must match Prisma's settings.
bgp … local-as 65020
DC side AS. eBGP to Prisma's infrastructure AS 65534.
peer SC-DC1 peer-as 65534 peer-address … local-address tunnel.60
Peers with Prisma's BGP address over the tunnel. Advertise DC subnets with a redistribution profile, as in the BGP group.
(reachability)
The entire infrastructure subnet must be reachable from the DC. Prisma uses it for control-plane traffic, and Palo Alto asks that the DC address be reachable by ICMP from it.

GRE VPNHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

GRE: Underlay First, Then Overlay

A GRE tunnel only works if the underlay (the route between the two tunnel endpoints) works. Then the overlay (routes into the tunnel interface, zone, rules) can carry traffic. GRE adds 24 bytes of headers and has no encryption, so MTU and, where needed, IPsec protection matter.

GRE VPNCONFIG ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

GRE Tunnel Configuration and Status

GRE on PAN-OS is configured under network tunnel gre and bound to a tunnel.<n> interface, which is what routing actually points at. Available from PAN-OS 9.0.

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
# set network tunnel gre <gre-name> local-address interface ethernet1/1 ip <local-ip> peer-address ip <remote-ip> tunnel-interface tunnel.<n> ttl 64 keep-alive enable yes interval 10 retry 3Create the GRE tunnel and bind it to a tunnel interface.Network > GRE Tunnels > Add
# set network interface tunnel units tunnel.<n> ip <tunnel-local-ip/mask>Give the tunnel interface an address so it can be a routed next hop.Network > Interfaces > Tunnel > Add
# set network interface tunnel units tunnel.<n> mtu 1400Lower the MTU. GRE adds 24 bytes of overhead.Network > Interfaces > Tunnel > Advanced > MTU
show network tunnel greAll GRE tunnels with state and keepalive status.Network > GRE Tunnels (Status)
show network tunnel gre name <gre-name>One tunnel in detail.Network > GRE Tunnels > select
show interface tunnel.<n>Tunnel interface state. With keepalives enabled this only reads up when they are succeeding.Network > Interfaces > Tunnel
show counter global | match greGRE encapsulation and decapsulation counters.CLI only
admin@fw-01(active)> show network tunnel gre
name        local-addr      peer-addr        tunnel-if   keep-alive  status
GRE-to-DC2  198.51.100.2    203.0.113.200    tunnel.5    enabled     up
GRE-Lab     198.51.100.2    192.0.2.77       tunnel.6    enabled     down   <-- keepalives failing

⚠ Verification note. show network tunnel gre isn't in Palo Alto's CLI cheat sheets or GRE admin pages, which configure and monitor GRE in the web interface (Network > GRE Tunnels). Confirm the command with ? on your release. Reliable alternatives: show interface tunnel.<n>, the System log filtered on ( subtype eq gre ) for tunnel up/down events, show session all filter protocol 47 for the GRE session itself, and ping source <tunnel-ip> host <peer-tunnel-ip>. GRE is IP protocol 47, and a security rule must permit it between the tunnel endpoints.

GRE VPNTEST ORDER ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Underlay Before Overlay — The Order That Saves Time

A GRE tunnel cannot come up if the peer is unreachable from the configured local address. Test the underlay first, always. Testing the overlay on a broken underlay tells you nothing you did not already know.

  1. Underlay reachability. ping source <local-address-ip> host <peer-ip> — the peer must be reachable from the GRE local address specifically, not just from the firewall generally.
  2. Underlay path. traceroute source <local-address-ip> host <peer-ip> to see what is in between.
  3. Is GRE permitted? Security policy must allow IP protocol 47 on the underlay zone. It is not permitted by default.
  4. Overlay reachability. ping source <tunnel-local-ip> host <tunnel-remote-ip> — this validates encapsulation and decapsulation end to end.
  5. Inner traffic policy. A separate security rule is needed for traffic entering or leaving the zone attached to tunnel.<n>.
admin@fw-01(active)> ping count 3 source 198.51.100.2 host 203.0.113.200    step 1: underlay
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss

admin@fw-01(active)> test security-policy-match from Untrust to Untrust source 198.51.100.2 destination 203.0.113.200 protocol 47
"Allow-GRE-Underlay" {
        application/service [ gre/gre/any/any ];
        action allow;
}                                                                step 3: proto 47 is permitted

admin@fw-01(active)> ping count 3 source 10.255.5.1 host 10.255.5.2          step 4: overlay
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss
SymptomLikely cause
Tunnel state DOWNUnderlay unreachable, security policy missing for protocol 47, or keepalives not being exchanged.
Tunnel UP but no traffic crossesMissing inner security policy, or routing does not point at the tunnel interface.
Small packets fine, large packets failMTU. Lower the tunnel MTU and consider a TCP MSS adjustment on the zone.

Two security rules, not one. GRE needs a rule permitting protocol 47 between the underlay zones, and a separate rule for the traffic riding inside the tunnel. Getting the first and forgetting the second produces a tunnel that reads perfectly healthy and carries nothing.

GRE VPNROUTING / MTU ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Routing over GRE, Keepalives and MTU

CommandDescription / usage
# set network virtual-router <vr> routing-table ip static-route <name> destination <remote-net/mask> nexthop ip-address <tunnel-remote-ip> interface tunnel.<n>Static route through the tunnel. Alternatively run BGP or OSPF over the tunnel interface.
show routing route | match tunnel.<n>Verify routes pointing at the tunnel.
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router <vr> ip <ip-behind-tunnel>Confirm the tunnel is selected as next hop.
show network tunnel gre name <name> | match keepKeepalive interval, retry count and status. Works peer-to-peer when both ends are PAN-OS.
ping source <tunnel-local-ip> do-not-fragment yes size 1372 host <tunnel-remote-ip>Path-MTU test through the tunnel. 1372 + 28 = 1400.

If the far end is not a Palo Alto, GRE keepalives may not be honoured. Use a tunnel monitor profile on tunnel.<n> instead — configure a monitor profile and a destination on the remote side, and the tunnel interface goes down when the monitor fails. That is what makes routing withdraw properly instead of black-holing.

GRE over IPsec

PAN-OS does not offer GRE-inside-IPsec as a single object. You build it by routing the GRE traffic through an IPsec tunnel and making the proxy-IDs match the GRE 5-tuple — the GRE local and peer addresses with protocol 47.

admin@fw-01(active)> show vpn ipsec-sa | match 203.0.113.200
Tun-DC2   GW-DC2   3   ESP   0x8f2a1b44   0x1c99e207   00h41m   the SA carrying the GRE
admin@fw-01(active)> show counter global filter packet-filter yes delta yes   with a proto-47 filter set
SD-WANCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

PAN-OS SD-WAN Building Blocks

Palo Alto SD-WAN is configured and orchestrated from Panorama with the SD-WAN plugin, which pushes the objects below to the branch and hub firewalls and can auto-build the VPN tunnels and BGP between them. Knowing which object makes which decision is the key to troubleshooting it.

ObjectWhereWhat it decides
Link tagObjects → TagsA name for a bundle of similar links (e.g. Broadband, LTE). Each link carries exactly one tag.
SD-WAN Interface ProfileNetwork → SD-WAN Interface ProfileCharacteristics of a physical link: its tag, link type (cable, fiber, LTE, MPLS…), bandwidth, and probing.
Ethernet interface (SD-WAN enabled)Network → InterfacesA Layer 3 interface with SD-WAN enabled and an interface profile applied.
Virtual SD-WAN interface (sdwan.x)Network → Interfaces → SD-WANA numbered group of VPN tunnels, or of direct internet (DIA) links, that you route traffic to.
Path Quality ProfileObjects → SD-WAN Link ManagementLatency, jitter and packet-loss thresholds (with sensitivity) at which a path counts as degraded.
Traffic Distribution ProfileObjects → SD-WAN Link ManagementHow to pick the path: Best Available Path, Top-Down Priority or Weighted Session Distribution, limited to the listed link tags.
SD-WAN policy rulePolicies → SD-WANFor matching traffic (zones, addresses, applications), which Path Quality and Traffic Distribution profiles apply.

The routing table chooses which motorway (sdwan.1 or sdwan.901). The SD-WAN policy chooses which lane of that motorway, based on live traffic reports (Path Quality) and lane rules (Traffic Distribution).

Without the SD-WAN plugin, the classic way to steer between ISPs on PAN-OS is PBF with path monitoring, or floating static routes with path monitoring (see Checking the Routing Table). Those use the normal routing/PBF logic, not SD-WAN path quality.

SD-WANCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

How SD-WAN Interacts with Routing and Policy

  1. PBF and routing come first. The route lookup must point the destination at a virtual SD-WAN interface (sdwan.x). If the route points at a physical interface or a plain tunnel instead, SD-WAN path selection never happens for that traffic.
  2. Zones and rules use the virtual interface. sdwan.x sits in a zone, and security and NAT rules are matched on that zone like any other interface.
  3. The SD-WAN policy rule matching the session supplies the Path Quality and Traffic Distribution profiles.
  4. Path selection picks a physical link (or a tunnel over a link) inside sdwan.x, limited to the link tags in the Traffic Distribution profile, and moves sessions when the path's quality crosses the thresholds.
QuestionFortiGate SD-WANPAN-OS SD-WAN
Where is it configured?On the FortiGate (config system sdwan), or via FortiManagerPanorama with the SD-WAN plugin, pushed to the firewalls
What groups the links?Members in zonesPhysical links (by tag) in virtual SD-WAN interfaces
What measures quality?Health checks (Performance SLA)Path monitoring against a Path Quality profile
What picks the path?SD-WAN rule mode (manual, best quality, lowest cost, maximize bandwidth)Traffic Distribution profile (Best Available, Top-Down, Weighted)
When does it apply?Only if the best route points to SD-WANOnly if the route (or PBF) egress is a virtual SD-WAN interface
Spoke-to-spoke on demandADVPN shortcutsNo ADVPN. Hub-and-spoke transit, or full-mesh VPN clusters built by Panorama

Lab Extension: SPOKE1-PA as an SD-WAN Branch

SPOKE1-PA gets an LTE link on ethernet1/4. Because PAN-OS SD-WAN is driven from Panorama, the configuration below is the set of Panorama objects in the order you create them, written as a settings sheet rather than firewall CLI.

// Panorama · SD-WAN template for SPOKE1-PA (GUI objects, shown as a settings sheet, not CLI)
Objects > Tags                              Broadband · LTE
Network > SD-WAN Interface Profile          SDWAN-BB    tag Broadband · link type Cable Modem · max download/upload per contract
                                            SDWAN-LTE   tag LTE · link type LTE/3G/4G/5G · max download/upload per contract
Network > Interfaces > ethernet1/1          Layer 3 · SD-WAN enabled · interface profile SDWAN-BB
Network > Interfaces > ethernet1/4          Layer 3 · SD-WAN enabled · interface profile SDWAN-LTE
Network > Interfaces > SD-WAN > sdwan.1     DIA group: ethernet1/1, ethernet1/4 · zone UNTRUST
Network > Interfaces > SD-WAN > sdwan.901   VPN group to the hub (tunnels auto-created by the plugin) · zone VPN
Virtual router default                      0.0.0.0/0 → sdwan.1 · corporate prefixes via BGP over sdwan.901
Objects > Path Quality Profile              PQ-VOICE   latency 150 ms · jitter 30 ms · loss 2 % · sensitivity high
                                            PQ-GENERAL latency 300 ms · jitter 100 ms · loss 5 %
Objects > Traffic Distribution Profile      TD-BB-FIRST  Top Down Priority · tags Broadband, LTE
Policies > SD-WAN                           VOICE    from TRUST · app sip, rtp · PQ-VOICE · TD-BB-FIRST
                                            DEFAULT  from TRUST · any · PQ-GENERAL · TD-BB-FIRST
What each line does

Purpose: Makes SPOKE1-PA an SD-WAN branch with two internet links (broadband preferred, LTE backup). Direct internet traffic and the VPN to the hub can both fail over between them, and voice gets stricter quality thresholds than everything else.

Tags and interface profiles

Tags Broadband · LTE
Name the two link bundles. Traffic Distribution profiles refer to links only through these tags.
SDWAN-BB / SDWAN-LTE
Attach the tag to each link and describe it: link type and bandwidth. Bandwidth matters for distribution and reporting.

Interfaces

ethernet1/1 / ethernet1/4 · SD-WAN enabled
Marks the physical links as SD-WAN links and applies their profiles.
sdwan.1 · DIA
Virtual interface grouping both ISP links for direct internet access. The default route points here, and it sits in UNTRUST, so NAT and security rules still say UNTRUST.
sdwan.901 · VPN
Virtual interface grouping the hub tunnels built over each link. BGP routes for corporate prefixes point here, in zone VPN.

Routing

0.0.0.0/0 → sdwan.1
Routing selects the virtual interface. The SD-WAN policy then picks broadband or LTE inside it.
corporate prefixes via BGP over sdwan.901
Hub and other-site traffic resolves to the VPN virtual interface, so SD-WAN path selection applies to it as well.

Profiles and policy

PQ-VOICE · 150/30/2 · sensitivity high
Voice moves off a path quickly once latency, jitter or loss exceed these values.
PQ-GENERAL · 300/100/5
More tolerant thresholds for everything else, to avoid needless path changes.
TD-BB-FIRST · Top Down Priority · Broadband, LTE
Use Broadband while it qualifies, and LTE only when it doesn't, so the expensive link is the last resort.
SD-WAN rule VOICE (above DEFAULT)
First match: SIP/RTP from TRUST gets PQ-VOICE. Everything else falls to DEFAULT.

Moving a route from a physical interface to sdwan.x changes the egress interface. Make sure the virtual interface is in the zone your NAT and security rules expect, or sessions start matching different rules. Commit and push from Panorama in a maintenance window.

SD-WANCONCEPT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Hub-and-Spoke and Spoke-to-Spoke with PAN-OS SD-WAN

The SD-WAN plugin builds VPN clusters: Panorama generates the IPsec tunnels between branches and hubs over each link, places them in VPN virtual SD-WAN interfaces, and configures BGP for the overlay. There's no ADVPN-style on-demand shortcut. Spoke-to-spoke traffic either transits the hub (hub-and-spoke cluster) or uses tunnels that Panorama built directly between branches (full-mesh designs, depending on plugin version).

CheckWhy
Tunnels exist per linkEach virtual VPN interface should hold a tunnel over every link that should carry it. A missing one means no failover path.
BGP routes point to the VPN virtual interfaceIf corporate routes resolve to a plain tunnel or the default route, SD-WAN path selection doesn't apply.
Path monitoring on the branch sideBranches initiate the tunnels and probe them. Hubs are responders and normally don't probe, so judge path health on the branch.
SD-WANDESIGN ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Spoke-to-Spoke Options on PAN-OS

OptionHow spoke-to-spoke worksTroubleshooting focus
Hub transit (this lab)Through the hub: tunnel.1 in, tunnel.2 out, intrazone VPN → VPN.Hub routes, route reflection, intrazone rule, hub capacity.
Full or partial mesh IPsecDirect tunnels between spokes that need them.Per-tunnel config drift, routing preference (direct vs via hub).
LSVPN (GlobalProtect satellites)Portal/gateway on the hub pushes config to satellites. Gateway-to-satellite tunnels plus routing.Satellite authentication, routes pushed, gateway status.
SD-WAN plugin (Panorama)Panorama builds hub-spoke or mesh VPN clusters and path selection.Generated config, path quality profiles, SD-WAN monitoring.

Whatever the overlay, the R·A·P method doesn't change: find the egress interface (and zone) for the flow, check translation, check the rule. Only the commands that show the overlay differ.

Troubleshooting PAN-OS SD-WAN

Follow the decision order: is the path up, which rule applies, what does path monitoring report, and which path did the session take?

show sdwan connection all                                 // paths per virtual interface: state, local/peer IP, tunnel
show sdwan rule vif sdwan.901                              // SD-WAN rules sending traffic to this virtual interface
show sdwan path-monitor stats vif sdwan.901              // latency, jitter, loss per path
show sdwan path-monitor parameter vif sdwan.901          // probe settings
show sdwan session distribution policy-name VOICE        // how sessions are spread across paths
show sdwan session path-select session-id <id>           // path chosen for one session, and why
show sdwan event                                          // path changes and quality events
show counter global filter delta yes                      // SD-WAN related counters
test routing fib-lookup virtual-router default ip <dst>  // does the route point to sdwan.x?
SymptomLikely causeCheck / fix
Traffic never fails overThe route points at a physical interface or tunnel, not sdwan.x.test routing fib-lookup. Point routes (or BGP next hops) at the virtual interface.
LTE used while broadband is fineDistribution method or tag order, or broadband exceeding a strict Path Quality profile.Traffic Distribution profile tag order, show sdwan path-monitor stats.
Sessions flap between pathsThresholds too strict or sensitivity too high for the link.Start with tolerant thresholds, then tighten. Check show sdwan event.
Path shows down on the hub onlyHubs are responders and don't probe.Check path state on the branch side.
Rule never usedEarlier SD-WAN rule matches first, or the match criteria (zone, app) differ.show sdwan rule vif, rule order in Panorama.
New interface traffic hits different security rulessdwan.x is in a different zone than the old interface.Zone of the virtual interface, test security-policy-match.

Sample — path quality with one link degraded

admin@branch-fw> show sdwan path-monitor stats all
VIF          Path             Latency  Jitter  Loss%   MOS   State
sdwan.1      ISP-A-to-Hub1        18ms     2ms   0.0%   4.3   up
sdwan.1      ISP-B-to-Hub1        41ms    11ms  28.4%   2.1   degraded   <-- exceeds the profile threshold
sdwan.2      LTE-to-Hub1          88ms    24ms   1.2%   3.6   up

Compare the measured figures against the thresholds in the path-quality profile before concluding anything. A path marked degraded is telling you it crossed a threshold you configured — that may mean the circuit is genuinely bad, or that the threshold is unrealistic for that circuit type. LTE will not meet a threshold designed for fibre.

time-box 15 minR: route → sdwan.x?path quality

High AvailabilityRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Building an Active/Passive HA Pair

Use it when two identical firewalls (same model, same PAN-OS, same licences and content) must act as one. Cable HA1 (control) and HA2 (data) between them, and connect each data port to the same switches.

// ===== PA-1 (preferred active) =====
set deviceconfig high-availability enabled yes
set deviceconfig high-availability group group-id 10 mode active-passive passive-link-state auto
set deviceconfig high-availability group group-id 10 peer-ip 10.255.0.2
set deviceconfig high-availability group group-id 10 election-option device-priority 90
set deviceconfig high-availability group group-id 10 election-option preemptive yes
set deviceconfig high-availability group group-id 10 state-synchronization enabled yes
set deviceconfig high-availability interface ha1 port ha1-a ip-address 10.255.0.1 netmask 255.255.255.252
set deviceconfig high-availability interface ha2 port ha2-a ip-address 10.255.1.1 netmask 255.255.255.252
set deviceconfig high-availability group group-id 10 monitoring link-monitoring link-group UPLINKS enabled yes failure-condition any interface [ ethernet1/1 ethernet1/2 ]
commit
// ===== PA-2: same, except peer-ip 10.255.0.1, its own HA1/HA2 IPs, device-priority 110 =====
What each line does

Purpose: Enables HA in active/passive mode, defines the peer and the HA links, makes PA-1 the preferred active unit, synchronises sessions, and fails over when an uplink fails.

high-availability enabled yes
Turns HA on.
group group-id 10 mode active-passive
Group ID (must match on both peers) and mode.
passive-link-state auto
The passive firewall keeps its data links up (not forwarding), so neighbours see link and failover is faster. The default shutdown is safer if Layer 2 loops are possible.
peer-ip 10.255.0.2
The peer's HA1 address.
election-option device-priority 90
A lower number = higher priority. PA-1 (90) is preferred over PA-2 (110).
election-option preemptive yes
Lets the preferred unit take back the active role when it recovers. Enable it on both peers if you want priority to decide.
state-synchronization enabled yes
Syncs the session table, forwarding table, ARP table and IPsec SAs over HA2, so sessions survive failover.
interface ha1 port ha1-a ip-address … · interface ha2 port ha2-a …
The control (HA1) and data (HA2) links. Add HA1 backup and heartbeat backup for resilience.
monitoring link-monitoring link-group UPLINKS … failure-condition any interface [ … ]
Fails over when any uplink in the group goes down. Add path monitoring for failures beyond the cable.

Verify and troubleshoot

1 · Pair formed

show high-availability state
show high-availability all

Good: Local active, peer passive, both HA1/HA2 up, config synchronised. If not: Peer not seen: HA1 cabling/IP, group-id, or PAN-OS/content mismatch.

2 · State sync

show high-availability state-synchronization

Good: Session sync counters increasing. If not: HA2 link or transport issue: sessions would drop on failover.

3 · Monitors

show high-availability link-monitoring
show high-availability path-monitoring

Good: Groups and members up. If not: A down member triggers or blocks failover.

4 · Controlled failover test

request high-availability state suspend
show high-availability state
request high-availability state functional

Good: The peer becomes active while this unit is suspended, then it returns. If not: No failover: the peer isn't healthy, or preemption/priority settings differ.

⚠ Syntax note. PAN-OS configuration-mode set commands. The structure follows Palo Alto documentation and published configurations. Use Tab/? while typing, run commit validate (or validate full) before commit, and check the GUI equivalent shown in each step.

High AvailabilityHOW IT WORKS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Hub & spokes

Active/Passive Failover in Motion

In an active/passive pair only the active firewall forwards traffic. HA1 carries hellos, heartbeats and config sync. HA2 carries session (and forwarding-table) sync, so existing sessions survive a failover. Link and path monitoring decide when the active should give up.

LinkCarriesIf it fails
HA1 (control)Hellos, heartbeats, HA state, config syncPeers can't see each other: risk of split brain. Use an HA1 backup link.
HA2 (data)Session table, forwarding tables, ARPFailover still happens, but sessions aren't synced and drop.
HA3 (A/A only)Packet forwarding between peers for asymmetric flowsAsymmetric sessions in active/active break.
High AvailabilityHOW MANY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

HA Links — How Many, and What Each One Does

Two firewalls are like two friends guarding one door. They need a walkie-talkie to say "I'm OK" every second (HA1). They need a notebook they share so both know who already came in (HA2). If both friends open the door at the same time, they also need a little window between them to hand people across (HA3).

ModeRequiredOptional backupsTotal you normally cable
Active/Passive2 — HA1, HA2HA1-backup, HA2-backup2 minimum, 4 recommended
Active/Active3 — HA1, HA2, HA3HA1-backup, HA2-backup (no HA3-backup exists)3 minimum, 5 recommended
LinkJobUnder the hood
HA1 · controlHellos, heartbeats, HA state, config sync, and management-plane sync of routing and User-ID.Layer 3, needs an IP. TCP 28769/28260 clear text, TCP 28 when encrypted. Heartbeats are ICMP.
HA1-backupTakes over if HA1 dies, so the peers do not both think they are alone.Separate physical port, different subnet from HA1. TCP 28770/28260.
Heartbeat backupExtra heartbeat over the MGT port.Port 28771. Recommended when HA1 or HA1-backup uses an in-band port.
HA2 · dataCopies sessions, forwarding tables, IPsec SAs and ARP tables to the peer.Layer 2, EtherType 0x7261 by default; IP (protocol 99) or UDP 29281 if it must cross subnets. One-way from active to passive, except HA2 keep-alive.
HA2-backupKeeps session sync alive if HA2 fails.Separate physical port, different subnet from HA2.
HA3 · forwardingActive/active only. Hands packets to the peer that owns the session — during session setup and for asymmetric flows.Layer 2, MAC-in-MAC, no IP, no encryption. No backup link: use a LAG for redundancy. Needs jumbo frames on anything in the path. If HA3 fails, the active-secondary goes non-functional.

HA1 is the one that matters most during an upgrade. Lose HA1 and HA1-backup and each peer thinks the other is dead — that is split brain. This is why the runbook's HA health gate checks HA1 link status: up before anything else.

HA4 is not part of this picture. It belongs to NGFW clusters, not to a classic two-firewall HA pair.

High AvailabilityACTIVE/PASSIVE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Active/Passive — One Works, One Watches

Two lifeguards. One sits in the tall chair and watches every swimmer. The other sits on the bench. Every second they wave at each other (HA1). The one in the chair keeps passing notes about every swimmer to the bench (HA2). When the chair lifeguard has to leave — say, to get new glasses (the upgrade) — the bench lifeguard climbs up and already knows every swimmer. Nobody drowns.

LinkWhat it is doing in the picture
HA1Ball bouncing both ways — "are you alive?" "yes, are you?" Config changes also ride here.
HA2Balls flowing one way only. The active copies its session table to the passive, so a failover does not drop live sessions.
Backups (dashed)Idle until the primary link fails. Optional, but strongly recommended.
High AvailabilityACTIVE/ACTIVE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Active/Active — Both Work, and They Hand Packets Across

Two shop cashiers, both open. A customer starts an order at till 1 but walks over to till 2 to pay. Till 2 does not start a new order — it slides the customer across the counter back to till 1, who owns that order. That slide across the counter is HA3. They still wave at each other (HA1) and still share the notebook (HA2).

During an active/active upgrade the survivor carries everything while its peer is suspended — including traffic that used to hairpin over HA3. Size for 100% on one box before the window, not during it.

High AvailabilityVERIFY ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Checking the Links — CLI and GUI

Run on both peers before the window, and again after each peer comes back.

admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state          roles plus HA1 / HA2 link status in one screen
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability all            full detail — find the HA1, HA1-backup, HA2 (and HA3 on A/A) blocks
Link State: Up                                             what you want to see under every configured link
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability interface ha2  HA2 counters — are sessions actually syncing
  • Health at a glance: Dashboard → High Availability widget. HA1, HA2 (and HA3) lights green.
  • Where HA1 / HA2 and their backups are configured: Device → High Availability → the Control Link (HA1), Control Link (HA1 Backup), Data Link (HA2) and Data Link (HA2 Backup) panels.
  • Where HA3 is configured (A/A only): Device → High Availability → Active/Active Config → Packet Forwarding.
Link downWhat breaksUpgrade decision
HA1 (no backup)Split-brain risk — both peers may go active.Stop. Fix before the window.
HA2Failover works but drops every live session.Stop. The whole point of a hitless upgrade is gone.
HA3 (A/A)Active-secondary goes non-functional; asymmetric flows fail.Stop. Fix the LAG / jumbo frames first.
A backup link onlyNo redundancy for that link.Proceed with care, record it in the change.

HA Status — The Essential Commands

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
show high-availability allComprehensive dump — state, peer, link and path monitoring, sync. Run this first.Device > High Availability
show high-availability stateLocal and peer state with the version-compatibility check.Dashboard > High Availability widget
show high-availability state-synchronizationSent and received sync message statistics — proves session sync is actually working.Device > High Availability
show high-availability link-monitoringLink-monitoring status for HA1, HA2 and HA3.HA > Link and Path Monitoring
show high-availability path-monitoringPath-monitoring status — which destinations are being probed for failover triggers.HA > Link and Path Monitoring
show high-availability transitionsCount of state transitions. A high number means flapping.Device > High Availability
show high-availability flap-statisticsDetailed flap counters — note the hyphen, it is one word to the parser.Device > High Availability
show high-availability control-link statisticsHA1 control-link message statistics.Device > High Availability
show high-availability interface ha2 | match bytesQuick confirmation that HA2 is passing session-sync data.HA > Backup links
show high-availability all | match configWhether the running config is in sync with the peer.Device > High Availability

Sample — a healthy pair

admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state
Group 1:
  Mode: Active-Passive
  Local Information:
      Version: 11.1.4-h7      State: active         (last 62 days)
      Preemptive: no          Priority: 100
  Peer Information:
      Version: 11.1.4-h7      State: passive        Priority: 110
      Mgmt IP: 10.10.0.12
  Version Compatibility: Match
  App-Threat Compatibility: Match
  Running Config Compatibility: Match
  HA1: up    HA1-backup: up    HA2: up
  State Sync: Enabled          State Sync Type: Ethernet
StateMeaning
active / passiveNormal active-passive operation.
initialJust booted, has not yet negotiated a role. Should not persist more than a couple of minutes.
suspendedTaken out of the group — by an operator, or automatically because the peer is on incompatible code. Recover with request high-availability state functional.
non-functionalFailed a monitored check — link, path, or a dataplane fault. Look at link and path monitoring output.
tentativeActive-active only. Just came up and is syncing before taking traffic.

Version Compatibility: Mismatch is not cosmetic. Peers more than one feature release apart will refuse to sync, and the older one suspends itself. During a staged upgrade this is expected and temporary; outside one, it means somebody upgraded a single peer and stopped.

High AvailabilityFAILOVER ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Suspend, Resume and Manual Sync

CommandDescription / usageGUI path
request high-availability state suspendSuspend HA on the local device — the peer takes over. The controlled way to test failover or take a box out for work.HA > Operational Commands > Suspend local device
request high-availability state functionalBring the device back into the HA group.HA > Operational Commands > Make local device functional
request high-availability sync-to-remote running-configPush the running config to the peer when auto-sync has failed.HA > Operational Commands > Sync to peer
request high-availability sessions-reestablish [force]Re-establish the HA1 link. Add force when HA1-backup is not configured.Device > High Availability
show high-availability session-reestablish-statusWhen HA1 or HA1-backup was last re-established.Device > High Availability
request high-availability clear-alarm-ledClear the HA alarm LED on hardware after a failover.CLI only
admin@fw-01(active)> request high-availability state suspend
Successfully changed HA state to suspended
admin@fw-01(suspended)> show high-availability state | match State   note the prompt changed
      State: suspended
... peer is now active; do the work ...
admin@fw-01(suspended)> request high-availability state functional
Successfully changed HA state to functional

Suspending is one command; the box will not un-suspend itself. If preemption is disabled — which it should be — the peer stays active after you go functional, and that is correct. Do not "fix" it by suspending the other peer as well.

The prompt tells you everything. admin@fw-01(suspended)> means you are on the box that is deliberately not carrying traffic. Look at the prompt before every command during a change window.

⚠ Verification note. request high-availability state suspend / functional, request high-availability sync-to-remote running-config and request high-availability clear-alarm-led are confirmed (PAN-OS XML API upgrade use case, Palo Alto community troubleshooting lists). request high-availability sessions-reestablish and show high-availability session-reestablish-status weren't found in the official HA documentation reviewed. Confirm with request high-availability ? on your release.

High AvailabilityLOGS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

HA Logs and Debug

CommandDescription / usage
less mp-log ha_agent.logThe HA agent log — where the reason for an unexpected failover is recorded.
tail follow yes mp-log ha_agent.logLive-tail during a controlled failover test.
debug ha-agent on debugIncrease HA-agent verbosity. Revert with debug ha-agent on info.

admin@fw-02(passive)> tail follow yes mp-log ha_agent.log
Apr 27 03:14:02 ha_agent: Path monitor group "wan-gateways" FAILED (2 of 2 destinations down)
Apr 27 03:14:02 ha_agent: Local device transitioning active -> non-functional
Apr 27 03:14:03 ha_agent: Peer 10.10.0.11 transitioning passive -> active

When a failover happens and nobody knows why, this log holds the answer and it is almost always one of three things: a monitored link went down, a path-monitor group failed, or a dataplane process crashed. All three are named explicitly in ha_agent.log at the moment of transition — search by timestamp.

Symptom after failoverCheck
Existing sessions droppedSession synchronisation: state-synchronization status, HA2 link health.

Always run troubleshooting commands on the active firewall. Sessions, counters and captures on the passive peer don't reflect live traffic.

System & SoftwarePERFORMANCE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

CPU, Memory and Throughput

Two planes, two commands. show system resources is the management plane; show running resource-monitor is the dataplane. Users complaining about slow traffic care about the second one; admins complaining about a slow web UI care about the first.

CommandPlaneDescription / usage
show system resourcesMPTop-style CPU and memory by management process.
show system resources followMPLive-updating. Ctrl-C to exit.
show running resource-monitorDPPer-core CPU, session table and packet rate.
show running resource-monitor secondDPPer-second granularity — catches short spikes the averages hide.
show running resource-monitor minuteDPPer-minute, with recent history.
show system statistics applicationDPLive throughput by application. Toggle views with the a and s keys.
show system statistics sessionDPLive per-session throughput.
show system logdb-quota / show system logdb-quota detailMPLog database quota and usage by log type.
admin@fw-01(active)> show running resource-monitor second
DP dp0:
Resource monitoring sampling data (per second):

CPU load (%) during last 60 seconds:
core  0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
      6  71  74  69  73  70  72  68
                                        core 0 is control; 1-7 are packet-processing
Resource utilization (%) during last 60 seconds:
session (average): 22        session (maximum): 26
packet buffer (average): 11  packet descriptor (average): 9

Look at the spread across packet-processing cores, not just the average. One core at 98% while the others idle means a single elephant flow pinned to that core — a large backup or a busy tunnel — and the box is effectively saturated even though average CPU looks comfortable. Averages hide the exact failure mode you are chasing.

System & SoftwareRESTART ✓ checked vs PAN docs Lab · Edge HA pair

Processes, Reboot and Shutdown

CommandImpactDescription / usage
show system software statusNoneWhich daemons are running or dead.
debug software restart process <process>VariesRestart one MP process — ikemgr, routed, useridd, management-server. Effect depends entirely on which one.
debug software restart process allSevereRestart every MP process.
debug software restart dataplaneSevereRestarts the dataplane. Every session drops.
request restart dataplaneSevereThe supported way to restart the dataplane. Still drops all sessions.
request restart systemOutageFull reboot.
request shutdown systemOutageGraceful shutdown. Somebody has to be on site to power it back on.

Restarting a process is not a diagnosis. It clears the symptom and destroys the evidence, and if a process needed restarting there is a reason worth knowing. Generate a tech-support file before the restart, or you will be reproducing the fault deliberately to get one.

On an HA pair, suspend the local device first (request high-availability state suspend) so the peer takes over cleanly, rather than letting a dataplane restart trigger an unplanned failover mid-restart.

User-ID lives on both planes, and they can disagree. The management plane learns mappings and the dataplane enforces them — when a user-based rule misbehaves, checking both is the first move.

admin@fw-01(active)> show user ip-user-mapping ip 10.10.20.55
IP address:       10.10.20.55 (vsys1)
User:             corp\jsmith
From:             AD-Agent (10.10.0.30)
Idle Timeout:     2412 s
Max. TTL:         6612 s

A user-based rule failing to match usually comes down to one of three things and in this order: no mapping exists for the address, the mapping is stale from a previous user of a DHCP lease, or the group membership has not been refreshed since the user was added to the group. Check ip-user-mapping first, then show user group name.

Management Access & HardeningRECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: Securing Administrative Access

Use it when building or auditing a firewall. Palo Alto's guidance is clear: keep the management interface on a dedicated, internal management network, restrict who can reach it, and never expose management (GUI/SSH) on internet-facing interfaces.

set deviceconfig system ip-address 10.99.0.10 netmask 255.255.255.0 default-gateway 10.99.0.1
set deviceconfig system permitted-ip 10.99.0.0/24
set deviceconfig system service disable-telnet yes disable-http yes
set network profiles interface-management-profile PING-ONLY ping yes
set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 interface-management-profile PING-ONLY
set mgt-config users jdoe-admin permissions role-based superuser yes
set deviceconfig system authentication-profile AUTH-ADMIN-MFA
commit
What each line does

Purpose: Puts management on its own network, limits who may connect, disables cleartext protocols, keeps the internet interface free of management services, and uses named admin accounts with MFA.

system ip-address · default-gateway
The out-of-band management interface on the management network.
system permitted-ip 10.99.0.0/24
Only these source addresses may connect to the management interface (Device > Setup > Interfaces > Management).
service disable-telnet yes disable-http yes
Only encrypted management (HTTPS, SSH).
interface-management-profile PING-ONLY on ethernet1/1
The internet-facing interface answers ping only, with no HTTPS/SSH/SNMP. Exposure of management on dataplane interfaces has been at the centre of several critical PAN-OS advisories.
mgt-config users jdoe-admin … superuser
Named accounts instead of a shared admin account, so actions are audited per person. Use admin roles for least privilege.
system authentication-profile AUTH-ADMIN-MFA
Admin logins via an authentication profile backed by RADIUS/SAML with MFA.

Recipe: Checking and Renewing Firewall Certificates

Use it when GlobalProtect, decryption, the GUI, syslog over SSL or Panorama links suddenly fail. Expired certificates are a classic cause. Check expiry dates regularly and renew before they lapse.

show sslmgr-store config-certificate-info
show log system direction equal backward | match cert
// renewal: generate a CSR (signed externally), then import the signed certificate with the same name
request certificate generate certificate-name GP-2027 name gp.example.com algorithm RSA rsa-nbits 2048 signed-by external
What each line does

Purpose: Lists certificates with their expiry dates, finds expiry warnings, and generates a CSR for renewal.

show sslmgr-store config-certificate-info
Certificate details including expiry dates (db-exp-date).
show log system … | match cert
System log entries about certificates, such as expiry warnings.
request certificate generate … signed-by external
Creates a key and CSR on the firewall (GUI: Device > Certificate Management > Certificates > Generate, Signed By External Authority). Export the CSR, have it signed, then import the signed certificate onto the same name.
Where a certificate is usedWhat breaks when it expires
SSL/TLS service profile of the GP portal/gatewayUsers can't connect: certificate warnings or errors
Forward Trust CA (decryption)Every decrypted site shows an error
Management GUI certificateBrowser warnings for admins
Syslog/LDAPS client certificates, Panorama device certificateLog forwarding, LDAP or Panorama connectivity fails

Neither is on the official cheat sheets. The GUI (Device > Certificate Management > Certificates, Expires column) is the documented view.

Upgrade · PlanSCOPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

What This Runbook Covers

An HA pair is two firewalls holding hands — one can take a nap (reboot) while the other keeps working. A standalone firewall is one firewall alone — when it naps, the door is closed.

Two upgrade paths live in this document. Every step is shown in CLI with the web-interface path beside it in a GUI PATH box, and the Firewall GUI and Panorama GUI groups walk the whole change click-by-click. Both paths assume you can reach the management plane, and both assume the firewall can reach updates.paloaltonetworks.com or that you have already uploaded the image manually.

PathUse whenTraffic impact
HA pairTwo firewalls in active/passive or active/activeBrief failover blips only, if sequenced correctly
StandaloneSingle firewall, no peerFull outage for the duration of the reboot

Every command below has been checked against the current PAN-OS Upgrade Guide and the PAN-OS CLI reference. Where a widely-circulated runbook command is wrong on modern PAN-OS, it is called out in Syntax Corrections rather than silently fixed — you will meet the old form in other people's documents.

Version strings in this guide use <target> as a placeholder. Substitute your actual target — for example 11.2.x-hN or 12.1.x. Do not copy a version number out of a runbook; read it off your own upgrade path.

Upgrade · PlanSTART HERE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Which Kind of Upgrade Is This?

A version number is an address: 12 is the city, .1 is the street, .4 is the house, -h2 is a new coat of paint on the same house. Moving house on the same street is easy. Moving to another city needs a map.

Reading a PAN-OS version:
   11 . 1 . 4 - h13
    |    |   |    |
    |    |   |    +-- HOTFIX       urgent fixes on top of a maintenance release
    |    |   +------- MAINTENANCE  bug fixes, same features
    |    +----------- FEATURE      new features, new behaviour
    +---------------- MAJOR        new generation (11 -> 12)
Upgrade typeExamplePath planning?HA version-gap risk?RollbackFollow
Hotfix11.1.4-h7 → 11.1.4-h13No — but base 11.1.0 must be on diskNoEasyPatch Route
Maintenance11.1.4 → 11.1.10NoNoEasyPatch Route
Feature11.1.x → 11.2.xYesOnly if peers end up 2+ releases apartHarder — needs the exported configCheck the Path, then the full runbook
Major11.x → 12.1Yes — plus hardware supportYes, if skipping on an HA pairHarderCheck the Path, Going to 12.1, full runbook

There is no PAN-OS 11.3 or 11.4. The feature releases run 10.1 → 10.2 → 11.0 → 11.1 → 11.2 → 12.1. When someone says "11.1 to 11.4" they almost always mean 11.1.x to 11.1.4 — a maintenance upgrade.

Upgrade · PlanMAJOR / FEATURE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

How to Check the Upgrade Path — Seven Checks

Before a long car trip you check four things: does the car go that far, which roads are open, where you must stop, and whether the people at home know you are coming. This page is that check list.

  1. Read what you run today. CLI: show system info | match "model|sw-version". GUI: Dashboard → General Information, or Device → Software (tick in Currently Installed).
  2. Can the hardware run the target? TechDocs → Compatibility Matrix → Supported OS Releases by Model. If your model has no tick under the target, stop — this is a hardware refresh, not an upgrade. Check the End-of-Life Summary for the support end date of the target too.
  3. Pick the target build, not just the release. Use Palo Alto's Support PAN-OS Software Release Guidance (LIVEcommunity) for the currently preferred maintenance release. On 11.1.3 and later, Device → Software → clear Base Releases to show preferred releases only.
  4. Read the path table. TechDocs → PAN-OS Upgrade Guide → Determine the Upgrade Path, with the version filter set to your target. Summary below.
  5. Panorama and friends first. Panorama, Log Collectors and WildFire appliances must be on the same or a later release than the firewalls. Check Panorama, Log Collector, Firewall, and WildFire Version Compatibility, and any plugin version tables (SD-WAN, DLP).
  6. Read the notes for every release on the path — including releases you skip. Release Notes (known issues, minimum content version), Upgrade/Downgrade Considerations and Changes to Default Behavior.
  7. Run the upgrade check report (standalone or from Panorama for managed firewalls) and clear its warnings before the window.

The path table in one view

Running todayDocumented path (standalone / Panorama-managed)
11.0 / 11.1 / 11.2Skip Software Version → directly to 12.1.
10.2.xSkip directly up to 11.2. Then 11.2 → 12.1 as a second hop.
10.1.xSkip up to three releases — directly up to 11.1. Then onward.
10.0.x and olderOne release at a time: install the latest preferred maintenance release of each, until you reach 10.1, then skip.

HA pairs: the skip feature is documented for standalone and Panorama-managed devices, and HA peers two or more feature releases apart suspend the older one (Peer version too old). Step HA pairs one feature release at a time unless TAC confirms otherwise. See Going to 12.1.

Two rules from the upgrade guide worth memorising

  • Upgrade from the latest maintenance release of each release on your path, not from an old build.
  • Never install a base image (x.y.0) unless it is your final target. Download it; do not install it.

Worked examples

From → toStandaloneHA pair
11.2.x → 12.11 hop1 hop
11.1.x → 12.11 hop (skip)2 hops: 11.2, then 12.1
10.2.x → 12.12 hops: skip to 11.2, then 12.13 hops: 11.1, 11.2, 12.1
PA-3200 on 11.1 → 12.1Not possible — PA-3200 stops at 11.1.
  • Device → Software → Check Now. What the box offers is the final word: if the target is not listed after Check Now, the box cannot reach it in one hop.

Patch and Maintenance Upgrades — The Short Route

Same house, fresh paint. You still move the furniture out of the way first (backup), and you still check the paint is dry before anyone leans on the wall (chassis-ready).

For a jump inside one feature release — 11.1.4 → 11.1.10, or 11.1.4-h7 → 11.1.4-h13 — the procedure is the same as the full runbook, minus the planning.

SectionPatch upgrade?
Pre-Change Checklist, Remote Access, Capture State, BackupYes — all of it
Disk SpaceYes — and do not delete the base image (x.y.0)
Software and ContentYes — check the target's minimum content version
HA Links, HA Preparation, HA UpgradeYes — same suspend / install / functional sequence
Check the Path, Going to 12.1Skip
RollbackUse Reverting to a Previous Maintenance Release only
The whole patch on one peer (HA: after suspend; standalone: this IS the outage at the reboot):
admin@fw-01> request system software check                         refresh the list
admin@fw-01> request system software info                          base image (x.y.0) must say Downloaded yes for a hotfix target
admin@fw-01> request system software download version <target>   non-disruptive
admin@fw-01> request system software install version <target>    wait for FIN / OK in show jobs id
admin@fw-01> request restart system                                 the reboot
admin@fw-01> show chassis-ready                                     yes = dataplane up
  • Device → Software → Check Now → Download (base first if needed) → Install → reboot when prompted.

Two peers on different maintenance builds of the same release for a few minutes is normal. Still finish both peers in the same window.

Palo Alto also documents a separate Install a PAN-OS Software Patch procedure with its own revert steps. This runbook does not cover it; follow that page if you use it.

The Upgrade Path — Rules That Bite Before You Type Anything

PAN-OS will not let you jump wherever you like. Three constraints govern the path, and violating any of them turns a clean maintenance window into a long night.

  1. You can now skip feature releases — within limits. The Skip Software Version Upgrade feature (PAN-OS 10.1 and later) lets a firewall jump up to three releases. Palo Alto's current path table says 11.0, 11.1 and 11.2 can go directly to 12.1. Older releases (10.0 and earlier) still climb one step at a time. See Going to PAN-OS 12.1.
  2. A hotfix needs its base image on the box. To land on 11.1.4-h13 the firewall must already have 11.1.0 downloaded. The base image only needs downloading, not installing.
  3. HA peers cannot drift more than one feature release apart. When they do, the older peer suspends itself with the message Peer version too old. If your path has multiple hops, both peers must land on each intermediate release before you move on. This is the rule that collides with skipping — an HA pair jumping 11.1 → 12.1 is two releases apart mid-change. See the HA warning in Going to PAN-OS 12.1.

Think of it as a staircase with no handrail. On old releases you can only take one step at a time, you must both be standing on the same step before either of you climbs again, and the step has to be delivered before you can stand on it.

Read the currently installed version and the content versions in one shot:
admin@fw-01(active)> show system info | match "sw-version|app-version|threat-version|hostname"  version and content in one line — your baseline record
hostname: fw-01
sw-version: 11.1.x-hN
app-version: 8951-9143
threat-version: 8951-9143

The release notes for every version you pass through list minimum content release requirements and known issues. Reading only the release notes for your final target is the single most common planning mistake.

Upgrade · Plan11.x → 12.1 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Going to PAN-OS 12.1 — Checks Before You Plan the Window

Before you buy new shoes, check they come in your size. Some older firewalls simply do not come in size 12 — no amount of upgrading will fit them.

1 · Can the hardware run 12.x at all?

ModelLast PAN-OS it supports12.1?
PA-220 / PA-220R10.2No
PA-3200 Series11.1No — stay on 11.1 or refresh hardware
PA-5200 Series11.2No — 11.2 is the ceiling
PA-7000 Series11.2 (card-dependent)No
PA-400 / PA-3400 / PA-5400 / PA-5450, VM-Series12.xYes

Per the Palo Alto compatibility matrix, 12.x support begins at 12.1.2. Never target 12.1.0 or 12.1.1. Re-check your exact model in Compatibility Matrix → Supported OS Releases by Model before the change — the table above is a summary, not a substitute.

2 · Which path?

Running todayStandalone / Panorama-managedHA pair (safe default)
11.2.xDirect to 12.1 (skip)Direct to 12.1 — one feature release apart, normal HA rules
11.1.xDirect to 12.1 (skip)11.1 → 11.2 → 12.1, both peers on each step
11.0.xDirect to 12.1 (skip)11.0 → 11.1 → 11.2 → 12.1, or confirm skip support for HA with TAC

HA + skip is the open question. The Skip Software Version feature is documented for standalone and Panorama-managed devices. The HA rule says peers two or more feature releases apart suspend the older one with Peer version too old. If you skip 11.1 → 12.1 on an HA pair, the peers sit two releases apart between the first and second reboot — with no redundancy while that lasts. Until the 12.1 HA upgrade page or TAC confirms otherwise, step HA pairs through 11.2.

3 · How a skip actually works

Download the target's base image and the target. Install ONLY the target.
admin@fw-01> request system software check                          refresh the list — skip-eligible 12.1 releases should now appear
admin@fw-01> request system software download version 12.1.0        base image — download only, never install
admin@fw-01> request system software download version <12.1 target> the release you will actually run
admin@fw-01> request system software install version <12.1 target>  one install, one reboot
  • Device → Software → Check Now. Download the 12.1 base image, then the 12.1 target. Install the target only.
  • If 12.1 is not listed after Check Now, the box is not skip-eligible — go via 11.2.

4 · Pre-checks that are easy to miss

CheckWhy
Panorama firstPanorama, its Log Collectors and WildFire appliances must be on the same or later release than the firewalls. Upgrade them first.
CertificatesSince 11.1, OpenSSL Security Level 2: RSA ≥ 2048 or ECDSA ≥ 256, SHA256 or better. Weak certs break after upgrade — fix them before.
Strata Logging ServiceInstall the device certificate on each HA peer before upgrading; the firewall switches to it for logging-service authentication.
Release notes for every skipped releaseSkipping the install does not skip the behaviour changes. Read Upgrade/Downgrade Considerations for 11.2 and 12.1.
Upgrade check reportPAN-OS can generate an upgrade check report (standalone or from Panorama for managed devices). Run it and clear the warnings before the window.
PluginsSD-WAN, DLP and other Panorama plugins have their own compatible-version tables. Check before Panorama goes to 12.1.

Pre-Change Checklist

Pack your bag the night before school. Everything on this list is packing — do it before the window, not during it.

Work top to bottom. Anything unchecked here becomes a problem at 2am.

ItemWhy it matters
Change window approvedReboots are non-negotiable. Standalone means outage; HA means failover risk.
Out-of-band accessConsole or a jump host on a different path. If the management interface does not come back, SSH will not save you.
Config and device state exported off-boxThe on-box snapshot is useless if the box itself is the problem. Device state also carries what Panorama pushed.
Tech-support file generatedTAC will ask for a pre-upgrade one. Generating it afterwards loses the before picture.
Content up to dateRelease notes state a minimum content version. Upgrading with stale content is a supported way to break App-ID.
HA fully in syncUpgrading an out-of-sync pair propagates the mismatch into the new version.
Disk space checked on both peersA full partition stops the download or the install. show system disk-space — and mind the 90% rule on /opt/pancfg.

Upgrade · PlanPLAYBOOK ✓ checked vs PAN docs

It Broke After an Upgrade or a Change

time-box 30 minchanged behaviourcommit diff
  1. What exactly changed? Use Config Audit (Device → Config Audit) between the last good and the current running config, or compare the candidate with the running config before committing a fix. For upgrades, compare the backup taken before the upgrade.
  2. Did anything fail to load? Check the system log around the upgrade and the commit for warnings. Run show jobs all for failed commits or content installs.
  3. Run the R·A·P checks on the failing flow. Most "upgrade" faults turn out to be a rule, NAT or route difference the tests reveal in minutes.
  4. Read the release notes for every version crossed, especially "Changes to default behaviour" and known issues. Content updates (App-ID) can also change which rule matches.
  5. Routing engine: moving from legacy virtual routers to the Advanced Routing Engine is a deliberate migration, not an upgrade side effect. Commands change from show routing to show advanced-routing.

Pre-change capture (attach to the change ticket): show system info, show routing route per VR, show routing protocol bgp summary, show vpn ike-sa, show high-availability state, show session info, plus a saved named config snapshot. Repeat afterwards and compare.

Upgrade · PreparePRE-STAGE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Opening Remote Access Before the Window

Make sure you have the key to the house before you lock the door behind you.

An upgrade is the worst possible time to discover you cannot reach the firewall from where you actually are. Sort access out days ahead, from a session you already have, while the firewall is healthy.

Do this before you start, never during. Every method below needs a commit, and a commit needs a working management session. If you are locked out already, you are going to the console or the data centre — there is no remote fix for a lockout.

Permitted IP addresses on the management interface

If the management interface has a permitted-IP list, only those sources can reach it. Adding your remote source is the single most common pre-upgrade access task.

admin@fw-01(active)> configure                                                enter configuration mode — the prompt changes from > to #

See what is already allowed — Tab after permitted-ip lists the current entries:
admin@fw-01(active)# show deviceconfig system permitted-ip                    which source addresses may reach the management interface

Add your remote source. Always a /32 for a single host:
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig system permitted-ip 203.0.113.45/32 description "upgrade-window jump host"  allow one host to reach management — everything unlisted is then blocked
admin@fw-01(active)# commit                                                   apply the candidate config — nothing above is live until this runs
admin@fw-01(active)# exit                                                     leave configuration mode, back to the > prompt

GUI: Device → Setup → Management → edit Management Interface Settings → add the address under Permitted IP Addresses → OK → Commit.

The permitted-IP list is all-or-nothing. An empty list means any source may reach the management interface. The moment you add your first entry, everything not listed is blocked — including the session you are typing in right now. Add your current source address in the same commit, or you will cut yourself off the instant it applies.

If Panorama pushes the list via a template

A template-pushed permitted-ip cannot be edited locally until you override it:

admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig system permitted-ip 203.0.113.45/32  allow that source address to reach the management interface
Server error : set failed, may need to override template object permitted-ip first

admin@fw-01(active)# override deviceconfig system permitted-ip             break the Panorama template lock so you can edit this locally
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig system permitted-ip 203.0.113.45/32  allow that source address to reach the management interface
admin@fw-01(active)# commit                                                apply the candidate config — nothing above is live until this runs

Cleaner alternative: add the entry to the Panorama template and push it to both peers at once. The local override works, but it drifts the firewall from its template and someone will "fix" that later by re-pushing — removing your access.

Upgrade · PrepareACCESS PATHS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Access Paths, Best to Worst

There is more than one way to reach a firewall remotely, and they are not equally good ideas. In order of preference:

MethodVerdict
Out-of-band console (terminal server / iLO)Best. Survives a failed boot, a bad commit and a wrong permitted-IP entry. The only path that works when the firewall does not.
VPN to the management network, then SSHVery good. No firewall management exposed publicly. Nothing to undo afterwards.
Jump host on the management networkGood. One permitted-IP entry, permanent, auditable.
GlobalProtect on the firewall itselfCareful. Fine day to day, useless when the box is mid-reboot — the thing you need access to is the thing that is down.
Interface management profile on a data interfaceLast resort. Works, but you are putting the management plane on a traffic-carrying interface.
Management interface directly on a public IPDo not. See the warning below.

Interface management profile on a data-plane interface

When there is genuinely no other path, you can enable SSH and HTTPS on a data interface's IP. Three things must all be right: the profile, the interface it is attached to, and a security policy permitting the traffic.

admin@fw-01(active)> configure                                                enter configuration mode — the prompt changes from > to #

1. Build a tightly scoped profile:
admin@fw-01(active)# set network profiles interface-management-profile MGMT-TEMP https yes  allow the web interface on whichever interface gets this profile
admin@fw-01(active)# set network profiles interface-management-profile MGMT-TEMP ssh yes  allow SSH on whichever interface gets this profile
admin@fw-01(active)# set network profiles interface-management-profile MGMT-TEMP ping yes  allow ping, so you can test reachability
admin@fw-01(active)# set network profiles interface-management-profile MGMT-TEMP permitted-ip 203.0.113.45/32  restrict it to one source — this is the whole security control

2. Attach it to the interface:
admin@fw-01(active)# set network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 interface-management-profile MGMT-TEMP  attach the profile to a data interface so its IP answers SSH and HTTPS
admin@fw-01(active)# commit                                                   apply the candidate config — nothing above is live until this runs
admin@fw-01(active)# exit                                                     leave configuration mode, back to the > prompt

3. Verify it took:
admin@fw-01(active)> show interface ethernet1/1                               detail for one interface, including any management profile applied

GUI: Network → Network Profiles → Interface Mgmt → Add. Then Network → Interfaces → the interface → Advanced → Management Profile.

Never expose the management plane to the internet without a source restriction. The permitted-ip inside the interface management profile is not optional decoration — it is the whole control. Palo Alto management interfaces have been actively scanned and exploited in the wild; an unrestricted HTTPS management surface on a public address will be found in hours, not weeks.

Name the profile something obviously temporary — MGMT-TEMP, not MGMT. Add its removal to the change closure checklist alongside re-enabling preemption. Temporary access that nobody removes is how a maintenance convenience becomes next year's audit finding.

Removing it afterwards

admin@fw-01(active)# delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 layer3 interface-management-profile  detach the profile — do this as soon as the change closes
admin@fw-01(active)# delete network profiles interface-management-profile MGMT-TEMP  remove the temporary profile entirely
admin@fw-01(active)# commit                                                   apply the candidate config — nothing above is live until this runs
Upgrade · PrepareACCESS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Connect and Confirm Which Box You Are On

Put a name sticker on each window. You do not want to switch off the wrong firewall.

Open a session to each peer in its own terminal tab and label them. The PAN-OS prompt tells you the HA role, which is the single most useful thing on the screen during an upgrade.

$ ssh admin@10.10.10.11     peer 1
$ ssh admin@10.10.10.12     peer 2

admin@fw-01(active)>       <- role is in the prompt
admin@fw-02(passive)>
admin@fw-02(suspended)>     <- after you suspend it

The prompt updates live. If you are sitting on a passive peer and it becomes active mid-upgrade, press Enter and the prompt will redraw with the new role. This is the fastest failover confirmation you have.
