Baseline Capture — Run on Both Peers

Take a photo of your room before you tidy it. Then you can tell exactly what moved.

Capture this into your change record before you touch anything. It is what you compare against afterwards, and what you hand TAC if it goes wrong.

admin@fw-01(active)> show system info                     everything about the box — model, serial, versions, uptime, mgmt IP

admin@fw-01(active)> show system info | match sw-version  just the running PAN-OS version
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state         the main HA summary — roles, sync status, link health
admin@fw-01(active)> show session info            session count and table utilisation
admin@fw-01(active)> show system resources        CPU and memory before the change
admin@fw-01(active)> show interface all            which links are up right now

You are taking a photograph of a healthy firewall. If something looks odd afterwards, the only way to know whether the upgrade caused it is to have the photograph.

  • Version and content: Dashboard → General Information widget.
  • HA roles and sync: Dashboard → High Availability widget.
  • Sessions and resources: Dashboard → System Resources widget; interfaces under Network → Interfaces (link state column).
Upgrade · PrepareBASELINE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Baseline Capture, Part 2: Reachability and Routing (ARP, Routes, Neighbours per VR/LR and VSYS)

Before moving house, write down which neighbours you could wave to and which roads led where. After the move, you check the same list.

Part 1 photographs the box. Part 2 photographs what the box could reach: which next hops and hosts answered ARP, how many routes each virtual router or logical router held, and which routing neighbours were up. After the upgrade, a missing ARP entry or a route count that dropped tells you exactly where to look, instead of "some users can't reach something".

Step 0 · Make the output easy to compare

admin@fw-01(active)> set cli pager off  print long tables without --more-- prompts
admin@fw-01(active)> show clock  timestamp at the top of the capture

Turn on session logging in your SSH client (PuTTY: Session > Logging, SecureCRT: File > Log Session) and save the file as <hostname>-PRE-<date>.txt. Run everything below on both HA peers.

Step 1 · ARP and IPv6 neighbours (what answered)

admin@fw-01(active)> show arp all  every ARP entry on every interface, with status
admin@fw-01(active)> show arp ethernet1/1  one interface, e.g. the WAN next hop
admin@fw-01(active)> show arp all | match "total ARP"  the entry counts, for a quick before/after number
admin@fw-01(active)> show neighbor interface all  IPv6 neighbour table, only if you run IPv6
In the ARP outputMeaningRecord it?
c completeThe host or next hop answered ARPYes. These are the things that were reachable.
s staticConfigured static ARP entryYes. It must survive the upgrade.
e expiringAbout to time out (idle host)Note, but don't treat as critical.
i incompleteARP sent, no replyYes. An already-broken entry is not an upgrade problem: knowing that saves an hour later.

Write down the critical next hops separately: the ISP gateway, the core switch, every BGP/OSPF neighbour, load balancers and VIPs, so you can test them by name afterwards.

Step 2 · Routing per virtual router (legacy routing engine)

admin@fw-01(active)> show routing route  all virtual routers; each block starts with "VIRTUAL ROUTER: "
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing route virtual-router default  one VR: repeat for every VR you have
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing route virtual-router vr-wan type static  statics only (repeat per type if useful)
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing fib virtual-router default  the forwarding table actually in use
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing protocol bgp summary  BGP peers, states and prefix counts
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing protocol bgp peer  per-peer detail incl. received/advertised counts
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing protocol ospf neighbor  OSPF neighbours and their state (Full?)
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing bfd details  BFD sessions, if BFD is configured
admin@fw-01(active)> show routing path-monitor  static routes with path monitoring, and their state

Step 2 (alternative) · Routing per logical router (Advanced Routing Engine)

admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing route  all logical routers
admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing route logical-router default  one LR: repeat for every LR
admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing fib  forwarding table
admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing bgp peer status logical-router default  BGP peer states per LR
admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing ospf neighbor logical-router default  OSPF neighbours per LR
admin@fw-01(active)> show advanced-routing static-route-path-monitor  monitored static routes

Step 3 · Multi-VSYS: capture per virtual system

Routing tables and ARP belong to virtual routers and interfaces, so Steps 1–2 already cover every VSYS. What is per-VSYS is the traffic and policy view. Switch context, capture, and switch back:

admin@fw-01(active)> show system info | match multi-vsys  is multi-vsys on? (on = repeat this step per vsys)
admin@fw-01(active)> set system setting target-vsys vsys2  commands now run in vsys2's context
admin@fw-01(active)> show session info  session count for this vsys
admin@fw-01(active)> show interface all  interfaces and their state as seen from this vsys
admin@fw-01(active)> set system setting target-vsys none  back to the full-firewall context

Also note which virtual router each VSYS uses (Device > Virtual Systems > the VSYS > Virtual Routers and Interfaces), so that after the upgrade you check the right VR for each tenant.

On an active/passive pair the passive firewall isn't forwarding traffic, so its ARP table and session counts are naturally small. Compare each peer with its own baseline. On the passive peer, dynamic routing neighbours normally aren't established either: that's expected, not a fault.

  • ARP: there's no full ARP table view in the web interface. show arp all is the reference.
  • Routes and neighbours: Network > Virtual Routers > More Runtime Stats (legacy), or Network > Routing > Logical Routers > More Runtime Stats (Advanced Routing).
Upgrade · PrepareHA HEALTH ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

HA Health — The Gate You Must Pass

Before you swap goalkeepers, make sure both are awake and wearing gloves.

Do not start an HA upgrade on a pair that is not healthy and in sync. Fix that first, in a separate change if necessary.

admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state                  the main HA summary — roles, sync status, link health
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability all                    full HA detail — use this when something looks wrong
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state-synchronization  session-sync statistics between the peers
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability path-monitoring        which monitored paths are up or down
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability link-monitoring        which monitored links are up or down

Filter to the lines that decide whether you proceed:

admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state | match "Mode|State|Configuration|Preempt"  the four lines that decide whether you proceed
Mode: Active-Passive
Local Information: State: active
Peer Information: State: passive
Configuration Synchronization: Enabled
Running Configuration: synchronized
Preemptive: yes              <- note this now; you will restore it later

Write down the current preemption setting. You are about to disable it. If you do not know whether it was on to begin with, you will either leave it off permanently or turn it on somewhere it was deliberately disabled.

What you want to seeWhat it means if you do not
Running Configuration: synchronizedPeers disagree. Force a sync and resolve before upgrading.
Peer State: passive (or active-secondary)Peer is suspended, non-functional or absent. Stop.
HA1 link status: upControl link down means split-brain risk during the upgrade.
HA2 link status: upSession sync is not happening; failover will drop sessions.
App/Threat versions match on bothContent mismatch. Install the same content on both peers first.
  • Dashboard → High Availability widget — local/peer state, Running Config, HA1/HA2 status, App and Threat versions side by side.
  • Device → High Availability → General → Election Settings shows Preemptive. Note it now.
Upgrade · PrepareBACKUP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Three Backups — Snapshot, Config Export, Device State

Save your homework on the computer and on a USB stick. If the computer breaks, the stick still has it.

These are different things and people routinely conflate them. Do all three, on both peers.

On-box named snapshot

admin@fw-01(active)> configure                                                enter configuration mode — the prompt changes from > to #
admin@fw-01(active)# save config to Pre_Upgrade_2026-08-24.xml                snapshot the config to the firewall's OWN disk — convenient, not a real backup
admin@fw-01(active)# exit                                                     leave configuration mode, back to the > prompt

Confirm it landed:
admin@fw-01(active)> show config saved Pre_Upgrade_2026-08-24.xml | match hostname  prove the snapshot exists and is readable

Off-box export

admin@fw-01(active)> scp export configuration from running-config.xml to user@10.20.30.40:/backups/fw-01-pre.xml  copy the live config to a remote server — THIS is the real backup
or, if you use TFTP:
admin@fw-01(active)> tftp export configuration from running-config.xml to 10.20.30.40  same thing over TFTP if you have no SCP target

Device state export — the fullest restore bundle

admin@fw-01(active)> configure                                                enter configuration mode
admin@fw-01(active)# save device-state                                        build device_state_cfg.tgz in /opt/pancfg/mgmt/device-state — Tab-complete to confirm on your release
admin@fw-01(active)# exit
admin@fw-01(active)> scp export device-state to user@10.20.30.40:/backups/        copy the bundle off the box
or:
admin@fw-01(active)> tftp export device-state to 10.20.30.40
BackupContainsUse it to
Named snapshot (on-box)Local running configQuick revert on a healthy box
Config export (off-box)Local running config only — not what Panorama pushedRebuild or roll back a standalone / locally managed firewall
Device state (off-box)Running config plus Panorama-pushed device-group and template settings. On a GlobalProtect portal, also its certificates and satellite list.Replace a dead firewall with a new one — import the bundle on the replacement

Device state is not "everything". It does not hold licences (re-fetch them from the support portal on a replacement), logs, software images or dynamic content. Encrypted secrets in the config are tied to the master key — if you use a custom master key, record it (securely) or the restored secrets will not decrypt.

The named snapshot lives on the firewall's own disk. If the appliance fails to boot, that copy is unreachable. The off-box export is the one that actually protects you — treat the snapshot as a convenience, not a backup.

  • Device → Setup → Operations → Save named configuration snapshot (on-box), then Export named configuration snapshot → running-config.xml (off-box, via browser), then Export device state (full bundle, via browser). Full walkthrough: Backing Up Without an SCP Server.
Upgrade · PrepareEVIDENCE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Pre-Upgrade Tech-Support File

A doctor wants to know how you felt before you got sick, not just after.

Generate on both peers. It is a background job, so start it early and collect it while downloads run.

admin@fw-01(active)> request tech-support dump                              generate the diagnostic bundle TAC will ask for — do it BEFORE the change
Exec job enqueued with jobid 599

admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs id 599                                       poll that job until it reports FIN / OK
wait for Status FIN / Result OK, then pull the file off the box

admin@fw-01(active)> scp export tech-support to user@10.20.30.40:/backups/  pull the tech-support file off the box

If you open a TAC case after a failed upgrade, the first request will be for a tech-support file from before the change. Generating one afterwards captures the broken state only, which halves its value.

  • Device → Support → Generate Tech Support File → Yes → Download when it finishes.
Upgrade · PreparePRE-FLIGHT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Check Disk Space Before You Download Anything

You cannot put a new toy in a full cupboard. Look inside the cupboard first.

Insufficient disk is one of the most common reasons an upgrade stalls, and it always announces itself at the least convenient moment — usually after a 1.2GB download has run for fifteen minutes. Thirty seconds up front avoids it.

admin@fw-01(active)> show system disk-space  free space per partition — run this BEFORE downloading anything
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/root       3.8G  3.1G  581M  85% /
/dev/sda5       7.6G  4.2G  3.0G  59% /opt/pancfg
/dev/sda6       3.8G  3.0G  666M  82% /opt/panrepo
/dev/sda8        88G  2.4G   81G   3% /opt/panlogs
PartitionHoldsMatters because
/opt/panrepoPAN-OS software imagesWhere your upgrade image lands. Full = download fails.
/opt/pancfgConfig, saved snapshots, dynamic contentBlocks downloads at 90% regardless of free bytes. See below.
/ (root)System files, debug logs, packet capturesNot used for operational storage, but a full root breaks upgrades and packet captures.
/opt/panlogsTraffic, threat and system logsUsually huge and rarely the problem. Clearing logs will not help panrepo.

The 90% rule on /opt/pancfg catches everyone. PAN-OS runs a strict percentage check — at 90% or above, downloads fail even with gigabytes free. You can be staring at 1.4GB available and still be refused. Get pancfg below 90%, not merely "roomy".

To see what is sitting on the box beyond the partition totals:

admin@fw-01(active)> show system files                  files on the box, including core dumps — press ? after "files" to see what your release offers

Add show system disk-space to your pre-change checklist and run it on both peers. They fill at different rates — the active peer generates far more log and report data than the passive one.

  • No partition view in the GUI — show system disk-space is CLI only. Cleanup of images and content is in the GUI (Device → Software and Dynamic Updates → X).
Upgrade · PrepareCLEANUP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Deleting Old Software Images

Throw out old toys — but never the one you are playing with, and never its box.

Old PAN-OS images live in /opt/panrepo and are usually the biggest easy win — each one is roughly a gigabyte and most firewalls accumulate several.

1. List what is actually on the box:
admin@fw-01(active)> debug swm list                      which PAN-OS images are sitting on the disk right now
Product   B  Version        Built                 Loaded
panos        11.1.0-c797    2024-05-11 00:52:43   2025-05-11 14:12:28
panos        11.1.4-h7      ...
panos        11.1.10        ...

2. Delete the ones you no longer need:
admin@fw-01(active)> delete software version 11.1.10     remove an old image — never the running version or its base image
admin@fw-01(active)> delete software version 11.1.4-h13  remove an old image — never the running version or its base image
admin@fw-01(active)> delete software version 11.1.4-h7   remove an old image — never the running version or its base image

3. Confirm the space came back:
admin@fw-01(active)> show system disk-space              free space per partition — run this BEFORE downloading anything

Two images you must not delete. The version currently running, and its base image. If you are on 11.1.4-h13, then 11.1.0 stays. The GUI protects you here — it simply will not offer an X on those rows. The CLI is less forgiving. Cross-check debug swm list against show system info | match sw-version before you delete anything.

Do not delete the base image of the version you are about to install either. Deleting 11.1.0 to make room for 11.1.4-h13 means the install will be rejected for a missing base image, and you will re-download the very file you just removed. See The Upgrade Path.

Stop it happening again

Operational mode (>) — not configure, no commit:
admin@fw-01(active)> show max-num-images         how many images of each type are kept today
admin@fw-01(active)> set max-num-images count 2  keep only 2 — range 2 to 64 — older ones are pruned automatically

This caps how many images PAN-OS retains, so old versions are pruned automatically rather than accumulating until an upgrade fails.

GUI: Device → Software → click the X at the right of any row you want removed. On Panorama, the same applies at Panorama → Software (its own images) and Panorama → Device Deployment → Software (images staged for managed firewalls) — the second of those is frequently the real culprit on a Panorama with a full disk.

⚠ Verification note. show max-num-images / set max-num-images count couldn't be confirmed in official Palo Alto documentation. Confirm with ? on your release. The software deletion commands (delete software version …) and show system disk-space (official form show system disk-space files adds inode usage) are standard.

Upgrade · PrepareCLEANUP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Deleting Old Content and Configuration Files

Dynamic content accumulates the same way images do, and it lands on /opt/pancfg — the partition with the 90% cliff.

Tab after "update" to list what is present, then delete the oldest:
admin@fw-01(active)> delete anti-virus update panup-all-antivirus-5649-6176  remove one old antivirus content file — only the installed one matters
admin@fw-01(active)> delete anti-virus update panup-all-antivirus-5650-6177  remove one old antivirus content file
admin@fw-01(active)> delete anti-virus update panup-all-antivirus-5651-6178  remove one old antivirus content file

admin@fw-01(active)> delete content update <filename>                        remove an old App and Threat content file
admin@fw-01(active)> delete wildfire update <filename>                       remove an old WildFire content file

Antivirus content updates daily, so a firewall that has been up for a year may be holding hundreds of these. They are the quietest disk consumer on the box and the safest thing to delete — only the currently installed version matters.

Saved configuration snapshots

Every save config to leaves a file behind. Runbooks that name snapshots by date build up years of them.

admin@fw-01(active)> show config saved          list what exists
admin@fw-01(active)> delete config saved <filename>  remove an old configuration snapshot

Other reclaimable files

admin@fw-01(active)> delete core file <filename>       process crash dumps
admin@fw-01(active)> delete debug-log <filename>        rotated .old debug logs — frees root
admin@fw-01(active)> delete debug-filter file <filename>  remove a saved debug filter file
admin@fw-01(active)> delete pcap directory <name>       forgotten packet captures
admin@fw-01(active)> delete report ...                   custom or predefined reports

Old tech-support files and packet captures are a classic hidden consumer. Someone captures traffic to troubleshoot, gets their answer, and the pcap sits on the root partition for two years. show system files will surface them.

GUI: Device → Dynamic Updates → the X on old Antivirus, Applications and Threats, and WildFire entries. Device → Setup → Operations for saved configuration snapshots.

Upgrade · PrepareCLEANUP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Logs, Automatic Cleanup and Quotas

Logs are the last thing to reach for, not the first — they are your evidence trail, and they usually live on a partition that was not the problem anyway.

admin@fw-01(active)> clear log system   WIPE the system log — destructive, and it frees panlogs, not panrepo
admin@fw-01(active)> clear log traffic  WIPE the traffic log — you lose the audit trail
admin@fw-01(active)> clear log threat   WIPE the threat log — you lose the audit trail

Clearing logs is destructive and usually solves the wrong problem. Logs sit on /opt/panlogs, which is typically the emptiest partition on the box. If /opt/panrepo is full, clearing the system log frees nothing useful — deleting old images is what fixes it. Check show system disk-space first and clear the partition that is actually full.

Built-in cleanup

admin@fw-01(active)> debug software disk-usage cleanup deep threshold 90  run the built-in cleanup at 90% instead of the 95% default — not persistent

Runs the internal cleanup routine at a lower threshold than the 95% default. It is not persistent across reboots and must be re-run each time. It may remove backup log files, so it can cost you data you wanted for analysis.

Quotas — the durable fix

admin@fw-01(active)> show system logdb-quota  how much space each log type is allowed to consume

GUI: Device → Setup → Management → Logging and Reporting Settings. Reducing quotas is a real fix; clearing logs is a one-off that buys you until next month.

Alert on it. The firewall writes a system log entry along the lines of Disk usage for / exceeds limit, 95 percent in use, cleaning filesystem. If you forward syslog, build an alert on that string — then disk pressure reaches you weeks before it reaches an upgrade window.

Some partitions cannot be cleaned from the CLI at all, because the files need root access. If show system disk-space shows a partition full and nothing above touches it, that is a TAC case, not a puzzle to solve with clever commands. Do not go looking for a root shell.

Upgrade · PrepareFIELD CASE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Field Case — panrepo at 80%, Install Blocked

An upgrade that would not proceed because /opt/panrepo had no room for the target image. What actually cleared it, in order:

1. Old antivirus content — frees /opt/pancfg:
> delete anti-virus update panup-all-antivirus-5649-6176  remove one old antivirus content file — only the installed one matters
> delete anti-virus update panup-all-antivirus-5650-6177  remove one old antivirus content file
> delete anti-virus update panup-all-antivirus-5651-6178  remove one old antivirus content file
> delete anti-virus update panup-all-antivirus-5653-6180  remove one old antivirus content file

2. Cached system event logs — frees /opt/panlogs:
> clear log system                                        WIPE the system log — destructive, and it frees panlogs, not panrepo

3. Old software images — frees /opt/panrepo, and this is what unblocked it:
> delete software version 11.1.10                         remove an old image — never the running version or its base image
> delete software version 11.1.4-h13                      remove an old image — never the running version or its base image
> delete software version 11.1.4-h7                       remove an old image — never the running version or its base image

> show system disk-space                                  free space per partition — run this BEFORE downloading anything
/opt/panrepo utilisation 80% -> 46%, roughly 4.1 GB reclaimed

Which step did the work. Step 3 is the one that fixed the blocked install — images and panrepo are the same partition. Step 1 helped a different partition that also benefits from headroom. Step 2 freed panlogs, which was almost certainly not the constraint. Worth knowing, because next time you can go straight to delete software version and keep your system log intact.

Before repeating this, check show system info | match sw-version and confirm you are not deleting the running version or its base image. In this case the box was running a 10.2 release, so removing 11.1 images was safe. On a firewall already running 11.1.4-h13, delete software version 11.1.4-h13 would be deleting the version underneath itself.

Upgrade · PrepareIMAGES ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Listing Images — check vs info

Check the menu before you order — you can only order what is on it.

Two commands, routinely mixed up, and the distinction matters when you are troubleshooting a download that will not appear.

CommandWhat it does
request system software checkRefreshes the list of available versions and shows what is loaded on the firewall.
request system software infoShows the software versions available for download, with size and whether each is already downloaded.
request system software info preferred(11.1.3 and later) Preferred releases only.
request system software info base(11.1.3 and later) Base releases only.
admin@fw-02(passive)> request system software info  list versions available to download, with a Downloaded flag
Version    Size   Released on           Downloaded
12.1.x-hN  1.3GB  (release date)         no
12.1.0     1.3GB  (release date)         yes
Downloaded=yes is what you are waiting for before you can install

Only versions for the next available release are shown — unless the box is skip-eligible (see Going to 12.1). If your target does not appear in the list, you are more than one feature release away from it — go back to The Upgrade Path.

  • Device → Software → Check Now. The Downloaded column and Currently Installed tick are the GUI twins of info.
Upgrade · PrepareDOWNLOAD ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Downloading the Image

Bring the new toy into the house early. It is not played with yet — it just sits in the box.

Download is non-disruptive. Do it well before the window — on a 3400-class box a 1.2GB image typically takes 15–20 minutes over a management link that is not congested.

admin@fw-01(active)> request system software download version <target>  pull the image onto the firewall — non-disruptive, do it early
Download job enqueued with jobid 595

admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs id 595                                   poll that job until it reports FIN / OK
poll until Status FIN and Result OK

Downloading to both peers in one command

admin@fw-01(active)> request system software download sync-to-peer yes version <target>  download once and push the image across to the HA peer
pulls the image once, then pushes it across HA1 to the peer

sync-to-peer yes saves a second internet pull and is useful when only one peer has a route to the update servers. Verify it actually arrived — run request system software info on the peer and confirm Downloaded: yes rather than assuming.

If the base image is missing

Landing on a hotfix requires the base image present on disk first:
admin@fw-01(active)> request system software download version 11.1.0     base — download only
admin@fw-01(active)> request system software download version 11.1.4-h13 target
You install only the target. The base image never gets installed.
  • Device → Software → Download on the base image (if hotfix) and the target. Watch progress in Tasks, bottom-right.
  • Repeat on the peer, or confirm it arrived there before the window.
Upgrade · PrepareCONTENT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Dynamic Updates — Content Before Software

Update the sticker book before you get the new album — the new album expects the new stickers.

Content goes on first, and it goes on both peers. Content installs do not require a reboot and are not synchronised by HA.

Download

admin@fw-01(active)> request content upgrade download latest     fetch the newest Applications and Threats content
Download job enqueued with jobid 597
admin@fw-01(active)> request anti-virus upgrade download latest  fetch the newest antivirus signatures
Download job enqueued with jobid 596
admin@fw-01(active)> request wildfire upgrade download latest    fetch WildFire signatures — errors harmlessly without the licence
Server error : There is not wildfire license on the box   expected without a WildFire subscription — not a failure

Install

admin@fw-01(active)> request content upgrade install version latest     activate the App and Threat content — no reboot needed
Content install job enqueued with jobid 601
admin@fw-01(active)> request anti-virus upgrade install version latest  activate the antivirus signatures — no reboot needed
Content install job enqueued with jobid 600

Verify

admin@fw-01(active)> request content upgrade check                            ask Palo Alto's servers what content is available
admin@fw-01(active)> request anti-virus upgrade check                         ask Palo Alto's servers what antivirus content is available
admin@fw-01(active)> show system info | match "app-version|threat-version|av-version"  confirm content installed — check the date is today or yesterday
confirm today's or yesterday's date on both peers, and that the two peers match
Command formNote
request content upgrade checkQueries Palo Alto's servers for available content versions.
request content upgrade infoLists content versions already on the firewall.
request content upgrade download latestlatest is accepted; an explicit version string also works.
request content upgrade install version latestDocumented form takes an explicit content version; latest is the convenient shorthand.

The WildFire error above is cosmetic on a box without the subscription, but do not train yourself to ignore errors during an upgrade. Read every one; decide it is harmless rather than assuming.

  • Device → Dynamic Updates → Check Now → Download → Install for Applications and Threats, then Antivirus (and WildFire if licensed). Repeat on the peer.
Upgrade · PrepareJOBS ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Watching Jobs — Nothing Is Instant

Putting cookies in the oven does not mean they are baked. Watch the timer.

Almost every request command returns a job ID and exits immediately. The command succeeding tells you the job was queued, not that it worked.

admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs id 595     poll that job until it reports FIN / OK
Enqueued          ID  Type      Status  Result  Completed
2026/08/24 21:04  595 Downld    FIN     OK      21:19:52

admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs all        every job the box knows about
admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs processed  jobs that have finished
admin@fw-01(active)> show jobs pending    jobs still queued or running
StatusMeaning
ACT / PENDStill running or queued. Keep waiting.
FIN + OKDone and successful. Proceed.
FIN + FAILDone and failed. Read the details column before retrying.

The command is show jobs id <jobid> — plural jobs. Many runbooks in circulation write show job id, which is not valid syntax.

  • Tasks link, bottom-right of every page = show jobs all. Click a task for its details.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)RECIPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Recipe

Recipe: HA Upgrade of an Active/Passive Pair (Condensed)

Use it when you need the short version of the HA upgrade. The detailed steps, checks and failure handling are in the surrounding Upgrade topics. Upgrade the passive unit first, fail over, then upgrade the other.

// on BOTH: confirm state and download the target release
show high-availability state
request system software check
request system software download version 11.1.x
// passive peer first
request high-availability state suspend
request system software install version 11.1.x
request restart system
request high-availability state functional
// move traffic to the upgraded unit: suspend the active peer, then upgrade it the same way
request high-availability state suspend
request system software install version 11.1.x
request restart system
request high-availability state functional
show high-availability state
What each line does

Purpose: The core command sequence for an HA upgrade, in order.

show high-availability state
Both peers healthy and synchronised before you start.
request system software download version …
Downloads the image (install the required content version first, per the release notes).
request high-availability state suspend
Takes the unit out of HA, so it won't become active while upgrading.
request system software install version … · request restart system
Installs and reboots into the new release.
request high-availability state functional
Returns the unit to HA after the upgrade.
(preemption)
If preemption is enabled, disable it during the upgrade so the failovers happen when you choose (see Disable Preemption). Re-enable it afterwards.

From PAN-OS 12.1.2 an HA upgrade orchestration workflow is also available (see the HA sequence topic). The manual sequence above works on all releases.

Upgrade · Execute (CLI)HA PREP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Disable Preemption

Tell the bossy goalkeeper: "Do not grab the gloves back the second you walk in." Otherwise he grabs them while he is still tying his shoes.

Preemption makes the higher-priority peer grab the active role back the moment it is capable of it. During an upgrade that means an unplanned failover at the exact moment a freshly rebooted, newly-versioned firewall comes up. Turn it off first.

Read the current setting before changing it:
admin@fw-01(active)> configure                                                enter configuration mode — the prompt changes from > to #
admin@fw-01(active)# show deviceconfig high-availability group election-option  read the current preemption setting before you change it
preemptive yes;

admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig high-availability group election-option preemptive no  stop the higher-priority peer grabbing back the active role mid-upgrade
admin@fw-01(active)# commit                                                   apply the candidate config — nothing above is live until this runs
admin@fw-01(active)# exit                                                     leave configuration mode, back to the > prompt

Verify from operational mode:
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state | match Preempt             is preemption on or off right now
Preemptive: no

The path is high-availability group election-option — with no group ID in it. On PAN-OS 7.0 and later the HA group is a single node; group-id is a value you set beneath it, not a selector you index into. See Syntax Corrections.

You only need to disable preemption on one peer, but the commit must succeed before you proceed. If you prefer belt-and-braces, doing it on both is harmless.

  • Device → High Availability → General → edit Election Settings → clear Preemptive → OK → Commit. Confirm the commit succeeded before going on.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)HA PREP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Link and Path Monitoring — Optional, Situational

Turn off the smoke alarm while you make toast on purpose — then turn it straight back on.

Some environments also disable link and path monitoring for the window, so that interfaces bouncing during a reboot do not trigger a failover on the peer that is still passing traffic.

admin@fw-01(active)> configure                                                enter configuration mode — the prompt changes from > to #
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig high-availability group monitoring link-monitoring enabled no  stop a bouncing interface triggering a failover during reboots
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig high-availability group monitoring path-monitoring enabled no  stop failed ping probes triggering a failover during reboots
admin@fw-01(active)# commit                                                   apply the candidate config — nothing above is live until this runs

Verify:
admin@fw-01(active)# show deviceconfig high-availability group monitoring     read the current link and path monitoring settings
admin@fw-01(active)# exit                                                     leave configuration mode, back to the > prompt
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability path-monitoring                   which monitored paths are up or down
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability link-monitoring                   which monitored links are up or down

Preemption is about who wants to be in charge. Monitoring is about who is allowed to declare themselves unfit. During a reboot both opinions become unreliable, so you mute them for the duration.

This is a genuine trade-off, not a free win. With monitoring disabled you also lose automatic failover for a real link failure during the window. Palo Alto's documented procedure disables preemption only. Disable monitoring if your environment has a history of spurious failovers on reboot; otherwise leave it alone — and either way, re-enable it the moment you are done.

  • Device → High Availability → Link and Path Monitoring → edit Link Monitoring and Path Monitoring → clear Enabled → OK → Commit.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)HA PREP ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Force a Config Sync

Copy the right homework onto your friend’s page — never copy the wrong one over the right one.

Run from the active peer. Only needed if the running config shows out-of-sync, but harmless to run as a belt-and-braces step before you start.

admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state | match Configuration       is the running config in sync between peers
Running Configuration: synchronized

If it is out-of-sync, push from active to peer:
admin@fw-01(active)> request high-availability sync-to-remote running-config  push THIS box's config to the peer — overwrites theirs, so direction matters

Re-check:
admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state | match Configuration       is the running config in sync between peers

This overwrites the peer's running configuration with the local one. Run it from the peer you know is correct — normally the active. Running it from the wrong box propagates the wrong config, and the wrong config is now on both firewalls.

  • Device → High Availability → Operational Commands → Sync to peer. Run it from the peer that has the correct config.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)SEQUENCE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

The Active/Passive Sequence

Two goalkeepers. One steps off to change boots while the other guards the net. Then they swap. The net is never empty.

Palo Alto's current documented manual procedure for active/passive is active-first: suspend the active peer to force a failover, upgrade it, return it to functional, then suspend the secondary and upgrade that.

The passive-first variant. Many field runbooks — including plenty that work fine — upgrade the passive peer first, verify it carries traffic after a deliberate failover, then upgrade the original active. That order tests the newly-upgraded box before committing both peers to the new version, which some teams prefer. Both orders are safe. What matters is that only one peer is ever out of service, and that you know which order you are following before you start.

✓ New in 12.1.2. From PAN-OS 12.1.2, Palo Alto adds an HA upgrade orchestration workflow (request workflow high-availability software install … ha-pair <serial1,serial2>, stoppable with request workflow terminate-job job-id <id>). The manual suspend → install → reboot → functional sequence here remains valid and is what earlier releases require.

Upgrade · Execute (CLI)STEP 1 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Suspend the Peer You Are About to Upgrade

Put up a "back in 5 minutes" sign. The other shop opens and customers walk next door.

Suspending removes the firewall from HA participation. It stops passing traffic and stops competing for the active role. This is what makes the upgrade safe.

admin@fw-01(active)> request high-availability state suspend        take THIS firewall out of HA — it stops passing traffic, peer takes over

Confirm — prompt changes and state reports suspended:
admin@fw-01(suspended)>
admin@fw-01(suspended)> show high-availability state | match State  local and peer role in two lines
Local Information: State: suspended
Peer Information: State: active

Verify from the other peer that it actually took over, and that traffic is genuinely flowing — do not take the state output as proof of service.

admin@fw-02(active)> show session info                           session count and how full the session table is
admin@fw-02(active)> show session all | match "flow|proto"       trim the session list to the useful columns
admin@fw-02(active)> show high-availability state | match State  local and peer role in two lines

This is your real failover test. If traffic does not recover here, stop — put the suspended peer back with request high-availability state functional and investigate. You have not installed anything yet, so nothing is lost. Discovering a broken failover after you have rebooted a peer onto a new version is a much worse place to be.

You can also drive the peer from the local box, which is useful when you only have a session to one side:

admin@fw-01(active)> request high-availability state peer suspend     suspend the OTHER firewall from this session
admin@fw-01(active)> request high-availability state peer functional  return the OTHER firewall to service from this session
  • Device → High Availability → Operational Commands → Suspend local device for high availability.
  • Confirm suspended in the bottom-right corner; on the peer, Dashboard HA widget shows active and Monitor → Traffic shows live sessions.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)STEP 2 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Install and Reboot

Change clothes, then have a nap. You are only ready to play when you are fully awake — that is chassis-ready: yes.

Install writes the image to the alternate partition. Nothing changes until the reboot.

admin@fw-01(suspended)> request system software install version <target>  write the image to the spare partition — no effect until reboot
Executing this command will install a new version of software. It will not take
effect until system is restarted. Do you want to continue? (y or n)  y    confirm — the install prompt wants a y before it queues the job
Software install job enqueued with jobid 332.

admin@fw-01(suspended)> show jobs id 332                                  poll that job until it reports FIN / OK
wait for FIN / OK — do NOT reboot before the install job finishes

admin@fw-01(suspended)> request restart system                            reboot NOW — no confirmation, no grace period
session drops; allow 10-15 minutes on a mid-range chassis before it answers again

After it comes back:

admin@fw-01(suspended)> show system info | match sw-version  just the running PAN-OS version
sw-version: <target>
admin@fw-01(suspended)> show high-availability state         the main HA summary — roles, sync status, link health
admin@fw-01(suspended)> show chassis-ready                   is the DATAPLANE up — 'yes' means it can pass traffic, not just answer SSH
yes     <- dataplane is up, not just the management plane

The management interface answers SSH well before the dataplane is ready. show chassis-ready returning yes is the signal to proceed. Bringing a peer back to functional while the dataplane is still initialising is how a "clean" upgrade drops traffic.

The firewall stays suspended across the reboot. That is intentional — it comes back on the new version without immediately trying to take traffic.

  • Device → Software → Install on the target → reboot when prompted, or Device → Setup → Operations → Reboot Device.
  • No GUI chassis-ready: SSH in and run it, or wait for Dashboard interfaces to show up plus a couple of minutes.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)STEP 3 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Return to Functional and Wait for Sync

Come back to the team, but sit on the bench first. Watch until you both know the same game plan (config synchronized).

admin@fw-01(suspended)> request high-availability state functional            put THIS firewall back into HA — it rejoins as passive

admin@fw-01(passive)>    <- active/passive: it comes back as passive

admin@fw-01(passive)> show high-availability state | match "State|Configuration"  role plus whether the config has synchronised
Local Information: State: passive
Peer Information: State: active
Running Configuration: synchronized

Do not move to the second peer until Running Configuration: synchronized appears. The two peers are now running different PAN-OS versions, which is expected and supported for the duration of the window — but only if the config is agreed between them.

You have one foot on each step of the staircase. It is a perfectly stable place to stand for a few minutes. It is not a place to stop for the night.

  • Operational Commands → Make local device functional for high availability. Bottom-right should show passive (A/P) or active (A/A).
  • Dashboard HA widget → Running Config: synchronized before you touch the second peer.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)STEP 4 ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Repeat on the Second Peer

Now the other goalkeeper changes boots. For these few minutes there is only one goalkeeper — be quick and careful.

Same three commands, other box. The upgraded peer takes over as active.

admin@fw-02(active)> request high-availability state suspend              take THIS firewall out of HA — it stops passing traffic, peer takes over
FW-01 (already on the new version) becomes active — verify traffic on it now

admin@fw-02(suspended)> request system software install version <target>  write the image to the spare partition — no effect until reboot
admin@fw-02(suspended)> show jobs id <jobid>                              poll one job — wait for Status FIN and Result OK
admin@fw-02(suspended)> request restart system                            reboot NOW — no confirmation, no grace period

after reboot:
admin@fw-02(suspended)> show system info | match sw-version               just the running PAN-OS version
admin@fw-02(suspended)> show chassis-ready                                is the DATAPLANE up — 'yes' means it can pass traffic, not just answer SSH
admin@fw-02(suspended)> request high-availability state functional        put THIS firewall back into HA — it rejoins as passive

Between suspending FW-02 and FW-02 coming back functional, you are running on a single firewall with no redundancy. That is the exposed part of the window. Keep it short and do not start unrelated troubleshooting in the middle of it.

  • Same clicks on FW-02: Suspend local device → Device → Software → Install → Reboot → Make local device functional.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)RESTORE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Restore Preemption and Monitoring

Turn the smoke alarm back on. Put everything back how you found it.

Undo exactly what you disabled — and only what you disabled. If preemption was already no before you started, leave it no.

admin@fw-01(active)> configure                                                enter configuration mode — the prompt changes from > to #
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig high-availability group election-option preemptive yes  restore automatic failback to the preferred peer
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig high-availability group monitoring link-monitoring enabled yes  restore link-failure detection
admin@fw-01(active)# set deviceconfig high-availability group monitoring path-monitoring enabled yes  restore path-failure detection
admin@fw-01(active)# commit                                                   apply the candidate config — nothing above is live until this runs
admin@fw-01(active)# exit                                                     leave configuration mode, back to the > prompt

admin@fw-01(active)> show high-availability state | match Preempt             is preemption on or off right now
Preemptive: yes

Putting the original active back in charge

If preemption is enabled and FW-01 has the higher priority, it will reclaim active on its own. If preemption stays disabled, force it:

On the current active (FW-02):
admin@fw-02(active)> request high-availability state suspend             take THIS firewall out of HA — it stops passing traffic, peer takes over
wait 1-2 minutes, confirm FW-01 is active and passing traffic
admin@fw-02(suspended)> request high-availability state functional       put THIS firewall back into HA — it rejoins as passive
admin@fw-02(passive)> show high-availability state | match "Mode|State"  just the roles — who is active, who is passive

Leaving preemption disabled after the window is one of the most common post-upgrade loose ends. It is invisible until months later, when a failover happens and the pair never fails back. Put it on the change closure checklist.

  • Election Settings → select Preemptive → OK → Commit (only if it was on before). Link and Path Monitoring → re-select Enabled → Commit.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)ACTIVE/ACTIVE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Active/Active Differences

Two shop tills, both open. When one closes to fix it, the other till takes every customer — make sure it can.

The command sequence is identical. Three things change.

  • Order does not matter. Either peer can go first. Documentation convention starts with active-primary.
  • Returning to functional gives you active, not passive. After request high-availability state functional expect active-primary or active-secondary, not passive.
  • Both peers pass traffic afterwards. Your validation must confirm sessions on both, not just one.
admin@fw-01(active-primary)> show high-availability state | match "Mode|State"  just the roles — who is active, who is passive
Mode: Active-Active
Local Information: State: active-primary
Peer Information: State: active-secondary

Capacity planning matters more here. In active/passive you were always running on one box. In active/active, suspending a peer means the survivor absorbs the full load — check that it can before the window, not during it.

  • Bottom-right shows active-primary / active-secondary. Monitor → Traffic filtered per firewall should show sessions on both.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)NO HA ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Single Firewall — Full Sequence

Only one shop, no neighbour. When it closes to fix it, it is simply closed. Do the tidying in daylight; close only for the actual fix.

No peer means no failover, no suspend step, and no way to hide the reboot. Everything else is the same, minus the HA sections.

  1. Baseline — show system info, show session info, show interface all.
  2. Back up — named snapshot plus off-box export, and a tech-support dump.
  3. Content first — download and install App/Threat and antivirus.
  4. Download the image — request system software download version <target>, plus the base image if you are landing on a hotfix.
  5. Install — request system software install version <target>, wait for show jobs id to report FIN/OK.
  6. Reboot — request restart system. This is the outage.
  7. Validate — show chassis-ready, version, sessions, interfaces, logs.
The whole standalone path, condensed:
admin@fw-01> show system info | match sw-version                              just the running PAN-OS version
admin@fw-01> configure                                                        enter configuration mode — the prompt changes from > to #
admin@fw-01# save config to Pre_Upgrade_2026-08-24.xml                        snapshot the config to the firewall's OWN disk — convenient, not a real backup
admin@fw-01# exit                                                             leave configuration mode, back to the > prompt
admin@fw-01> scp export configuration from running-config.xml to user@10.20.30.40:/backups/  copy the live config off the box to a remote server
admin@fw-01> request tech-support dump                                        generate the diagnostic bundle TAC will ask for — do it BEFORE the change
admin@fw-01> request content upgrade download latest                          fetch the newest Applications and Threats content
admin@fw-01> request content upgrade install version latest                   activate the App and Threat content — no reboot needed
admin@fw-01> request system software download version <target>                pull the image onto the firewall — non-disruptive, do it early
admin@fw-01> show jobs id <jobid>                                             poll one job — wait for Status FIN and Result OK
admin@fw-01> request system software install version <target>                 write the image to the spare partition — no effect until reboot
admin@fw-01> show jobs id <jobid>                                             poll one job — wait for Status FIN and Result OK
admin@fw-01> request restart system                                           reboot NOW — no confirmation, no grace period
  • Click-by-click version: Standalone — GUI Sequence.
Upgrade · Execute (CLI)OUTAGE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Managing the Outage

The lights coming on does not mean the oven is hot. Wait until you see real cookies (sessions).

PhaseTypical durationImpact
Content download + install10–25 minNone
Image download15–20 minNone
Software install5–15 minNone — writes to the alternate partition
Reboot10–20 minFull outage
Dataplane initialisation2–5 min after SSH answersPartial — mgmt up, traffic not yet

The last row catches people out. The box answers SSH, someone declares success, and the change is closed while traffic is still black-holing. show chassis-ready must return yes, and you must see real sessions, before you call it done.

Only the reboot is the outage. Everything before it is preparation you can do in daylight — which is exactly why you should, leaving the window itself as short as possible.

Where Everything Lives in the Web Interface

Every CLI step in this runbook has a GUI equivalent. The web interface is the better choice when you have no SCP or TFTP target to export a config to, when the change is being run by someone who does not live in the CLI, or when you want a second pair of eyes watching a screen rather than a scrollback buffer.

TaskWhere
Current versionDashboard → General Information widget, or Device → Setup → Management
HA healthDashboard → High Availability widget
Config backupDevice → Setup → Operations
Tech-support fileDevice → Support
Content updatesDevice → Dynamic Updates
PAN-OS imagesDevice → Software
Preemption settingDevice → High Availability → Election Settings
Link / path monitoringDevice → High Availability → Link and Path Monitoring
Suspend / make functionalDevice → High Availability → Operational Commands
RebootDevice → Setup → Operations → Reboot Device
Job statusTasks (bottom-right corner of every page)

The CLI tells you what happened. The GUI shows you what is happening. During a reboot the Dashboard High Availability widget updates on its own, which beats re-running show high-availability state every thirty seconds.

The bottom-right corner of the web interface is the most under-used part of it. Tasks is the GUI equivalent of show jobs all, and the small status area next to it shows the local HA state live — the same information the CLI prompt gives you.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaNO SCP NEEDED ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Backing Up Without an SCP Server

This is the strongest argument for the GUI path. The CLI can only push a config to a remote host — if you have no SCP or TFTP server, you have no off-box backup. The web interface downloads it straight to your laptop through the browser.

  1. Device → Setup → Operations. The Configuration Management panel holds every backup option.
  2. Save named configuration snapshot. Name it something dated — Pre_Upgrade_2026-08-24. This is the on-box copy, the GUI twin of save config to.
  3. Export named configuration snapshot. Pick running-config.xml from the dropdown, click OK, and the browser downloads the file. This is your real off-box backup.
  4. Save it somewhere that is not the firewall — change ticket, file share, anywhere you can reach when the appliance is down.
  5. Export device state. Same panel. Downloads the full bundle — running config plus everything Panorama pushed. This is what you import onto a replacement firewall.
  6. Repeat on the peer. HA does not do this for you.
ButtonWhat it actually does
Save named configuration snapshotWrites a copy to the firewall's own disk. Convenient, not a backup.
Export named configuration snapshotDownloads a saved snapshot through your browser.
Export configuration versionDownloads any previously committed version by number.
Export device stateRunning config plus Panorama-pushed device-group and template settings (and, on a GlobalProtect portal, certificates and satellites). The fullest restore bundle — but no licences, logs or images.
Load named configuration snapshotLoads a snapshot into the candidate config. Still needs a commit.

Tech-support file

Device → Support → Generate Tech Support File, click Yes. When it finishes, a Download link appears — again, straight through the browser, no server required.

The export dialog is a dropdown of snapshots that already exist. If you skipped step 2, there is nothing useful to select. Save first, then export — people miss this and end up exporting a snapshot from six months ago.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaCONTENT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Dynamic Updates in the GUI

Device → Dynamic Updates. One row per update type, with a Currently Installed marker showing what is live.

  1. Check Now (bottom of the page) to refresh the list from Palo Alto's servers.
  2. Find Applications and Threats. Compare Currently Installed against the minimum version in your target release's release notes.
  3. Click Download on the version you want. When it completes the Action link changes from Download to Install.
  4. Click Install. No reboot needed.
  5. Repeat for Antivirus, and for WildFire if you hold that subscription.
  6. Repeat all of it on the peer. Content is not synchronised by HA.

The Action link changing from Download to Install is the GUI's way of telling you the download finished — the same signal as a job reaching FIN/OK. Rows you have no licence for simply will not offer a download, which is cleaner than the CLI's There is not wildfire license on the box error.

Offline content

No internet from the management interface? Download the content file from the support portal on a machine that does have access, then Upload at the bottom of the Dynamic Updates page and choose Install From File.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaSOFTWARE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Downloading and Installing PAN-OS

Device → Software. This page is the GUI equivalent of request system software info — a version list with a Downloaded column and a Currently Installed marker.

  1. Check Now to refresh the available versions.
  2. On PAN-OS 10.2.10 and later 10.2 releases, and on 11.1.3 and later, the page shows preferred releases and their base releases by default. The Base Releases and Preferred Releases checkboxes filter the view — clearing one shows only the other.
  3. Download the base image first if your target is a hotfix. For 11.1.4-h13 that means downloading 11.1.0 as well. The base image is downloaded only, never installed.
  4. Download your target version. Watch progress in the dialog or in Tasks.
  5. Install once Downloaded shows a tick. Nothing changes until the reboot.
  6. When prompted to reboot, click Yes. If you are not prompted, go to Device → Setup → Operations → Reboot Device.

Only versions for the next available release are listed — unless the box is skip-eligible (see Going to 12.1). If your target is not there, you are more than one feature release away from it — see The Upgrade Path. Clicking Check Now repeatedly will not conjure it.

No internet from the management interface

Download the image from the Palo Alto Networks support portal on another machine, then use Upload at the bottom of the Software page and Install From File. The base-image rule still applies — upload both files.

If a download errors partway, click Check Now again to refresh the image list before retrying. A stale list is a common cause of a download that will not start.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaHA SEQUENCE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

HA Pair — Full GUI Sequence

Same shape as the CLI sequence, and the same active-first ordering. Two browser tabs, one per peer, is the sane way to run it.

  1. Back up both peers — save and export the config, generate tech-support files. See Backing Up Without an SCP Server.
  2. Update content on both peers — Device → Dynamic Updates.
  3. Download the image on both peers — Device → Software. Download only; do not install yet.
  4. Disable preemption. Device → High Availability → edit Election Settings → clear Preemptive → OK → Commit. One peer only, but the commit must succeed before you go further. Note what it was set to first.
  5. Suspend the active peer. Device → High Availability → Operational Commands → Suspend local device for high availability. Confirm the state shows suspended in the bottom-right corner.
  6. Verify the failover worked — on the other peer, check the Dashboard High Availability widget shows it active, and confirm real traffic in Monitor → Traffic. If traffic has not recovered, make the peer functional again and stop.
  7. Install on the suspended peer — Device → Software → Install, then reboot when prompted.
  8. Wait for it to come back, then confirm the version in the Dashboard General Information widget.
  9. Make it functional — Operational Commands → Make local device functional for high availability. Expect passive in active/passive, active in active/active.
  10. Wait for config sync. Dashboard → High Availability widget → Running Config: synchronized. Do not proceed until you see it.
  11. Repeat steps 5–10 on the second peer.
  12. Re-enable preemption — Election Settings → select Preemptive → OK → Commit. Only if it was enabled to begin with.
CLI commandGUI equivalent
request high-availability state suspendOperational Commands → Suspend local device for high availability
request high-availability state functionalOperational Commands → Make local device functional for high availability
request high-availability state peer suspendOperational Commands → Suspend peer device (or switch context to the peer)
request high-availability sync-to-remote running-configOperational Commands → Sync to peer
show high-availability stateDashboard → High Availability widget
show jobs allTasks, bottom-right corner
show chassis-readyNo direct equivalent — see the warning below

The GUI has no show chassis-ready button. The web interface answering does not mean the dataplane is up. If you have any CLI access at all, SSH in and run show chassis-ready before making a peer functional. Failing that, wait for the Dashboard interface widget to show links up and give it a couple of extra minutes.

Standalone — GUI Sequence

The HA steps drop out entirely. What remains is preparation, one reboot, and validation.

  1. Device → Setup → Operations — save a named snapshot, then export it to your laptop.
  2. Device → Support — generate and download a tech-support file.
  3. Device → Dynamic Updates — Check Now, download and install Applications and Threats, then Antivirus.
  4. Device → Software — Check Now, download the base image if your target is a hotfix, then download the target.
  5. Install the target. Still no impact at this point.
  6. Reboot when prompted, or Device → Setup → Operations → Reboot Device. This is the outage.
  7. Validate — Dashboard General Information for the version, Monitor → Traffic for real sessions, Monitor → System log for errors.

Same trap as the CLI path, and worse in a browser: the login page returning feels like success. It only means the management plane is up. Confirm actual traffic in Monitor → Traffic before you close the change.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaSCOPE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

When to Drive the Upgrade From Panorama

The teacher (Panorama) must know the new lesson before the class (firewalls) learns it.

Panorama is the right tool when you are upgrading more than a couple of firewalls, when the firewalls have no direct internet access but Panorama does, or when you want one audit trail across a fleet. It is the wrong tool for a single standalone firewall — that is more clicks, not fewer.

Upgrade Panorama before the firewalls it manages. Panorama must be running the same or a later PAN-OS release than its managed devices. Upgrading a firewall past its Panorama breaks management until Panorama catches up. Check the Panorama, Log Collector, Firewall and WildFire Version Compatibility matrix before you start.

OrderComponent
1Panorama (and its HA peer, if it has one)
2Log Collectors
3WildFire appliances
4Firewalls

Panorama deploys images and content, and it can reboot devices for you. It does not handle HA suspend and failover — those are still done on each firewall, either from its own web interface or by switching context to it from within Panorama. That split is the main thing to understand about the Panorama path.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaCONTENT ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Deploying Content From Panorama

Panorama → Device Deployment → Dynamic Updates.

  1. Check Now for the latest updates. If one is available, the Action column shows a Download link.
  2. Download the content release you need, if it is not already present on Panorama.
  3. Install, then tick the firewalls to receive it, and click OK.
  4. Select both peers of every HA pair. Content is not synchronised between peers, so both must be selected explicitly.

This is where Panorama genuinely saves time. Pushing content to forty firewalls is one dialog here versus forty separate logins — and it happens well before the change window, since content installs are non-disruptive.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaSOFTWARE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

Deploying PAN-OS — The Two Checkboxes That Matter

"Group HA Peers" means "send both goalkeepers to change boots at once". Never tick it during an upgrade.

Panorama → Device Deployment → Software. Images are listed per firewall model, so PanOS_3400-11.1.4-h13 is a different row from the 5400 equivalent. Click Install in the Action column of the row matching the models you are upgrading.

The Deploy Software file dialog then offers two checkboxes, and getting them wrong is the main way this goes badly.

CheckboxSet it toWhy
Group HA PeersCleared, for HA upgradesLeaving it selected upgrades both peers of a pair together. That is a full outage for that pair. Clear it and select one peer at a time.
Reboot device after installSelectedSaves a separate reboot trip. If you leave it cleared, reboot each device manually from Device → Setup → Operations afterwards.

Group HA Peers is the single most dangerous control on this page. It sounds like a convenience — keep my pairs together — and it is exactly the opposite of what you want during an upgrade. Palo Alto's documented HA procedure says to make sure it is not selected, every time.

Standalone firewalls

Simpler: click Install, select all the non-HA firewalls you are upgrading, select Reboot device after install, and click OK. Grouping is irrelevant with no peers, but each one takes a real outage — batch them by change window, not by convenience.

Confirming what landed

Panorama → Managed Devices shows the Software Version and HA status for every firewall in one table. It is the fastest fleet-wide verification you have.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaHA SEQUENCE ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

HA Pairs From Panorama — Passive First

This ordering differs from the firewall-GUI procedure. The Panorama-driven procedure upgrades the passive peer first, verifies it, then suspends the active peer and upgrades that. The standalone firewall procedure earlier in this runbook goes active-first. Both are documented and both are safe — but decide which one you are following before you start, and do not mix them mid-change.

  1. Content to both peers — Panorama → Device Deployment → Dynamic Updates.
  2. Disable preemption on the first peer of each pair. Switch context to the firewall, Device → High Availability → Election Settings → clear Preemptive → Commit. One peer per pair is enough.
  3. Deploy to the passive peer. Panorama → Device Deployment → Software → Install on the right model row. Select only the passive peer of each pair (active-secondary for active/active). Group HA Peers cleared, Reboot device after install selected. OK.
  4. Wait for the reboot to finish. Do not start the next step early.
  5. Verify in Panorama → Managed Devices that the version is correct and the upgraded peer is still passive.
  6. Suspend the active peer. Switch context to it → Device → High Availability → Operational Commands → Suspend local device. The upgraded peer takes over — confirm traffic is flowing on it.
  7. Deploy to the now-suspended peer — same dialog, this time selecting the other half of each pair. Group HA Peers still cleared, Reboot device after install still selected.
  8. Wait for it to come back, then Make local device functional from its Operational Commands.
  9. Wait for config sync, then re-enable preemption where you disabled it.

Panorama does the boring, repeatable part — shipping images and rebooting. The judgement calls, suspend and make-functional, stay on the firewall. That division is why the Panorama path still needs someone watching each pair rather than one big OK button.

Step 6 is the failover test, exactly as in the CLI path. If traffic does not recover when you suspend the active peer, make it functional again and stop — at that point only one peer has been upgraded and you can still walk away cleanly.

Upgrade · GUI & PanoramaAIR-GAPPED ✓ checked vs PAN docs Runbook

When Panorama Has No Internet Access

The deployment steps are identical; only the source of the image changes. Instead of Check Now and Download, you upload the files to Panorama first.

  1. On a machine with internet access, download the PAN-OS image for each firewall model you are upgrading from the Palo Alto Networks support portal. Model-specific — a 3400 image will not deploy to a 5400.
  2. Download the base image too, if your target is a hotfix.
  3. Download the content release files you need.
  4. In Panorama, Panorama → Device Deployment → Software → Upload and select each image file.
  5. Same for content: Panorama → Device Deployment → Dynamic Updates → Upload.
  6. Deploy exactly as in HA Pairs From Panorama — Install, Group HA Peers cleared, Reboot device after install selected.

Upload everything for every model and every hop before the window opens. Discovering a missing base image with a peer already suspended is a bad place to be, and downloading a 1.2GB file from the support portal at that moment is not a fast recovery.
